q: For 2025, a qualifying relative's gross income must be less than what amount?
explain: The gross income test for a qualifying relative uses the exemption amount, which is $5,200 for 2025. It was $5,050 for 2024 and $4,700 for 2023.

q: Maria's husband died in June 2025. She has not remarried and has no dependents. What is the best filing status for her 2025 return?
choices: Single
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing jointly
Head of household
explain: A surviving spouse can file jointly for the year the spouse died. Qualifying surviving spouse status is only for the two years after the year of death, and it requires a dependent child.

q: A U.S. person must file Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) Form 114 (FBAR) when the aggregate value of their foreign financial accounts exceeds what amount at any time during the year?
explain: The FBAR threshold is an aggregate maximum value over $10,000 at any time during the calendar year. The $50,000 and $75,000 figures are Form 8938 thresholds for an unmarried taxpayer living in the U.S.
source: IRS: Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR); 31 CFR 1010.350

q: For 2025, a child's unearned income above what amount may be taxed at the parent's rate under the kiddie tax rules?
explain: For 2025 the Form 8615 threshold is $2,700. It was $2,600 for 2024.

q: To file as head of household, an unmarried taxpayer must have paid what share of the cost of keeping up a home for the year?
choices: At least one-third
At least half
More than half
All of it
explain: Head of household requires paying more than half the cost of keeping up a home that was the main home of a qualifying person for more than half the year (a dependent parent may live elsewhere).

q: Dana, single, owned and lived in her home for three years and sold it in 2025 at a $310,000 gain. She has not excluded gain on another home in the past two years. How much of the gain is taxable?
explain: She meets the two-out-of-five-year ownership and use tests, so up to $250,000 is excluded for a single filer. $310,000 minus $250,000 leaves $60,000 taxable.

q: Absent an alternate valuation election, the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally:
choices: The decedent's adjusted basis
Fair market value on the date of death
Zero
The lower of the decedent's basis or fair market value
explain: Inherited property generally takes a basis equal to fair market value at the date of death (or the alternate valuation date if the executor elects it).

q: Leo received stock as a gift. The donor's basis was $10,000 and the fair market value at the time of the gift was $8,000. Leo later sells it for $7,000. What is his recognized gain or loss?
choices: No gain or loss
$1,000 loss
$3,000 loss
$2,000 gain
explain: When fair market value (FMV) at the gift is below the donor's basis, the basis for figuring a loss is the FMV at the gift, $8,000. Selling for $7,000 gives a $1,000 loss.

q: A single taxpayer has a $10,000 net capital loss for 2025 and no other capital transactions. How much can be deducted against ordinary income in 2025, and how much carries over?
choices: $10,000 deducted, $0 carried over
$3,000 deducted, $7,000 carried over
$1,500 deducted, $8,500 carried over
$0 deducted, $10,000 carried over
explain: Net capital losses offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income ($1,500 if married filing separately). The rest carries forward indefinitely.

q: What is the maximum percentage of Social Security benefits that can be included in taxable income?
explain: Depending on provisional income, 0%, up to 50%, or up to 85% of benefits are taxable. 85% is the ceiling.

q: Which distribution is subject to the 10% additional tax on early distributions?
choices: From a 401(k) after separating from the employer in the year the employee turned 56
From an individual retirement arrangement (IRA) at age 45 to pay qualified higher education expenses
From an individual retirement arrangement (IRA) at age 52 to buy a car
Up to $10,000 from an individual retirement arrangement (IRA) at age 40 for a first-time home purchase
explain: Buying a car is not an exception. Separation from service at 55 or later (qualified plans only), higher education expenses (IRAs), and the $10,000 first-time homebuyer amount (IRAs) are all exceptions.

q: For 2025, what is the maximum health savings account (HSA) contribution for an individual under age 55 with family high deductible health plan (HDHP) coverage?
explain: The 2025 limits are $4,300 self-only and $8,550 family, plus a $1,000 catch-up at 55 or older. $8,300 was the 2024 family limit.

q: What is the 2025 standard deduction for a single filer under 65 who is not blind?
explain: P.L. 119-21 (the 2025 reconciliation act) raised the 2025 amount from $15,000 to $15,750. $14,600 was 2024 and $16,100 is 2026, both outside this exam's tax year.
source: Form 1040 instructions (2025); IRC 63(c)(7) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: A married couple filing jointly with 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $300,000 paid $45,000 of state income and property taxes. What is their maximum itemized deduction for state and local taxes?
explain: For 2025 the state and local tax (SALT) cap is $40,000 ($20,000 married filing separately). It phases down only when MAGI exceeds $500,000 ($250,000 married filing separately), so this couple gets the full $40,000.
source: Schedule A instructions (2025); IRC 164(b)(7) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: For 2025, what is the maximum child tax credit per qualifying child before any phaseout?
explain: P.L. 119-21 raised the credit to $2,200 per qualifying child for 2025. The refundable portion (additional child tax credit) is capped at $1,700 per child.
source: Schedule 8812 instructions (2025); IRC 24(h) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: A married couple filing jointly, both age 66 with valid Social Security numbers (SSNs), has 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $120,000 and takes the standard deduction. What is their total enhanced deduction for seniors?
choices: $0, because they don't itemize
explain: For 2025 through 2028, each qualifying individual 65 or older gets up to $6,000, whether or not they itemize. The phaseout starts at MAGI over $150,000 for joint filers, so both spouses get the full amount.
source: Schedule 1-A instructions (2025); IRC 151(d)(5)(C) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: Cash contributions to a public charity are generally deductible up to what percentage of adjusted gross income (AGI)?
explain: The 60% limit for cash gifts to 50%-limit organizations applies for 2025. Capital gain property to public charities is generally limited to 30%, and gifts to most private nonoperating foundations to 30% (cash) or 20% (capital gain property).

q: A taxpayer with 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $80,000 had $9,000 of unreimbursed medical expenses and itemizes. How much is deductible?
explain: Only medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI are deductible. 7.5% of $80,000 is $6,000, so $9,000 minus $6,000 leaves $3,000.

q: For a home bought in 2025, interest is deductible on acquisition debt up to what amount (married filing jointly)?
choices: No limit
explain: The $750,000 limit ($375,000 married filing separately) applies to debt incurred after December 15, 2017. P.L. 119-21 made it permanent. The $1,000,000 limit applies only to grandfathered older debt.

q: A sole proprietor has $50,000 of net profit on Schedule C for 2025 and no wages. What is the self-employment tax, rounded to the nearest dollar?
explain: Net earnings subject to self-employment (SE) tax are 92.35% of net profit: $46,175. Multiply by 15.3% to get $7,064.78, about $7,065. Half of that is an adjustment to income.

q: A single taxpayer earned $250,000 in wages in 2025. What is the additional Medicare tax?
explain: The 0.9% additional Medicare tax applies to wages over $200,000 for a single filer. $50,000 times 0.9% is $450.

q: A married couple filing jointly has 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $280,000, including $40,000 of net investment income. What is their net investment income tax?
explain: Net investment income tax (NIIT) is 3.8% of the lesser of net investment income ($40,000) or MAGI over $250,000 ($30,000). 3.8% of $30,000 is $1,140.

q: A taxpayer had 2024 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $180,000. To avoid the underpayment penalty for 2025 using the prior-year safe harbor, withholding and timely estimates must equal at least what percentage of the 2024 tax?
explain: The prior-year safe harbor is 100% of last year's tax, raised to 110% when prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000 ($75,000 married filing separately).

q: In 2025 Ana earned $120,000 from Employer A and $80,000 from Employer B. Each employer withheld 6.2% Social Security tax on her full wages there. What excess Social Security tax can she claim as a credit?
explain: Total withheld is $12,400. The 2025 wage base is $176,100, so the maximum is $10,918.20. The excess, $1,481.80, is claimed on Schedule 3.
source: IRS Pub 505 (2025); SSA 2025 contribution and benefit base

q: A minister receives a housing allowance that meets the exclusion rules. How is it treated?
choices: Excluded from income tax and from self-employment tax
Included in income tax and excluded from self-employment tax
Excluded from income tax but included in net earnings for self-employment tax
Included for both income tax and self-employment tax
explain: A qualifying housing allowance is excluded for income tax, but ministers (unless exempt via Form 4361) must include it when figuring self-employment tax.

q: For 2025, what is the annual limit on tax-free 529 plan distributions for elementary and secondary school expenses per beneficiary?
choices: No limit
explain: The K-12 limit is $10,000 per beneficiary for 2025. P.L. 119-21 raises it to $20,000 starting in 2026, which is outside this exam's tax year.

q: A couple filed jointly, and the wife's share of the refund was applied to her husband's past-due child support. Which form should she file to get her share back?
choices: Form 8857
Form 8379
Form 843
Form 1040-X
explain: Form 8379 is the injured spouse allocation, used when a joint refund is offset for one spouse's separate debt. Form 8857 is for innocent spouse relief from a joint tax liability.

q: For a calendar-year individual, the fourth 2025 estimated tax payment is generally due on:
choices: December 15, 2025
December 31, 2025
January 15, 2026
April 15, 2026
explain: Individual estimates are due April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15 of the next year. December 15 is the fourth installment for calendar-year corporations.

q: A claim for refund is generally timely if filed within:
choices: 2 years from the date the return was filed
3 years from the date the return was filed or 2 years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later
3 years from the due date of the return only
6 years from the date the return was filed
explain: The general refund statute is the later of 3 years from filing or 2 years from payment. A return filed early is treated as filed on the due date.

q: A married couple elects gift-splitting and gives their son $38,000 in 2025. They make no other gifts. Which statement is correct?
choices: No gift tax return is required
Form 709 must be filed to elect gift-splitting, and there is no taxable gift
$19,000 is a taxable gift that uses part of the unified credit
Each spouse must pay gift tax on $19,000
explain: The 2025 annual exclusion is $19,000 per donee, so splitting covers $38,000. But the election itself requires filing Form 709, even when no taxable gift results.

q: What is the basic exclusion amount for estates of decedents dying in 2025?
explain: The 2025 basic exclusion is $13,990,000. $13,610,000 was 2024. P.L. 119-21 sets $15,000,000 starting in 2026.

q: Which statement about Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) and Form 8938 is correct?
choices: Both are attached to Form 1040
FBAR is filed electronically with Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN); Form 8938 is attached to the income tax return
Form 8938 replaces the FBAR for taxpayers who file it
Both have the same reporting thresholds
explain: FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) goes to FinCEN through the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) e-filing system. Form 8938 is filed with the income tax return. Filing one does not satisfy the other, and the thresholds differ.
source: IRS: Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements

q: To let a surviving spouse use a deceased spouse's unused exclusion (DSUE), the executor must:
choices: Do nothing; portability is automatic
File a timely and complete Form 706, even if no estate tax is due
File Form 709 for the surviving spouse
Attach a statement to the final Form 1040
explain: Portability requires an election on a timely filed, complete Form 706. Rev. Proc. 2022-32 gives a simplified late election up to five years after death when no return was otherwise required.

q: Form 706 is generally due how long after the decedent's date of death?
choices: 6 months
9 months
12 months
15 months
explain: Form 706 is due 9 months after death. A 6-month extension to file is available with Form 4768.

q: Which of the following can be an S corporation shareholder?
choices: A nonresident alien
A C corporation
A partnership
An estate
explain: Eligible shareholders include individuals who are U.S. citizens or residents, estates, and certain trusts and exempt organizations. Nonresident aliens, partnerships, and corporations are not eligible.

q: For an S election to take effect for the current calendar tax year, Form 2553 must generally be filed no later than:
choices: January 31
March 15
April 15
June 15
explain: The election must be made no more than 2 months and 15 days after the start of the tax year it is to take effect, which is March 15 for a calendar year. Late election relief exists under Rev. Proc. 2013-30.

q: Raj contributes land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and fair market value (FMV) of $100,000, subject to a $30,000 mortgage the partnership assumes, for a 25% interest. What is Raj's basis in his partnership interest?
explain: Start with $40,000, subtract the $30,000 liability he is relieved of, then add back his 25% share of it ($7,500): $17,500.

q: For a property transfer to a corporation to qualify for nonrecognition under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 351, the transferors must control what percentage of the corporation immediately after the exchange?
explain: Control means at least 80% of the total combined voting power and at least 80% of the total shares of each other class of stock.

q: A C corporation owns 30% of another domestic C corporation and receives a $100,000 dividend. What is the dividends-received deduction, before any taxable income limit?
explain: The dividends received deduction (DRD) is 50% for less than 20% ownership, 65% for 20% to less than 80%, and 100% for 80% or more in the same affiliated group.

q: How are guaranteed payments for services treated?
choices: Not deductible by the partnership; not self-employment income to the partner
Deductible by the partnership; ordinary income and self-employment income to the partner
Treated as a distribution reducing the partner's basis
Subject to income tax withholding as wages
explain: Guaranteed payments are generally deductible by the partnership and reported to the partner as ordinary income subject to self-employment tax. Partners are not employees, so no W-2.

q: Form 1065 for a calendar-year partnership is due on:
choices: January 31
March 15
April 15
September 15
explain: Partnership returns are due the 15th day of the 3rd month after year-end. A 6-month extension (Form 7004) moves it to September 15.

q: A business owner spends $400 on a restaurant meal with a client in 2025 to discuss business. How much is deductible?
explain: Business meals are generally 50% deductible. The temporary 100% restaurant rule applied only to 2021 and 2022.

q: For tax years beginning in 2025, what is the maximum Section 179 expense deduction?
explain: P.L. 119-21 raised the limit to $2,500,000, reduced dollar for dollar once qualifying property placed in service exceeds $4,000,000. $1,250,000 was the pre-act 2025 figure.
source: Form 4562 instructions (2025); IRC 179(b) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: A business buys new equipment in March 2025 (after January 19, 2025) and places it in service the same month. What bonus depreciation percentage is available?
explain: P.L. 119-21 restored 100% bonus depreciation for qualified property acquired after January 19, 2025. Property acquired earlier and placed in service in 2025 gets 40%.
source: Form 4562 instructions (2025); IRC 168(k) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: A new business incurs $53,000 of start-up costs. How much can it elect to deduct immediately, before amortizing the rest?
explain: The $5,000 immediate deduction is reduced dollar for dollar by start-up costs over $50,000. $5,000 minus $3,000 is $2,000. The rest is amortized over 180 months.

q: What is the maximum deduction for business gifts to one recipient during the year?
explain: Business gifts are limited to $25 per recipient per year. Incidental costs like engraving or shipping don't count toward the limit.

q: What is the 2025 standard mileage rate for business use of a vehicle?
choices: 65.5 cents
67 cents
70 cents
72.5 cents
explain: The 2025 business rate is 70 cents per mile. It was 67 cents in 2024.

q: Under the simplified method for a home office, what is the maximum deduction?
explain: The simplified method allows $5 per square foot for up to 300 square feet, a maximum of $1,500.

q: For 2025, a C corporation's charitable contribution deduction is generally limited to what share of its taxable income (figured with certain modifications)?
explain: For 2025 the limit is 10% of taxable income figured without the deduction and certain other items, with a 5-year carryforward. P.L. 119-21 adds a 1% floor starting in 2026.

q: An individual actively participates in a rental activity and has 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $120,000. What is the maximum special allowance for rental losses?
explain: The $25,000 allowance is reduced by 50% of MAGI over $100,000. $20,000 over times 50% is $10,000, leaving $15,000.

q: A small tax-exempt organization may file Form 990-N (e-Postcard) if its annual gross receipts are normally:
choices: $25,000 or less
$50,000 or less
$200,000 or less
$500,000 or less
explain: Organizations with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less may file the 990-N. Form 990-EZ is for gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000.
source: IRS: Annual electronic filing requirement for small exempt organizations (Form 990-N)

q: For 2025, employer contributions to a simplified employee pension individual retirement arrangement (SEP-IRA) for an employee are limited to the lesser of 25% of compensation or:
explain: The 2025 defined contribution limit is $70,000. $69,000 was 2024 and $23,500 is the 2025 401(k) elective deferral limit.

q: A taxpayer rents out a vacation home for 12 days in 2025 and uses it personally the rest of the year. How is the rental income treated?
choices: Reported in full with expenses allocated
Not reported, and no rental expenses are deducted
Reported, with losses fully deductible
Reported as self-employment income
explain: If a dwelling unit used as a home is rented fewer than 15 days, the rental income is not reported and the rental expenses are not deductible.

q: A domestic trust must file Form 1041 if it has gross income for the year of at least:
explain: A trust must file if it has any taxable income or gross income of $600 or more, or has a nonresident alien beneficiary.

q: Under Circular 230, an enrolled agent must complete continuing education of at least how many hours per year (within the 72-hour cycle requirement)?
choices: 12 hours, including 1 hour of ethics
16 hours, including 2 hours of ethics
24 hours, including 2 hours of ethics
24 hours, including 4 hours of ethics
explain: Enrolled agents (EAs) need 72 hours per 3-year enrollment cycle, with a minimum of 16 hours each year, 2 of which must be ethics.

q: Under Circular 230, a contingent fee is prohibited for which service?
choices: Preparing an original tax return
Services rendered in connection with the IRS's examination of an original return
A claim for refund filed solely about statutory interest or penalties
Services in a judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code
explain: Circular 230 bars contingent fees for preparing an original return. The other three are listed exceptions where a contingent fee may be charged.

q: A client asks for their records back, but there is a fee dispute. Under Circular 230, the practitioner must:
choices: Keep all records until the fee is paid
Return the client's records needed to comply with federal tax obligations, though copies may be kept
Return only the original documents the client mailed in
Send the records to the IRS
explain: Section 10.28 requires promptly returning client records necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations, even if a fee dispute exists. The practitioner may keep copies.

q: A paid preparer must keep a copy of each return prepared, or a list of the taxpayers and their identifying numbers, for how long?
choices: 1 year after the close of the return period
3 years after the close of the return period
6 years after the return is filed
Until the statute of limitations on collection expires
explain: Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6107(b) requires keeping a completed copy or a list for 3 years after the close of the return period.

q: Which statement about Form 8821 is correct?
choices: It authorizes the designee to represent the taxpayer before the IRS
It authorizes the designee to inspect and receive confidential tax information but not to represent the taxpayer
It can only be granted to enrolled agents, CPAs, and attorneys
It allows the designee to sign the taxpayer's return
explain: Form 8821 is a tax information authorization. Representation requires Form 2848, which only eligible practitioners can hold.

q: The federally authorized tax practitioner privilege under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7525 applies to all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Noncriminal tax matters before the IRS
Noncriminal tax proceedings in federal court brought by or against the United States
Criminal tax matters
Advice given by an enrolled agent on a civil audit issue
explain: The 7525 privilege covers only noncriminal tax matters. It also does not cover written communications promoting participation in a tax shelter.

q: If a taxpayer omits more than 25% of the gross income stated on the return, the IRS generally has how long after the return was filed to assess tax?
choices: 3 years
6 years
10 years
No limit
explain: The normal assessment period is 3 years. A substantial omission of more than 25% of gross income extends it to 6 years. Fraud or no return means no limit.

q: The IRS generally has how long after assessment to collect a tax?
choices: 3 years
6 years
10 years
20 years
explain: The collection statute expiration date (CSED) is generally 10 years from assessment. Some events, such as a pending offer in compromise or bankruptcy, suspend it.

q: An individual qualifies for a guaranteed installment agreement only if the tax owed, not counting penalties and interest, is no more than:
explain: A guaranteed agreement requires $10,000 or less in tax, full payment within 3 years, and filing and payment compliance for the prior 5 years. Streamlined agreements go up to $50,000 assessed.

q: After receiving a notice of intent to levy and notice of right to a hearing, how long does a taxpayer have to request a Collection Due Process hearing with Form 12153?
choices: 10 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
explain: A timely collection due process (CDP) request must be filed within 30 days of the notice date. After that, only an equivalent hearing is available, without Tax Court review.

q: The trust fund recovery penalty equals what share of the unpaid trust fund taxes?
explain: The trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6672 is 100% of the unpaid withheld income tax and employee share of Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA), assessed against responsible persons who willfully failed to pay.

q: After receiving a statutory notice of deficiency addressed to a taxpayer in the United States, how long does the taxpayer have to petition the Tax Court?
choices: 30 days
60 days
90 days
150 days
explain: The petition is due within 90 days, or 150 days if the notice is addressed to someone outside the United States. The 30-day letter comes earlier and offers Appeals.

q: An electronic return originator (ERO) that keeps a signed Form 8879 must retain it for how long?
choices: 1 year
2 years
3 years from the return due date or the IRS received date, whichever is later
7 years
explain: EROs keep Form 8879 for 3 years from the return due date or the date the IRS received the return, whichever is later.

q: A specified tax return preparer must e-file individual returns if they reasonably expect to file how many or more individual income tax returns in the year?
explain: Preparers who reasonably expect to file more than 10 (that is, 11 or more) individual or trust returns must e-file, unless an exception applies. Form 8948 documents paper-filed exceptions.

q: Under the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Safeguards Rule, a paid tax preparer must:
choices: Keep client files on paper only
Maintain a written information security plan
Register their software with Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)
Get IRS approval before using cloud storage
explain: Tax preparers are financial institutions under the FTC Safeguards Rule and must have a written information security program. IRS Pub 5708 gives a template.
source: IRS Pub 4557; IRS Pub 5708; 16 CFR Part 314

q: Ines is a citizen of Brazil who is not an exempt individual and does not claim the closer connection exception. She was present in the United States 140 days in 2025, 120 days in 2024, and 90 days in 2023. What is her residency status for 2025 under the substantial presence test?
choices: Nonresident alien, because she was present fewer than 183 days in 2025
Resident alien, because her total days over three years exceed 300
Nonresident alien, because her weighted day count is 170
Resident alien, because her weighted day count is 195
explain: The test counts all 2025 days, one-third of 2024 days, and one-sixth of 2023 days: 140 + 40 + 15 = 195, which is at least 183, and she was present at least 31 days in 2025. Being under 183 days in the current year alone does not make her a nonresident; that only matters for the closer connection exception, which she does not claim.

q: A student in the United States on an F-1 visa who substantially complies with the visa requirements is an exempt individual, and does not count days of presence for the substantial presence test, unless the student has already been exempt as a teacher, trainee, or student for any part of more than how many calendar years?
explain: A student is generally not an exempt individual if he or she was exempt as a teacher, trainee, or student for any part of more than 5 calendar years, unless the student shows no intent to reside permanently and has substantially complied with the visa. The 2 calendar year figure is the teacher and trainee rule (exempt in 2 of the prior 6 years), a common mix-up.

q: Mei, a citizen of China, had never been in the United States before she entered as a lawful permanent resident (green card holder) on September 20, 2025. She remained in the United States through December 31, 2025, and does not meet the substantial presence test for 2025. What is her residency status for 2025?
choices: Dual-status alien: nonresident through September 19 and resident beginning September 20, 2025
Nonresident alien for all of 2025, because she was present fewer than 183 days
Resident alien for all of 2025, because she held a green card at some time during the year
Nonresident alien for 2025, with residency beginning January 1, 2026
explain: Under the green card test, when a person does not also meet the substantial presence test, the residency starting date is the first day in the calendar year on which the person is present in the United States as a lawful permanent resident. Mei is therefore a resident only from September 20, making 2025 a dual-status year; the green card does not make her a resident for the whole year.

q: All of the following statements about an individual with a dual-status tax year who does not elect to be treated as a U.S. resident for the entire year are true EXCEPT:
choices: The individual cannot use the head of household tax rates
An individual who is a resident on the last day of the year files Form 1040 and attaches a statement for the nonresident part of the year
The individual cannot file a joint return
An individual who is a resident on the last day of the year may claim the standard deduction
explain: A dual-status taxpayer cannot claim the standard deduction, even if he or she is a resident at year end. The other statements are true: head of household rates are not available, the return form depends on status on the last day of the year, and a joint return is possible only if a dual-status individual married to a U.S. citizen or resident elects to file jointly.
source: IRS Pub 519 (2025); IRS: Taxation of Dual-Status Individuals

q: Tom, a U.S. citizen, is married to Ana, a nonresident alien. For 2025 they elect to treat Ana as a U.S. resident for income tax purposes. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both spouses are taxed on their worldwide income and must file a joint return for the year of the choice
Only Ana's U.S.-source income is subject to U.S. tax
Tom may file as head of household because his spouse is a nonresident alien
The election applies only to 2025 and must be made again each year
explain: When the choice is made, both spouses are treated as U.S. residents for the entire year, are taxed on worldwide income, and must file a joint return for the year of the choice. The election stays in effect for later years until it is terminated, so it does not have to be remade each year.

q: All of the following statements about an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) are true EXCEPT:
choices: It is issued to individuals who have a federal tax purpose but are not eligible for a Social Security number
An application or renewal is made on Form W-7
It expires if it is not used on a U.S. federal tax return for any 3 consecutive tax years
It qualifies the holder to claim the earned income tax credit
explain: An ITIN is for federal tax purposes only; it does not authorize work in the United States or provide eligibility for Social Security benefits or the earned income tax credit. The other statements are true: it is for people not eligible for a Social Security number (SSN), Form W-7 is used to apply or renew, and it expires on December 31 after the third consecutive tax year of non-use.
source: IRS: Individual Taxpayer Identification Number; IRS: Renew an ITIN

q: Which statement about the Identity Protection Personal Identification Number (IP PIN) is correct?
choices: It is a six-digit number that is valid for one calendar year, and a new one is generated each year
It is available only to taxpayers who have been confirmed victims of identity theft
It is a permanent five-digit number that stays the same for every future return
Parents cannot obtain an IP PIN for their dependents
explain: An IP PIN is a six-digit number valid for one calendar year, and a new IP PIN is generated each year. Anyone with a Social Security number (SSN) or individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN) who can verify identity may enroll, not just identity theft victims, and parents and guardians can request IP PINs for dependents.
source: IRS: Get an Identity Protection PIN

q: Ruth, age 67, is single and not blind. Her only 2025 income is $17,000 of taxable pension and interest income. No advance premium tax credit was paid for her and no other special filing situation applies. Is she required to file a 2025 return?
choices: Yes, because her gross income exceeds $15,750
Yes, because her gross income exceeds $5,200
No, because her gross income is less than $17,750
No, because taxpayers age 65 or older are never required to file
explain: For 2025 a single filer age 65 or older must file if gross income is at least $17,750 (the $15,750 basic standard deduction plus the $2,000 additional amount). Ruth's $17,000 is below that, so she is not required to file. The $15,750 figure is the threshold for a single filer under 65.
source: Form 1040 instructions (2025), Chart A; IRS Pub 501 (2025)

q: Leah, age 16, is single, not blind, and claimed as a dependent by her parents. In 2025 she earned $3,000 of wages and $1,000 of bank interest. Must she file a 2025 return?
choices: No, because her unearned income is not more than $1,350
No, because her earned income is not more than $15,750
Yes, because her gross income of $4,000 is more than $3,450
Yes, because any dependent with unearned income must file
explain: A dependent must file if gross income is more than the larger of $1,350 or earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450. Here that is $3,000 + $450 = $3,450, and her gross income is $3,000 + $1,000 = $4,000, so she must file. Passing the separate unearned-income and earned-income tests does not end the analysis; the gross income test still applies.
source: Form 1040 instructions (2025), Chart B; Rev. Proc. 2024-40

q: Luis is a U.S. citizen whose tax home and abode are in Spain on April 15, 2026. He does not file Form 4868. To be timely, by what date must he file his 2025 Form 1040 (attaching a statement explaining the extension)?
choices: April 15, 2026
August 15, 2026
October 15, 2026
explain: A U.S. citizen or resident living outside the United States and Puerto Rico with a tax home abroad on the regular due date gets an automatic 2-month extension, to June 15, 2026, and attaches a statement showing eligibility. October 15, 2026 is available only by also filing Form 4868 by June 15. Interest still runs on unpaid tax from April 15.

q: Which statement about Form 4868 for a 2025 individual income tax return is correct?
choices: It extends the due date for both filing and paying the tax to October 15, 2026
It must be approved by the IRS before the extension takes effect
It gives an automatic extension to file until October 15, 2026, but tax is still due by April 15, 2026
It gives an automatic extension to file until December 15, 2026
explain: Form 4868 filed by April 15, 2026 gives an automatic 6-month extension to file, to October 15, 2026. It does not extend the time to pay, so interest and possibly the late payment penalty apply to tax paid after April 15, 2026.

q: Elena's husband died in February 2023. She has not remarried. Her daughter, age 10, whom she claims as a dependent, lived with her all of 2025, and Elena paid all the costs of keeping up the home. Elena was entitled to file a joint return for 2023. What is her most favorable filing status for 2025?
choices: Married filing jointly
Qualifying surviving spouse
Head of household
Single
explain: Qualifying surviving spouse status is available for the 2 years after the year of death (2024 and 2025 here) if the taxpayer has not remarried, could have filed jointly in the year of death, and keeps up a home for a dependent child or stepchild. It uses joint return rates and the $31,500 standard deduction, which beats head of household ($23,625). Married filing jointly is allowed only for the year of death.

q: Rosa and her husband separated, and he moved out of their home on August 1, 2025. Their son lived with Rosa all year, she paid all the household costs, and she can claim him as a dependent. They are not divorced or legally separated at year end, and they will not file a joint return. What is Rosa's 2025 filing status?
choices: Married filing separately
Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
explain: To be considered unmarried for head of household purposes, the spouse must not have lived in the home during the last 6 months of the year. Her husband lived there through July 31, which is within the last 6 months (July through December), so Rosa cannot use head of household and must file married filing separately if they do not file jointly. Single status requires being unmarried on December 31.

q: Daniel is unmarried. He paid more than half the cost of keeping up his widowed mother's apartment for all of 2025. She lives alone across town, and he can claim her as a dependent. What is Daniel's best filing status for 2025?
choices: Single, because his mother did not live with him
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing separately
explain: A dependent parent does not have to live with the taxpayer for head of household status, as long as the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of keeping up the parent's main home for the entire year and can claim the parent as a dependent. The live-with requirement that disqualifies other relatives does not apply to a parent.

q: Carlos, age 22 and single, lived all of 2025 with his brother Marco, age 23, a full-time student who is not disabled. Carlos provided all of Marco's support. Is Marco Carlos's qualifying child?
choices: Yes, because Marco is a full-time student under age 24
Yes, because a brother meets the relationship test and Carlos provided all his support
No, because Marco is not younger than Carlos
No, because a student must be under age 19 to be a qualifying child
explain: To meet the age test, a qualifying child must be younger than the taxpayer (or the spouse if filing jointly), in addition to being under 19, or under 24 if a full-time student, unless permanently and totally disabled. Marco is older than Carlos, so he fails the age test even though he is a student under 24. Carlos would have to look at the qualifying relative rules instead.

q: Sofia, age 18, lived with her parents all of 2025 and did not provide over half of her own support. She married in 2025 and she and her husband file a 2025 joint return only to claim a refund of income tax withheld; neither would owe tax on a separate return. Which statement is correct?
choices: Her parents cannot claim her because she filed a joint return
Her parents can claim her only as a qualifying relative
Her parents can claim her only if she files married filing separately
Her parents can claim her as a qualifying child because the joint return was filed only to claim a refund of withheld tax
explain: The joint return test does not disqualify a child who files a joint return only to claim a refund of income tax withheld or estimated tax paid. That exception would not apply if the couple filed jointly to claim a credit such as the American opportunity credit.

q: Kayla, age 6, lived all of 2025 with her mother Ana and her grandmother Rosa. Ana's 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) is $35,000 and Rosa's is $30,000. Kayla is a qualifying child of both. Ana does not claim Kayla. Can Rosa claim Kayla as a qualifying child?
choices: Yes, because Ana did not claim her
Yes, because Rosa is the older taxpayer
No, because Rosa's AGI is not higher than the highest AGI of any parent who can claim Kayla
No, because only a parent can ever claim a qualifying child
explain: When a parent can claim the child but no parent does, another taxpayer may claim the child only if that taxpayer's AGI is higher than the highest AGI of any parent who can claim the child. Rosa's $30,000 is lower than Ana's $35,000, so she cannot. Simply having the parent decline to claim the child is not enough.

q: Mark and Jen are divorced. Their son lived with Jen for 250 nights in 2025. Jen signed Form 8332 releasing her claim to the son's exemption for 2025, and Mark attaches it to his return. Which benefit may Mark claim for the son?
choices: Head of household filing status
The earned income credit
The child and dependent care credit
The child tax credit
explain: Under the special rule for divorced or separated parents, a release lets the noncustodial parent claim the child as a dependent and for the child tax credit or credit for other dependents. It does not allow the noncustodial parent to claim head of household status, the earned income credit, the child and dependent care credit, or the exclusion for dependent care benefits; those stay with the custodial parent.

q: All of the following relatives can be a taxpayer's qualifying relative without living with the taxpayer all year EXCEPT:
choices: A cousin
A father-in-law
A niece
A stepmother
explain: Cousins are not on the list of relatives who do not have to live with the taxpayer, so a cousin can be a qualifying relative only by living with the taxpayer all year as a member of the household. Nieces and nephews, in-laws, and stepparents are all on the relationship list.

q: Four siblings provided all of their mother's 2025 support: Ana 45%, Ben 30%, Clara 15%, and David 10%. The mother's gross income was under $5,200, she lived alone, and no one else provided support. Which statement about a multiple support agreement is correct?
choices: Only Ana may claim her, because she provided the most support
Any one of Ana, Ben, or Clara may claim her if each of the others who provided over 10% signs a statement agreeing not to claim her
Any of the four siblings may claim her, including David
No one may claim her, because no single person provided over half her support
explain: Under a multiple support agreement, a person who provided over 10% of the support may claim the dependent if together the eligible group provided over half, and every other person who provided over 10% signs a written statement not to claim. David provided exactly 10%, not over 10%, so he cannot claim her and does not need to sign. The claimant uses Form 2120 to identify the others.

q: All of the following statements about Form 8379, Injured Spouse Allocation, are true EXCEPT:
choices: It may be filed with the original joint return or later by itself
A separate Form 8379 must be filed for each year the taxpayer wants a share of an offset refunded
It may generally be filed within 3 years from the due date of the original return (including extensions) or 2 years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later
It relieves the requesting spouse of liability for an understatement of tax on the joint return
explain: Form 8379 only recovers the injured spouse's share of a joint overpayment that was applied to the other spouse's past-due debt. Relief from liability for an understatement on a joint return is innocent spouse relief, requested on Form 8857, a separate procedure. The other three statements match the Form 8379 instructions.

q: After a 2025 federally declared disaster, the IRS postponed filing and payment deadlines for taxpayers in the covered counties. Which statement is correct?
choices: Taxpayers with an IRS address of record in the covered area get the relief automatically and do not need to contact the IRS
Every affected taxpayer must file Form 4868 to receive the postponement
Relief applies only to taxpayers who physically lived in the area on the date of the disaster, even if their records were elsewhere
Taxpayers who live outside the area cannot receive relief even if the records they need are located in the area
explain: The IRS automatically provides filing and penalty relief to any taxpayer with an IRS address of record in the disaster area, with no need to contact the agency. Taxpayers outside the area whose necessary records are located in the area can also qualify and should call the IRS disaster hotline. No Form 4868 is needed for the postponement.
source: IRS newsroom: California wildfire victims qualify for tax relief (2025); IRC 7508A

q: Joe and Kim file jointly and enrolled in Marketplace coverage for 2025. Joe's modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $52,000 and Kim's is $28,000. They claim their son, age 17, whose only income was $4,000 of wages, so he is not required to file. What household income and family size do they use on Form 8962?
explain: Household income is the MAGI of the taxpayer and spouse plus the MAGI of dependents who are required to file a return. The son is not required to file, so his wages are left out: $52,000 + $28,000 = $80,000. Family size counts everyone in the tax family, including dependents claimed, so it is 3.

q: A married couple living together received advance premium tax credit for 2025 Marketplace coverage. Neither is a victim of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment, and they decide to file separately. Which statement is correct?
choices: Each spouse may claim half of the premium tax credit
They may claim the credit only if household income is under 400% of the federal poverty line
The spouse who enrolled in the plan may claim the full credit
Neither spouse can claim the premium tax credit
explain: A married taxpayer who files separately is generally not an applicable taxpayer for the premium tax credit, unless the domestic abuse or spousal abandonment exception applies. They must still file Form 8962 to reconcile the advance payments. For 2025, income above 400% of the federal poverty line does not by itself bar the credit.

q: Raj and Priya file jointly and live in the United States. During 2025 the total value of their foreign bank accounts peaked at $140,000 and was $90,000 on December 31, 2025. They have no other foreign financial assets. Which statement is correct?
choices: They must file Form 8938 and a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)
They must file Form 8938 but not a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)
They must file a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) but not Form 8938
They do not need to file Form 8938 or a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)
explain: For joint filers living in the United States, Form 8938 is required only if specified foreign financial assets exceed $100,000 on the last day of the year or $150,000 at any time. Neither threshold is met ($90,000 and $140,000). The FBAR is required because the aggregate value of the foreign accounts exceeded $10,000 at some point during the year.

q: Noah, age 12, has $5,000 of interest income and no other income for 2025. He does not itemize. His parents are married and file jointly. How much of Noah's income is taxed at his parents' rate on Form 8615?
explain: Net unearned income is unearned income minus $2,700 (when the child does not itemize), limited to taxable income: $5,000 - $2,700 = $2,300. His taxable income is $5,000 - $1,350 = $3,650, so the $2,300 limit applies. The $3,650 figure is his total taxable income, not the part taxed at the parents' rate.

q: A child must file Form 8615 for 2025. The child's parents are married but file separate returns. Whose tax rate is used to figure the child's tax on net unearned income?
choices: The parent with the greater taxable income
The parent with the lower taxable income
The parent who provided more of the child's support
Either parent, as the parents choose
explain: When the parents file separate returns, the return of the parent with the greater taxable income is used. If the parents were divorced or legally separated, the custodial parent's return would generally be used instead.

q: In 2025 Maria paid her housekeeper, age 45, cash wages of $2,700, paid as $675 in each calendar quarter. The housekeeper is Maria's household employee and is not related to her. Maria paid no household wages in 2024. Which statement is correct?
choices: Maria must withhold Social Security and Medicare tax because wages reached $2,700
Maria owes Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax on the wages
Maria must withhold federal income tax from the wages
Maria has no federal household employment tax obligation for this employee for 2025
explain: For 2025, Social Security and Medicare taxes apply only if cash wages to one household employee are $2,800 or more, and FUTA applies only if total cash wages are $1,000 or more in a calendar quarter. Maria paid $2,700 and $675 per quarter, so neither applies, and income tax withholding is never required unless the employee asks and the employer agrees.

q: Hal and his wife, both U.S. citizens, owned their home as joint tenants with right of survivorship, with no other joint tenants. Hal paid the entire purchase price. When Hal died in 2025 the home was worth $900,000. How much is included in Hal's gross estate?
explain: A qualified joint interest between spouses, where the spouses are the only joint tenants, is included at one-half of its value regardless of who paid: $900,000 x 50% = $450,000. The contribution test that would include the full $900,000 applies to joint owners who are not spouses (or when the surviving spouse is not a U.S. citizen).

q: Gina and her brother bought land as joint tenants with right of survivorship for $400,000. Gina paid $300,000 and her brother paid $100,000. When Gina died in 2025 the land was worth $600,000. How much is included in Gina's gross estate?
explain: For joint tenants who are not spouses, the full value is included except the part attributable to the survivor's contribution. Gina furnished 75% of the cost ($300,000 / $400,000), so $600,000 x 75% = $450,000 is included. The 50% rule ($300,000) applies only to qualified joint interests between spouses.

q: In January 2024 Walter transferred ownership of a $1,000,000 policy on his life to his daughter, who was also the beneficiary. He kept no rights in the policy. Walter died in November 2025 and the daughter collected $1,000,000. How much of the proceeds is included in Walter's gross estate?
choices: $0, because Walter held no incidents of ownership at death
$19,000, the annual exclusion amount
The policy's cash surrender value on the date of the transfer
explain: A transfer of a life insurance policy within 3 years of death is pulled back into the gross estate if the proceeds would have been included under section 2042 had the decedent kept the policy. Walter transferred it about 22 months before death, so the full $1,000,000 is included even though he held no incidents of ownership when he died.

q: Ellen died in 2025 owning a $500,000 traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA, no basis) payable to her two adult children. Which statement is correct?
choices: The IRA is included in her gross estate, and distributions are income in respect of a decedent taxable to the children, who may deduct estate tax attributable to the IRA
The IRA is included in her gross estate, and distributions are tax-free to the children because of a stepped-up basis
The IRA is excluded from her gross estate because it passes by beneficiary designation
The IRA is excluded from her gross estate, and distributions are taxable to the children
explain: An IRA payable to beneficiaries is included in the decedent's gross estate as an annuity or other payment receivable by reason of surviving the decedent. Distributions are also income in respect of a decedent to the children, with no stepped-up basis, and a section 691(c) deduction is allowed for federal estate tax paid on that income. Passing outside the probate estate does not keep it out of the gross estate.

q: Paul, a U.S. citizen, died in 2025 and left his entire estate outright to his wife, who is not a U.S. citizen. Which statement about the estate tax marital deduction is correct?
choices: The unlimited marital deduction applies because the spouses were married at death
The marital deduction is allowed only if the spouse becomes a citizen within 9 months
A marital deduction is allowed up to $190,000
No marital deduction is allowed unless the property passes to the spouse in a qualified domestic trust (QDOT)
explain: If the surviving spouse is not a U.S. citizen, the marital deduction is generally denied unless the property passes in a qualified domestic trust, which may be set up and funded before the estate tax return is filed. The $190,000 figure is the 2025 gift tax annual exclusion for gifts to a noncitizen spouse, not an estate tax marital deduction.

q: Frank died in 2025 with a gross estate of $18,000,000. Funeral and administration expenses and debts total $500,000. His will leaves $3,000,000 to a qualified public charity and the rest to his children. What is his taxable estate?
explain: Taxable estate is the gross estate minus deductions: $18,000,000 - $500,000 - $3,000,000 = $14,500,000. The estate tax charitable deduction has no percentage-of-income limit. The $510,000 choice subtracts the $13,990,000 basic exclusion, but the exclusion works through the unified credit and is not a deduction in figuring the taxable estate.

q: At Ruth's death in 2025 her estate held stock worth $10,000,000 and land worth $6,000,000. The executor sold the stock 4 months after death for $9,200,000; it would have been worth $8,800,000 six months after death. The land was worth $5,600,000 six months after death. The estate owes estate tax, and the alternate valuation election reduces both the gross estate and the tax. What is the gross estate if the executor elects alternate valuation?
explain: Under alternate valuation, property is valued 6 months after death, except property sold or distributed within 6 months is valued on the date of disposition. So the stock is $9,200,000 (sale date) and the land is $5,600,000: total $14,800,000. Using $8,800,000 for the stock ($14,400,000) ignores the sale-date rule.

q: Victor, a U.S. citizen, died in 2025 with a gross estate of $12,500,000. During his life he made $2,000,000 of adjusted taxable gifts after 1976. Must his executor file Form 706?
choices: No, because his gross estate is below $13,990,000
Yes, because the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts of $14,500,000 exceeds $13,990,000
Only if estate tax is due after the unified credit
Only if the executor wants to elect portability
explain: The filing threshold is the basic exclusion amount ($13,990,000 for 2025 deaths), reduced by adjusted taxable gifts and any specific exemption used. Equivalently, $12,500,000 + $2,000,000 = $14,500,000 exceeds $13,990,000, so a return is required whether or not tax is due. Comparing only the gross estate to $13,990,000 is the common error.

q: Sam died in 2025 survived by his wife. His taxable estate was $3,500,000, his adjusted taxable gifts were $500,000, and he had no deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) from a prior spouse. His executor timely files Form 706 and elects portability. What is the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount?
explain: DSUE is the lesser of the basic exclusion amount or the decedent's applicable exclusion amount minus the sum of the taxable estate and adjusted taxable gifts: $13,990,000 - ($3,500,000 + $500,000) = $9,990,000. The $10,490,000 choice forgets to subtract the adjusted taxable gifts.

q: Alma died on March 10, 2025. Her estate had $15,000 of gross income in its first year, and the executor chose a fiscal year ending February 28, 2026. When is the estate's first Form 1041 due, without extension?
choices: December 10, 2025
April 15, 2026
explain: An estate with gross income of $600 or more must file Form 1041, due the 15th day of the 4th month after its tax year ends. The year ends February 28, 2026, so the return is due June 15, 2026; Form 7004 can extend it 5 1/2 months. December 10, 2025 is the 9-month Form 706 deadline, and April 15 applies only to a calendar-year return.

q: Which of the following 2025 transfers requires the donor to file Form 709? Assume no other gifts.
choices: $60,000 of tuition paid directly to a university for a grandson
$25,000 paid directly to a hospital for a friend's surgery
$500,000 of cash given outright to the donor's wife, a U.S. citizen
$25,000 paid to a university for a grandson's room and board
explain: Tuition paid directly to an educational organization and medical costs paid directly to the provider are not gifts at all, and outright gifts to a U.S. citizen spouse generally need no return because of the unlimited marital deduction. Room and board is not tuition, so the $25,000 is a gift to the grandson that exceeds the $19,000 annual exclusion and must be reported.

q: In 2025 Ken, a U.S. citizen, gave his wife, who is not a U.S. citizen, $200,000 in cash. He made no other gifts. Which statement is correct?
choices: The taxable gift is $10,000 and Ken must file Form 709
There is no taxable gift because of the unlimited marital deduction
The taxable gift is $181,000 and Ken must file Form 709
The taxable gift is $10,000 but no Form 709 is required
explain: Gifts to a spouse who is not a U.S. citizen do not qualify for the unlimited marital deduction, but for 2025 the annual exclusion for such gifts is $190,000. $200,000 - $190,000 = $10,000 taxable gift, and a return is required because present-interest gifts exceeded $190,000. The $181,000 choice wrongly uses the regular $19,000 exclusion.

q: Which statement about the due date of a Form 709 for gifts made in 2025 is correct?
choices: It is due April 15, 2026, and an extension of the donor's income tax return on Form 4868 also extends the time to file Form 709
It is due 9 months after the date of the gift
It is due April 15, 2026, and a Form 4868 extension also extends the time to pay any gift tax
It is due October 15, 2026, with no extension needed
explain: Form 709 for 2025 gifts is generally due April 15, 2026. Extending the income tax return with Form 4868 also extends Form 709, or the donor can file Form 8892, but neither extends the time to pay gift tax. The 9-month period is the estate tax return deadline.

q: All of the following are requirements or effects of electing gift-splitting for 2025 EXCEPT:
choices: The spouses may choose to split some gifts to third parties and not others made during the year while married
Neither spouse may be a nonresident who is not a U.S. citizen at the time of the gift
The spouses must have been married at the time of the gift
The consenting spouse becomes jointly and severally liable for the gift tax on the split gifts
explain: Consent to gift-splitting is effective for the entire calendar year, so all gifts by either spouse to third parties during the year while married must be split. The other three statements are correct conditions or effects of the election.

q: In 2025 Ivan transferred $10,000 in cash to an irrevocable trust for his nephew. The trust accumulates income, and the nephew will receive the property at age 30. The nephew has no right to withdraw any of the gift now. Ivan made no other gifts and has made no prior taxable gifts. Which statement is correct?
choices: No Form 709 is required because the gift is under $19,000
No gift occurs until the nephew turns 30
Form 709 is required only if the gift exceeds $19,000
Form 709 is required, the full $10,000 is a taxable gift, and the unified credit covers it so no gift tax is paid
explain: A gift of a future interest does not qualify for the annual exclusion, so Form 709 must be filed for it regardless of amount and the full $10,000 is a taxable gift. Because Ivan has no prior taxable gifts, the unified credit absorbs the tax. The $19,000 exclusion applies only to present interests.

q: Which of the following 2025 gifts is a direct skip for generation-skipping transfer tax purposes?
choices: A gift to an unrelated friend who is 40 years younger than the donor
A gift to the donor's niece, who is 30 years younger than the donor
A gift to a grandson whose father (the donor's son) died before the gift
A gift to the donor's wife, who is 45 years younger than the donor
explain: A direct skip is a transfer subject to gift or estate tax to a skip person, meaning someone two or more generations below the donor. An unrelated person born more than 37 1/2 years after the donor is assigned two generations down, so the friend is a skip person. A spouse is always in the donor's generation, a niece is one generation down, and the predeceased parent rule moves the grandson up one generation.

q: In 2025 Diego, a U.S. citizen, received a $120,000 cash gift from his grandmother, a nonresident alien living in Mexico. Diego files his 2025 Form 1040 on time without an extension. Which statement is correct?
choices: Diego must include the $120,000 in gross income
Diego must report the gift on Form 3520, due April 15, 2026, but the gift is not taxable income
Diego must file Form 709 because the gift exceeds $19,000
No reporting is required because gifts from foreign individuals are reported only above $200,000
explain: A U.S. person who receives more than $100,000 in gifts or bequests from a nonresident alien individual or foreign estate during the year must report them on Form 3520. For an individual it is due on the 15th day of the 4th month after year end (April 15, 2026), or the 15th day of the 10th month if the income tax return is extended. The gift itself is not income, and Form 709 is filed by donors, not recipients.

q: In 2025 Lena, a U.S. citizen, contributed $150,000 in cash to a foreign partnership in exchange for a 5% interest. Which form must she file to report the contribution?
choices: Form 8865
Form 3520
Form 5471
No form, because her interest is less than 10%
explain: A U.S. person who contributes property to a foreign partnership is a Category 3 filer of Form 8865 if, immediately after the contribution, she owns at least 10%, or if the property contributed (with related contributions in the prior 12 months) exceeds $100,000. Her $150,000 contribution meets the second test even though her interest is only 5%. Form 5471 is for foreign corporations.

q: In May 2026 Omar learns he should have filed a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) for 2025 because his foreign accounts exceeded $10,000. He has not filed anything. Which statement is correct?
choices: The FBAR was due April 15, 2026, but filers automatically get an extension to October 15, 2026, with no request required
He must file Form 4868 to extend the FBAR
The FBAR is attached to his Form 1040 and follows its due date
The FBAR is due June 30 each year with no extension
explain: The FBAR is due April 15 following the calendar year, and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) grants an automatic extension to October 15 with no specific request needed. It is filed electronically with FinCEN through the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) E-Filing System, not with the tax return. June 30 was the pre-2017 due date.
source: FinCEN: BSA Electronic Filing Requirements for the FBAR (FinCEN Form 114)

q: A U.S. citizen holds each of the following. Which one is reportable on Form 8938 (if the filing threshold is met) but NOT on the Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)?
choices: A savings account at a bank in France
Signature authority, with no financial interest, over his employer's foreign bank account
A rental house in Italy owned directly
Stock certificates of a German corporation held directly, not in an account
explain: Foreign stock held directly rather than in a financial account is a specified foreign financial asset for Form 8938 but is not a financial account for the FBAR. A foreign bank account is reportable on both, directly held foreign real estate is reportable on neither, and signature-only authority is an FBAR item but not a Form 8938 item.
source: IRS: Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR Requirements

q: On her timely filed 2025 return, Nadia reported gross income of $200,000 but omitted $8,000 of dividends from foreign corporation stock she holds directly. There is no fraud. How long does the IRS have to assess tax for 2025? Assume she filed every required information return, including Form 8938.
choices: 3 years after the return was filed
6 years after the return was filed
10 years after the return was filed
There is no time limit
explain: The 6-year period applies if omitted gross income exceeds 25% of reported gross income, or if the omission is more than $5,000 and is attributable to a specified foreign financial asset reportable under section 6038D (determined without the dollar thresholds). The $8,000 is only 4% of reported income, so the 25% test fails, but the foreign asset rule applies.

q: In 2025, Mia's employer gave her a transit pass worth $400 each month for all 12 months. She has no other transportation fringe benefits. How much of the transit pass value must be included in her wages?
explain: For 2025 the monthly exclusion for transit passes is $325, so $75 a month is taxable ($400 minus $325). Over 12 months that is $900. The $1,020 choice uses the 2024 limit of $315.
source: Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.17; IRC 132(f); IRS Pub 15-B (2025)

q: All of the following are included in federal gross income EXCEPT:
choices: Interest on a general obligation bond issued by the State of New Jersey
Original issue discount that accrued in 2025 on a corporate bond bought at original issue
Interest on a Series I savings bond cashed in 2025 to pay for a vacation
Interest the IRS paid on a delayed federal income tax refund
explain: Interest on obligations of a state or political subdivision is generally excluded from federal gross income, although it is still reported as tax-exempt interest on the return. Original issue discount (OID) must be included as it accrues even though no cash is received, and savings bond interest is federally taxable unless the education exclusion applies.

q: Rosa and Tom file jointly for 2025. They cashed qualified Series EE bonds for $8,000 ($5,000 principal and $3,000 interest) and paid $10,000 of qualified tuition for their daughter that year. Their modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) for the exclusion, including the bond interest, is $164,250. How much of the interest can they exclude?
explain: Because qualified expenses exceed the bond proceeds, all $3,000 of interest is eligible before the income limit. For 2025 the joint phaseout runs from $149,250 to $179,250, so MAGI that is $15,000 into the $30,000 range cuts the exclusion by half: $3,000 x 50% = $1,500. Excluding the full $3,000 ignores the phaseout.

q: Lisa bought shares of a U.S. corporation 10 days before the ex-dividend date and sold them 20 days after the ex-dividend date. She received a $500 dividend that the payer reported in Form 1099-DIV box 1b as qualified. How should Lisa treat the dividend?
choices: As a qualified dividend, because the payer reported it in box 1b
As a nondividend distribution that reduces her basis
As an ordinary dividend, because she did not hold the stock more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date
As a short-term capital gain
explain: To get qualified dividend rates, the shareholder must hold the stock more than 60 days during the 121-day period beginning 60 days before the ex-dividend date. Lisa held the shares about 30 days, so the dividend is taxed at ordinary rates even though the payer showed it in box 1b.

q: Carlos has owned shares of a corporation for five years with an adjusted basis of $1,000. In 2025 he received $1,500 reported in Form 1099-DIV box 3 (nondividend distributions). What is the result for 2025?
choices: $1,500 ordinary dividend income
No income, and his basis becomes negative $500
His basis is reduced to zero and he reports $500 of ordinary income
His basis is reduced to zero and he reports a $500 long-term capital gain
explain: A nondividend distribution is a return of capital that first reduces stock basis. Once basis reaches zero, the excess is capital gain, long-term here because he held the shares more than a year. Basis can never go below zero.

q: In 2025 Diane, a casual gambler, won $8,000 reported on Form W-2G and had $11,000 of documented gambling losses. She itemizes deductions. How much of her gambling losses can she deduct for 2025?
explain: For 2025, wagering losses are deductible as an itemized deduction only to the extent of wagering gains, so the deduction is $8,000. The $7,200 choice applies the 90 percent limit added by P.L. 119-21, which only applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

q: In 2025 a lender canceled $20,000 of Ben's credit card debt and issued Form 1099-C. Immediately before the cancellation, Ben's total liabilities were $100,000 and the fair market value of all his assets was $90,000. How much canceled debt must he include in income?
explain: The insolvency exclusion is limited to the amount by which liabilities exceed the fair market value of assets immediately before the cancellation. Ben was insolvent by $10,000, so he excludes $10,000 on Form 982 and includes the other $10,000. Excluding all $20,000 ignores the limit.

q: Ken, a U.S. citizen, met the physical presence test and had 219 qualifying days in 2025. He earned $120,000 of foreign earned income during those days. What is his maximum foreign earned income exclusion for 2025?
explain: The 2025 exclusion limit is $130,000, prorated by qualifying days: $130,000 x 219/365 = $78,000. That is less than his $120,000 of foreign earned income, so $78,000 is the maximum. The $75,900 choice prorates the 2024 limit of $126,500.
source: Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.39; IRC 911(b)(2); IRS Pub 54 (2025); Form 2555 instructions (2025)

q: Ana is a degree candidate at a university. In 2025 she received a $20,000 scholarship. She used $12,000 for tuition and required fees, $1,000 for books required for her courses, and $7,000 for room and board. How much of the scholarship is taxable?
explain: A scholarship is tax-free only to the extent it pays qualified tuition and related expenses, which include fees, books, supplies and equipment required for courses. Room and board is not a qualified expense, so $7,000 is taxable. The $8,000 choice wrongly treats required books as taxable.

q: Joe sells handmade furniture as a hobby, not a business. In 2025 he had $5,000 of hobby income and $6,000 of hobby expenses. How does this affect his 2025 return?
choices: He reports $5,000 of income and cannot deduct the expenses
He reports no income because his expenses exceed his income
He reports $5,000 of income and deducts $5,000 of expenses as an itemized deduction
He reports a $1,000 loss on Schedule C
explain: Hobby income is included in gross income. Hobby expenses would be miscellaneous itemized deductions subject to the 2 percent floor, which are not allowed for 2025, so none are deductible. The idea of deducting expenses up to income was the rule before 2018.

q: For 2024 Sara filed as single and itemized deductions of $15,100, including $6,000 of state income tax. The 2024 standard deduction for a single filer was $14,600. In 2025 she received a $1,200 state income tax refund for 2024. How much of the refund is taxable in 2025?
explain: Under the tax benefit rule, a recovery is taxable only to the extent the earlier deduction reduced tax. Her itemized deductions exceeded the standard deduction by $500 ($15,100 minus $14,600), so only $500 of the refund is taxable. Including the full $1,200 ignores the fact that $700 gave her no tax benefit.
source: IRC 111; Rev. Proc. 2023-34; IRS Pub 525 (2025), Recoveries

q: For calendar year 2025, a third party settlement organization (such as a payment app) must file Form 1099-K for a payee only when the payee's gross payments for goods and services:
choices: Exceed $600, regardless of the number of transactions
Exceed $2,500, regardless of the number of transactions
Exceed $5,000, regardless of the number of transactions
Exceed $20,000 and the number of transactions exceeds 200
explain: P.L. 119-21 retroactively restored the pre-2021 threshold, so a third party settlement organization (TPSO) reports only when payments exceed $20,000 and there are more than 200 transactions. The other amounts are earlier or transition thresholds that do not apply for 2025. Income is taxable whether or not a Form 1099-K is issued.
source: IRC 6050W(e); P.L. 119-21; IRS newsroom, IRS issues FAQs on Form 1099-K threshold under the One, Big, Beautiful Bill (Oct. 23, 2025)

q: In 2025 Nina, age 40, made a $7,000 nondeductible traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA) contribution (her only basis) and converted $7,000 to a Roth IRA later that year. On December 31, 2025, the value of her only other traditional IRA, a rollover IRA, was $63,000. She has no simplified employee pension (SEP) or Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) IRAs. How much of the conversion is taxable?
explain: Under the pro rata rule on Form 8606, the nontaxable share is basis divided by the year-end value of all traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs plus the amount converted: $7,000 / ($63,000 + $7,000) = 10%. So $700 is nontaxable and $6,300 is taxable. Treating the conversion as fully tax-free ignores the other IRA.

q: Leo, age 45, has a Roth individual retirement arrangement (IRA) with $20,000 of regular contributions, a $30,000 conversion made in 2022 (fully taxable when converted), and $10,000 of earnings. He withdraws $35,000 in 2025 and no exception to the early distribution tax applies. What is the result?
choices: $0 included in income; $15,000 subject to the 10% additional tax
$0 included in income; no additional tax
$15,000 included in income and subject to the 10% additional tax
$10,000 included in income and subject to the 10% additional tax
explain: Roth distributions come first from regular contributions ($20,000), then from conversions, first in first out, then earnings. The next $15,000 comes from the 2022 conversion, which was already taxed, so nothing is included in income. Because the 5-year period for that conversion runs from 2022 through 2026, the $15,000 is subject to the 10% additional tax, or $1,500.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.408A-6, Q/A-5 and Q/A-8; IRC 408A(d)(3)(F); IRS Pub 590-B (2025)

q: Maya, age 62, made her first Roth individual retirement arrangement (IRA) contribution on April 10, 2021, and designated it for tax year 2020. On what date does her 5-year period for qualified Roth IRA distributions end, so that distributions after it can be qualified?
choices: December 31, 2024 (qualified starting January 1, 2025)
April 10, 2025
December 31, 2025 (qualified starting January 1, 2026)
April 10, 2026
explain: The 5-year period begins on January 1 of the tax year for which the first contribution was made, not the date it was deposited. A contribution for 2020 starts the clock on January 1, 2020, so the five years are 2020 through 2024. Counting from 2021 because the deposit was made in 2021 is the common mistake.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.408A-6, Q/A-2; IRC 408A(d)(2)(B); IRS Pub 590-B (2025)

q: Omar, age 45, left his job in 2025 and took a $50,000 distribution from his 401(k). The plan withheld 20% ($10,000). Within 60 days he deposited the $40,000 he received into a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA). He did not make up the withheld amount. How much of the distribution is included in his 2025 gross income?
explain: Only the amount actually rolled over within 60 days is tax-free, so the $10,000 that was withheld and not replaced from other funds is taxable, and it is also subject to the 10% additional tax because he is under 59½. The $10,000 withheld is credited as tax paid. Answering $0 assumes the withholding counts as rolled over.
source: IRC 402(c); IRC 3405(c); IRS Pub 575 (2025); IRS Rollovers of Retirement Plan and IRA Distributions page

q: Which of the following transactions is subject to the one-rollover-per-year limit for individual retirement arrangements (IRAs)?
choices: A conversion from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA
A trustee-to-trustee transfer between two traditional IRAs
A 60-day rollover of a distribution from one traditional IRA into another traditional IRA
A rollover from a 401(k) plan to a traditional IRA
explain: The limit applies to 60-day IRA-to-IRA rollovers: only one is allowed in any 1-year period across all of a person's IRAs. Roth conversions, trustee-to-trustee transfers and plan-to-IRA rollovers are not counted.
source: IRC 408(d)(3)(B); IRS Rollovers of Retirement Plan and IRA Distributions page; IRS Pub 590-A (2025)

q: Ruth failed to take a $10,000 required minimum distribution from her traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA) for 2025. She takes the missed amount and files Form 5329 within the correction window, and she does not request a waiver. What is her excise tax on the shortfall?
explain: The excise tax on a required minimum distribution (RMD) shortfall is 25%, reduced to 10% if the shortfall is corrected within the correction window: $10,000 x 10% = $1,000. The $5,000 choice uses the old 50% rate that SECURE 2.0 replaced.
source: IRC 4974(a) and (e); Form 5329 instructions (2025); IRS Pub 590-B (2025)

q: Grace has a vested 401(k) balance of $120,000 and has never had a plan loan. What is the most she can borrow in 2025 without the loan being treated as a taxable distribution?
explain: A plan loan is not a distribution if it does not exceed the lesser of $50,000 or the greater of half the vested balance or $10,000. Half of $120,000 is $60,000, so the $50,000 cap controls. The loan also must generally be repaid within 5 years.

q: An individual retirement arrangement (IRA) owner died in 2025. All of the following beneficiaries are eligible designated beneficiaries EXCEPT:
choices: The owner's 35-year-old son, who is not disabled or chronically ill
The owner's surviving spouse
The owner's 12-year-old child
The owner's brother, who is 8 years younger than the owner
explain: Eligible designated beneficiaries are the surviving spouse, the owner's minor child, a disabled or chronically ill person, and anyone not more than 10 years younger than the owner. An adult child who is not disabled or chronically ill is a designated beneficiary who must empty the account by December 31 of the year containing the 10th anniversary of the death.

q: Helen, age 74, has a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA). In 2025 she had the IRA trustee pay $120,000 directly to a public charity (not a donor advised fund or supporting organization). How much can she exclude from income as a qualified charitable distribution?
explain: The 2025 qualified charitable distribution (QCD) limit is $108,000 per IRA owner, so the other $12,000 is a taxable distribution. The $105,000 figure was the 2024 limit, and $100,000 was the limit before SECURE 2.0 indexing began.

q: Rick sold business equipment in 2025 for $60,000. He bought it for $50,000 and had claimed $30,000 of depreciation. How is his gain treated?
choices: $40,000 section 1231 gain
$30,000 ordinary income and $10,000 section 1231 gain
$10,000 ordinary income and $30,000 section 1231 gain
$40,000 ordinary income
explain: Adjusted basis is $20,000 ($50,000 minus $30,000), so the gain is $40,000. Under section 1245, gain up to the depreciation taken ($30,000) is ordinary income, and the $10,000 above original cost is section 1231 gain.

q: Ivy is single. Her 2025 taxable income is $55,000, which includes $15,000 of long-term capital gains and qualified dividends. How much of the $15,000 is taxed at the 0% rate?
explain: Her ordinary taxable income is $40,000. The 2025 0% bracket for single filers goes up to $48,350 of taxable income, so $8,350 of the gains fit in it and the remaining $6,650 is taxed at 15%. The $7,025 choice uses the 2024 threshold of $47,025.
source: Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.03; IRC 1(h); Form 1040 instructions (2025), Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet
