q: On December 10, 2025, Ted sold 100 shares of XYZ with a basis of $7,000 for $5,000. On December 28, 2025, he bought 100 shares of XYZ for $5,500. What is the result?
choices: $2,000 loss allowed; basis of new shares $5,500
$2,000 loss disallowed; basis of new shares $5,500
$2,000 loss allowed; basis of new shares $7,500
$2,000 loss disallowed; basis of new shares $7,500
explain: Buying substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after a loss sale is a wash sale, so the $2,000 loss is disallowed. The disallowed loss is added to the basis of the new shares: $5,500 + $2,000 = $7,500, and the holding period of the old shares carries over.

q: Amy bought 100 shares for $6,000. Later the company had a 3-for-2 stock split. In 2025 she sold 50 of her shares for $3,000. What is her gain?
explain: After the split she holds 150 shares with the same $6,000 total basis, or $40 a share. The 50 shares sold have a basis of $2,000, so the gain is $3,000 minus $2,000 = $1,000. Using the pre-split $60 a share gives the wrong answer of $0.

q: Which of the following exchanges can qualify as a like-kind exchange under section 1031 for 2025?
choices: A business truck exchanged for another business truck
A rental building in the United States exchanged for a rental building in Mexico
Shares of stock exchanged for shares of another corporation's stock
A rental house in Ohio exchanged for vacant land held for investment in Texas
explain: Since 2018, like-kind treatment is limited to real property held for business or investment. Improved and unimproved U.S. real property are like-kind to each other. Personal property such as trucks no longer qualifies, U.S. and foreign real property are not like-kind, and stock never qualified.

q: Nora was granted incentive stock options on January 2, 2022. On March 1, 2023, she exercised options for 1,000 shares at $10 a share when the fair market value was $25. She sold the shares on June 1, 2025, for $40 a share. How is the 2025 sale reported for regular tax?
choices: $15,000 ordinary income and $15,000 long-term capital gain
$15,000 long-term capital gain only
$30,000 long-term capital gain and no ordinary income
$40,000 long-term capital gain
explain: She held the shares more than 2 years from grant and more than 1 year from exercise, so this is a qualifying disposition. Her regular tax basis is the $10 exercise price, giving a $30,000 long-term capital gain with no ordinary income. Treating the $15 spread at exercise as ordinary income is the rule for a disqualifying disposition or a nonstatutory option.
source: IRC 421(a); IRC 422(a)(1); IRS Pub 525 (2025), Incentive Stock Options

q: All of the following digital asset transactions in 2025 are taxable events EXCEPT:
choices: Exchanging bitcoin for ether
Using bitcoin to buy a car
Moving bitcoin from one wallet the taxpayer owns to another wallet the taxpayer owns
Receiving bitcoin as payment for freelance services
explain: Digital assets are treated as property, so exchanging them for other property or using them to pay for goods is a sale, and receiving them for services is ordinary income at fair market value. Moving digital assets between the taxpayer's own wallets is not a sale or exchange.
source: IRS Notice 2014-21; IRS Frequently Asked Questions on Digital Asset Transactions; Form 1040 instructions (2025)

q: Gina was self-employed all of 2025 with a Schedule C net profit of $40,000. She paid health insurance premiums of $600 a month for a policy in her own name. Beginning September 1, 2025, she was eligible for subsidized coverage through her spouse's employer but declined it. What is her self-employed health insurance deduction?
explain: The deduction is not allowed for any month the taxpayer is eligible to participate in a subsidized plan of an employer of the taxpayer or spouse, even if coverage is declined. Only January through August qualify: 8 x $600 = $4,800, which is well under her net profit limit.

q: Paul is single, age 40, and covered by a retirement plan at work. His 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $83,000 and he contributes $7,000 to a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA). How much can he deduct?
explain: For 2025 the phaseout for a single filer covered by a workplace plan runs from $79,000 to $89,000. He is $4,000 into the $10,000 range, so the deduction is reduced by 40%: $7,000 x 60% = $4,200. The $2,800 choice uses the 2024 range of $77,000 to $87,000.
source: IRS News Release (Nov. 1, 2024), 401(k) limit increases to $23,500 for 2025, IRA limit remains $7,000; IRC 219(g); IRS Pub 590-A (2025)

q: Erin is single with 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $91,000. She paid $2,500 of interest on a qualified student loan. How much student loan interest can she deduct?
explain: For 2025 the deduction phases out for single filers with MAGI between $85,000 and $100,000. She is $6,000 into the $15,000 range, so the $2,500 is reduced by 40% ($1,000), leaving $1,500. The $667 choice uses the 2024 range of $80,000 to $95,000.

q: Kim, single, is a restaurant server, a qualifying tipped occupation, and has a valid Social Security number (SSN). In 2025 she received $30,000 of qualified tips, and her modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $170,000. What is her deduction for qualified tips?
explain: The deduction is capped at $25,000, then reduced by $100 for each $1,000 of MAGI over $150,000. Her MAGI is $20,000 over, so the reduction is $2,000 and the deduction is $25,000 minus $2,000 = $23,000. The $28,000 choice wrongly applies the reduction to the full $30,000 of tips before the cap.
source: IRC 224(b); P.L. 119-21 sec. 70201; IRS newsroom, One, Big, Beautiful Bill: How to take advantage of no tax on tips and overtime

q: Dan and Lia file jointly for 2025 with modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $210,000. Dan, a nonexempt employee with a valid Social Security number (SSN), received $42,000 of overtime pay at time-and-a-half that is required under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Of that amount, $14,000 is the half-time premium above his regular rate. What is their deduction for qualified overtime compensation?
explain: Only the overtime pay in excess of the regular rate (the half-time premium) is qualified overtime compensation, so the deduction is $14,000. That is under the $25,000 joint cap and their MAGI is below the $300,000 phaseout threshold. The $12,500 figure is the cap for a non-joint return.
source: IRC 225(b), (c) and (e); P.L. 119-21; IRS newsroom, What to know about the No Tax on Overtime deduction

q: Sam is single and in his second year of graduate school. In 2025 he paid $12,000 of qualified tuition, and his modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $85,000. What is the largest education credit he can claim?
choices: $1,000 lifetime learning credit
$2,000 lifetime learning credit
$2,400 lifetime learning credit
$2,500 American opportunity credit
explain: The American opportunity credit is limited to the first four years of postsecondary education, so a graduate student uses the lifetime learning credit: 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses, or $2,000. That amount phases out between $80,000 and $90,000 of MAGI for single filers, so it is cut in half to $1,000.
source: IRC 25A(c) and (d); IRS Pub 970 (2025), ch. 2 and 3

q: In 2025 Jen paid her son's $10,000 first-year college tuition with a $10,000 distribution from his 529 plan. She also wants to claim the American opportunity credit using $4,000 of that tuition. What is the tax result of that choice?
choices: She cannot claim the credit for any expense paid with 529 funds
The earnings allocable to the $4,000 become taxable and are also subject to the 10% additional tax
There is no tax effect because the 529 distribution equaled total tuition
The earnings allocable to the $4,000 become taxable, but the 10% additional tax does not apply to them
explain: The same expenses cannot be used for both the credit and a tax-free 529 distribution, so qualified expenses for the 529 drop to $6,000 and part of the earnings becomes taxable. The 10% additional tax does not apply to amounts taxable only because expenses were used for an education credit, which often makes claiming the credit worthwhile.

q: Which of the following is a requirement for a tax-free rollover from a 529 plan to a Roth individual retirement arrangement (IRA) in 2025?
choices: The 529 account must have been maintained for the 15-year period ending on the date of the distribution
Lifetime rollovers for the beneficiary may not exceed $50,000
The Roth IRA must belong to the 529 account owner rather than the beneficiary
Contributions made within the 3 years before the distribution may be rolled over
explain: The 529 account must have been open for at least 15 years, the Roth IRA must be the beneficiary's, the lifetime limit is $35,000, and contributions made in the 5-year period ending on the distribution date cannot be rolled over. Each year's rollover is also limited by the beneficiary's annual Roth IRA contribution limit.

q: In February 2025 Victor gave stock with a basis of $10,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to his father. His father died in November 2025 and left the same stock to Victor in his will. The stock was worth $110,000 at the date of death. What is Victor's basis in the stock?
choices: $110,000, but only if Form 706 is filed for the father's estate
explain: When appreciated property is given to a decedent within 1 year before death and passes back to the donor or the donor's spouse, there is no step-up. The basis is the decedent's adjusted basis just before death, which is Victor's original $10,000 carryover basis. The $110,000 choice applies the normal date-of-death rule.

q: Martha set up a revocable living trust and transferred her brokerage account to it. She is the trustee and can revoke the trust at any time. How is the trust's 2025 investment income taxed?
choices: The trust pays tax on all of it at trust tax rates on Form 1041
It is tax-exempt until the trust becomes irrevocable
Martha reports it on her own Form 1040 because it is a grantor trust
The trust beneficiaries report it on Schedule K-1 as it accrues
explain: A trust that the grantor can revoke is a grantor trust, and its income, deductions and credits are treated as the grantor's. Martha reports the income on her own return. A revocable trust also does not remove the assets from her estate.
source: IRC 671; IRC 676(a); Form 1041 instructions (2025), Grantor Type Trust

q: All of the following are true of a 2025 qualified charitable distribution (QCD) EXCEPT:
choices: The individual retirement arrangement (IRA) owner must be at least age 70½ on the date of the distribution
The amount counts toward the owner's required minimum distribution for the year
The amount is excluded from income, so it is not also deducted as a charitable contribution
The distribution can be paid to a donor advised fund
explain: A QCD must go directly from the IRA trustee to a charity described in section 170(b)(1)(A), but supporting organizations and donor advised funds are excluded. QCDs are a strong planning tool for people who take the standard deduction, because they keep the gift out of adjusted gross income (AGI) and still satisfy the required minimum distribution (RMD).

q: Frank was born in March 1952 and turns 73 in 2025. He has a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA) and decides to take his first required minimum distribution on March 15, 2026. What is the main tax consequence of waiting?
choices: He must take both his 2025 and 2026 required minimum distributions (RMDs) in 2026, and both are taxable in 2026
He owes the 25% excise tax because the 2025 required minimum distribution (RMD) was due by December 31, 2025
His 2025 required minimum distribution (RMD) is taxable on his 2025 return even though he receives it in 2026
He can skip the 2025 required minimum distribution (RMD) entirely
explain: The first RMD can be delayed until April 1 of the year after the owner turns 73, but the second RMD is still due by December 31 of that same year. Waiting puts two distributions in 2026, which may push Frank into a higher bracket. Distributions are taxed in the year received.

q: Rita retired and began receiving a single-life annuity from her employer's qualified plan on January 1, 2025, when she was 63. Her cost in the plan (after-tax contributions) is $52,000. She received 12 monthly payments of $1,500 in 2025. Using the Simplified Method, how much of the 2025 payments is taxable?
explain: For a single-life annuity starting at age 63, the Simplified Method uses 260 anticipated payments. The tax-free part is $52,000 / 260 = $200 a month, or $2,400 for the year, so $18,000 minus $2,400 = $15,600 is taxable. Treating all $18,000 as taxable ignores her cost recovery.

q: Under their 2025 divorce decree, Laura transferred a rental property to her former husband, Mark. Laura's adjusted basis was $200,000 and the fair market value was $500,000. What are the tax results?
choices: Laura recognizes $300,000 of gain and Mark's basis is $500,000
Laura recognizes no gain and Mark's basis is $500,000
Laura recognizes no gain and Mark's basis is $200,000
Mark reports $500,000 of income as a property settlement
explain: A transfer of property to a spouse, or to a former spouse incident to divorce, is treated like a gift: no gain or loss is recognized and the recipient takes the transferor's adjusted basis. Mark's basis is $200,000, so he will bear the built-in gain if he later sells, which matters when negotiating a settlement.

q: Kevin pays his former spouse $2,000 a month in cash under a divorce decree executed in November 2018 that has never been modified. The payments otherwise meet the definition of alimony. How are his 2025 payments treated?
choices: Not deductible by Kevin and not taxable to his former spouse
Deductible by Kevin but not taxable to his former spouse
Not deductible by Kevin but taxable to his former spouse
Deductible by Kevin and taxable to his former spouse
explain: The repeal of the alimony deduction applies only to divorce or separation instruments executed after December 31, 2018, or older instruments modified to adopt the new rule. Kevin's 2018 decree keeps the old treatment: he deducts the payments and his former spouse includes them in income.

q: Raul and Elena live together all year in Texas, a community property state, and have no agreement changing the character of their income. In 2025 Raul earned wages of $80,000 and Elena earned wages of $20,000. If they file separate returns, how much wage income does each report?
choices: Raul $100,000; Elena $0
explain: In a community property state, wages earned by either spouse during the marriage are community income, owned half by each. On separate returns each spouse generally reports half of the total community wages, $50,000 each. Reporting only one's own wages ignores state community property law.

q: Tina has a $50,000 net operating loss (NOL) carryover from 2022. For 2025, her taxable income computed without any NOL deduction and without the qualified business income deduction is $40,000. How much of the NOL can she deduct in 2025, and how much carries forward?
choices: $40,000 deducted; $10,000 carried forward
$32,000 deducted; $18,000 carried forward
$50,000 deducted; nothing carried forward
$32,000 deducted; the rest expires
explain: For NOLs arising after 2017, the deduction is limited to 80% of taxable income figured without the NOL and qualified business income (QBI) deductions: $40,000 x 80% = $32,000. The remaining $18,000 carries forward indefinitely. Deducting the full $40,000 is the pre-2018 rule.

q: Harold died in March 2025. He had a $30,000 long-term capital loss carryover that came entirely from his own separately owned investments. His widow files a 2025 joint return with no other capital transactions. What happens to the carryover?
choices: The full $30,000 is deductible on the final joint return
$3,000 is deductible on the 2025 joint return and the rest can be used by the widow in later years
$3,000 is deductible on the 2025 joint return and the rest cannot be carried to any later year
The carryover transfers to Harold's estate for use on Form 1041
explain: A decedent's capital loss carryover can be used only on the final return, where the usual $3,000 limit applies. Any remaining carryover attributable to the decedent cannot be passed to the surviving spouse or the estate. This is a reason to consider harvesting gains before a spouse with large carryovers dies.

q: Which item that caused alternative minimum tax in 2024 can generate a credit for prior year minimum tax on Form 8801 in 2025?
choices: The adjustment for state and local taxes deducted for regular tax
Tax-exempt interest from specified private activity bonds
The standard deduction, which is not allowed for alternative minimum tax (AMT)
The adjustment for the bargain element of incentive stock options exercised and held at year end
explain: The minimum tax credit is based on AMT caused by deferral items, which only change the timing of income, such as the incentive stock option (ISO) adjustment. Exclusion items such as taxes, the standard deduction and private activity bond interest permanently differ between the two systems and do not create a credit.

q: Gabe, single, has one sole proprietorship that had a qualified business loss of $10,000 in 2024 and $50,000 of qualified business income (QBI) in 2025. His 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction is $100,000, and he has no real estate investment trust (REIT) dividends or publicly traded partnership (PTP) income. What is his 2025 QBI deduction?
explain: A negative QBI amount carries forward and reduces QBI in the next year, so 2025 QBI is $50,000 minus $10,000 = $40,000. His taxable income is under the 2025 threshold of $197,300, so the deduction is 20% of $40,000 = $8,000, which is less than 20% of taxable income ($20,000). The $10,000 choice ignores the carryover.
source: IRC 199A(c)(2); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.27; Form 8995 instructions (2025)

q: Rachel and her former husband filed a joint return showing a correct tax that was never paid. He kept the money. Which type of relief can Rachel request for this underpayment?
choices: Equitable relief
Innocent spouse relief
Separation of liability relief
Injured spouse allocation
explain: Innocent spouse relief and separation of liability relief apply only to understated tax. Equitable relief is the only type that can cover an underpayment of tax properly shown on a joint return. All three are requested on Form 8857, while injured spouse claims on Form 8379 deal with refund offsets.
source: IRC 6015(b), (c) and (f); IRS Innocent Spouse Relief page; IRS Pub 971

q: Diego had almost no income in the first half of 2025 and then sold a business asset in November at a large gain. He made no estimated payments until January 2026. What planning tool can reduce or eliminate an underpayment penalty for the earlier quarters?
choices: Filing Form 1040-X to spread the gain over four quarters
Requesting a penalty waiver on Form 843 for first-time abatement before filing
Electing to treat the January payment as made on April 15, 2025
Using the annualized income installment method on Form 2210, Schedule AI
explain: The annualized income installment method figures each required payment based on income actually earned through the end of each period. Because the gain came in November, the required payments for earlier periods are small. This is figured on Form 2210 Schedule AI and attached to the return.

q: Lou, a cash-method taxpayer, received a $5,000 check for consulting services on December 30, 2025. The check was good, but he did not deposit it until January 5, 2026. In which year must he report the income?
choices: 2026, because cash-method taxpayers report income when deposited
Either year, at his choice
2025, because he had the check and could have cashed it
2026, because the bank did not credit the funds until 2026
explain: Under the constructive receipt doctrine, income is reported when it is credited or made available without substantial restriction. Receiving a good check in 2025 is receipt in 2025 even if it is deposited later. For timing planning, a taxpayer wanting income in 2026 must arrange to be paid in 2026, not just delay the deposit.

q: A married couple is deciding whether to file separately for 2025. All of the following benefits are unavailable to a married taxpayer filing separately EXCEPT:
choices: The child tax credit
The lifetime learning credit
The student loan interest deduction
The deduction for qualified tips
explain: The child tax credit can be claimed on a separate return, subject to its own rules. Education credits, the student loan interest deduction and the new deduction for qualified tips all require a joint return if the taxpayer is married.

q: Lena suspects her husband underreports his business income. They live together and could save some tax by filing jointly for 2025. What is the main reason she might choose married filing separately?
choices: She would qualify for head of household status
She could later switch to a joint return without any time limit
Married filing separately always produces the lowest total tax
On a separate return she is responsible only for the tax on her own return, not joint and several liability
explain: Spouses who file jointly are jointly and severally liable for the entire tax, including tax on the other spouse's unreported income. Filing separately limits her liability to her own return, which can be worth a higher tax bill. Head of household requires living apart from the spouse for the last 6 months of the year.

q: Jay and Kate filed a 2025 joint return on April 10, 2026. In June 2026 they want to amend and file separate returns instead. Which statement is correct?
choices: They can file Forms 1040-X within 3 years to change to separate returns
They can change to separate returns only if both spouses sign a written agreement
They cannot change from a joint return to separate returns after the due date of the return
They can change only if the IRS approves a private letter ruling request
explain: Once the due date has passed, spouses who filed jointly cannot elect to file separately for that year, except that a decedent's executor may in some cases. The reverse is allowed: separate filers can generally switch to a joint return within 3 years by filing Form 1040-X.

q: When a paid preparer signs a taxpayer's 2025 Form 1040, the preparer's declaration under penalties of perjury is based on:
choices: Only the documents the taxpayer provided in writing
An audit of the taxpayer's books and records
The taxpayer's oral statement that the return is correct
All information of which the preparer has any knowledge
explain: The taxpayer declares under penalties of perjury that the return is true, correct and complete to the best of his or her knowledge and belief. The preparer's declaration states it is based on all information of which the preparer has any knowledge, so a preparer cannot ignore information that suggests the return is wrong.
source: Form 1040 (2025), Sign Here jurat; IRC 6065; Treasury Circular 230 sec. 10.22

q: All of the following are deductible medical expenses for a taxpayer who itemizes EXCEPT:
choices: Batteries and repairs for a hearing aid
Fees for a weight-loss program to treat obesity diagnosed by a physician
Nicotine patches bought without a prescription
Fees for a stop-smoking program
explain: Amounts paid for drugs that do not require a prescription, such as nicotine gum or patches, are not medical expenses; insulin is the only nonprescription exception. Fees for a stop-smoking program are deductible, as are hearing aid batteries and a weight-loss program that treats a diagnosed disease.

q: Helen is 62 years old at the end of 2025. She paid $6,000 in 2025 for a qualified long-term care insurance contract. How much of the premium can she include in her medical expenses on Schedule A, before the 7.5% of adjusted gross income (AGI) floor?
explain: For 2025, the eligible long-term care premium limit for a person older than 60 but not older than 70 at year end is $4,810, so only $4,810 of the $6,000 counts. $6,020 is the limit for someone older than 70, and $1,800 is the limit for ages 51 to 60.

q: In 2025 Rosa drove her own car 600 miles round trip for outpatient treatment at a licensed hospital, paid $24 for parking, and stayed 3 nights near the hospital in a room she shared with her husband, who went along to help her. The room cost $140 per night, and they spent $180 on meals. Using the standard rate, what is her total deductible medical travel and lodging before the 7.5% floor?
explain: Mileage is 600 x $0.21 = $126, plus $24 parking = $150. Lodging is limited to $50 per person per night, so the cap is $100 per night for two people, giving 3 x $100 = $300; meals are not deductible. Total is $150 + $300 = $450. Using the full $140 room rate would give $570.
source: IRS Pub 502 (2025); IRS 2025 standard mileage rates (IR-2024-312)

q: A taxpayer who itemizes for 2025 paid all of the following taxes. All are deductible on Schedule A, subject to the state and local tax (SALT) limit, EXCEPT:
choices: State income tax withheld from wages
Real estate tax on a main home in New Jersey
A yearly state tax on a personal car based only on its value
Real property tax on a vacation home in Spain
explain: Foreign real property taxes are not deductible on Schedule A. State income taxes, U.S. real estate taxes, and personal property taxes that are based on value alone and imposed yearly are deductible, subject to the 2025 SALT limit.

q: On June 30, 2025, Paul refinanced the mortgage on his main home with a 30-year loan and paid $3,000 in points. None of the proceeds was used to improve the home. He made 6 monthly payments in 2025. How much of the points can he deduct for 2025?
explain: Points paid to refinance a mortgage generally are not deductible in full in the year paid; they are deducted over the life of the loan. $3,000 / 360 payments = $8.33 per payment, x 6 payments = $50. Deducting all $3,000 is allowed only for points on a loan to buy or build the main home that meets all the tests.

q: In 2025 Karen took a $40,000 home equity line of credit secured by her main home. She used $25,000 to remodel her kitchen and $15,000 to pay off credit cards. Her total mortgage debt is well under the $750,000 limit. She paid $3,200 of interest on the line in 2025. How much is deductible as home mortgage interest?
explain: Interest on a home equity loan is deductible only to the extent the proceeds were used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing the loan. $25,000 / $40,000 x $3,200 = $2,000. The $15,000 used for credit cards is personal interest and is not deductible.
source: IRS Pub 936 (2025); Instructions for Schedule A (Form 1040) (2025); IRC 163(h)(3)

q: How are private mortgage insurance premiums paid in 2025 on a loan to buy a main home treated on the 2025 return?
choices: Deductible as home mortgage interest with no income limit
Deductible as home mortgage interest, reduced once adjusted gross income (AGI) exceeds $100,000
Not deductible, because the itemized deduction for mortgage insurance premiums has expired
Deductible as a medical expense subject to the 7.5% floor
explain: The itemized deduction for mortgage insurance premiums expired and is not available on 2025 returns. The phaseout above $100,000 of AGI applied when the deduction existed, which is why that choice is tempting.

q: For 2025, Sam paid $8,000 of investment interest. His investment income was $3,000 of taxable interest, $2,000 of nonqualified dividends, and $4,000 of qualified dividends. He has no other investment expenses and makes no election. How much investment interest can he deduct, and what happens to the rest?
choices: $5,000 deducted; $3,000 carried forward to 2026
$5,000 deducted; $3,000 is lost
$8,000 deducted
$9,000 limit, so all $8,000 deducted
explain: Investment interest is deductible only up to net investment income. Without the election, qualified dividends are excluded, so investment income is $3,000 + $2,000 = $5,000. The disallowed $3,000 carries forward to the next year. Counting the qualified dividends ($9,000) requires the election.
source: Form 4952 and instructions; Instructions for Schedule A (Form 1040) (2025); IRC 163(d)

q: A taxpayer elects on Form 4952 to treat $4,000 of qualified dividends as investment income so that more investment interest is deductible. What is the effect of the election?
choices: The $4,000 is no longer eligible for the qualified dividend or capital gain tax rates
The $4,000 is still taxed at the qualified dividend rates
The $4,000 becomes exempt from the net investment income tax
The election can be made only for net capital gain, not qualified dividends
explain: A taxpayer may elect to include qualified dividends and net capital gain in investment income, but amounts elected are not eligible to be taxed at the qualified dividend or capital gain rates. The election lets more interest be deducted at the cost of losing the preferential rate on that amount.

q: Gina has 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $100,000. She gave a public charity publicly traded stock she held for 3 years, with a fair market value of $40,000 and a basis of $10,000. She made no other contributions and makes no special election. What is her 2025 charitable deduction?
choices: $10,000, with no carryover
$30,000, with $10,000 carried over for up to 5 years
explain: Long-term capital gain property given to a 50% limit organization is deductible at fair market value but limited to 30% of AGI: 30% x $100,000 = $30,000. The $10,000 excess carries over for up to 5 years. The 60% limit applies to cash gifts, not appreciated property.

q: Leo wrote a single $300 check to his church in 2025 and received nothing in return. Which record must he have to deduct it?
choices: A canceled check or bank statement alone is enough
Form 8283 attached to his return
A qualified appraisal
A contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the church
explain: No deduction is allowed for a single contribution of $250 or more unless the donor has a contemporaneous written acknowledgment from the organization, obtained by the earlier of the filing date or the due date including extensions. A bank record alone is enough only for gifts under $250. Form 8283 and appraisals apply to noncash gifts.

q: Which of the following 2025 contributions to a public charity requires the donor to obtain a qualified appraisal?
choices: A painting with a claimed deduction of $8,000
Publicly traded stock with a claimed deduction of $50,000
A $10,000 cash gift
Used clothing in good condition with a claimed deduction of $400
explain: Noncash property with a deduction over $5,000 per item or group of similar items is reported in Section B of Form 8283 and requires a qualified appraisal. Publicly traded securities are reported in Section A in any amount and need no appraisal, even above $5,000.

q: In August 2025 a storm in a federally declared disaster area damaged Tom's home. The decrease in fair market value was $30,000, his basis was $200,000, and insurance paid $10,000. The loss is not a qualified disaster loss. His 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) is $60,000. What is his deductible casualty loss?
explain: The loss is the $30,000 decrease in value less $10,000 insurance = $20,000. Subtract $100 for the event = $19,900, then subtract 10% of AGI ($6,000) = $13,900. Stopping before the 10% of AGI reduction gives $19,900.

q: Nora, who itemizes, reported $12,000 of gambling winnings for 2025 and has records of $10,000 of gambling losses. She is not a professional gambler. How much can she deduct as gambling losses?
explain: For 2025, gambling losses are an other itemized deduction allowed up to the amount of gambling winnings, so all $10,000 is deductible. The rule limiting the deduction to 90% of losses ($9,000) was added by P.L. 119-21 but applies only to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
source: Instructions for Schedule A (Form 1040) (2025); IRC 165(d) as amended by P.L. 119-21, sec. 70114

q: A nonresident alien files Form 1040-NR for 2025 with effectively connected wage income. All of the following may be claimed as itemized deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040-NR) EXCEPT:
choices: State and local income taxes
Gifts to U.S. charities
Casualty losses from a federally declared disaster
Home mortgage interest on a U.S. residence
explain: Schedule A (Form 1040-NR) has lines only for state and local income taxes, gifts to U.S. charities, casualty and theft losses from a federally declared disaster, and certain other itemized deductions. Home mortgage interest, real estate taxes, and medical expenses are not on the schedule.

q: For 2025, a single taxpayer can claim the qualified business income (QBI) deduction using the simplified Form 8995 if taxable income before the QBI deduction is not more than:
explain: The 2025 threshold is $197,300 for single and most other filers and $394,600 for married filing jointly. $191,950 was the 2024 figure and $182,100 was the 2023 figure.
source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.27

q: Dr. Lee, single, runs a consulting practice that is a specified service trade or business. Her 2025 taxable income before the qualified business income (QBI) deduction is $260,000, and the business produced $150,000 of QBI. What is her QBI deduction from this business?
explain: For 2025 the specified service trade or business (SSTB) phase-in range for a single filer runs from $197,300 to $247,300. Above $247,300 an SSTB is not a qualified trade or business, so the deduction is $0. 20% of QBI ($30,000) would apply only at or below the $197,300 threshold.
source: Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.27; IRC 199A(d)(3)

q: Mike, single, has $80,000 of qualified business income (QBI) from a sole proprietorship that is not a specified service trade or business (SSTB). His 2025 taxable income before the QBI deduction is $70,000, and he has no net capital gain or qualified dividends. What is his QBI deduction?
explain: The deduction is the lesser of 20% of QBI ($16,000) or 20% of taxable income before the QBI deduction minus net capital gain (20% x $70,000 = $14,000). The taxable income limit controls, so the deduction is $14,000.

q: Ann and Ben file jointly with 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $50,000. They paid $8,000 of qualifying day care for their two children, ages 4 and 7, so both could work. Neither receives dependent care benefits. What is their child and dependent care credit?
explain: For 2025, expenses are limited to $6,000 for two or more qualifying persons, and the credit rate is 20% for AGI over $43,000. $6,000 x 20% = $1,200. Applying 20% to the full $8,000 gives $1,600, which ignores the dollar limit.

q: Carla, head of household with 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $90,000, paid $9,000 for day care for her two children under 13. She excluded $5,000 of employer dependent care benefits from income. What is her child and dependent care credit?
explain: The $6,000 dollar limit for two children is reduced by the $5,000 of excluded benefits, leaving $1,000. At AGI over $43,000 the rate is 20%, so the credit is $1,000 x 20% = $200. Forgetting the reduction gives $1,200.

q: Raj and Priya file jointly with 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $100,000. Their dependents are their 17-year-old son and Raj's mother, who lives with them and qualifies as their dependent. Both dependents are U.S. citizens with Social Security numbers (SSNs). How much credit for other dependents can they claim?
explain: A child who is 17 at year end cannot be used for the child tax credit (CTC), but he and the dependent mother each qualify for the $500 nonrefundable credit for other dependents, for $1,000. $4,400 wrongly treats both as CTC qualifying children.

q: Linda's dependent son, age 19, is in his first year of college and enrolled full time. She paid $3,000 of qualified tuition in 2025, and her modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $60,000. How much of her American opportunity tax credit is refundable?
explain: The American opportunity tax credit (AOTC) is 100% of the first $2,000 plus 25% of the next $2,000: $2,000 + $250 = $2,250. Up to 40% is refundable: $2,250 x 40% = $900. $1,000 is 40% of the $2,500 maximum, which applies only with $4,000 of expenses.

q: Jake, single, paid $10,000 of qualified graduate school tuition for himself in 2025. His modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $85,000. What is his lifetime learning credit?
explain: The lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses, or $2,000. For 2025 it phases out between $80,000 and $90,000 of MAGI for single filers: ($90,000 - $85,000) / $10,000 = 50%, so the credit is $1,000. $2,500 is the American opportunity tax credit (AOTC) maximum.

q: Joe and Mia file jointly for 2025. Their only foreign income is dividends from a U.S. mutual fund, reported on Form 1099-DIV, with $450 of foreign tax paid. Which statement is correct?
choices: They must file Form 1116 because the foreign tax exceeds $300
The election to skip Form 1116 applies only to foreign wages
They may only deduct the foreign tax on Schedule A
They may claim the $450 credit without Form 1116, but they cannot carry foreign taxes to or from any other year
explain: A taxpayer can claim the foreign tax credit without Form 1116 if all foreign income is passive, it is reported on a payee statement such as Form 1099-DIV, and creditable foreign taxes are not over $300 ($600 on a joint return). With the election, no carryover to or from that year is allowed. The $300 limit applies only to non-joint returns.

q: Dana, single with one qualifying child, had $30,000 of wages in 2025. She also had $8,000 of taxable interest and $4,500 of dividends. Which statement is correct about her earned income credit?
choices: She qualifies because the investment income limit for 2025 is $13,500
Investment income does not affect the earned income credit (EIC) if she has a qualifying child
She does not qualify because her investment income of $12,500 exceeds the 2025 limit of $11,950
She qualifies for a reduced credit equal to the excess over $11,950
explain: For 2025 the EIC is not allowed if investment income exceeds $11,950. Her $8,000 + $4,500 = $12,500 is over the limit, so she gets no credit. The limit applies whether or not there is a qualifying child, and there is no partial credit.

q: Each of the following single taxpayers has no qualifying child and meets every earned income credit (EIC) requirement except as stated. Who can claim the earned income credit for 2025?
choices: Ed, age 24 at the end of 2025, not a dependent
Fay, age 64 at the end of 2025, not a dependent
Gus, age 66 at the end of 2025, not a dependent
Hal, age 30, claimed as a dependent by his parent
explain: Without a qualifying child, the taxpayer must be at least 25 but under 65 at the end of the year and cannot be anyone's dependent. Fay at 64 qualifies. Ed is too young, Gus is too old, and Hal is a dependent. The temporary age rules for 2021 do not apply to 2025.

q: In 2025 the IRS made a final determination that Kim's earned income credit (EIC) claim for 2024 was due to reckless or intentional disregard of the rules, but not fraud. For how long is she barred from claiming the EIC?
choices: The next 2 tax years
She is not barred but must file Form 8862 next year
The next 5 tax years
The next 10 tax years
explain: A final determination of reckless or intentional disregard of the rules bars the EIC for 2 tax years. The 10-year ban applies only to fraud. After the ban ends, she must generally file Form 8862 to claim the credit again.

q: A paid preparer must complete Form 8867, Paid Preparer's Due Diligence Checklist, for a 2025 client claiming any of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Earned income credit
Credit for other dependents
Lifetime learning credit
Head of household filing status
explain: Form 8867 covers the earned income credit (EIC), the child tax credit (CTC), additional child tax credit (ACTC) and credit for other dependents (ODC), the American opportunity tax credit (AOTC), and head of household filing status. The lifetime learning credit is not covered. The AOTC is covered, which is why the education credit choice is tempting.

q: In 2025 Ray and Sue, filing jointly with modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $150,000, finalized the adoption of a U.S. child with special needs. They paid $3,000 of qualified adoption expenses. No credit was claimed for this child before. Which statement is correct?
choices: Their credit is limited to the $3,000 they paid
Their credit is $16,810, and none of it is refundable
Their credit is $17,280, and up to $5,000 of it is refundable
Their credit is $17,280, and all of it is refundable
explain: For a U.S. special needs adoption that becomes final in 2025, the full $17,280 is allowed regardless of actual expenses. Under P.L. 119-21, up to $5,000 per child is refundable starting in 2025; the rest is nonrefundable and can carry forward 5 years. $16,810 is the 2024 figure.
source: Instructions for Form 8839 (2025); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.04; IRC 23(a)(3) and 23(h) as amended by P.L. 119-21

q: Olga, single, had household income of 250% of the federal poverty line for 2025. Her advance premium tax credit exceeded her allowed premium tax credit by $2,500. How much must she repay?
explain: For 2025, the repayment limit for a single filer with household income from 200% to under 300% of the poverty line is $975. $1,950 is the limit for other filing statuses in that band, and full repayment applies only at 400% or more.

q: Lena paid $24,000 for rooftop solar panels on a second home she uses as a residence and does not rent out. Installation was completed in October 2025, and she has enough tax liability to use any credit. What residential clean energy credit can she claim for 2025?
choices: $0, because the home is not her main home
explain: The residential clean energy credit is 30% of the cost for property placed in service in 2025: $24,000 x 30% = $7,200. For solar electric property the home does not have to be the main home. P.L. 119-21 ends the credit for expenditures made after December 31, 2025, and an expenditure is made when installation is completed, so this one qualifies.
source: Instructions for Form 5695 (2025); IRS FAQs on P.L. 119-21 energy credit changes; IRC 25D

q: In 2025 Victor installed a qualifying heat pump costing $8,000 and qualifying exterior windows costing $3,000 in his main home. He has enough tax liability to use any credit. What is his energy efficient home improvement credit?
explain: The credit is 30% of costs. The heat pump gives $2,400, capped at $2,000. The windows give $900, capped at $600 for windows within the $1,200 general limit. $2,000 + $600 = $2,600. $3,300 is 30% of the total cost without any caps.

q: Ivan and Joy file jointly with 2025 adjusted gross income (AGI) of $48,000. Each contributed $2,000 to a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA). Both are over age 18, neither is a student or a dependent, and they took no distributions. What is their saver's credit?
explain: For 2025, joint filers with AGI over $47,500 but not over $51,000 get a 20% rate. Eligible contributions are $2,000 each, or $4,000, so the credit is $4,000 x 20% = $800. $2,000 would be the 50% rate, which applies only at AGI of $47,500 or less.

q: What is the 2025 alternative minimum tax (AMT) exemption amount for married taxpayers filing jointly, before any phaseout?
explain: The 2025 AMT exemption is $137,000 for joint filers and qualifying surviving spouses. $133,300 was the 2024 amount and $126,500 the 2023 amount; $88,100 is the 2025 amount for single and head of household filers.
source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.11

q: Rita, single, has 2025 alternative minimum taxable income of $700,000. What is her alternative minimum tax (AMT) exemption?
explain: The $88,100 exemption is reduced by 25% of alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) over $626,350. ($700,000 - $626,350) x 25% = $18,412.50, so the exemption is $88,100 - $18,412.50 = $69,687.50. Using 50% instead of 25% gives $51,275.
source: Instructions for Form 6251 (2025); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.11; IRC 55(d)

q: In figuring 2025 alternative minimum taxable income, all of the following are added back or included EXCEPT:
choices: State and local taxes deducted on Schedule A
The standard deduction
The bargain element of incentive stock options exercised and held at year end
Charitable contributions deducted on Schedule A
explain: Charitable contributions are allowed for both regular tax and alternative minimum tax (AMT), so they are not an adjustment. Taxes deducted on Schedule A are added back, the standard deduction is not allowed for AMT, and the spread on incentive stock options (ISOs) exercised and kept at year end is an adjustment.

q: Which alternative minimum tax (AMT) item can create a minimum tax credit that may be used in a later year?
choices: The standard deduction
State income taxes deducted on Schedule A
Tax-exempt interest on specified private activity bonds
The bargain element of an incentive stock option exercised and held
explain: The minimum tax credit is allowed only for AMT caused by deferral items, such as the incentive stock option (ISO) adjustment, which reverses when the stock is sold. The standard deduction, itemized taxes, and private activity bond interest are exclusion items that create a permanent difference and do not generate the credit.

q: For 2025, a household employer must withhold and pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on a household employee's cash wages once the employer pays that employee at least:
explain: The 2025 threshold is $2,800 of cash wages to any one household employee. $2,700 was the 2024 figure, $3,000 is the 2026 figure, and $1,000 in a quarter is the separate Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) test.
source: Instructions for Schedule H (Form 1040) (2025); IRC 3121(a)(7)(B) and 3121(x)

q: In 2025 the Parks paid a 30-year-old nanny $2,400 in cash wages: $1,200 in the third quarter and $1,200 in the fourth quarter. They did not withhold income tax. Which statement is correct?
choices: They owe no household employment taxes
They owe Social Security and Medicare taxes but not Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax
They owe Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax but not Social Security and Medicare taxes, and must file Schedule H
They owe both Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) and Social Security and Medicare taxes
explain: Social Security and Medicare apply only if cash wages to one employee reach $2,800 in 2025, and $2,400 is below that. FUTA applies if total cash wages to household employees are $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter, which happened, so Schedule H is required for the FUTA tax.

q: Hana, a U.S. citizen, had 2025 total tax of $5,000 and federal withholding of $4,100. She made no estimated payments. Her 2024 tax was $6,000. Is she subject to the underpayment penalty for 2025?
choices: Yes, because withholding was less than 90% of her 2025 tax
Yes, because withholding was less than 100% of her 2024 tax
No, because her 2025 tax minus withholding is less than $1,000
No, because she can pay the $900 balance by April 15, 2026
explain: No penalty applies if the tax shown on the return minus withholding is less than $1,000: $5,000 - $4,100 = $900. She fails the 90% and 100% tests, but the $1,000 exception still protects her. Simply paying the balance by the due date does not by itself avoid the penalty.

q: Each of the following can reduce or eliminate an individual's 2025 underpayment of estimated tax penalty EXCEPT:
choices: Having had no tax liability for a full 12-month 2024 tax year as a U.S. citizen
Using the annualized income installment method when most income was received late in the year
A waiver for a taxpayer who retired after reaching age 62 in 2025 and had reasonable cause
Paying the full balance due with a return filed by April 15, 2026
explain: The penalty is figured on each installment that was paid late, so paying the full balance with a timely return does not remove it. The no-tax-liability exception, the annualized income method (Schedule AI), and the waiver for retirement after age 62 with reasonable cause are all recognized relief.

q: Mark had large investment income early in 2025 and made no estimated payments. In December he raised his wage withholding so total 2025 withholding equaled 100% of his 2024 tax. His 2024 adjusted gross income (AGI) was $90,000. How is the December withholding treated for the underpayment penalty?
choices: As paid on the dates actually withheld, so the first three installments are underpaid
It counts only toward the January 15, 2026 installment
It cannot be counted because withholding after September 15 is ignored
As paid in equal amounts on each installment due date unless he elects otherwise, so no penalty applies
explain: Withholding is treated as paid in equal amounts on each due date unless the taxpayer shows otherwise. Spread evenly, his withholding covers 25% of 100% of his 2024 tax for each installment, so no penalty applies. That is why late-year withholding can fix an underpayment and late estimates cannot.

q: An employee of a church that elected to be exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes must pay self-employment tax on church employee income of at least what amount for 2025?
explain: Church employee income of $108.28 or more is subject to self-employment (SE) tax. The $400 net earnings test applies to other self-employment income, not to church employee income.

q: In 2025 Pat earned $150,000 of wages subject to Social Security tax and had $60,000 of net profit from a side business on Schedule C. What is Pat's self-employment tax, rounded to the cent?
explain: Net earnings are $60,000 x 92.35% = $55,410. Only $176,100 - $150,000 = $26,100 is left for Social Security: $26,100 x 12.4% = $3,236.40. Medicare applies to all of it: $55,410 x 2.9% = $1,606.89. Total $4,843.29. Ignoring the wages gives $8,477.73.

q: Ed, a farmer who has never used the farm optional method before, had 2025 gross farm income of $9,000 and net farm profit of $1,500. If he uses the farm optional method, what are his net earnings from self-employment?
explain: The farm optional method is available because gross farm income is not more than $10,860. Net earnings equal two-thirds of gross farm income, up to $7,240: 2/3 x $9,000 = $6,000. $1,385 is the regular method result ($1,500 x 92.35%).

q: Liz had one employer in 2025, which mistakenly withheld $11,500 of Social Security tax from her wages. How does she recover the excess?
choices: Ask her employer to adjust the overcollection, and file Form 843 if the employer does not
Claim the excess as a credit on Schedule 3 of her Form 1040
Deduct the excess on Schedule A
It cannot be recovered
explain: When a single employer withholds too much Social Security tax, the employee cannot claim the excess as a credit on the income tax return; the employer should adjust it, and if not, the employee files Form 843. The Schedule 3 credit is for excess caused by two or more employers.

q: Tim and Ursula file jointly for 2025. Tim earned $100,000 from Employer A and $50,000 from Employer B. Ursula earned $60,000 from one employer. Each employer withheld 6.2% Social Security tax on all wages paid. What credit for excess Social Security tax can they claim?
explain: Excess Social Security tax is figured separately for each spouse. Tim's total wages of $150,000 are under the 2025 wage base of $176,100, and Ursula had one employer, so there is no excess. Combining the spouses' $210,000 would wrongly give ($210,000 - $176,100) x 6.2% = $2,101.80.
source: IRS Tax Topic 608; Instructions for Schedule SE (Form 1040) (2025); IRC 31(b)

q: Rev. Ana was ordained in 2023 and had net self-employment (SE) earnings of $400 or more, part of it from ministerial services, in both 2023 and 2024. By what date must she file Form 4361 to request exemption from SE tax?
choices: The due date of her 2023 return
Within 2 years after ordination, regardless of earnings
The due date, including extensions, of her 2024 return
Any time before the IRS assesses SE tax
explain: Form 4361 must be filed by the due date, including extensions, of the return for the second tax year in which the minister had $400 or more of net SE earnings, any part from ministerial services. Her second such year is 2024.

q: All of the following statements about an approved Form 4361 exemption are true EXCEPT:
choices: It must be based on religious opposition to accepting public insurance, not economic reasons
It is irrevocable once approved
It applies only to earnings from ministerial services
It also exempts the minister's ministerial earnings from federal income tax
explain: The Form 4361 exemption covers only self-employment tax on ministerial earnings; those earnings remain subject to income tax. The exemption must rest on religious opposition, not economic reasons, it is irrevocable, and it does not apply to other self-employment income.

q: Which statement about the 2025 combat zone pay exclusion is correct?
choices: Enlisted members may exclude all military pay for months served in a combat zone, but commissioned officers other than warrant officers may exclude only up to the highest rate of enlisted pay plus any imminent danger pay
All service members exclude the same capped amount each month
The exclusion applies only to months in which the member served the entire month in the combat zone
Excluded combat pay can never be counted as earned income for the earned income credit (EIC)
explain: Enlisted members and warrant officers exclude all qualifying pay, while other commissioned officers are capped at the highest rate of enlisted pay plus imminent danger or hostile fire pay. Service in any part of a month counts as the whole month, and a member may elect to include nontaxable combat pay in earned income for the EIC.

q: Sgt. Diaz, an enlisted member, arrived in a combat zone on March 28, 2025 and left on September 3, 2025. For how many months of 2025 can he exclude his military pay?
explain: Service in a combat zone for any part of a month is treated as service for the whole month. March through September is 7 months. Counting only full months gives 5.

q: A service member serving in a combat zone generally has deadlines for filing returns and paying tax extended by the time in the combat zone plus how many days after leaving it?
choices: 60 days
90 days
120 days
180 days
explain: The period of service in a combat zone, plus any continuous qualified hospitalization, plus the next 180 days is disregarded in determining whether tax acts such as filing and paying were timely.

q: Beth inherited her father's traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA) and withdrew the entire $100,000 balance in 2025, all of it taxable. The federal estate tax attributable to the IRA was $35,000. She itemizes. How does she get a benefit for that estate tax on her 2025 income tax return?
choices: She deducts $35,000 as an itemized deduction on Schedule A
She subtracts $35,000 from the distribution as an adjustment to income
She claims a $35,000 credit against her income tax
She gets no benefit because the estate paid the estate tax
explain: A recipient of income in respect of a decedent can deduct the estate tax attributable to it under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 691(c). Individuals may claim it only as an itemized deduction on Schedule A, line 16. It is not an adjustment to income or a credit.
source: IRS Pub 559 (2025); Instructions for Schedule A (Form 1040) (2025); IRC 691(c)

q: All of the following are income in respect of a decedent EXCEPT:
choices: Wages the decedent earned but had not been paid at death
A distribution to a beneficiary from the decedent's traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA)
Interest accrued on savings bonds up to the date of death but not yet received
Shares of stock the decedent owned at death that the beneficiary later sells
explain: Income in respect of a decedent (IRD) is income the decedent had a right to but had not received, such as unpaid wages, IRA balances, and accrued interest. IRD does not get a stepped-up basis. Stock owned at death is not IRD; it gets a basis equal to fair market value at death.

q: Kai, single, sold his main home in 2025 for a $320,000 gain. He meets the ownership and use tests and excludes $250,000. His other income is $180,000 of wages, so his modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) is $250,000. He has no other investment income. What is his net investment income tax?
explain: Gain excluded under section 121 is not net investment income (NII), but the $70,000 taxable gain above the exclusion is. The net investment income tax (NIIT) is 3.8% of the smaller of NII ($70,000) or MAGI over $200,000 ($50,000): $50,000 x 3.8% = $1,900. Taxing all $70,000 gives $2,660.
source: Instructions for Form 8960 (2025); IRC 1411(a)(1) and 1411(c)(1)(A)(iii); IRC 121

q: All of the following are generally included in net investment income for the net investment income tax (NIIT) EXCEPT:
choices: Interest from a bank savings account
Rental income from a passive rental property
Gain from the sale of publicly traded stock
Distributions from a traditional IRA
explain: Distributions from qualified plans and IRAs are excluded from net investment income, as are wages, self-employment (SE) income, Social Security, and tax-exempt interest. Interest, passive rents, and capital gains on stock are included.

q: Nina files married filing separately for 2025. She had $60,000 of Medicare wages and $100,000 of net earnings from self-employment (Schedule SE, line 6). What is her additional Medicare tax?
explain: The married filing separately (MFS) threshold is $125,000. Her wages are under it, so no tax on wages. The self-employment (SE) threshold is reduced by wages: $125,000 - $60,000 = $65,000. SE income over that is $100,000 - $65,000 = $35,000, x 0.9% = $315. Using the $200,000 single threshold would wrongly give $0.

q: Omar, a restaurant server, received $3,000 of cash tips in 2025 that he did not report to his employer, all in months when his tips were $20 or more. Which form does he use to figure the Social Security and Medicare tax on these tips?
choices: Form 4137
Form 8919
Form 8959
Schedule SE
explain: Form 4137 figures Social Security and Medicare tax on tips not reported to the employer, including allocated tips, and the tax goes on Schedule 2. Form 8919 is for misclassified workers, Form 8959 is the additional Medicare tax, and Schedule SE is for self-employment income.

q: Rosa received a Form 1099-NEC for 2025, but she filed Form SS-8 and received an IRS determination that she was an employee. How does she pay her share of Social Security and Medicare tax on that pay?
choices: Schedule SE, at the full 15.3% rate
No tax is due because the employer must pay it all
Form 4137
Form 8919, for the employee share only
explain: Form 8919 is used by a worker who was an employee but was treated as an independent contractor, and it figures only the employee share of Social Security and Medicare tax. Schedule SE would charge both halves, which is the common mistake.
source: IRS About Form 8919; Instructions for Form 8919 (2025)

q: Ken bought his main home in 2008 and claimed the $7,500 first-time homebuyer credit. He still lives in the home in 2025. What repayment of the credit is due on his 2025 return?
choices: $500 on Schedule 2, without Form 5405
$500 with Form 5405 attached
The entire unpaid balance
None, because the 15-year repayment period ended with the 2024 return
explain: Credits for homes bought in 2008 were repaid in 15 equal installments of 6 2/3% beginning with the 2010 return, so the last installment was due on the 2024 return. Nothing is due for 2025 while the home remains his main home.
source: IRC 36(f)(1) and 36(f)(7); Instructions for Form 5405 (Rev. Nov. 2024)

q: Jill, age 50 and not disabled, took a $3,000 distribution from her health savings account (HSA) in 2025 and used it for a vacation. What are the tax consequences?
choices: $3,000 is included in income, with no additional tax
$3,000 is included in income, plus a $300 additional tax
$3,000 is included in income, plus a $600 additional tax
Nothing, if she repays it by year end
explain: An HSA distribution not used for qualified medical expenses is included in income and is subject to a 20% additional tax unless the owner is disabled, dies, or is 65 or older. $3,000 x 20% = $600, reported on Schedule 2. The 10% rate applies to individual retirement arrangement (IRA) early distributions and to HSA testing period failures.

q: Leo, age 45, took a $10,000 distribution from his traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA) in 2025. His Form 1099-R shows code 1 in box 7, and no exception applies. Which statement is correct?
choices: He owes a $1,000 additional tax and may enter it directly on Schedule 2 without filing Form 5329
He owes a $2,500 additional tax on Form 5329
He must file Form 5329 to report a $1,000 additional tax
No additional tax applies if he included the distribution in income
explain: The 10% additional tax on early distributions is $10,000 x 10% = $1,000. When code 1 is correctly shown on all Forms 1099-R and the full amount is subject to the tax, the taxpayer does not need Form 5329 and enters the tax directly on Schedule 2, line 8. The 25% rate applies only to Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) IRA distributions within the first 2 years.

q: A domestic limited liability company (LLC) has three individual members. It has never filed Form 8832 or Form 2553. For federal income tax purposes, the LLC is classified as:
choices: A disregarded entity
A partnership
A C corporation, because state law gives its members limited liability
An S corporation
explain: Under the check-the-box default rules, a domestic eligible entity with two or more members is a partnership unless it elects otherwise, so it files Form 1065. Limited liability under state law does not make an LLC a corporation; only a single-member LLC is disregarded by default.

q: A limited liability company (LLC) that had been taxed as a partnership since 2019 filed Form 8832 to be classified as an association taxable as a corporation, effective January 1, 2023. Assuming no IRS permission and no change in ownership, what is the earliest effective date for a new election to change its classification again?
choices: January 1, 2024
January 1, 2026
January 1, 2028
It can never change its classification again
explain: After an entity changes its classification by election, it cannot change again by election during the 60 months following the effective date of that election. Sixty months after January 1, 2023 runs through December 31, 2027, so the earliest new effective date is January 1, 2028. The IRS can permit an earlier change, for example after more than 50% of the ownership changes, but that is not the case here.

q: All of the following are requirements for a married couple's unincorporated business to be treated as a qualified joint venture instead of a partnership EXCEPT:
choices: The only members of the venture are the spouses, and they file a joint return
Both spouses materially participate in the business
Both spouses elect not to be treated as a partnership
Each spouse must own exactly 50% of the business
explain: A qualified joint venture requires that the spouses be the only members, file jointly, both materially participate, and elect out of partnership treatment; the business also cannot be held in the name of a state-law entity such as a limited liability company (LLC). Equal ownership is not required: income, deductions and credits are divided according to each spouse's interest, and each spouse files a separate Schedule C (or F) and Schedule SE.
source: IRC 761(f); IRS, Election for Married Couples Unincorporated Businesses; Form 1065 instructions (2025)

q: Tom is the only member of a domestic limited liability company (LLC) that has never filed Form 8832. In 2025 the LLC hired two employees. Which statement is correct?
choices: Because it has employees, the LLC is now classified as a corporation for income tax purposes
Tom reports the LLC's income on his Schedule C, but the LLC must use its own employer identification number (EIN) to report and pay employment taxes
The LLC must file Form 1065 because it has employees
Tom may report the employees' wages on Form 941 under his Social Security number
explain: A single-member LLC owned by an individual is disregarded for income tax, so its income goes on the owner's Schedule C. For employment tax purposes, however, it is treated as a corporation, and the IRS says a single-member LLC that must file employment or excise taxes needs its own EIN.
source: Treas. Reg. 301.7701-2(c)(2)(iv) and 301.7701-3(b)(1)(ii); IRS, Do You Need a New EIN

q: In which situation must a partnership obtain a new employer identification number (EIN)?
choices: It changes its name and moves its office to another state
One partner sells her interest to a new partner, and the partnership continues
It converts to a state-law limited liability company (LLC) that continues to be classified as a partnership
It ends, and the remaining owners begin a new partnership
explain: IRS guidance says a partnership needs a new EIN if it incorporates, if a partner takes it over as a sole proprietorship, or if it ends and a new partnership begins. A change of name or location, a change in ownership that does not terminate the partnership, and a conversion to an LLC classified as a partnership do not require a new EIN.
source: IRS, Do You Need a New EIN; IRS Pub 541 (12/2025)

q: A new partnership has three partners: Ann, an individual with a calendar tax year, who owns a 40% interest in profits and capital; and two C corporations that each own a 30% interest in profits and capital and each use a fiscal year ending June 30. The partnership has no business purpose for another year and makes no section 444 election. What is its required tax year?
choices: The calendar year, because Ann is the largest single partner
The fiscal year ending June 30
The year that results in the least aggregate deferral, computed without regard to majority interest
Any year the partnership chooses on its first return
explain: A partnership must first use the majority interest tax year, which is the tax year of one or more partners who together own more than 50% of profits and capital. The two corporations together own 60% and share a June 30 year end, so June 30 is required. The least aggregate deferral test applies only when there is no majority interest year and the principal partners do not share a year.

q: A partnership has three corporate partners. Corp A owns 45% of profits and uses a fiscal year ending March 31. Corp B owns 45% and uses a fiscal year ending June 30. Corp C owns 10% and uses the calendar year. Profits and capital interests are the same. Under the least aggregate deferral rule, which tax year must the partnership use?
choices: Year ending March 31
Year ending June 30
Calendar year
Any of the three, because no partner owns more than 50%
explain: No year is held by partners owning more than 50%, and the principal partners (5% or more) have different years, so the least aggregate deferral test applies. Aggregate deferral is the sum of each partner's months of deferral times its profits share: March 31 = (3 x 0.45) + (9 x 0.10) = 2.25; June 30 = (9 x 0.45) + (6 x 0.10) = 4.65; December 31 = (3 x 0.45) + (6 x 0.45) = 4.05. March 31 produces the least deferral.

q: A newly formed partnership's required tax year is the calendar year. It is not part of a tiered structure and wants to make a section 444 election on Form 8716 instead of using the calendar year. Which fiscal year end can it elect?
choices: June 30
August 31
September 30
March 31
explain: A new entity's section 444 election is limited to a year with a deferral period of 3 months or less, measured from the end of the elected year to the end of the required year. September 30 to December 31 is 3 months, while August 31 would be 4 months and June 30 would be 6. An electing partnership must also file Form 8752 and make any required payment under section 7519.
source: IRC 444(b); Form 8716 (Rev. August 2021) instructions; IRS Pub 538

q: Ana started a dog-breeding activity in 2021. Its net results were: 2021 loss, 2022 profit, 2023 loss, 2024 profit, and 2025 profit. Under the section 183 presumption, how is the activity treated for 2025?
choices: Presumed to be engaged in for profit, because it had a profit in at least 3 of the last 5 years
Presumed to be a hobby, because it had losses in 2 of the last 5 years
Presumed to be a hobby, because the profit test for this activity is 2 of 7 years
No presumption applies until the activity has 5 consecutive profitable years
explain: An activity is presumed to be engaged in for profit if gross income exceeds deductions in 3 or more of the 5 consecutive years ending with the year in question. Ana had profits in 2022, 2024 and 2025, so the presumption applies for 2025. The 2-of-7-year test applies only to breeding, training, showing or racing horses.

q: In 2025 Rosa's sole proprietorship made the following payments in the course of its business. Rosa must report each payment on a Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC EXCEPT:
choices: $1,200 paid to an unincorporated freelance graphic designer for services
$3,000 of legal fees paid to a law firm organized as a professional corporation
$900 of office rent paid to an individual landlord
$5,000 paid to an S corporation for janitorial services
explain: Payments to corporations, including S corporations, are generally exempt from Form 1099 reporting, but attorneys' fees are an exception and must be reported even when paid to a corporation. For 2025 the threshold for nonemployee compensation and rents is $600, so the $1,200 and $900 payments are reportable; the $2,000 threshold applies only to payments made after December 31, 2025.
source: Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC (Rev. April 2025); IRC 6041(a); P.L. 119-21, sec. 70433

q: Under the general due date rules for 2025 information returns (before any weekend or holiday adjustment), Form 1099-NEC reporting nonemployee compensation must be filed with the IRS by:
choices: January 31, whether filed on paper or electronically
February 28 if filed on paper, or March 31 if filed electronically
February 15, the same date it must be furnished to the recipient
March 15, the due date of a calendar-year partnership return
explain: Section 6071(c) requires Form 1099-NEC to be filed with the IRS by January 31, the same date it must be furnished to the recipient, with no later date for electronic filing. The February 28 (paper) and March 31 (electronic) dates apply to Form 1099-MISC.
source: Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC (Rev. April 2025); IRC 6071(c)

q: All of the following statements about 2025 Forms W-2 are true EXCEPT:
choices: Copy A must be filed with the Social Security Administration (SSA) by the same date that employee copies must be furnished
An extension of time to file Copy A with the Social Security Administration (SSA) is not automatic, and only one 30-day extension may be requested on Form 8809
An employer that must file 10 or more information returns in total during the year must file Forms W-2 electronically
Filing Form 8809 automatically extends the time to furnish employee copies by 30 days
explain: Form 8809 relates to filing Copy A with the SSA, and that 30-day extension is not automatic. An extension of time to furnish employee copies is a separate request (on Form 15397) and is also not automatically granted. For 2025, both the SSA filing and employee copies were due February 2, 2026, because January 31 fell on a Saturday.
source: General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3 (2025); IRC 6071(c)

q: A new employee hired in March 2025 never gives his employer a Form W-4. The employer must withhold federal income tax as if the employee:
choices: Checked Married filing jointly and made no other entries
Claimed single status with one withholding allowance
Checked Single or Married filing separately and made no entries in Steps 2 through 4
Claimed exemption from withholding
explain: Under the current Form W-4 rules, an employee who does not furnish a W-4 is treated as single or married filing separately with no other adjustments. Withholding allowances were eliminated from the W-4 starting in 2020, so the old single-with-zero-or-one-allowance rule no longer applies.

q: Lee contributes a building with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $90,000, subject to a $50,000 mortgage he took out five years ago to buy it, to a partnership for a 40% interest in capital, profits and losses. The partnership assumes the mortgage, and Lee's share of partnership liabilities is 40%. What gain does Lee recognize, and what is his basis in the partnership interest?
choices: No gain; basis $0
Gain $10,000; basis $0
Gain $30,000; basis $0
No gain; basis $20,000
explain: Lee's basis starts at $20,000, is reduced by the $50,000 liability he is relieved of, and is increased by his 40% share of it ($20,000): $20,000 - $50,000 + $20,000 = -$10,000. Basis cannot go below zero, so the $10,000 excess (the net relief of $30,000 minus his $20,000 basis) is gain treated as from a sale or exchange, and his basis is zero. Gain is figured on the net decrease in liabilities, not on the full $50,000.

q: Carla and Dan form an equal partnership. Carla contributes land with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $50,000. Dan contributes $50,000 in cash. Two years later the partnership sells the land for $56,000. Using the traditional method under section 704(c), how much of the $26,000 tax gain is allocated to Carla?
explain: The $20,000 built-in gain that existed at contribution ($50,000 - $30,000) must be allocated to Carla, the contributing partner. The remaining $6,000 of appreciation after contribution is shared equally, so Carla's total is $20,000 + $3,000 = $23,000 and Dan's is $3,000. Splitting the whole $26,000 equally ignores section 704(c).

q: In 2025 Eve receives a fully vested 20% capital interest in a partnership in exchange for services. The interest is worth $30,000, and she can transfer it immediately. How does Eve treat the transaction?
choices: No income, because receiving a partnership interest is a nontaxable contribution under section 721
$30,000 of capital gain
$30,000 of ordinary income in 2025, and her basis in the interest is $30,000
No income until she sells the interest, when all gain is ordinary income
explain: Section 721 nonrecognition covers contributions of property, not services. The fair market value of a capital interest received for services is ordinary compensation income in the first year it is transferable or not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, and that amount becomes her basis. A profits interest received for services, by contrast, is generally not taxed on receipt.

q: Mia's basis in her partnership interest was $40,000 on January 1, 2025. For 2025 her Schedule K-1 shows: ordinary business income $15,000, tax-exempt interest $2,000, section 179 deduction $3,000, and charitable contributions $1,000. She received a $10,000 cash distribution, and her share of partnership liabilities increased by $6,000. What is her basis on December 31, 2025?
explain: Basis increases for income (including tax-exempt income) and for an increased share of liabilities, which is treated as a cash contribution, and decreases for distributions and for deductions such as section 179 and charitable contributions. $40,000 + $15,000 + $2,000 + $6,000 - $10,000 - $3,000 - $1,000 = $49,000. Leaving out the liability increase gives $43,000.

q: Sam's adjusted basis in his partnership interest, including his share of liabilities, is $8,000 at the end of 2025 before his share of the year's results. His share of the partnership's 2025 ordinary loss is $12,000, and he has no other partnership items. Considering only the basis limitation, how much loss can Sam deduct for 2025?
choices: $8,000, with $4,000 carried forward
explain: A partner's distributive share of loss is allowed only to the extent of the adjusted basis of the partner's interest at the end of the partnership year. Sam deducts $8,000, his basis drops to zero, and the $4,000 excess carries forward until he has basis to absorb it. The at-risk and passive activity rules are applied after this basis limit.

q: Ava, the general partner, and Ben, a limited partner, each contribute $40,000 cash to a limited partnership and share profits and losses equally. The partnership then borrows $60,000 on a recourse loan. Ben has not guaranteed the loan and has no obligation to contribute more capital. What is Ben's basis in his partnership interest?
explain: A recourse liability is shared by the partners who bear the economic risk of loss for it. A limited partner who has not guaranteed the debt or lent to the partnership generally bears no risk of loss, so all $60,000 is Ava's share (her basis is $100,000) and Ben's basis stays at his $40,000 contribution. The $70,000 answer wrongly shares the recourse debt by profit ratios, which is the general rule for nonrecourse debt.

q: Under the partnership agreement, Gina is to receive 30% of the partnership's ordinary income, figured before any guaranteed payments, but not less than $25,000 for the year. For 2025 the partnership's ordinary income before guaranteed payments is $60,000. How much of Gina's $25,000 is a guaranteed payment?
explain: Gina's 30% distributive share is $18,000 ($60,000 x 30%). The partnership must pay the $7,000 needed to reach her $25,000 minimum regardless of income, so that $7,000 is a guaranteed payment. Only the excess of the minimum over the distributive share is guaranteed, not the full amount.

q: Hal is a limited partner in a state-law limited partnership. He holds his interest as a passive investor and takes no part in management. In 2025 the partnership paid him a $20,000 guaranteed payment for consulting services he actually performed, and his distributive share of ordinary business income was $30,000. How much is included in his net earnings from self-employment, before the 92.35% adjustment?
explain: A limited partner's distributive share of partnership income is excluded from net earnings from self-employment, but guaranteed payments for services actually rendered are not excluded. Hal includes the $20,000 guaranteed payment only. A general partner would include both the guaranteed payment and the distributive share of trade or business income.
source: IRC 1402(a)(13); Schedule SE instructions (2025); Partner's Instructions for Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) (2025)

q: Maria's basis in her partnership interest is $12,000. In 2025 she receives a $15,000 cash distribution that does not liquidate her interest. Her share of partnership liabilities does not change, and the partnership has no unrealized receivables or inventory. What is the result?
choices: No gain; her basis becomes negative $3,000
$3,000 gain, generally capital gain; her basis becomes $0
$15,000 of ordinary income; her basis stays $12,000
No gain until she sells her interest; her basis becomes $0
