explain: When $100,000 or more accumulates on any day, the tax must be deposited by the close of the next business day. A monthly depositor that triggers this rule becomes a semiweekly depositor immediately for the rest of the calendar year and for the following calendar year.

q: An employer had 15 employees in 2025, and each earned more than $7,000. It is not in a credit reduction state, and it paid all required state unemployment tax on time. What is its 2025 Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA) tax after the credit for state unemployment tax?
explain: FUTA tax is 6.0% of the first $7,000 of each employee's wages, reduced by a credit of up to 5.4%, for a net rate of 0.6%. 15 x $7,000 x 0.6% = $630. $6,300 ignores the credit, and $5,670 is the credit itself.

q: In May 2025 the city condemned a warehouse that Tomas, a calendar-year taxpayer, held for use in his business, and he realized a gain on the award in 2025. To postpone the gain under Section 1033, by what date must he buy like-kind replacement real property?
choices: December 31, 2027
December 31, 2028
December 31, 2029
explain: For real property held for business or investment that is condemned, the replacement period ends 3 years after the close of the first tax year in which any part of the gain is realized: December 31, 2025 plus 3 years is December 31, 2028. December 31, 2027 is the general 2-year period that applies to other involuntary conversions.

q: A fire completely destroyed a delivery van used only in Kim's business in 2025. The van's adjusted basis was $18,000 and its fair market value before the fire was $25,000. There was no salvage value, and insurance paid $10,000. What is Kim's casualty loss?
explain: When business property is completely destroyed, the loss is the adjusted basis minus salvage value and reimbursement, without regard to the decline in fair market value: $18,000 - $10,000 = $8,000. The $100 reduction applies only to personal-use property, so $7,900 is wrong, and $15,000 wrongly starts from fair market value.

q: Nora is single, and her 2025 taxable income before the qualified business income (QBI) deduction is $400,000, with no net capital gain. Her sole proprietorship, which is not a specified service trade or business (SSTB), has $300,000 of qualified business income, paid $80,000 of W-2 wages, and holds qualified property with an unadjusted basis immediately after acquisition (UBIA) of $1,000,000, all still within its depreciable period. What is her 2025 QBI deduction?
explain: Her taxable income is above the 2025 phase-in range ($197,300 to $247,300), so the deduction is the lesser of 20% of QBI ($60,000) or the greater of 50% of W-2 wages ($40,000) or 25% of wages plus 2.5% of UBIA ($20,000 + $25,000 = $45,000). The limit is $45,000, which is also less than 20% of taxable income ($80,000).
source: IRC 199A(b)(2), (b)(3); Instructions for Form 8995-A (2025); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.27

q: For purposes of the qualified business income deduction, all of the following are specified service trades or businesses (SSTBs) EXCEPT:
choices: An engineering firm
A dental practice
A law firm
An investment management firm
explain: The SSTB definition borrows the list of fields in section 1202(e)(3)(A) but expressly removes engineering and architecture. Health (including dentists), law, and investing and investment management are SSTBs.

q: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for an individual to aggregate trades or businesses for the qualified business income (QBI) deduction?
choices: The same person or group owns 50% or more of each business for a majority of the tax year, including the last day
All items of each business are reported on returns with the same tax year
None of the businesses is a specified service trade or business (SSTB)

The businesses meet all three factors: same or customarily offered together products or services, shared facilities or centralized elements, and operation in coordination with or reliance on each other
explain: The businesses need to meet only two of the three factors, not all three. The ownership, same tax year, and no-SSTB requirements are all mandatory. Once aggregated, the businesses must generally be reported that way consistently in later years.

q: A retailer had gross receipts of $800,000 in 2024. In 2025 it spent $8,000 on eligible access expenditures to remove barriers for disabled customers in its building, which was first placed in service in 1985. What is its 2025 disabled access credit?
explain: The credit is 50% of eligible access expenditures over $250 and up to $10,250: ($8,000 - $250) x 50% = $3,875. The business qualifies because its prior-year gross receipts did not exceed $1,000,000. $4,000 ignores the $250 floor, and $5,000 is the maximum credit.

q: All of the following statements about the small employer health insurance premium credit (Form 8941) are correct EXCEPT:
choices: The employer generally must pay a uniform percentage, not less than 50%, of the premium cost for each enrolled employee
The coverage generally must be a qualified health plan offered through a Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP) Marketplace
As part of the general business credit, an unused credit is generally carried back 1 year and forward 20 years
An eligible employer can claim the credit for any number of tax years as long as it meets the requirements each year
explain: The credit is available only for a credit period of 2 consecutive tax years. The uniform 50% contribution, SHOP coverage, and the general business credit carryback and carryforward rules are all correct. The maximum credit is 50% of premiums (35% for tax-exempt employers).

q: A startup C corporation first had gross receipts in 2022, and its 2025 gross receipts were $3 million. Its 2025 research credit is $700,000. As a qualified small business, what is the maximum amount it can elect to apply against its payroll taxes for 2025?
choices: $0, because it has been in business more than 3 years
explain: A qualified small business has gross receipts under $5 million for the year and no gross receipts before the 5-tax-year period ending with that year, which this company meets. For tax years beginning after December 31, 2022, the election limit is $250,000 plus an additional $250,000, or $500,000. $250,000 was the limit for earlier years.

q: A C corporation that is not a farming business or an insurance company has a net operating loss (NOL) of $200,000 for its 2025 tax year. How is the NOL used?
choices: It is carried forward indefinitely, with no carryback
It is carried back 2 years, then forward 20 years
It is carried back 5 years, then forward indefinitely
It is carried forward 20 years, with no carryback
explain: NOLs arising in tax years beginning after 2020 generally cannot be carried back and carry forward indefinitely, deductible up to 80% of taxable income in a carryforward year. The 2-year carryback is limited to farming losses and certain insurance companies, and the 5-year carryback applied only to 2018 through 2020 losses.

q: Leo runs his business from a home office that meets the exclusive and regular use tests and uses the regular (actual expense) method. In 2025 his gross income from the business was $5,000, and his business expenses not related to the home were $2,000. The business portion of his home expenses was: mortgage interest $1,500 (fully deductible as an itemized deduction), utilities and insurance $1,000, and depreciation $1,200. How much depreciation carries over to 2026?
explain: The deduction is limited to gross income from the business use of the home less expenses not related to the home: $5,000 - $2,000 = $3,000. Mortgage interest is subtracted first (leaving $1,500), then operating expenses ($1,000, leaving $500), and depreciation last. $500 of depreciation is allowed and $700 carries over.

q: In which situation can a self-employed taxpayer deduct expenses for part of the home that is NOT used exclusively for business?
choices: Space used regularly to store inventory for a retail business when the home is the business's only fixed location
A room used to meet clients during the day and as a family TV room in the evening
A guest bedroom used for administrative work most days and for occasional overnight guests
A kitchen table used every day for bookkeeping
explain: The exclusive use test has two exceptions: regular use for storage of inventory or product samples of a retail or wholesale business whose only fixed location is the home, and use as a daycare facility. Any personal use of a client meeting room or administrative office fails the exclusive use test.

q: A C corporation that is not a tax shelter had gross receipts of $28 million in 2022, $32 million in 2023, and $34 million in 2024. Which statement is correct for its 2025 tax year?
choices: It may use the cash method, because its 2022 gross receipts were under $31 million
It may use the cash method, because its average gross receipts are under $35 million
It must use an accrual method, because its average annual gross receipts for 2022 through 2024 exceed $31 million
It must use an accrual method, because any year over $30 million disqualifies it
explain: A C corporation can use the cash method for 2025 only if average annual gross receipts for the 3 prior tax years do not exceed $31 million. ($28M + $32M + $34M) / 3 = $31.33 million, which exceeds the limit. The test uses the 3-year average, not any single year.
source: IRC 448(a), (b)(3), (c); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.31; Instructions for Form 1120 (2025)

q: All of the following statements about Form 3115 are correct EXCEPT:
choices: For an automatic change, the original Form 3115 is attached to the timely filed return (including extensions) for the year of change, and a signed copy is sent to the IRS
No user fee is required for a change filed under the automatic change procedures
A non-automatic change request is generally filed during the tax year for which the change is requested, with a user fee
A positive section 481(a) adjustment is generally taken into income entirely in the year of change
explain: A positive section 481(a) adjustment is generally spread over 4 tax years (the year of change and the next 3), while a negative adjustment is generally taken entirely in the year of change. The other statements correctly describe automatic and non-automatic filing procedures.

q: A C corporation's retained earnings were $200,000 at the beginning of 2025. For 2025, net income per books was $90,000, taxable income was $110,000, and it paid $30,000 of cash dividends. It had no other changes in retained earnings. What is the ending balance on Schedule M-2?
explain: Schedule M-2 analyzes unappropriated retained earnings per books: beginning balance plus net income per books minus distributions. $200,000 + $90,000 - $30,000 = $260,000. Using taxable income ($110,000) gives the wrong answer of $280,000, because M-2 uses book income.
source: Form 1120 (2025), Schedule M-2; Instructions for Form 1120 (2025)

q: A C corporation reports 2025 net income per books of $150,000 after deducting $30,000 of federal income tax expense. Its books also include a $5,000 fine paid to a government agency and $4,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest. There are no other differences. What is its taxable income on Schedule M-1?
explain: Schedule M-1 starts with book income, adds back federal income tax per books and nondeductible expenses, and subtracts book income that is not taxable: $150,000 + $30,000 + $5,000 - $4,000 = $181,000. Federal income tax and the fine are not deductible, and the bond interest is tax exempt.

q: Which corporation must file Schedule M-3 instead of Schedule M-1 with its 2025 Form 1120?
choices: A corporation with total assets of $12 million at the end of its tax year
A corporation with total assets of $8 million and gross receipts of $40 million
A corporation with total assets of $11 million during the year but $9.9 million at the end of its tax year
A corporation with total receipts of $200,000 and total assets of $240,000
explain: A corporation filing Form 1120 must file Schedule M-3 if its total assets at the end of the tax year are $10 million or more. The test uses year-end assets, not mid-year assets or gross receipts. A corporation with total receipts and total assets under $250,000 does not have to complete Schedules L, M-1 or M-2 at all.
source: Instructions for Schedule M-3 (Form 1120); Form 1120 (2025), Schedule K, question 13

q: In 2025 Ken sold stock with a basis of $10,000 to his sister for $7,000, its fair market value. Later in 2025 his sister sold the stock to an unrelated buyer for $11,000. How much gain does his sister recognize?
explain: Ken's $3,000 loss is disallowed because a sibling is a related person. His sister's basis is her $7,000 cost, so her realized gain is $4,000, but it is recognized only to the extent it exceeds Ken's disallowed loss: $4,000 - $3,000 = $1,000.

q: In 2025 a C corporation lends $8,000 interest free to a shareholder. It is the only loan outstanding between them, and tax avoidance is not a principal purpose of the loan. How does Section 7872 apply?
choices: Forgone interest is treated as a dividend to the shareholder
Forgone interest is treated as compensation to the shareholder
Section 7872 does not apply, because the aggregate outstanding loans are $10,000 or less
The entire $8,000 is treated as a distribution
explain: Below-market corporation-shareholder loans are subject to Section 7872, but the rule does not apply on any day the aggregate outstanding loans between the borrower and lender are $10,000 or less, unless tax avoidance is a principal purpose. Above that amount, forgone interest on a corporation-shareholder loan would generally be treated as a distribution.

q: A car dealer sells a car to a customer who pays $6,000 in cash on June 2, 2025, and $5,000 in cash on June 10, 2025, for the same car. What is the dealer's Form 8300 obligation?
choices: No Form 8300 is required, because no single payment exceeded $10,000
File Form 8300 by June 17, 2025, 15 days after the first payment
File Form 8300 by June 25, 2025, 15 days after the payment that brought the total over $10,000
File Form 8300 by January 31, 2026
explain: Related payments received within one year are added together, and a report is due within 15 days after the payment that causes the total to exceed $10,000. $6,000 + $5,000 = $11,000 on June 10, so Form 8300 is due by June 25, 2025. January 31 is the deadline for the written statement to the payer, not the Form 8300 itself.

q: A sole proprietor made the following payments in the course of business in 2025. Which one requires a 2025 Form 1099?
choices: $1,500 to a law firm organized as a corporation for legal services
$2,000 to a corporation for office supplies
$500 to an unincorporated freelance designer
$5,000 of rent paid to a real estate agent who manages the property
explain: Payments to corporations are generally exempt from Form 1099 reporting, but the exemption does not apply to attorneys' fees, so the $1,500 is reported on Form 1099-NEC. For 2025 the general threshold is $600 (the $2,000 threshold applies to payments made after December 31, 2025), so the $500 payment is not reported, and rents paid to real estate agents are excluded.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.6041-3(p)(1); IRC 6041(a) as amended by P.L. 119-21; Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC

q: In 2025 a business pays $3,000 for services to an independent contractor who has not furnished a taxpayer identification number. How much must the business withhold as backup withholding?
explain: Backup withholding is 24% of reportable payments when the payee fails to furnish a correct taxpayer identification number (TIN): $3,000 x 24% = $720. The payer reports the withholding on Form 945 and on the payee's Form 1099-NEC.

q: Under the fixed date method safe harbor for an accountable plan, an employee is treated as substantiating expenses and returning excess amounts within a reasonable period if the employee:
choices: Substantiates within 30 days and returns any excess within 60 days after the expense is paid or incurred
Substantiates within 60 days and returns any excess within 120 days after the expense is paid or incurred
Substantiates within 90 days and returns any excess within 180 days after the expense is paid or incurred
Substantiates and returns any excess by the end of the tax year
explain: Under the fixed date method, an advance within 30 days of the expense, substantiation within 60 days, and return of excess within 120 days are treated as reasonable. The 30-day figure applies to when an advance is paid, not to substantiation.

q: Under the common-law rules, the IRS groups the facts that show whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor into which three categories?
choices: Behavioral control, financial control, and the type of relationship of the parties
Hours worked, place of work, and method of payment
Supervision, training, and length of service
Business license, written contract, and Form W-9
explain: Evidence of the degree of control and independence falls into behavioral control, financial control, and the type of relationship. No single fact, such as a written contract or method of payment, decides the issue. Either the business or the worker can file Form SS-8 to request an IRS determination.
source: IRS Pub 15-A (2025); IRS About Form SS-8

q: All of the following are requirements for a business to obtain Section 530 relief from federal employment taxes for workers it treated as independent contractors EXCEPT:
choices: It obtained a Form SS-8 determination before treating the workers as independent contractors
It had a reasonable basis for not treating the workers as employees
It filed all required federal information returns, such as Forms 1099, consistent with that treatment
It did not treat any worker holding a substantially similar position as an employee
explain: Section 530 relief requires a reasonable basis, reporting consistency (filing required information returns), and substantive consistency (no similar worker treated as an employee). A prior Form SS-8 determination is not a requirement.
source: IRS Pub 15-A (2025), Relief provision; Revenue Act of 1978, section 530

q: When advising a client on choice of entity for 2025, all of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
choices: A C corporation's taxable income is taxed at a flat 21% rate
C corporation earnings distributed as dividends are taxed again to the shareholders
An S corporation shareholder who works in the business should receive reasonable compensation subject to employment taxes
A C corporation may claim the qualified business income deduction on its business income
explain: The Section 199A deduction is available to individuals and certain trusts and estates, including owners of sole proprietorships, partnerships and S corporations, but not to C corporations. The 21% flat rate, double taxation of dividends, and reasonable compensation for S corporation shareholder-employees are all correct.

q: Throughout every month of 2024, a company had 40 full-time employees (averaging at least 30 hours a week) and 30 part-time employees who each worked 80 hours a month. It is not part of a controlled group, and no seasonal worker exception applies. Is it an applicable large employer (ALE) for 2025?
choices: No, because only full-time employees are counted, and it has 40
No, because part-time employees count as half an employee each, for a total of 55 that is rounded down
Yes, because it has 60 full-time and full-time equivalent employees, so it must file Forms 1094-C and 1095-C for 2025
Yes, because it has 70 total employees, so it must file Forms 1094-B and 1095-B for 2025
explain: Full-time equivalents are figured by adding the monthly hours of non-full-time employees (up to 120 each) and dividing by 120: 30 x 80 = 2,400 / 120 = 20. 40 + 20 = 60, which is at least 50, so the company is an ALE for 2025 and files Forms 1094-C and 1095-C. Headcount alone (70) is not the test.
source: IRS Determining if an employer is an applicable large employer; Instructions for Forms 1094-C and 1095-C (2025); IRC 4980H(c)(2)(A), (E)

q: A simple trust's governing instrument allocates capital gains and trustee fees to principal (corpus). For 2025 the trust has $10,000 of taxable interest, a $5,000 capital gain, and $1,000 of deductible trustee fees. It distributes its $10,000 of fiduciary accounting income to the beneficiary as required. What is the trust's income distribution deduction?
explain: Fiduciary accounting income is $10,000 because the gain and fees are charged to corpus, but distributable net income (DNI) is $10,000 of interest minus the $1,000 of fees, or $9,000; the capital gain allocated to corpus is excluded from DNI. The distribution deduction is the lesser of the required distribution ($10,000) or DNI ($9,000), so it is $9,000. Choosing $10,000 ignores the DNI ceiling.
source: IRC 643(a)(3), 643(b), 651(a) and (b); Form 1041 instructions (2025), Schedule B

q: A complex trust has 2025 distributable net income (DNI) of $20,000, all taxable interest. The trust instrument requires the trustee to pay $12,000 of income to Ann each year. The trustee also makes a discretionary distribution of $15,000 to Ben. How much must Ben include in his 2025 gross income?
explain: Under the tier rules, income required to be distributed currently (Ann's $12,000) absorbs DNI first. Only the remaining DNI of $8,000 ($20,000 minus $12,000) is available for the second-tier discretionary distribution, so Ben includes $8,000. A pro rata split of DNI across both distributions ($11,111) is wrong because first-tier amounts take priority.
source: IRC 662(a)(1) and (2); Form 1041 instructions (2025), Schedule B

q: For 2025, a simple trust has $6,000 of taxable interest and $4,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest and no expenses. It distributes all $10,000 of its income to the beneficiary as required. What is the trust's income distribution deduction?
explain: Tax-exempt interest is included in distributable net income (DNI), so DNI is $10,000, but the distribution deduction cannot include items not included in the trust's gross income. The deduction is therefore limited to the $6,000 of taxable interest, and the beneficiary reports $6,000 of taxable interest and $4,000 of tax-exempt interest. Deducting the full $10,000 would let tax-exempt income generate a deduction.

q: A complex trust has 2025 taxable interest of $8,000 and $1,000 of deductible trustee fees. The trustee makes a discretionary distribution of $3,000 of income to a beneficiary. The trust has no other items. What is the trust's 2025 taxable income?
explain: Distributable net income (DNI) is $7,000 ($8,000 minus $1,000), so the full $3,000 distribution is deductible. A complex trust's exemption is $100, so taxable income is $8,000 minus $1,000 minus $3,000 minus $100, or $3,900. The $300 exemption applies only to a trust required to distribute all income currently, and $600 is the exemption for an estate.

q: On February 20, 2026, the trustee of a calendar-year complex trust distributes $5,000 to a beneficiary and wants it treated as a 2025 distribution. Which statement is correct?
choices: The trustee must file Form 1041-T by March 6, 2026, the 65th day after year end
The trustee may elect under section 663(b) to treat it as paid on December 31, 2025, and the election is made on the 2025 Form 1041 filed by its due date, including extensions
The election is not available because only estates may use the 65-day rule
The distribution can be treated as a 2025 distribution only if it is made by January 31, 2026
explain: Section 663(b) lets an estate or complex trust treat amounts paid within the first 65 days of the year as paid on the last day of the prior year; February 20 is within 65 days. The election is made on the return for the year the distribution is treated as made, no later than its due date including extensions, and becomes irrevocable after that date. Form 1041-T, due by the 65th day, is a different election under section 643(g) that allocates estimated tax payments to beneficiaries.

q: All of the following statements about Form 1041 filing for 2025 are true EXCEPT:
choices: A trust generally must adopt a calendar year
An estate's first tax year may be any period of 12 months or less that ends on the last day of a month
Form 7004 gives an estate or trust an automatic 6-month extension of time to file Form 1041
A calendar-year trust must file its 2025 Form 1041 and give Schedules K-1 to beneficiaries by April 15, 2026
explain: Form 7004 gives an estate or trust an automatic 5 1/2-month extension to file Form 1041, not 6 months. The other statements are correct: trusts generally use a calendar year, an estate may choose a fiscal year, and a calendar-year return and the K-1s are due April 15, 2026.

q: A complex trust has 2025 taxable income of $16,650, all ordinary income. Using the 2025 tax rate schedule for estates and trusts, what is the trust's regular income tax?
explain: For 2025 the top 37% rate for estates and trusts starts at taxable income over $15,650, and the tax at that point is $3,777. The tax is $3,777 plus 37% of $1,000 ($16,650 minus $15,650), or $4,147. A flat 37% on the full $16,650 ($6,161) ignores the lower brackets.

q: A calendar-year trust terminated and distributed all its assets to its sole beneficiary in 2025. In its final year the trust had $4,000 of gross income and $9,000 of deductible trustee and legal fees (section 67(e) expenses). Which statement is correct?
choices: The $5,000 excess is lost because a trust's deductions cannot pass to a beneficiary
The beneficiary may deduct the $5,000 excess deduction on her 2025 return and carry any unused part to 2026
The beneficiary may deduct the $5,000 excess deduction only on her 2025 return, and it keeps its character as a deduction in arriving at adjusted gross income (AGI)
The trust reports a $5,000 net operating loss that the beneficiary carries forward 20 years
explain: Under section 642(h)(2), deductions in the final year that exceed gross income pass to the beneficiaries who succeed to the property. The beneficiary may claim them only in her tax year in which or with which the trust terminates, and each item keeps its character; section 67(e) expenses are deductions in arriving at AGI and are reported on the final Schedule K-1, box 11. Unlike an unused capital loss carryover, excess deductions cannot be carried forward to later years.
source: IRC 642(h); Treas. Reg. 1.642(h)-2; Form 1041 instructions (2025), Schedule K-1 box 11

q: Rosa died on May 10, 2025. Her executor chose a fiscal year ending April 30 for the estate and expects the estate to owe $8,000 of income tax for its first tax year. Which statement about estimated tax is correct?
choices: The estate must make quarterly estimated payments because it expects to owe $1,000 or more
The estate must pay estimated tax only if it does not file Form 1041 by the 15th day of the 4th month
The estate is not required to pay estimated tax for any tax year ending before May 10, 2027
The executor must pay estimated tax under Form 1041-T by the 65th day of the year
explain: A decedent's estate does not have to pay estimated tax for any tax year ending before the date 2 years after the decedent's death, so no estimated payments are required for years ending before May 10, 2027. The $1,000 test applies to trusts and to estates after that 2-year period. Form 1041-T is used to allocate estimated payments to beneficiaries, not to pay estimated tax.

q: A promoter persuades Dan to transfer his home and his consulting business to a series of trusts he controls. The trusts pay Dan's mortgage, groceries and family vacations and deduct them as trust expenses, and Dan reports no business income. How does the IRS treat this arrangement?
choices: The trusts are respected as separate taxpayers, but only half of the expenses are deductible
The arrangement is an abusive trust; Dan is taxed on the income as if the trusts did not exist, and the personal living expenses are not deductible
The income is taxed to the trusts at trust rates, and Dan owes only gift tax on the transfers
The arrangement is valid if each trust files Form 1041 and issues Schedules K-1
explain: The IRS treats such arrangements as abusive trust schemes: a trust over which the grantor keeps control is disregarded, and all of its income is taxed to the grantor. Personal living expenses such as food, housing and recreation are not deductible by a trust any more than by an individual, and income earned by Dan cannot be assigned to another entity. Filing Form 1041 does not make the arrangement valid.
source: IRS: Abusive Trust Tax Evasion Schemes, Questions and Answers; Form 1041 instructions (2025); IRC 671, 677

q: All of the following are requirements for an organization to be exempt under section 501(c)(3) EXCEPT:
choices: It must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes
None of its net earnings may inure to any private shareholder or individual
It may not attempt to influence legislation as a substantial part of its activities
It may endorse political candidates as long as the activity is not a substantial part of its operations
explain: A 501(c)(3) organization is absolutely prohibited from participating in any political campaign for or against a candidate; there is no insubstantial-part exception for campaign activity. The insubstantial-part test applies only to lobbying (influencing legislation). The other choices state actual requirements.

q: Which of the following organizations may apply for 501(c)(3) recognition on Form 1023-EZ?
choices: A newly formed nonprofit corporation that will run a food pantry, projects gross receipts of $30,000 in each of its first 3 years, and has $20,000 of assets
A newly formed church with projected gross receipts of $40,000
A limited liability company formed to provide scholarships, with $10,000 of assets
A nonprofit corporation projecting $80,000 of gross receipts in its second year and holding $50,000 of assets
explain: Form 1023-EZ is available only if projected annual gross receipts do not exceed $50,000 in any of the next 3 years (or actual receipts did not exceed $50,000 in any of the past 3 years) and total assets do not exceed $250,000; the food pantry meets both tests. Churches and limited liability companies (LLCs) are not eligible to use Form 1023-EZ, and the $80,000 projection exceeds the $50,000 limit.
source: Instructions for Form 1023-EZ (Rev. January 2025); IRS: Do you have the required financial information?

q: A newly formed chamber of commerce wants IRS recognition of exemption as a business league under section 501(c)(6). Which application should it file?
choices: Form 1023, filed on paper
Form 1024-A, filed electronically
Form 1024, filed electronically through Pay.gov
Form 1023-EZ, filed electronically
explain: Business leagues and chambers of commerce under section 501(c)(6), and most other 501(c) organizations, apply on Form 1024, which must be submitted electronically through Pay.gov. Form 1024 is not used by 501(c)(3) organizations (Form 1023 or 1023-EZ) or 501(c)(4) organizations (Form 1024-A).

q: Which statement about the 2025 annual information return for an exempt organization is correct?
choices: A private foundation with gross receipts normally under $50,000 may file Form 990-N
An organization with gross receipts of $180,000 and total assets of $520,000 at year end may file Form 990-EZ
An organization with gross receipts of $180,000 and total assets of $450,000 at year end may file Form 990-EZ
An organization whose gross receipts are normally $40,000 must file Form 990-EZ
explain: Form 990-EZ may be filed if gross receipts are less than $200,000 and total assets are less than $500,000 at year end, so the organization with $450,000 of assets qualifies, but the one with $520,000 of assets must file Form 990. Private foundations file Form 990-PF regardless of size, and an organization with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less may file Form 990-N rather than 990-EZ.
source: IRS: Form 990 Series, Which Forms Do Exempt Organizations File; IRC 6033

q: A 501(c)(3) organization had all of the following income in 2025. Each is excluded from unrelated business taxable income EXCEPT:
choices: Dividends from its stock portfolio
Royalties from licensing its name and logo
Rent from an office building it owns free of debt
Rent from an office building it bought with borrowed money that is still outstanding
explain: Dividends, royalties and rents from real property are generally excluded from unrelated business taxable income (UBTI), but the exclusions do not apply to income from debt-financed property. Rent from the leveraged building is unrelated debt-financed income and is included in UBTI in proportion to the acquisition debt. Rent from the debt-free building stays excluded.

q: An exempt organization operates two unrelated trades or businesses in 2025. Business A has net income of $30,000 and Business B has a net loss of $12,000. Neither has any net operating loss (NOL) carryover. What is the organization's unrelated business taxable income for 2025?
explain: Under section 512(a)(6), unrelated business taxable income (UBTI) is computed separately for each unrelated trade or business, and a loss from one cannot offset income from another, so Business A's $30,000 stands alone (Business B's loss carries forward as its own NOL). The $1,000 specific deduction then reduces total UBTI to $29,000. Netting the businesses ($17,000 after the specific deduction) is the pre-2018 approach.

q: A small calendar-year 501(c)(3) organization eligible to file Form 990-N did not file anything for 2022, 2023 or 2024. Which statement is correct?
choices: Its exemption is automatically revoked as of May 15, 2025, the due date of its third missed annual notice
Its exemption is revoked only after the IRS sends a notice and the organization fails to respond within 90 days
No revocation occurs because Form 990-N filers are not subject to automatic revocation
Its exemption is automatically revoked as of January 1, 2022, the start of the first missed year
explain: An organization that fails to file a required Form 990, 990-EZ, 990-PF or 990-N for 3 consecutive years automatically loses its exemption, effective on the original due date of the third missed return or notice. For a calendar-year organization the 2024 Form 990-N was due May 15, 2025. To be reinstated, the organization must apply again; revocation is not retroactive to the first missed year.
source: IRC 6033(j); IRS: Automatic Revocation of Exemption

q: Nora turns 61 in 2025 and participates in her employer's 401(k) plan, which permits catch-up contributions. What is the maximum elective deferral she can make for 2025?
explain: For 2025 the elective deferral limit is $23,500, and a participant who attains age 60, 61, 62 or 63 during the year may make a catch-up of $11,250 instead of the regular $7,500. Nora's maximum is $23,500 plus $11,250, or $34,750. $31,000 is the limit for a participant age 50 to 59 or 64 and older, and $35,750 uses 2026 figures.
source: IRS News Release IR-2024-285; Notice 2024-80; IRC 414(v)(2)(E)

q: All of the following statements about Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) individual retirement arrangement (IRA) plans for 2025 are true EXCEPT:
choices: An employee age 61 in a plan subject to the regular $16,500 deferral limit may defer up to $21,750
A distribution taken within 2 years of first participating, with no exception, is subject to a 25% additional tax instead of 10%
During the first 2 years of participation, a tax-free transfer may be made only to another SIMPLE IRA
An employer that never had a SIMPLE IRA plan may set one up for 2025 as late as the due date of its 2025 return, including extensions
explain: A new SIMPLE IRA plan generally must be set up between January 1 and October 1 of the year; it is a simplified employee pension (SEP), not a SIMPLE IRA, that can be set up as late as the return due date including extensions. The other statements are true: the 2025 limit is $16,500 plus a $5,250 catch-up for ages 60 to 63 ($21,750), and the 2-year rule raises the additional tax to 25% and limits tax-free moves to other SIMPLE IRAs.

q: Carla is a sole proprietor with no employees. Her 2025 Schedule C net profit is $100,000 and her self-employment tax is $14,130. Her simplified employee pension (SEP) plan provides for a 25% contribution rate. What is the maximum deductible SEP contribution for herself?
explain: A self-employed person's compensation is net earnings reduced by the deductible half of self-employment (SE) tax and by the contribution itself, so a 25% plan rate becomes a 20% reduced rate (25% divided by 125%). Net profit of $100,000 minus $7,065 (half of SE tax) is $92,935, and 20% of that is $18,587. Applying 25% to $92,935 ($23,234) ignores the reduction for her own contribution.
source: IRS Pub 560 (2025), chapter 5; IRS: Self-Employed Individuals, Calculating Your Own Retirement Plan Contribution and Deduction

q: Marco, age 45, is a sole proprietor with no employees who sponsors a one-participant (solo) 401(k) plan. His 2025 Schedule C net profit is $60,000 and the deductible half of his self-employment tax is $4,239. What is the maximum total contribution (elective deferrals plus employer nonelective contribution) he can make for 2025?
explain: His employer nonelective contribution is limited to 20% of net earnings after the half self-employment (SE) tax deduction: $60,000 minus $4,239 equals $55,761, and 20% of that is $11,152. He may also defer the full $23,500 elective deferral limit, for a total of $34,652, which is under the $70,000 annual additions limit. Using 25% of $55,761 ($13,940) to reach $37,440 ignores the self-employed reduced rate.
source: IRS Pub 560 (2025); Notice 2024-80; IRS: One-Participant 401(k) Plans

q: Each of the following one-participant plans is not in its final plan year. Which one must file Form 5500-EZ for the 2025 plan year?
choices: A solo 401(k) with $240,000 of assets at the end of the plan year, sponsored by an owner who has no other plans
A solo 401(k) with $190,000 of assets and a profit-sharing plan with $110,000 of assets, both sponsored by the same owner
A simplified employee pension (SEP) with $400,000 of assets
A Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) individual retirement arrangement (IRA) plan with $300,000 of assets
explain: A one-participant plan must file an annual return (Form 5500-EZ, or Form 5500-SF electronically) when the total year-end assets of all the sponsor's one-participant plans exceed $250,000; here $190,000 plus $110,000 equals $300,000, so both plans must file. A single plan with $240,000 is under the threshold. SEPs and SIMPLE IRA plans are IRA-based and do not file the Form 5500 series.
source: IRS: Are the assets in your client's one-participant plans more than $250,000?; IRS: Form 5500 Corner

q: Ken owns 100% of a corporation that sponsors a profit-sharing plan. In 2025 Ken sells land to the plan for its fair market value of $50,000. What is the initial excise tax on this transaction?
choices: None, because the sale was at fair market value
$5,000, paid by the plan
$7,500 for each year in the taxable period, paid by Ken
$50,000, paid by the corporation
explain: A sale of property between a plan and a disqualified person, such as the 100% owner of the employer, is a prohibited transaction even at fair market value. The disqualified person who participates pays an initial tax of 15% of the amount involved ($50,000 times 15%, or $7,500) for each year in the taxable period, and a 100% additional tax applies if the transaction is not corrected.
source: IRC 4975(a), (b), (c)(1)(A) and (e)(2); IRS Pub 560 (2025), Prohibited Transactions

q: All of the following statements comparing qualified retirement plans with nonqualified deferred compensation (NQDC) plans are true EXCEPT:
choices: A qualified plan must meet nondiscrimination rules, but an unfunded NQDC plan may cover only a select group of executives
An employer generally deducts NQDC only in its tax year in which the employee includes the amount in income
Amounts deferred under an unfunded NQDC plan that complies with section 409A generally are not taxed to the employee until paid
Employer contributions to a qualified plan are taxable to employees when contributed, to the extent they are vested
explain: Employer contributions to a qualified plan are not taxed to employees until distributed, even if vested; that tax deferral, together with the employer's current deduction, is the main advantage of qualification. The other statements are true: NQDC plans may favor highly compensated employees, the employer's deduction is matched to the employee's inclusion, and compliant unfunded deferrals are taxed when paid.

q: Lucia, a cash-method farmer, had her soybean crop damaged by hail in August 2025 and received crop insurance proceeds in October 2025. All of the following are requirements for her to elect to postpone reporting the proceeds until 2026 EXCEPT:
choices: She uses the cash method of accounting
She received the proceeds in the same tax year the crop was damaged
Under her normal business practice, she would have included more than 50% of the income from the damaged crop in a later year
She makes a separate election for each crop she grows in the same farming business
explain: One election covers all crops representing a single trade or business; it is not made crop by crop. The other three choices are the actual conditions for postponing crop insurance proceeds to the year after the damage.

q: In 2025 Ruth, a farmer, pledged her corn as collateral for a $40,000 Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC) loan and elected to report the loan proceeds as income on her 2025 Schedule F. Which statement is correct?
choices: She must generally report all CCC loans received in 2025 and later years the same way
She may switch back to treating future CCC loans as loans in any later year without IRS consent
She must report the $40,000 again as income when she repays the loan
The election is available only to accrual-method farmers
explain: A farmer may elect to treat a CCC loan as income in the year received, and once she does so she must generally report all CCC loans in that year and later years the same way. A later sale of the redeemed commodity is reported as sale proceeds minus her basis, so she does not include the $40,000 again. A forfeiture of pledged crops in full payment is treated as a sale of the crops.

q: Hank is a cash-method cattle rancher whose principal business is farming. He normally sells 100 head of beef cattle a year. Because of a drought that caused his county to be designated for federal disaster assistance, he sold 250 head in 2025. Under the weather-related sales rule, income from how many head may he elect to report in 2026 instead of 2025?
choices: 0, because the rule applies only to draft, breeding and dairy livestock
explain: A cash-method farmer may postpone to the next year the income from livestock sold in excess of the number normally sold, when the sale was caused by weather conditions that led to a federal assistance designation. The excess is 250 minus 100, or 150 head. The one-year postponement under section 451(g) applies to the excess livestock sold. The replacement-property rule for draft, breeding and dairy animals is the separate section 1033(e).

q: Elena, a farmer, uses Schedule J to average her farm income on her 2025 return. All of the following statements are true EXCEPT:
choices: Her base years are 2022, 2023 and 2024
She can use income averaging even if she was not farming in the base years
Gain from the sale of farmland can be included in her elected farm income
Her elected farm income cannot exceed her taxable income
explain: Elected farm income does not include gain from the sale of land (or of development, grazing or similar rights), even though gain on other farm property used regularly in the business can qualify. The other statements are true: the 2025 base years are 2022 through 2024, base-year farming is not required, and elected farm income is limited to taxable income.

q: For 2025, Olga's gross income is $96,000 from farming and $24,000 of wages. She did not file early. Which statement correctly describes her estimated tax requirement for 2025?
choices: She must make four quarterly payments based on 90% of her 2025 tax, because farm income must be at least 90% of gross income for the special rule
She qualifies for the special farmer rule and may make one estimated payment by January 15, 2026, figured using 66 2/3% of her 2025 tax instead of 90%
She qualifies for the special farmer rule only if her farm income is at least 75% of her gross income
She is exempt from estimated tax for 2025 because farmers are never charged an underpayment penalty
explain: A qualified farmer is one whose gross income from farming is at least two-thirds of total gross income for the current or prior year; Olga's farm income is 80% ($96,000 of $120,000). A qualified farmer makes one required installment due January 15 of the next year, figured with 66 2/3% substituted for 90%, or may skip it by filing the return and paying all tax by March 1 (March 2, 2026, for 2025 returns because March 1 falls on a Sunday). Farmers are not exempt from the underpayment penalty.
source: IRC 6654(i), 7503; IRS Pub 225 (2025), chapter 15; IRS FAQ: Estimated Tax, Farmers and Fishermen

q: Tom, a retired landowner, rents his farmland to a tenant under a crop-share lease and does not materially participate in the farming operation. In 2025 he sold his share of the crops for $30,000. How should he report this income?
choices: On Schedule F, subject to self-employment tax
On Schedule F, but not subject to self-employment tax
On Form 4835, with the net income carried to Schedule E, and not subject to self-employment tax
On Schedule C as rental income subject to self-employment tax
explain: A landowner who receives crop-share rent and does not materially participate reports the income and expenses on Form 4835 and carries the net income or loss to Schedule E (Form 1040), page 2. Because he does not materially participate, the crop-share income is rental income excluded from net earnings from self-employment. Schedule F is for a landowner who materially participates.

q: All of the following statements about depreciation of farm property are true EXCEPT:
choices: New farm machinery whose original use begins with the farmer after 2017 is 5-year property
A farmer is not required to use the 150% declining balance method for farm property placed in service after 2017, other than 15-year and 20-year property
A farmer who elects out of the uniform capitalization rules under section 263A must use the alternative depreciation system for farm property placed in service while the election is in effect
Grain bins and fences placed in service in 2025 are 5-year property if they are new
explain: Grain bins, cotton ginning assets, fences and other land improvements are specifically excluded from the 5-year class for new farm machinery and equipment. The other statements are true: new farm machinery placed in service after 2017 is 5-year property, the 150% declining balance requirement for farm property was removed after 2017 except for 15-year and 20-year property, and electing out of section 263A requires alternative depreciation system (ADS).
source: IRC 168(b)(2), 168(e)(3)(B)(vii), 263A(e)(2); IRS: Tax reform changes to depreciation deduction affect farmers' bottom line

q: Maria and her husband Jorge file a joint 2025 return. Maria works 1,800 hours as an employee nurse (not an owner) and spends 800 hours managing their rental properties. Jorge has no job and spends 400 hours on the rentals. Do they qualify as real estate professionals so that the rental activity is not automatically passive?
choices: Yes, because together they spent 1,200 hours, which is more than 750
Yes, because Maria spent more than 750 hours in real property businesses
No, because neither spouse separately meets both the more-than-half test and the more-than-750-hours test
No, because hours spent on rental properties never count toward the test
explain: To qualify, more than half of a taxpayer's personal services must be in real property trades or businesses in which he or she materially participates, and those services must exceed 750 hours. On a joint return, one spouse must meet both tests separately. Maria fails the more-than-half test (800 of 2,600 hours) and Jorge fails the 750-hour test, and their hours cannot be combined for this purpose.

q: In 2025 Grace rented her lake house to unrelated tenants at a fair rental price for 150 days. She rented it to her brother for 10 days at half the fair rental price, and she used it herself for 6 days. Is the house treated as used as a residence for 2025?
choices: No, because Grace herself used it only 6 days, which is not more than 14
No, because 16 personal-use days do not exceed 10% of the 160 days it was rented
Yes, because 16 personal-use days exceed 15 days, the greater of 14 days or 10% of the 150 fair rental days
Yes, because any rental to a relative makes the property a residence
explain: Days rented to a family member at less than a fair rental price are personal-use days, so Grace has 16 personal-use days (10 plus 6). The test is the greater of 14 days or 10% of the days rented at a fair rental price; only the 150 fair rental days count, so the threshold is 15 days, and 16 exceeds it. Counting the 10 below-market days as rental days produces the wrong 16-day threshold.

q: Sam owns a beach house that he rented at a fair rental price for 90 days in 2025 and used personally for 30 days. It was vacant the rest of the year. His 2025 utilities, insurance and maintenance for the house total $12,000. How much of the $12,000 is allocable to the rental use?
explain: When a dwelling unit is used for personal purposes during the year, rental expenses are allocated using the ratio of days rented at a fair rental price to the total days the unit was used for any purpose. That ratio is 90 divided by 120 (90 rental plus 30 personal), or 75%, so $9,000 is allocable to rental use. Days the house was vacant are not counted, so using 90 of 365 days ($2,959) is wrong.

q: In December 2025 Paula signed a 1-year lease with a new tenant starting January 1, 2026. She received $2,000 for January rent, $2,000 for the last month's rent, and a $2,000 security deposit she plans to return at the end of the lease. Also in December, a former tenant paid her $3,000 to cancel his lease. Paula uses the cash method. How much rental income must she report for 2025 from these receipts?
explain: Advance rent is income in the year received, regardless of the period covered, so both the January rent and the last month's rent ($4,000) are 2025 income. A payment to cancel a lease is rent in the year received ($3,000). A security deposit she intends to return is not income when received, so the total is $7,000.

q: Lena owns a condo that she rents to vacationers. In 2025 the average guest stay was 5 days, she provided no significant personal services, and she never used the condo personally. She worked 120 hours on the activity, and no other individual worked more hours than she did. The activity produced a loss. Which statement is correct?
choices: The activity is a rental activity, and she can deduct up to $25,000 of the loss under the active participation allowance
The activity is not treated as a rental activity under the passive activity rules, and because she materially participated, the loss is not passive
The loss is passive because all rental activities are passive unless she is a real estate professional
The loss is not deductible because she did not spend more than 500 hours on the activity
explain: An activity in which the average period of customer use is 7 days or less is not a rental activity for the passive activity rules, so the $25,000 allowance for rental real estate does not apply, but the activity is also not automatically passive. Instead, the material participation tests apply, and she meets the test for more than 100 hours with no other individual participating more. Her loss is therefore nonpassive.
source: Treas. Reg. 1.469-1T(e)(3)(ii)(A); Treas. Reg. 1.469-5T(a)(3); IRS Pub 925 (2025)

q: A landlord paid for each of the following on a residential rental property in 2025. Each is a currently deductible repair EXCEPT:
choices: Repainting the interior of a unit between tenants
Patching a small leak in the roof
Replacing a single broken window pane
Replacing the entire roof
explain: An expense must be capitalized as an improvement if it results in a betterment, a restoration or an adaptation of the property; replacing the entire roof is a restoration of a major component of the building, so it is depreciated rather than deducted. Repainting, patching a leak and replacing a broken pane keep the property in ordinary operating condition and are deductible repairs.

q: All of the following are practice before the IRS under Circular 230 EXCEPT:
choices: Corresponding with the IRS on behalf of a client about a proposed adjustment
Representing a client at a conference with a revenue agent
Appearing as a witness for a taxpayer before the IRS
Rendering written advice on a transaction having a potential for tax avoidance
explain: Practice before the IRS covers all matters connected with a presentation to the IRS about a taxpayer's rights, privileges, or liabilities, including corresponding, representing clients at conferences, and rendering written advice on arrangements with avoidance potential. Any individual may appear as a witness for a taxpayer or furnish information at the IRS's request without being a practitioner.

q: Which of the following individuals may represent the taxpayer named before the IRS under the limited practice rules?
choices: A neighbor with tax experience representing a retired couple in an examination
A part-time volunteer bookkeeper representing the nonprofit corporation she helps
A CPA currently suspended from practice before the IRS representing his own father
A regular full-time employee of an individual employer representing that employer
explain: Limited practice lets a regular full-time employee of an individual employer represent that employer, along with immediate family members, bona fide officers or full-time employees of corporations, and similar listed relationships. A person under suspension or disbarment may not engage in limited practice at all, even for a family member, and a neighbor or part-time volunteer is not in any listed category.

q: Dana is an unenrolled preparer who has obtained an Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion every year since 2024, including the current year. In 2025 she prepared and signed Victor's 2024 Form 1040. Which representation may Dana provide for Victor?
choices: Representing him before an Appeals officer after the examination of his 2024 return
Representing him before a revenue officer collecting the balance due on his 2024 return
Representing him in an examination of his 2023 return, which another preparer prepared and signed
Representing him before a revenue agent examining his 2024 return
explain: An Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP) Record of Completion holder may represent clients only for returns she prepared and signed, and only before revenue agents, customer service representatives, and similar IRS employees, including the Taxpayer Advocate Service. She may not represent clients before Appeals or on collection matters, even for a return she prepared.
source: IRS: Understanding Tax Return Preparer Credentials and Qualifications; IRS Pub 947

q: To obtain an Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion, a non-exempt unenrolled preparer must complete 18 hours of continuing education, consisting of:
choices: 6 hours of the Annual Federal Tax Refresher course, 10 hours of other federal tax law, and 2 hours of ethics
15 hours of federal tax law and 3 hours of ethics
16 hours of federal tax law and 2 hours of ethics, with no required course
10 hours of the Annual Federal Tax Refresher course, 6 hours of federal tax law, and 2 hours of ethics
explain: The Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP) requires 18 hours: a 6-hour Annual Federal Tax Refresher (AFTR) course with test, 10 hours of other federal tax law, and 2 hours of ethics. Exempt individuals skip the AFTR course but still need 15 hours (10 federal tax law, 3 federal tax law updates, 2 ethics), and all participants must have an active preparer tax identification number (PTIN) and consent to Circular 230 Subpart B and 10.51.
source: IRS: General Requirements for the Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion

q: Marco is a paid preparer with a valid preparer tax identification number (PTIN) but no professional credential, and he did not participate in the Annual Filing Season Program. He prepared and signed Elena's 2024 return in 2025. If the IRS examines that return, Marco:
choices: May represent Elena before a revenue agent because he signed the return
May represent Elena only if she signs Form 8821
May represent Elena only before customer service representatives
May not represent Elena before the IRS
explain: PTIN holders with no credential and no Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP) Record of Completion may only prepare returns. They may represent clients only for returns prepared and filed on or before December 31, 2015, so a return prepared in 2025 gives Marco no representation rights. Form 8821 only lets a designee receive information.
source: IRS: Understanding Tax Return Preparer Credentials and Qualifications; IRS Pub 947

q: Kim worked continuously for 7 years as an IRS revenue agent regularly applying and interpreting the income tax provisions of the Code. She left the IRS 4 years ago and now wants to become an enrolled agent. Which statement about whether she must pass the Special Enrollment Examination (SEE) is correct?
choices: She may be enrolled without the exam because she has more than 5 years of continuous service
She may be enrolled without the exam only if she passes a suitability check within 1 year
She must pass the SEE because she did not apply within 3 years after leaving the IRS
She must pass only Part 3 of the SEE
explain: A former IRS employee with at least 5 years of continuous qualifying employment may be enrolled without the exam, but the application must be made within 3 years from the date of separation. Kim has the service but waited 4 years, so she must qualify by examination like any other applicant.

q: Omar passed all three parts of the Special Enrollment Examination (SEE), but his application for enrollment was denied because he had not filed two required federal income tax returns. Which statement is correct?
choices: He may file a written protest within 30 days of receiving the denial notice and may reapply once he becomes current on his tax liabilities
He must retake the SEE before he can reapply
He is barred from reapplying for 5 years
He may practice under temporary recognition while his protest is pending
explain: An applicant denied enrollment may file a written protest within 30 days of receiving the notice of denial, and an applicant denied for a tax compliance failure may reapply after becoming current. Temporary recognition is granted only in unusual circumstances and is not automatic while a protest is pending.

q: Under Circular 230, enrolled agents renew their enrollment every 3 years in groups based on the last digit of the Social Security number (SSN). An enrolled agent whose SSN ends in 3 is in the same renewal group as an enrolled agent whose SSN ends in:
explain: Enrolled agents are grouped by the last digit of the SSN (or taxpayer identification number): 0, 1, 2, or 3; 4, 5, or 6; and 7, 8, or 9. An SSN ending in 3 falls in the 0 to 3 group, while 4 belongs to the next group.
source: Treasury Circular 230, 10.6(d); IRS: Enrolled Agent Renewal

q: Paula became an enrolled agent on July 15, 2025, and her first enrollment cycle ends December 31, 2026. What is the minimum continuing education she must complete for this cycle?
choices: 72 hours, including 6 hours of ethics
36 hours, including 4 hours of ethics
34 hours, including 2 hours of ethics
32 hours, including 4 hours of ethics
explain: A new enrollee must complete 2 hours of qualifying continuing education (CE) for each month enrolled during the cycle, and enrollment for any part of a month counts as a full month: July 2025 through December 2026 is 18 months, times 2 hours = 36 hours. She also needs 2 hours of ethics for each enrollment year in the cycle (2025 and 2026), or 4 hours. The full 72-hour requirement applies only to a complete 3-year cycle.

q: An enrolled agent attends a continuous 175-minute live seminar on partnership taxation from a qualified sponsor. How many continuing education (CE) hours may she claim?
explain: A contact hour is 50 minutes of continuous participation, and credit is granted only for full contact hours. 175 minutes divided by 50 is 3.5, so only 3 full contact hours may be claimed.

q: An enrolled agent fails to meet the renewal requirements. After the IRS gives notice and 60 days to respond, she still does not qualify and is placed on the roster of inactive enrolled agents. Which statement is correct?
choices: She may keep practicing until the end of the calendar year
She may still use the term enrolled agent on her letterhead
She may be reinstated by filing a renewal application with proof of the required continuing education (CE), but her status terminates if she does not do so within 3 years
Her enrollment is immediately and permanently revoked
explain: An individual placed in inactive status is ineligible to practice and may not use the enrolled agent designation. She may return to active status by filing a renewal application and showing the required CE, but must do so within three years of being placed in inactive status or her status terminates.

q: A revenue agent asks an enrolled agent to produce a client's 2023 brokerage statements. Neither the enrolled agent nor the client has them. Under Circular 230, the enrolled agent must:
choices: Promptly notify the revenue agent and provide any information she has about who may have the records
Subpoena the brokerage firm for the statements
Independently verify where the records are by contacting third parties
Withdraw from the representation
explain: When the requested records are not in the possession of the practitioner or the client, the practitioner must promptly notify the requesting IRS employee and provide any information about the identity of anyone who may have them. The practitioner must make reasonable inquiry of the client but is not required to contact third parties or independently verify the client's information.

q: While preparing Lena's 2025 return, Sam, an enrolled agent, learns that Lena failed to report $12,000 of consulting income on her 2023 return, which another preparer filed. Under Circular 230, Sam must:
choices: File an amended 2023 return for Lena without her consent
Notify the IRS of the omission
Refuse to prepare her 2025 return until she amends the 2023 return
Promptly advise Lena of the omission and its consequences under the Code and regulations
explain: A practitioner who knows that a client has made an error in or omission from a return must advise the client promptly of the omission and the consequences under the Code and regulations. Circular 230 does not require the practitioner to notify the IRS or to amend the return himself, and the decision to amend belongs to the client.

q: An enrolled agent relies on a staff accountant's work in preparing a client's return, and the staff accountant made an error. Under Circular 230, the enrolled agent is presumed to have exercised due diligence if she:
choices: Used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the staff accountant
Did not personally review the return
Obtained the client's signature on Form 8879
Holds errors and omissions insurance
explain: A practitioner is presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on another person's work if she used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating that person, taking into account the nature of the relationship. Signature forms and insurance have nothing to do with the presumption.

q: An enrolled agent repeatedly ignores a revenue agent's scheduled meeting dates without explanation, hoping the examination will stall until the assessment period runs out. Which Circular 230 section most directly prohibits this conduct?
choices: 10.23, prompt disposition of pending matters
10.26, notaries
10.29, conflicting interests
10.31, negotiation of taxpayer checks
explain: Section 10.23 provides that a practitioner may not unreasonably delay the prompt disposition of any matter before the IRS. Deliberately stalling an examination to run out the statute is exactly that conduct; the other sections address unrelated duties.

q: Beth, an enrolled agent, wants to hire Tom, whom she knows is currently suspended from practice before the IRS. Under Circular 230, Beth may NOT:
choices: Have Tom prepare written responses to an IRS revenue agent's information document request for a client
Hire Tom to answer the office phones
Hire Tom to maintain the office computers
Have Tom schedule client appointments
explain: A practitioner may not knowingly, directly or indirectly, accept assistance from a person under disbarment or suspension if the assistance relates to a matter constituting practice before the IRS (Circular 230, 10.24(a)). Preparing written responses to an IRS document request in an examination is practice before the IRS, so Beth may not use Tom for it.

q: While employed by the IRS, Raj personally and substantially participated as a revenue agent in the examination of Acme Corp's 2022 return. He has now left the IRS and is an enrolled agent. Under Circular 230, Raj may represent Acme Corp in that same examination matter:
choices: After 1 year from leaving the IRS
After 2 years from leaving the IRS
Only with Acme's informed written consent
At no time, because the restriction has no expiration
explain: A former government employee who personally and substantially participated in a particular matter involving specific parties may not represent or knowingly assist any party in that matter, with no time limit. The 2-year rule applies to matters that were only under the employee's official responsibility, and the 1-year rule applies to Treasury rules.

q: Carla is both an enrolled agent and a commissioned notary public. She represents Mr. Ortiz in an IRS examination. Under Circular 230, Carla:
choices: May notarize documents in the matter if she charges no fee
May notarize documents in the matter if Mr. Ortiz consents in writing
May not perform any official act as a notary for a matter in which she is employed as agent
May notarize documents only for her own tax matters
explain: A practitioner may not take acknowledgments, administer oaths, certify papers, or perform any official act as a notary public for any IRS matter in which she is employed as counsel, attorney, or agent, or in which she may be in any way interested. Client consent and waiving the fee do not change the rule.

q: On March 3, 2025, Leo received written notice that the IRS would examine his 2023 return. On May 20, 2025, his enrolled agent filed an amended 2023 return claiming a refund for a missed credit. Under Circular 230, may the enrolled agent charge a contingent fee for the amended return?
choices: No, contingent fees are never allowed for amended returns
Yes, because the amended return was filed within 120 days of Leo receiving written notice of the examination
Yes, but only if the fee is under 20% of the refund
No, because the amended return was filed more than 60 days after the notice
explain: A contingent fee is allowed for an amended return or refund claim filed within 120 days of the taxpayer receiving written notice of an examination of, or written challenge to, the original return. March 3 to May 20 is 78 days, well within the 120-day window.

q: Ivy, an enrolled agent, offers to review clients' prior-year returns and prepare amended returns for a fee equal to 25% of any refund. No IRS examination or challenge is involved. Under Circular 230:
choices: The arrangement is a prohibited contingent fee
The arrangement is permitted because amended returns are not original returns
The arrangement is permitted if the client signs a written fee agreement
The arrangement is permitted if the percentage is reasonable
explain: A fee based on a percentage of the refund reported on a return is a contingent fee, and contingent fees are prohibited except in the listed exceptions. An amended return qualifies only when filed within 120 days of written notice of an examination or challenge, which is not the case here. The key follows the text of Circular 230, 10.27, which is what the exam tests. In Ridgely v. Lew (D.D.C. 2014) a court barred the IRS from enforcing this rule against ordinary refund claims, but the regulation itself was not changed.

q: Ellen, an enrolled agent, has a fee dispute with a client who asks for his records back. Ellen's state law permits a practitioner to retain a client's records during a fee dispute. Under Circular 230, Ellen:
choices: May keep all records until the fee is paid
Must return all records, because Circular 230 overrides state law
Must send the records to the IRS for safekeeping
Need only return the records that must be attached to the client's return, but must give the client reasonable access to review and copy the other necessary records
explain: When state law allows retention in a fee dispute, the practitioner need only return records that must be attached to the taxpayer's return. She must still give the client reasonable access to review and copy any other retained records needed for federal tax compliance.

q: Under Circular 230, the records of the client that a practitioner must return on request include all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Bank statements the client gave the practitioner
A 2023 return the practitioner prepared and was paid for in a prior engagement, which the client needs to prepare his 2025 return
An appraisal prepared by a third party and provided to the practitioner
A 2025 return the practitioner prepared that she is withholding until the client pays the fee for preparing it
explain: Records of the client include documents the client provided, third-party materials provided to the practitioner, and returns the practitioner prepared in a prior representation if the client needs them for current tax obligations. They do not include documents the practitioner prepared that she is withholding pending payment of the fees for those documents.

q: Gary, an enrolled agent, represents two business partners whose interests in an IRS matter may conflict. Each gives informed consent orally at a meeting on June 2. Under Circular 230, the written confirmation of the consent must be obtained:
choices: Before the meeting
Only if the IRS requests it
Within 60 days after the representation ends
Within a reasonable period, but no later than 30 days after the oral consent
explain: Each affected client must waive the conflict by giving informed consent confirmed in writing. The written confirmation may follow the informed consent within a reasonable period, but no later than 30 days.

q: A practitioner obtains written conflict-of-interest consents from two clients. The representation of both clients ends on September 30, 2025. Under Circular 230, the practitioner must keep the consents until at least:
choices: September 30, 2026
September 30, 2027
September 30, 2028
September 30, 2031
explain: Copies of written conflict consents must be retained for at least 36 months from the date the representation of the affected clients ends, and provided to the IRS on request. 36 months after September 30, 2025 is September 30, 2028.

q: Under Circular 230, which statement may an enrolled agent use in an advertisement?
choices: Certified by the IRS to prepare returns
IRS-certified tax specialist
Enrolled to practice before the Internal Revenue Service
Former partner of the IRS
explain: Enrolled agents may describe themselves as enrolled to represent taxpayers before, enrolled to practice before, or admitted to practice before the IRS. They may not use the term certified or imply an employer or employee relationship with the IRS.

q: An enrolled agent publishes a fee of $350 for preparing a basic Form 1040 in a newspaper ad that last ran on February 1, 2025. Under Circular 230, she may not charge more than $350 for that service until at least:
choices: February 15
March 3
May 2
The end of the filing season
explain: A practitioner must charge no more than the published rate for at least 30 calendar days after the last date on which the fee schedule was published. February has 28 days in 2025, so 30 days after February 1 is March 3.

q: A client wants her 2025 federal refund deposited into the enrolled agent's business bank account so the agent can deduct the preparation fee and send her the rest. Under Circular 230, the enrolled agent:
choices: May do so with the client's written consent
May do so if the fee is disclosed on the return
May not direct or accept the refund into an account the practitioner owns or controls
May do so if the account is a trust account
explain: A practitioner may not endorse or otherwise negotiate a government check issued to a client for a federal tax liability, including directing or accepting payment by any means, electronic or otherwise, into an account owned or controlled by the practitioner or an associated firm. Client consent does not create an exception.

q: An enrolled agent drafts a client's will and a trust agreement as part of an estate tax engagement. Which Circular 230 provision addresses this?
choices: 10.32, which states that nothing in Circular 230 authorizes persons who are not members of the bar to practice law
10.27, which treats such services as a contingent fee
10.3, which gives enrolled agents unlimited authority in estate matters
10.37, which permits drafting legal instruments as written advice
explain: Section 10.32 states that nothing in Circular 230 may be construed as authorizing persons who are not members of the bar to practice law. Enrollment gives unlimited representation rights before the IRS, not authority to practice law.

q: A client with $52,000 of wages tells her enrolled agent she gave $40,000 in cash to her church in 2025 but has no receipts. Under Circular 230, the enrolled agent:
choices: May claim the deduction because a practitioner may rely on client information without verification
Must refuse the engagement
Must report the client to the IRS
Must make reasonable inquiries because the information appears incorrect or incomplete
explain: A practitioner generally may rely in good faith without verification on information the client provides, but may not ignore the implications of information known to him and must make reasonable inquiries if it appears incorrect, inconsistent, or incomplete. Large cash gifts relative to income with no records call for inquiry, especially since substantiation rules apply.

q: Under the accuracy-related penalty regulations, the reasonable basis standard is:
choices: A relatively high standard, significantly higher than not frivolous or not patently improper
Met by any position that is not frivolous
The same as the more likely than not standard
Higher than the substantial authority standard
explain: Reasonable basis is a relatively high standard of tax reporting, significantly higher than not frivolous or not patently improper, and it is not met by a merely arguable or colorable claim. It is lower than substantial authority, which in turn is lower than more likely than not.

q: An enrolled agent who has never prepared a return involving a foreign trust accepts such an engagement. Under Circular 230, she may attain the necessary competence by:
choices: Consulting with experts in the relevant area or studying the relevant law
Nothing further, because enrollment establishes competence in all federal tax matters
Obtaining the client's written waiver of competence
Charging a reduced fee
explain: Competent practice requires the knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation needed for the matter. A practitioner may become competent through various methods, such as consulting with experts in the relevant area or studying the relevant law.

q: Under Circular 230, an individual with principal authority for overseeing a firm's federal tax practice may be disciplined if he:
choices: Through willfulness, recklessness, or gross incompetence fails to take reasonable steps to ensure the firm has adequate compliance procedures, and firm members engage in a pattern or practice of noncompliance
Has any employee who makes a single inadvertent math error
Delegates return review to another enrolled agent
Shares this authority with another partner
explain: Individuals who have or share principal authority must take reasonable steps to ensure adequate compliance procedures, and are subject to discipline for willful, reckless, or grossly incompetent failures that are accompanied by a pattern or practice of noncompliance, or for failing to act promptly on a known pattern. A single inadvertent error by staff does not meet that standard, and more than one person may share the authority.

q: When giving written advice on a federal tax matter, a practitioner may NOT:
choices: Base the advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions
Rely in good faith on the reasonable advice of another competent person
Take into account the possibility that the return will not be audited
Relate the applicable law to the relevant facts
explain: Circular 230 requires written advice to rest on reasonable assumptions, consider all relevant facts, and relate the law to the facts. In evaluating a federal tax matter, the practitioner may not take into account the possibility that a return will not be audited or that a matter will not be raised on audit.

q: Under Circular 230, all of the following are incompetence and disreputable conduct EXCEPT:
choices: Willfully failing to file one's own federal tax return
Willfully preparing a return for compensation without a current or otherwise valid preparer tax identification number (PTIN)
Advertising a fixed fee for preparing Form 1040
Being suspended from practice as a CPA by a state licensing authority
explain: Disreputable conduct includes willfully failing to file a required federal return, willfully preparing or signing returns without a valid PTIN, and disbarment or suspension as an attorney, CPA, or actuary by a state or federal authority. Publishing fixed fees for routine services is expressly permitted by 10.30(b).

q: Under Circular 230, a practitioner may be sanctioned for violating the standards in 10.34 (returns), 10.35 (competence), 10.36 (procedures), or 10.37 (written advice) if the violation was:
choices: Willful only
Willful, reckless, or the result of gross incompetence
The result of any negligence
Committed on at least 3 returns
