explain: A practitioner may be sanctioned for willfully violating any Part 10 rule other than 10.33, and for recklessly or through gross incompetence violating 10.34, 10.35, 10.36, or 10.37. Ordinary negligence is not the standard, and the best practices in 10.33 are aspirational.

q: Which statement about sanctions under Circular 230 is correct?
choices: A censure bars the practitioner from practice for 1 year
A disbarred practitioner is automatically reinstated after 5 years
A monetary penalty may be imposed only on the individual practitioner, never on the firm
A monetary penalty may not exceed the gross income derived or to be derived from the conduct, and may be imposed in addition to or instead of censure, suspension, or disbarment
explain: A censure is a public reprimand and the practitioner may continue to practice, possibly subject to conditions. A monetary penalty may not exceed the gross income derived or to be derived from the conduct, may be in addition to or in lieu of other sanctions, and may also be imposed on a firm that knew or reasonably should have known of the conduct. Reinstatement after disbarment requires a petition, not an automatic return.

q: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who was disbarred from practice before the IRS may petition for reinstatement:
choices: After 1 year
After 3 years
After 5 years
Never
explain: A disbarred or suspended practitioner may petition for reinstatement after 5 years following the sanction, or immediately after a shorter suspension ends. Reinstatement is granted only if the IRS is satisfied the person is not likely to engage in further misconduct and reinstatement is not contrary to the public interest.

q: A taxpayer files a Collection Due Process hearing request based solely on a position the IRS has identified as frivolous, and the IRS notifies him that it is a specified frivolous submission. Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6702, he can avoid the frivolous submission penalty by:
choices: Paying the underlying tax within 90 days
Withdrawing the submission within 30 days after the notice
Requesting a Tax Court review
Filing Form 843
explain: The 6702(b) penalty applies to specified submissions, including collection due process (CDP) hearing requests, installment agreement and offer in compromise applications, and taxpayer assistance order applications, that rest on a frivolous position or reflect a desire to delay or impede tax administration. The penalty does not apply if the person withdraws the submission within 30 days after the IRS notice.

q: The IRS treats all of the following as badges (indicators) of fraud EXCEPT:
choices: Keeping two sets of books
Inability to explain substantial increases in net worth over several years
Destroying records just after an examination begins
Following the advice of the taxpayer's return preparer
explain: Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) indicators of fraud include multiple sets of books, unexplained increases in net worth, destruction of records especially after an examination starts, and failure to follow the advice of an accountant, attorney, or return preparer. Following a preparer's advice is the opposite of the listed indicator.

q: Ana, a paid preparer, charged $3,000 to prepare a return that takes an undisclosed position lacking substantial authority, and she knew or reasonably should have known of the position. There is no reasonable cause. What is her Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6694(a) penalty for that return?
explain: The 6694(a) penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived (or to be derived) from the return. 50% of $3,000 = $1,500, which exceeds $1,000. 75% applies only under 6694(b).

q: A preparer earned an $8,000 fee for a return on which he willfully understated the client's tax. He is assessed and pays a 6694(a) penalty of $4,000 for the same return. What additional amount does he owe under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6694(b)?
explain: The 6694(b) penalty is the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived: 75% of $8,000 = $6,000. Under 6694(b)(3) it is reduced by the $4,000 already paid under 6694(a), so the additional amount is $2,000 and the total is $6,000.

q: For a position that is NOT a tax shelter or reportable transaction, a preparer avoids the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6694(a) unreasonable position penalty if:
choices: There is substantial authority for the position, or the position is properly disclosed and has a reasonable basis
The position has a reasonable basis, whether or not disclosed
The position is more likely than not to be sustained, in all cases
The client signs a statement accepting responsibility
explain: A position is unreasonable unless there is substantial authority for it, or, if it is properly disclosed, there is a reasonable basis for it. For tax shelters and reportable transactions, the preparer must reasonably believe the position would more likely than not be sustained.

q: A preparer receives notice and demand for an Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6694(a) penalty and wants to contest it without paying the full amount. He must:
choices: Petition the Tax Court within 90 days
File Form 12153 within 30 days
Pay 25% of the penalty within 60 days and request a collection due process (CDP) hearing

Within 30 days of the notice and demand, pay at least 15% of the penalty and file a claim for refund, then sue in district court within 30 days after the claim is denied or, if it is not acted on, within 30 days after 6 months from filing
explain: Deficiency procedures do not apply to preparer penalties, so there is no Tax Court petition. The preparer may pay at least 15% within 30 days after notice and demand and file a refund claim; collection of the rest is then stayed if he begins a district court suit within 30 days after the claim is denied or after 6 months pass without action.

q: Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6107(a), a paid preparer must furnish the taxpayer a completed copy of the return:
choices: Within 30 days after filing
By the return's due date
Only if the taxpayer requests it in writing
Not later than the time the return is presented for the taxpayer's signature
explain: A tax return preparer must furnish a completed copy of the return or claim to the taxpayer not later than the time it is presented for the taxpayer's signature. Failure triggers the 6695(a) penalty unless due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect.

q: Jill, the signing preparer who completed a client's paper return, is unexpectedly hospitalized. Under the regulations, another preparer in her firm may sign the return if he:
choices: Reviews the entire preparation of the return and then signs it as preparer
Has a preparer tax identification number (PTIN) and signs Jill's name
Obtains the taxpayer's consent to sign without review
Signs only the taxpayer's name
explain: If the signing preparer is unavailable, another preparer must review the entire preparation of the return and then sign it. Signing another person's name or signing without review would subject the firm to the 6695(b) penalty for failure to sign properly.

q: A tax firm employs the following people. Who is required to have a preparer tax identification number (PTIN)?
choices: A receptionist who scans client documents
A data entry clerk who keys in figures without making any substantive determinations
An employee who interviews clients and decides what to enter on their returns using software, but does not sign them
An outside expert who advises on a single credit without preparing substantially all of any return
explain: A PTIN is required of any individual who is compensated for preparing, or assisting in preparing, all or substantially all of a return or claim for refund, even if he does not sign. Clerical workers who make no substantive determinations and an outside expert who advises on one item are not required to have one.

q: Which statement about preparer tax identification numbers (PTINs) is correct?
choices: A PTIN is issued once and never expires
A PTIN expires on December 31 of the year for which it is issued and must be renewed for the next year
Enrolled agents who do not prepare returns do not need a PTIN
A preparer may use the employer identification number (EIN) of his employer in place of a PTIN
explain: PTINs expire on December 31 of the calendar year for which they are issued, so preparers renew annually. All enrolled agents must have a valid PTIN to maintain active status, and the preparer's own PTIN, not the employer's EIN, goes in the preparer identification field (the EIN is reported separately for the firm).
source: IRS News: PTIN Renewal Period; Treas. Reg. 1.6109-2(a) and (e); Treasury Circular 230, 10.4(a)

q: Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6060 and its regulations, a person who employs signing tax return preparers must keep a record of each preparer employed during the return period, showing the preparer's:
choices: Name, taxpayer identification number, and principal place of work
Name and number of returns prepared
Name, compensation, and credentials
Name, home address, and date of hire
explain: The employer must retain a record of the name, taxpayer identification number, and principal place of work of each signing preparer employed during the return period, the 12-month period beginning July 1, and keep it available for inspection for 3 years after the close of that period. Failures are subject to the 6695(e) penalty.

q: A paid preparer endorses a client's federal refund check and cashes it, keeping the preparation fee and giving the client the rest. Which statement is correct?
choices: This is allowed if the client signs a written authorization
Only Circular 230 applies, so non-enrolled preparers face no penalty
This is allowed if the preparer is also an enrolled agent
The preparer is subject to the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6695(f) penalty for negotiating the check
explain: IRC 6695(f) imposes a penalty on any preparer who endorses or negotiates a refund check issued to a taxpayer for a return the preparer prepared. The only exception is for a bank that is a preparer and deposits the full check into the taxpayer's account (or cashes it and remits all of it) without having made a loan against the refund; Circular 230 10.31 separately bars practitioners.

q: A paid preparer files a 2025 return claiming head of household status, the earned income credit, the child tax credit, and the American opportunity tax credit (AOTC). She met the due diligence requirements only for the AOTC. How many Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6695(g) penalties may apply to this return?
explain: A separate 6695(g) penalty applies for the head of household (HOH) determination and for each credit for which due diligence was not met. She failed for HOH, the earned income credit (EIC), and the child tax credit (CTC), so three penalties may apply, and none applies to the AOTC.

q: A signing preparer e-filed a client's 2025 return claiming the earned income credit on March 10, 2026; the return was due April 15, 2026. Under the due diligence regulations, the preparer must keep Form 8867 and the supporting records until at least:
choices: March 10, 2028
April 15, 2028
March 10, 2029
April 15, 2029
explain: Due diligence records must be kept for 3 years from the latest of the return's due date (without extensions) or, for a signing preparer who e-files, the date the return was filed. The later date is April 15, 2026, so the records must be kept until April 15, 2029.

q: For 2025, Maria (who claims no qualified business income deduction) reported tax of $73,000. The correct tax was $80,000. Is the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6662 substantial understatement penalty triggered?
choices: Yes, because the understatement exceeds $5,000
Yes, because any understatement over 5% is substantial
No, because the $7,000 understatement does not exceed $8,000, the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000
No, because the penalty applies only to corporations
explain: For an individual, an understatement is substantial if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown or $5,000. The understatement is $80,000 - $73,000 = $7,000, and 10% of $80,000 = $8,000, which is greater than $5,000, so $7,000 is not substantial. The 5% figure applies only to taxpayers claiming a 199A deduction.

q: A C corporation (not a personal holding company) reported tax of $2,750,000 for 2025. The correct tax was $3,000,000. Does the corporation have a substantial understatement under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6662?
choices: Yes, because the understatement exceeds $10,000
Yes, because the understatement exceeds 5% of the correct tax
No, because the $250,000 understatement does not exceed $300,000
No, because corporations are subject only to the $10,000,000 test
explain: For a C corporation, an understatement is substantial if it exceeds the lesser of 10% of the tax required to be shown (or $10,000 if greater) or $10,000,000. 10% of $3,000,000 = $300,000, which is less than $10,000,000, and the $250,000 understatement does not exceed it.

q: On his 2025 return, Ken claimed a value for property that was 225% of its correct value, causing a $14,000 underpayment. What is his accuracy-related penalty?
explain: A claimed value of 150% or more of the correct amount is a substantial valuation misstatement (20%), but 200% or more is a gross valuation misstatement, which raises the rate to 40%. 225% is gross, so the penalty is 40% x $14,000 = $5,600.

q: Under the regulations, negligence for purposes of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6662 accuracy-related penalty is strongly indicated when a taxpayer:
choices: Takes a position supported by substantial authority
Fails to include on a return an amount of income shown on an information return
Files on extension
Relies on a revenue ruling that is later revoked
explain: Negligence is strongly indicated when a taxpayer fails to include income shown on an information return, or fails to make a reasonable attempt to check a deduction or credit that would seem too good to be true. Negligence also includes failing to keep adequate books and records or to substantiate items.

q: The IRS proves that part of Carl's $40,000 underpayment is attributable to fraud. Carl cannot show that any portion is not due to fraud. Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6663, his civil fraud penalty is:
explain: Once the IRS establishes that any portion of an underpayment is attributable to fraud, the entire underpayment is treated as fraud unless the taxpayer proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence. The penalty is 75% x $40,000 = $30,000, and the 20% accuracy-related penalty does not apply to the same portion.

q: Under the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7216 regulations, a preparer who wants to use a client's return information to market non-tax financial products must obtain the client's written consent:
choices: Before the information is used, in a signed and dated consent; if no duration is stated, it is effective for 1 year from the date signed
Within 30 days after using the information
Only if the information is disclosed outside the firm
As a condition of preparing the return
explain: Consent must be obtained before any use or disclosure, must be knowing and voluntary, and must be signed and dated by the taxpayer. If the consent states no duration, it is effective for one year from the date signed, and conditioning return preparation on consent makes it involuntary.

q: The IRS receives a client's Form 2848 on June 10, 2025. Line 3 lists "Income, 1040, 2021 through 2030." Which tax years will the IRS record on the Centralized Authorization File (CAF) system?
choices: 2021 through 2025 only
2021 through 2028
2021 through 2030
None, because a Form 2848 that lists future years is returned
explain: The IRS will not record future years that go more than 3 years past December 31 of the year it receives the form. December 31, 2025 plus 3 years is December 31, 2028, so 2021 through 2028 are recorded and 2029 and 2030 are not. Listing future years is allowed, so the form is not returned for that reason.

q: Marco and Elena filed a joint 2024 Form 1040. Both want the same enrolled agent to represent them in the examination of that return. How should the power of attorney be handled?
choices: One Form 2848 signed by both spouses is sufficient
Only the spouse listed first on the return needs to file Form 2848
No Form 2848 is needed because the enrolled agent prepared the return
Each spouse must file a separate Form 2848, even though they name the same representative
explain: When spouses give powers of attorney for a joint return, each must submit a separate Form 2848, even if they authorize the same representative. A single form signed by both spouses is not accepted, and preparing the return does not by itself authorize representation.

q: Which statement about who signs Form 2848 for a taxpayer that is not an individual is correct?
choices: For a corporation, any shareholder who owns at least 10% of the stock may sign
For an estate with three co-executors, all three co-executors must sign
For a trust, a trustee with authority to bind the trust signs, and Form 56 is attached to identify the current trustee
For a partnership under the centralized audit regime of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 (BBA), every partner must sign
explain: A trustee with authority to bind the trust signs with the title of trustee, and Form 56 is attached to identify the trustee. A corporation signs through an officer with legal authority to bind it, an estate needs only one co-executor with authority to bind the estate, and a BBA partnership signs through its partnership representative (or designated individual).

q: A law student working in a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic is named on a client's Form 2848 under designation k. The taxpayer signed the form on February 3, 2025. If nothing else is filed, what happens to the student's authorization on the Centralized Authorization File (CAF)?
choices: It stays on the CAF until the taxpayer revokes it
It expires 45 days after the taxpayer signed
The CAF automatically removes the student 130 days after the taxpayer's signature date
It expires at the end of the calendar year
explain: Qualifying students and law graduates use designation k and must be authorized under Circular 230 section 10.7(d). The CAF automatically purges the student or law graduate as representative 130 days after the taxpayer's signature date. The 45-day period is the time a representative has to sign after the taxpayer signs, not an expiration date.
source: Form 2848 instructions (Rev. 09/2021), Part II designation k; Circular 230, 10.7(d)

q: Unless line 5b limits the authority, a representative named on Form 2848 may do all of the following for the listed tax matters EXCEPT:
choices: Sign a consent to extend the time to assess tax
Sign a closing agreement
Receive and inspect the taxpayer's confidential tax information
Endorse or negotiate a refund check issued to the taxpayer
explain: A representative may generally perform any act the taxpayer can perform for the listed matters, including signing agreements, consents and waivers such as a statute extension or closing agreement. Representatives are never authorized to endorse or otherwise negotiate a government check issued for a federal tax liability, including directing it into an account they control.

q: Under Treas. Reg. 1.6012-1(a)(5), a representative may sign a client's income tax return, if Form 2848 specifically grants that authority, in which situation?
choices: The client is too busy with work to review the return before the due date
The client has been continuously in Puerto Rico for 90 days before the due date
The client has been continuously outside the United States for at least 60 days before the due date
The client wants the return e-filed a few days sooner
explain: An agent may sign an income tax return only for disease or injury, continuous absence from the United States for at least 60 days before the due date, or other good cause with specific IRS permission. Puerto Rico is treated as part of the United States for this rule, so time spent there does not count as absence. The authority must be granted on line 5a, and an agent who files a paper return attaches the Form 2848.

q: A client's Form 2848 names enrolled agent Rosa and specifically allows her to substitute or delegate. Rosa properly files the documents to substitute enrolled agent Daniel for herself. Who is now recognized as the client's representative?
choices: Only Daniel
Both Rosa and Daniel
Only Rosa, until the client signs a new Form 2848
Neither, until the IRS approves the change in writing
explain: After a substitution, only the newly recognized representative is the taxpayer's representative. After a delegation, both the original and the new representative are recognized. Either action is allowed only when the power of attorney specifically permits it.

q: A client wants to revoke a Form 2848 that names her former enrolled agent, without naming anyone new. She has a copy of the form. How should she revoke it?
choices: Call the Practitioner Priority Service and ask that the representative be removed
Write "REVOKE" across the top of the first page, sign and date it below that, and mail or fax it to the IRS
File a new Form 2848 that lists no representative
Have the former enrolled agent file Form 56
explain: To revoke without naming a new representative, the taxpayer writes "REVOKE" across the top of the first page with a current signature and date and sends it to the IRS. Without a copy, she sends a signed and dated statement listing the matters, periods and representatives being revoked. A representative who wants out instead writes "WITHDRAW" on the form in the same way.
source: Form 2848 instructions (Rev. 09/2021), Revocation of power of attorney; IRS Pub 947

q: In 2025 a client has a Form 2848 on the Centralized Authorization File (CAF) naming CPA Lee for income tax, 2022 through 2024. She then files a new Form 2848 naming enrolled agent Ortiz for the same matters. She does not check line 6 or attach a copy of the earlier form. What is the result?
choices: Lee and Ortiz are both authorized
The IRS rejects the new form until Lee withdraws
Lee's authority is generally revoked, and only Ortiz is authorized for those matters
Lee stays the primary representative and Ortiz only receives copies of notices
explain: When the IRS records a new Form 2848 on the CAF, it generally revokes earlier powers of attorney for the same matters. To keep Lee, the client had to check the line 6 box and attach a copy of each power of attorney she wanted to remain in effect.

q: A client has a Form 8821 on file naming her bookkeeper for 2023 and 2024 income tax. She later files Form 2848 naming an enrolled agent for the same years and does not mention the Form 8821. What happens to the bookkeeper's authorization?
choices: It remains in effect, because filing Form 2848 does not revoke a Form 8821
It is automatically revoked when the Form 2848 is recorded
It is converted into a power of attorney for the bookkeeper
It is suspended until the enrolled agent's representation ends
explain: The Form 2848 instructions state that filing Form 2848 will not revoke any Form 8821 in effect. A new Form 2848 revokes earlier Forms 2848 for the same matters, and a new Form 8821 revokes earlier Forms 8821, unless the taxpayer keeps them, but the two forms do not cancel each other.
source: Form 2848 instructions (Rev. 09/2021), Line 6; Form 8821 instructions (Rev. 09/2021), Line 5

q: A client gives her enrolled agent a power of attorney drafted by her lawyer instead of Form 2848. It contains all the information the IRS requires. What must the enrolled agent do to have it recorded on the Centralized Authorization File (CAF)?
choices: Nothing; the IRS records any power of attorney valid under state law
Have the client sign a new Form 2848, which replaces the lawyer's document
Have the document notarized and filed with Form 56
Attach a completed Form 2848; the client does not have to sign it, but the enrolled agent must sign the Part II declaration
explain: The IRS accepts a power of attorney other than Form 2848 if it meets the requirements of section 601.503(a) of the IRS Statement of Procedural Rules. It can be recorded on the CAF only if a completed Form 2848 is attached. Because the other document is the operative grant, the taxpayer need not sign the attached Form 2848, but the representative must sign the Declaration of Representative.

q: Walter has become incapacitated. Years ago he signed a durable power of attorney valid under state law naming his friend Gina, who is not eligible to practice before the IRS. The document lacks some of the information the IRS requires. Which statement is correct?
choices: Gina may sign Form 2848 for Walter naming an individual who is eligible to practice, and attach a statement signed under penalty of perjury that the durable power of attorney is valid under state law
No one can act for Walter before the IRS because any power of attorney ends when the taxpayer becomes incapacitated
Gina may represent Walter herself under designation f (family member)
The IRS will act only on a court guardianship order
explain: A power of attorney generally ends on incapacity, but a durable power of attorney continues. If the durable document lacks required information, the attorney-in-fact may sign Form 2848 for the taxpayer with a statement under penalty of perjury that the document is valid under the governing state law. Because Gina cannot practice before the IRS and is not a family member, she must name someone who can.
source: IRS Pub 947 (Rev. 02/2018), Non-IRS powers of attorney; 26 CFR 601.503(b)(4)

q: An enrolled agent gets a client's electronic signature on Form 2848 through a remote signing platform. How may the form be submitted to the IRS?
choices: By fax to the Centralized Authorization File (CAF) unit for the client's state
Online, using the IRS submission tool at IRS.gov/Submit2848
By mail, with a cover letter confirming the electronic signature
By any method, as long as the enrolled agent also signs electronically
explain: Forms 2848 with electronic or digitized signatures must be submitted online. Digital, electronic or typed-font signatures are not valid on forms filed by mail or fax. For a remote electronic signature, the submitter must also authenticate the taxpayer's identity.
source: Form 2848 instructions (Rev. 09/2021), Where To File; Electronic signatures

q: Which statement about a Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number is correct?
choices: It is the same number as the representative's preparer tax identification number (PTIN)
It shows that the holder is authorized to practice before the IRS
It must be renewed each enrollment cycle
It is a unique nine-digit number the IRS assigns to a representative, and it does not indicate authority to practice
explain: The CAF number is a unique nine-digit identifier the IRS assigns to a representative. It is not a Social Security number (SSN), employer identification number (EIN), PTIN or enrollment card number, and having one does not mean the person is recognized or authorized to practice. A representative without one enters "None" and the IRS issues one.

q: A client wants to authorize her outside accounting firm, organized as a partnership, as a single entity to receive her tax information. Which form allows this?
choices: Form 8821, because a designee may be an individual, corporation, firm, organization or partnership
Form 2848, because a firm may be named as representative if it employs an enrolled agent
Either form, at the client's choice
Neither form; only individuals may be named on either form
explain: Form 8821 can name any individual, corporation, firm, organization or partnership to inspect or receive tax information. Form 2848 authorizes an individual who is eligible to practice before the IRS, so a firm cannot be the named representative.
source: Form 8821 instructions (Rev. 09/2021); Form 2848 instructions (Rev. 09/2021), Purpose of Form

q: A mortgage lender has a borrower sign Form 8821 so the lender can verify the borrower's income. The form is not being used to resolve a tax matter. When must the IRS receive it?
choices: Within 45 days of the taxpayer's signature date
Within 60 days of the taxpayer's signature date
Within 120 days of the taxpayer's signature date
At any time within 3 years after the year it is signed
explain: When Form 8821 authorizes disclosure for income verification and not for help with a tax matter, the IRS must receive it within 120 days of the taxpayer's signature date. The 120-day rule does not apply when the form is used to resolve a tax matter.

q: Under the IRS Conference and Practice Requirements, when should a written protest or supporting statement for a scheduled conference generally be submitted?
choices: At the start of the conference
At least 5 business days before the conference
At least 30 calendar days before the conference
Within 10 days after the conference
explain: Written submissions should reach the IRS official at least five business days before the conference, and if that is not possible the conference should be postponed to a mutually agreeable date. Additional supporting facts may be submitted within a reasonable time after the conference.

q: During an examination, a revenue agent has asked an enrolled agent several times for the client's nonprivileged bank statements. The enrolled agent keeps failing to provide them, and the exam has stalled. What may the revenue agent do?
choices: Contact the client directly for the information, after getting permission from the agent's immediate supervisor
Disqualify the enrolled agent from the case immediately
Issue a notice of deficiency the next day without further contact
Nothing, because the IRS may never bypass a recognized representative
explain: When a representative unreasonably delays or hinders an examination by not furnishing nonprivileged information after repeated requests, the employee may ask the immediate supervisor for permission to contact the taxpayer directly. Bypassing the representative does not by itself disqualify the representative, though the matter may be referred to the Office of Professional Responsibility.

q: A preparer finishes a client's 2025 return and hands it to the client to sign. At that moment she asks the client to sign a consent allowing her to share the client's return information with her insurance agency affiliate. Is this request permitted under the 7216 regulations?
choices: Yes, as long as the consent is signed and dated
Yes, if the consent lasts no more than one year
No, because a consent for solicitation of business unrelated to tax return preparation cannot be requested after the completed return is provided to the taxpayer for signature
No, because return information may never be disclosed to anyone outside the preparer's firm
explain: Reg. 301.7216-3(b)(2) bars requesting consent to use or disclose return information to solicit business unrelated to tax return preparation after the preparer provides the completed return for signature. Disclosures with a valid consent are allowed in general, so the timing is the problem here.

q: Without obtaining a consent under the 7216 regulations, a tax return preparer may do all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Use the client's federal return information to prepare the client's state income tax return
Use the client's return information to market the preparer's life insurance products to that client
Compile a list of client names and addresses to solicit additional tax return preparation services
Disclose the client's return information to the IRS
explain: Using return information to solicit products or services other than tax return preparation requires a written consent. Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7216(b) and Reg. 301.7216-2 allow, without consent, use to prepare the taxpayer's state or local returns, a client list used only to solicit tax return preparation services, and disclosures to the IRS.

q: An enrolled agent wants to see whether the IRS assessed penalties, posted payments and made adjustments to a client's 2023 account after the return was filed. Which transcript should she request?
choices: Tax return transcript
Wage and income transcript
Verification of non-filing letter
Tax account transcript
explain: A tax account transcript shows basic return data plus changes made after filing, such as assessments, penalties and payments. A tax return transcript shows the line items from the original return as filed and does not reflect later changes. A record of account combines the two.
source: IRS, Transcript types for individuals and ways to order them; IRS Transcript Delivery System page

q: A client has not filed returns for several years and kept no records. To retrieve the client's transcripts through the Transcript Delivery System (TDS), what does the enrolled agent need?
choices: A properly executed Form 2848 or Form 8821 for the client on file with the IRS, plus access to e-Services
A Form 4506 signed by the client for each year
The client's IRS Online Account username and password
A Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request for each year
explain: TDS is available to Circular 230 practitioners and electronic return originators (EROs), but only when a properly executed Form 2848 or Form 8821 is on file for the client. A wage and income transcript from TDS then shows W-2 and 1099 data for the unfiled years. Using the client's own login credentials is not the authorized method.
source: IRS Transcript Delivery System (TDS) page; Form 8821 instructions; Form 2848 instructions (Rev. 09/2021)

q: Midway through a civil examination, a revenue agent who had been asking about large cash deposits abruptly suspends the exam and will not say why. What is the best course for the enrolled agent?
choices: Keep sending the agent explanations of the deposits to speed things up
Treat it as routine and wait for the 30-day letter
Recognize that this can signal a possible fraud referral to Criminal Investigation, stop volunteering information and advise the client to consult a criminal tax attorney
Rely on the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7525 privilege to protect all further communications with the client
explain: Under Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 25.1.3.3, when an examiner develops firm indications of fraud, the examiner suspends the exam without disclosing the reason to the taxpayer or representative. A sudden unexplained suspension is a red flag, and the client needs criminal tax counsel. The 7525 privilege does not apply in criminal matters, so communications with an enrolled agent would not be protected.

q: The Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) lists "badges" (indicators) of fraud that examiners look for. All of the following are badges of fraud EXCEPT:
choices: Keeping two sets of books
Omitting an entire source of income
Being unable to explain dealings in large sums of currency
Taking a deduction based on a reasonable reading of an unclear regulation
explain: Indicators of fraud include multiple sets of books or no records, omitting entire sources of income, unexplained dealings in currency and attempts to hinder the exam. A good-faith position on an unclear rule is not an indicator of fraud. No single indicator proves fraud; fraud is shown through affirmative acts.

q: A family of four reports monthly spending on food, clothing, housekeeping supplies, personal care and miscellaneous items that is less than the IRS National Standards amount for a family of four. How much does the IRS allow for these items on the collection financial statement?
choices: The full National Standards amount for their family size, without questioning the amount actually spent
Only the amount actually spent
The lesser of the amount actually spent or the National Standards amount
Nothing, until receipts are provided for each category
explain: Taxpayers are allowed the total National Standards amount monthly for their family size without questioning the amount actually spent. The lesser-of-actual-or-standard rule applies to most Local Standards, such as housing and utilities, not to the National Standards.

q: A taxpayer's actual monthly rent and utilities are $2,600. The IRS Local Standard for housing and utilities for her county and family size is $2,200. She cannot full pay her liability within six years. How much will the IRS generally allow for housing and utilities?
choices: $2,400, the average of the two
$0, because housing is a conditional expense
explain: For Local Standards such as housing and utilities, the taxpayer is allowed the amount actually spent or the standard, whichever is less. The lesser of $2,600 and $2,200 is $2,200. Higher actual expenses may be allowed only if the taxpayer shows the standard is inadequate.

q: A taxpayer owes $30,000 and can full pay the entire liability, including projected penalties and interest, within six years and before the collection statute expires. Her housing costs exceed the Local Standard, and she makes minimum credit card payments. Which is correct?
choices: The IRS must cap every expense at the published standards
Credit card payments are never allowed in a collection financial analysis
She must substantiate every expense with receipts before an agreement can be considered
Under the six-year rule, the IRS may allow expenses above the standards, including minimum credit card payments, if the liability can be paid in full within six years
explain: The six-year rule lets the IRS allow living expenses above the standards and other expenses, such as minimum credit card payments, when the liability can be paid in full within six years. The taxpayer provides financial information but generally does not have to substantiate reasonable expenses.
source: IRS Collection Financial Standards (Six-Year Rule); IRM 5.14.1.4.1

q: Nina timely filed her 2021 Form 1040 on April 18, 2022, showing a balance due she never paid. The tax was assessed in May 2022. There was no fraud. She files a Chapter 7 petition on March 1, 2025. Is the 2021 income tax dischargeable?
choices: Yes, because the return was filed on time
Yes, because the tax was assessed more than 240 days before the petition
No, because the return was last due within 3 years before the petition
No, because income taxes can never be discharged in bankruptcy
explain: Income tax is a priority debt, and not discharged, if the return was last due, including extensions, within 3 years before the petition. The 2021 return was due April 18, 2022, which is less than 3 years before March 1, 2025. Meeting the 240-day assessment test does not help when the 3-year test fails.

q: Omar timely filed his 2018 return on April 1, 2019. After he signed Form 872 extending the assessment period, an exam ended with additional tax assessed on September 1, 2024. He has never submitted an offer in compromise and has no prior bankruptcy. He files a Chapter 7 petition on February 1, 2025. Is the additional tax dischargeable?
choices: No, because it was assessed within 240 days before the petition
Yes, because the return was due more than 3 years before the petition
Yes, because the return was filed more than 2 years before the petition
No, because signing Form 872 makes the tax nondischargeable
explain: Tax assessed within 240 days before the petition is a priority tax that is not discharged. September 1, 2024 to February 1, 2025 is 153 days, which is within 240 days. The 3-year and 2-year tests are met, but all three must be satisfied.

q: Victor never filed a 2017 return. In 2020 the IRS prepared a substitute for return under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6020(b) and assessed the tax. Victor files a Chapter 7 petition in 2025 and still has not filed a 2017 return. There was no fraud. Is the 2017 tax dischargeable?
choices: Yes, because more than 3 years have passed since the return due date
Yes, because the tax was assessed more than 240 days before the petition
No, because a return prepared by the IRS under IRC 6020(b) is not a "return" for discharge purposes, so no return was filed
No, because any tax over 5 years old is excluded from bankruptcy
explain: Tax is not discharged if a required return was not filed. The Bankruptcy Code's definition of "return" includes one prepared under IRC 6020(a) with the taxpayer's cooperation but excludes an IRS substitute for return under 6020(b). A late-filed return filed within 2 years before the petition also blocks discharge.
source: 11 USC 523(a)(1)(B) and flush language of 523(a); IRC 6020

q: A client finds a private letter ruling issued to an unrelated taxpayer on facts nearly identical to his own. Which statement is correct?
choices: The client may rely on it as binding precedent against the IRS
It may not be used or cited as precedent; it binds the IRS only for the taxpayer who requested it, if the facts were fully and accurately described
It has the same weight as a revenue ruling
It has the force and effect of a Treasury regulation
explain: Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6110(k)(3), a written determination such as a private letter ruling (PLR) may not be used or cited as precedent. A PLR binds the IRS only for the requesting taxpayer. A revenue ruling, which is published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin, carries more weight than a PLR.
source: IRC 6110(k)(3); IRS, Understanding IRS Guidance: A Brief Primer

q: Which statement about temporary Treasury regulations is correct?
choices: They are binding only on the IRS, never on taxpayers
They remain in effect until Congress repeals them
They may be issued without notice and expire after 1 year
They must also be issued as proposed regulations and expire within 3 years after issuance
explain: Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7805(e) requires every temporary regulation to also be issued as a proposed regulation, and it expires within 3 years after it is issued. Temporary regulations are effective when published in the Federal Register.

q: For purposes of the substantial authority standard in Treas. Reg. 1.6662-4, all of the following count as authority EXCEPT:
choices: Proposed regulations
A private letter ruling issued after October 31, 1976
Revenue procedures
A conclusion reached in a respected tax treatise
explain: The regulation lists the Code, proposed, temporary and final regulations, revenue rulings and procedures, treaties, court cases, committee reports, the Blue Book, private letter rulings (PLRs) and technical advice memorandums (TAMs) issued after October 31, 1976, and other Bulletin guidance as authority. Conclusions in treatises, legal periodicals and opinions of tax professionals are not authority, though the sources they cite may be.

q: A client relied on an example in an IRS publication that turns out to misstate the law, and an understatement results. Which statement is correct?
choices: The publication binds the IRS, so the client owes no additional tax
The law controls the client's tax liability, but reasonable good-faith reliance on the publication is considered in deciding whether penalties apply
The client is automatically liable for the 20% accuracy-related penalty
The client may cite the publication as precedent in Tax Court
explain: IRS publications are informal guidance that is not published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin, so they are not binding on the IRS and have no precedential value. If informal guidance misstates the law, the law controls, but the taxpayer's reasonable reliance is relevant to penalties that have a reasonable cause standard.
source: IRS, General overview of taxpayer reliance on guidance published in the Internal Revenue Bulletin and FAQs; IRM 4.10.7.2

q: A provision of a U.S. income tax treaty conflicts with a provision of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). Under IRC 7852(d), which statement is correct?
choices: The treaty always prevails because treaties are ratified by the Senate
The Code always prevails because it is domestic law
Neither the treaty nor the law has preferential status by reason of its being a treaty or a law
The IRS chooses whichever provision produces more tax
explain: IRC 7852(d)(1) gives neither a treaty nor a statute preferential status just because it is a treaty or a law. Courts generally resolve a true conflict by applying the provision that is later in time. A taxpayer who claims a treaty overrides the Code generally must disclose that position.
source: IRC 7852(d)(1); IRC 6114; Whitney v. Robertson, 124 U.S. 190 (1888)

q: A foreign corporation with a U.S. sales office takes the position on its return that, under a tax treaty, its U.S. business profits are not attributable to a U.S. permanent establishment and are not taxable. How must it report this position?
choices: It need not report it, because a treaty automatically overrides the Code
On Form 8275, Disclosure Statement
Only on Form W-8BEN-E given to its customers
On Form 8833, Treaty-Based Return Position Disclosure, attached to its return
explain: Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6114 requires a taxpayer who takes the position that a treaty overrules or modifies an internal revenue law to disclose it, and the regulations require a completed Form 8833. The position that effectively connected income is not attributable to a permanent establishment is specifically listed as requiring disclosure. Failure to disclose triggers the IRC 6712 penalty.

q: An examiner asks a client to extend the assessment period for her 2022 Form 1040. Which statement is correct?
choices: Form 872 extends the period to a fixed date, while Form 872-A is open-ended and generally ends 90 days after a notice ending the agreement is sent
Form 872-A extends the period to a fixed date, while Form 872 is open-ended
Refusing to sign either form results in a penalty
The client must agree to extend for all issues on the return; limiting the extension is not allowed
explain: Form 872 is a fixed-date consent, and Form 872-A is an open-ended consent that generally stays open until 90 days after the taxpayer or the IRS sends notice ending it (for example on Form 872-T). The taxpayer may refuse or ask to limit the extension to specific issues, and refusing carries no penalty, though the IRS will generally issue a notice of deficiency.

q: Regarding an agreement to extend the assessment period under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6501(c)(4), all of the following are true EXCEPT:
choices: The agreement must be in writing and made before the assessment period expires
The IRS must notify the taxpayer of the right to refuse or to limit the extension to particular issues
The extended period may be extended again by later written agreements made before it expires
It may be used to extend the assessment period for the federal estate tax
explain: IRC 6501(c)(4) allows a written extension agreement made before the period expires and allows later agreements to extend it again. It excludes the estate tax imposed by chapter 11. Each time it asks, the IRS must notify the taxpayer of the right to refuse or limit the extension.

q: Hana did not file her 2021 Form 1040 and requested no extension. Her employer withheld $4,000, and her correct 2021 tax is $2,500. She files the 2021 return claiming a $1,500 refund on May 1, 2025. How much will the IRS refund?
explain: An original return claiming a refund is treated as a claim filed the same day as the return, so the look-back period is 3 years before May 1, 2025, which starts May 1, 2022. Withholding is deemed paid on April 15, 2022, the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ended, which falls outside the look-back period. The allowable refund is $0.

q: Ray timely filed his 2021 return on April 10, 2022, reporting $10,000 of tax, fully covered by withholding. After an exam he paid an additional $6,000 on July 1, 2024. On September 15, 2025 he files a claim for refund of $9,000 based on an overlooked deduction. What is the maximum refund allowed?
explain: An early return is treated as filed on the April 2022 due date, so the 3-year period from filing ended in April 2025, before the claim. Because the claim is filed later but within 2 years of the July 1, 2024 payment, the refund is limited to tax paid in the 2 years before the claim (on or after September 15, 2023). Only the $6,000 payment falls in that window, so the maximum refund is $6,000.

q: Under the mitigation provisions (sections 1311 through 1314 of the Internal Revenue Code), which situation may allow correction of an error in a tax year otherwise closed by the statute of limitations?
choices: The taxpayer simply forgot to claim a deduction in a year that closed several years ago
An item of income was included in the taxpayer's income for a closed year in error, and a determination for an open year requires the same item to be included in that open year
The taxpayer wants to revoke an election made in a closed year
The IRS discovers new evidence of unreported income in a closed year, with no related determination
explain: Mitigation applies only to the circumstances listed in Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 1312, such as double inclusion of an item of gross income, after a determination and generally when a party has maintained an inconsistent position. The error is corrected as if one year remained on the statute. It is not a general way to reopen closed years for ordinary errors.

q: Karen's 2024 Form 1040, showing a refund, was due April 15, 2025. She sends it on April 15 by FedEx Ground, which is not on the IRS list of designated private delivery services, and the IRS receives it on April 21. When is the return treated as filed?
choices: April 15, 2025, because she shipped it on the due date
April 21, 2025, the date the IRS received it
April 15, 2025, because any commercial carrier receipt proves timely filing
April 18, 2025, because carriers get a 3-day grace period
explain: The timely-mailing-is-timely-filing rule applies to U.S. mail and to private delivery services the IRS has designated, such as FedEx 2Day or UPS Next Day Air. FedEx Ground is not designated, so the return is filed when the IRS receives it. Had she used a designated service, the date recorded by the carrier would count as the postmark date.
source: IRC 7502(a), (f); Treas. Reg. 301.7502-1; IRS, Private delivery services (PDS)

q: A taxpayer in Hawaii e-files through an authorized transmitter at 9:30 p.m. Hawaii time on the filing due date. At that moment it is already the next day in the Eastern time zone. Is the return timely?
choices: Yes, because the electronic postmark is judged in the taxpayer's time zone
No, because e-filed returns are judged in Eastern time
No, because the electronic postmark rule applies only to paper returns
Yes, but only if the taxpayer also mails a paper copy
explain: A return sent through an authorized electronic return transmitter is treated as filed on the date of the electronic postmark, if that date is on or before the due date. When the taxpayer and the transmitter are in different time zones, the taxpayer's time zone controls.

q: Carla receives a math error notice dated June 2, 2025 that assesses additional 2024 tax because a dependent's Social Security number (SSN) was invalid for the child tax credit. She believes the SSN is valid. Which statement is correct?
choices: She may petition the Tax Court within 90 days of the math error notice
She may request abatement within 60 days after the notice is sent; the IRS must then abate, and any reassessment must follow the deficiency procedures
She may only file Form 843 and wait for a decision
She must pay the tax first and then sue for a refund
explain: A math or clerical error notice is not a notice of deficiency, so it carries no right to petition the Tax Court. Within 60 days after the notice is sent, the taxpayer may request abatement, and the IRS must abate. To reassess, the IRS must then use the deficiency procedures, which give Tax Court rights.

q: A client asks you to get a copy of her filed 2021 Form 1040, including attachments. What is the proper way to request it?
choices: A Freedom of Information Act request to the IRS Disclosure Office
Form 4506, Request for Copy of Tax Return
Form 4506-T, Request for Transcript of Tax Return
Form 911
explain: The IRS says not to use Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) for copies of tax returns or transcripts. A copy of the actual return is requested on Form 4506, and transcripts on Form 4506-T or through Transcript Delivery System (TDS) or online access. FOIA is for other agency records, such as an examination file.
source: IRS, Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) guidelines

q: Which of the following is tax evasion rather than tax avoidance?
choices: Deferring the sale of appreciated stock until January to push the gain into the next year
Contributing the maximum to a 401(k) plan to reduce taxable wages
Depositing cash receipts into an undisclosed account and leaving them off the return
Holding stock more than one year so the gain qualifies as long-term
explain: Avoidance is reducing tax by legitimate means and is not a crime. Evasion involves an affirmative act to evade or defeat a tax, such as deceit or concealment. Willful evasion is a felony under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7201, punishable by up to 5 years in prison.

q: The IRS establishes that part of a taxpayer's $40,000 underpayment for 2022 is due to fraud. The taxpayer proves by a preponderance of the evidence that $10,000 of the underpayment is not due to fraud. What is the civil fraud penalty?
explain: Once the IRS shows part of an underpayment is due to fraud, the entire underpayment is treated as fraud except any portion the taxpayer proves by a preponderance is not. The fraud portion is $40,000 minus $10,000, or $30,000, and the penalty is 75% of that, or $22,500. The $8,000 choice applies 20% to the whole amount, which is the accuracy-related penalty rate.

q: A taxpayer takes a return position contrary to a Treasury regulation because she believes in good faith that the regulation is invalid. To avoid the disregard-of-regulations portion of the accuracy-related penalty, she should disclose the position on:
choices: Form 8275-R, Regulation Disclosure Statement
Form 8275, Disclosure Statement
Form 8833
No form; disclosure cannot help with this penalty
explain: Positions contrary to a regulation are disclosed on Form 8275-R, and the position must have a reasonable basis and represent a good-faith challenge to the regulation's validity. Form 8275 is used for other positions, including those contrary to a rule such as a revenue ruling. Disclosure never avoids the negligence portion of the penalty.

q: An individual's correct 2025 tax is $60,000, but the return shows $45,000. Of the $15,000 understatement, $10,000 comes from a non-tax-shelter item that was adequately disclosed on Form 8275 and has a reasonable basis. Is there a substantial understatement of income tax?
choices: Yes, because $15,000 exceeds $6,000
Yes, because $5,000 equals the $5,000 floor
No, because the $5,000 remaining understatement does not exceed $6,000
No, because filing Form 8275 eliminates all accuracy-related penalties
explain: The understatement is reduced by items adequately disclosed with a reasonable basis: $15,000 minus $10,000 leaves $5,000. For an individual, it is substantial only if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the correct tax ($6,000) or $5,000, so the threshold is $6,000. Because $5,000 does not exceed $6,000, there is no substantial understatement.

q: The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) generally accepts cases that meet its criteria. All of the following meet TAS case acceptance criteria EXCEPT:
choices: The taxpayer has had a delay of more than 30 days in resolving a tax account problem
The taxpayer did not get a response or resolution by the date the IRS promised
A levy on the taxpayer's wages leaves her unable to pay rent
The taxpayer disagrees with an examiner's interpretation of the law and wants TAS to decide the issue
explain: TAS criteria include economic burden (such as economic harm or an immediate threat of adverse action), a delay of more than 30 days, no response by a promised date and failed IRS systems. A disagreement over the merits of an audit adjustment belongs with Appeals or the courts, not TAS.

q: A client receives a notice of deficiency dated June 2, 2025 and files Form 911 with the Taxpayer Advocate Service on June 20, 2025. Which statement is correct?
choices: Filing Form 911 extends the time to petition the Tax Court until Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) resolves the case
Filing Form 911 does not suspend the 90-day period to petition the Tax Court
Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) will file the Tax Court petition for the client
A Form 911 can be filed only by an attorney
explain: Form 911 states that signing the request does not suspend any periods for the taxpayer to act, such as petitioning the Tax Court, and is not a substitute for legal or administrative action. The client must still petition within 90 days of the notice date. A representative may file Form 911 by attaching a copy of Form 2848, Form 8821 or another power of attorney.

q: Dee received her Identity Protection Personal Identification Number (IP PIN) in early 2026. In March 2026 her preparer e-files Dee's 2025 Form 1040 but leaves off the IP PIN. What happens?
choices: The return is accepted and the IRS sends a letter requesting the IP PIN
The e-filed return is rejected and must be corrected with the IP PIN and resubmitted
The return is accepted because IP PINs are required only on paper returns
The return is accepted because IP PINs apply only to prior-year returns
explain: An incorrect or missing IP PIN causes an e-filed return to be rejected; a paper return is delayed until it can be verified. An IP PIN is valid for one calendar year and must be used on any federal return filed during that year, including prior-year returns.
source: IRS, Get an identity protection PIN (IP PIN)

q: Sam's e-filed return is rejected because another return was already filed using his Social Security number (SSN). He cannot e-file. What should he do?
choices: File a paper return and attach Form 14039, Identity Theft Affidavit, to the back of it
Wait for a CP2000 notice before taking any action
File Form 4506 to get a copy of the fraudulent return before filing his own
File Form 911; the IRS will not accept his return until Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) approves it
explain: When a misused SSN or individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN) prevents e-filing, Form 14039 is attached to the back of a paper return mailed to the usual filing location. Form 14039 can also be submitted online when it is not attached to a return. If the IRS sends a letter asking him to verify his identity, he should follow that letter instead.
source: Form 14039 (Rev. 2-2026) instructions; IRS Identity theft guide for individuals

q: An enrolled agent's client wants to contest a tax liability in court. Which statement about the enrolled agent's role is correct?
choices: Enrolled agents are automatically admitted to practice before the U.S. Tax Court
Enrolled agents may represent clients in U.S. district court because they have unlimited practice rights before the IRS
A nonattorney may be admitted to practice before the U.S. Tax Court by passing the Court's written examination, but cannot represent clients in district court or the Court of Federal Claims
Enrolled agents may represent clients in the Court of Federal Claims but not in the Tax Court
explain: Tax Court Rule 200 allows a nonattorney to be admitted by passing the Court's written examination, with at least two sponsors. District courts and the Court of Federal Claims admit only attorneys, apart from parties appearing for themselves. Unlimited practice before the IRS does not include practice before the courts.
source: Tax Court Rule 200(a)(3), (c); RCFC 83.1(a); 28 USC 1654; Circular 230, 10.3

q: Of the trial courts that hear federal tax disputes, which one allows a jury trial?
choices: U.S. Tax Court
U.S. Court of Federal Claims
U.S. Tax Court under the small tax case procedure
U.S. district court, in a refund suit
explain: A refund suit in district court may be tried by a jury at either party's request. The district court and the Court of Federal Claims both require paying the tax and filing a refund claim first. The Tax Court hears cases before payment without a jury, and its small tax case decisions (up to $50,000 per year) cannot be appealed and are not precedent.

q: Maria cannot pay the $30,000 balance due on her 2025 Form 1040 by April 15, 2026, unless she sells a rental property at a price well below its value. She lives in the United States and files Form 1127 before April 15. If the IRS grants the extension, it generally cannot exceed:
choices: 90 days
6 months
12 months
18 months
explain: An extension to pay tax shown on a return for undue hardship (more than an inconvenience, such as a sale at a sacrifice price) is generally limited to 6 months, or longer only if the taxpayer is abroad. The 18-month limit (plus up to 12 more in exceptional cases) applies to an extension to pay a deficiency, not the tax shown on the return. Interest still runs during any extension.

q: Victor owes $58,000 of assessed income tax, penalties and interest for prior years. He wants a payment plan and files Form 9465 by mail with no payment. Under the Form 9465 instructions in effect for 2025, what must he also do?
choices: Complete and attach Form 433-F, Collection Information Statement
Nothing more, as long as he agrees to pay by direct debit
File Form 656 because balances over $50,000 cannot be paid in installments
Request a guaranteed installment agreement under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6159(c)
explain: When the balance on Form 9465 is greater than $50,000, the instructions require the taxpayer to complete and attach Form 433-F so the IRS can evaluate ability to pay. The simple payment plan (formerly streamlined), which needs no financial statement, is limited to $50,000 or less. A guaranteed agreement requires tax of $10,000 or less.

q: Kim, an individual wage earner, owes an assessed balance of $38,000 in tax, penalties and interest. All her returns are filed. She asks for an installment agreement paid by direct debit that will pay the balance in full within 72 months, well before the collection statute expiration date. Which statement is correct?
choices: She qualifies for a guaranteed installment agreement
She must submit Form 433-A before any agreement can be granted
She can generally get the agreement without submitting a collection information statement
The IRS must file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien before granting the agreement
explain: Individual balances of $50,000 or less that will be paid within the collection statute qualify for a streamlined agreement (renamed a simple payment plan in 2025), which does not require a collection information statement. A guaranteed agreement is only for tax of $10,000 or less paid within 3 years.
source: IRM 5.14.5.2; IRS SB/SE Interim Guidance SBSE-05-0325-0008 (Mar. 3, 2025); Form 9465 instructions (Rev. July 2024)

q: Lena filed her 2025 Form 1040 on time but could not pay the balance. She entered into an installment agreement, and $8,000 of tax remained unpaid at the start of a month while the agreement was in effect. What is the failure-to-pay penalty for that month?
choices: $0, because the penalty stops during an installment agreement
explain: For an individual who filed on time, the failure-to-pay rate drops from 0.5% to 0.25% per month while an installment agreement is in effect: $8,000 x 0.25% = $20. The $40 answer uses the normal 0.5% rate, which still applies if the return was filed late.

q: The 10-year collection statute is suspended during each of the following periods EXCEPT:
choices: While a request for an installment agreement is pending
The 30 days after the IRS rejects an installment agreement request
While an offer in compromise is pending
While an installment agreement is in effect and being paid
explain: The collection statute expiration date (CSED) is suspended while an installment agreement request is pending, for 30 days after a rejection or termination, and during a timely appeal. It is not suspended while the agreement itself is in effect, because Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6331(k)(3) excludes that period.

q: Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6159, the IRS may terminate an existing installment agreement for any of the following reasons EXCEPT:
choices: The taxpayer misses an installment payment
The taxpayer fails to pay a new tax liability when it is due
The taxpayer fails to provide a financial condition update the IRS requested
The IRS applies the taxpayer's refund to the balance owed under the agreement
explain: Missed installments, failure to pay later liabilities and failure to give a requested financial update are statutory grounds for termination. Refunds are routinely applied to the balance during an agreement, and the taxpayer still makes the regular payment, so an offset is not a default. The IRS generally must give 30 days' notice before terminating an agreement.

q: An offer in compromise may be based on all of the following grounds EXCEPT:
choices: Doubt as to liability
Doubt as to collectibility
Effective tax administration
Reasonable cause for the penalties assessed
explain: The three grounds for compromise are doubt as to liability, doubt as to collectibility, and effective tax administration (economic hardship or public policy and equity). Reasonable cause is a basis for penalty abatement, requested separately, not a ground for an offer.

q: Andre, who does not meet the low-income certification guidelines, submits a doubt as to collectibility offer of $15,000 on the lump sum option. How much must he send with Form 656?
explain: A lump sum offer (5 or fewer payments) must include 20% of the offer amount plus the $205 application fee: $15,000 x 20% = $3,000, plus $205 = $3,205. Under the periodic payment option he would instead send the first proposed monthly payment with the fee.

q: Paolo's 2022 tax was assessed from an IRS substitute for return, and he has records showing he owes much less. The liability has not been decided by any court. If he submits a doubt as to liability offer on Form 656-L, which is correct?
choices: He must pay the $205 application fee and 20% of the offer
He must also submit Form 433-A (OIC)
No application fee or deposit is required, but he must explain in writing why the tax is wrong
He cannot use Form 656-L for a substitute for return assessment
explain: A doubt as to liability offer has no application fee or deposit, and the taxpayer must include a written statement and documents showing why the assessed tax is incorrect. It is barred only where the liability was established by a final court decision. Form 433-A (OIC) supports doubt as to collectibility offers.

q: Before the IRS will consider an offer in compromise from an individual who operates a business with employees, the taxpayer must meet all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Have filed all required tax returns
Have made all required estimated tax payments for the current year
Have made the federal tax deposits for the current quarter and the two preceding quarters
Have paid at least half of the total liability
explain: Form 656 requires filing compliance, current-year estimated payments and, for employers, deposits for the current quarter and two preceding quarters. There is no requirement to pay part of the liability before applying; the only upfront amounts are the fee and the 20% or first periodic payment.

q: Which statement about an offer in compromise that the IRS has accepted for processing and is still evaluating is correct?
choices: The IRS generally may not levy, and the collection statute is suspended while it is pending
Penalties and interest stop accruing while it is pending
If the IRS does not reject it within 12 months, it is deemed accepted
The IRS may not file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien while it is pending
explain: Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6331(k)(1) bars levy while an offer is pending, for 30 days after rejection and during a timely appeal, and the collection statute expiration date (CSED) is suspended for those periods. An offer is deemed accepted only if not rejected within 24 months of submission. Penalties and interest continue, and the IRS may file a notice of federal tax lien (NFTL) during consideration.

q: At the end of an office audit of his 2023 return, Omar signs Form 870 agreeing to a $6,000 deficiency. Which is a consequence of signing?
choices: He gives up any right to a later refund claim for 2023
He keeps the right to petition the Tax Court for the $6,000
The IRS may no longer examine any other item on his 2023 return
The IRS may assess and collect the deficiency immediately without issuing a notice of deficiency
explain: Form 870 waives the restrictions on assessment, so the IRS can assess right away without a 90-day letter, and Omar cannot take that amount to the Tax Court. He can still pay and file a refund claim, then sue in a district court or the Court of Federal Claims if it is denied.

q: Which statement correctly compares the Collection Appeals Program (CAP) with a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing?
choices: A CAP decision is binding and cannot be reviewed by a court, while a CDP determination can be petitioned to the Tax Court
Both allow the taxpayer to dispute the amount of a liability for which a notice of deficiency was received
CAP is available only after a Notice of Federal Tax Lien has been filed
CDP covers the rejection or termination of an installment agreement, but CAP does not
explain: Appeals' CAP decision is binding on both sides with no judicial review, while a CDP determination may be petitioned to the Tax Court within 30 days. CAP covers proposed or filed liens, levies, seizures, and rejected, modified or terminated installment agreements. CAP never allows a challenge to the liability itself.

q: Rita received a Final Notice of Intent to Levy and Notice of Your Right to a Hearing dated March 3, 2025. She mailed Form 12153 on October 15, 2025. Which is correct?
choices: She is entitled to a collection due process (CDP) hearing because she filed within one year
Her request is too late for any Appeals hearing
She may receive an equivalent hearing, but she cannot petition the Tax Court and the IRS is not barred from levying
Her equivalent hearing suspends the collection statute until Appeals issues its decision
explain: A CDP request must be made within 30 days of the levy notice. A late request filed within one year of the notice date gets an equivalent hearing, which results in a decision letter that cannot be taken to court. During an equivalent hearing the law does not prohibit levy and the collection statute is not suspended.

q: Ben received a notice of deficiency for 2022 but did not petition the Tax Court, and the tax was assessed. He then received a levy notice and filed a timely collection due process (CDP) request. Which issue may he raise at the hearing?
choices: That a deduction disallowed in the notice of deficiency should be allowed
That the tax should be reduced because the examiner made a legal error
A collection alternative such as an installment agreement or an offer in compromise
None, because receiving a notice of deficiency bars any CDP hearing
explain: At a CDP hearing the taxpayer may raise collection alternatives, spousal defenses and the appropriateness of the levy. The existence or amount of the liability may be challenged only if the taxpayer did not receive a notice of deficiency or otherwise have a chance to dispute it, so Ben cannot relitigate the deduction.

q: Nadia has a Notice of Federal Tax Lien on file. She wants to refinance her home at a lower rate to free up cash for her installment payments, but the new lender insists its mortgage be ahead of the IRS lien. The lien itself will remain. What should she request?
choices: A certificate of release
A certificate of discharge
A certificate of subordination
Withdrawal of the notice of federal tax lien (NFTL)
explain: A certificate of subordination lets a named creditor move ahead of the federal tax lien on specific property without removing the lien; it is requested on Form 14134 at least 45 days before the transaction. Discharge removes the lien from a specific property, release ends the lien when the debt is paid or unenforceable, and withdrawal removes the public notice.

q: Hugo owes $40,000 secured by a federal tax lien and wants a certificate of discharge for a parcel he is selling under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6325(b)(1), without any payment. His remaining property is subject to a $30,000 mortgage that has priority over the federal lien. What must the fair market value of his remaining property be, at a minimum?
explain: Under 6325(b)(1), the remaining property must be worth at least double the sum of the unpaid tax liability and the senior liens: 2 x ($40,000 + $30,000) = $140,000. The $110,000 choice doubles only the tax and then adds the mortgage.

q: Which statement about the withdrawal of a Notice of Federal Tax Lien is correct?
choices: A withdrawal extinguishes the lien and the underlying tax liability
The IRS has no authority to withdraw a notice of federal tax lien (NFTL) while any tax remains unpaid
A withdrawal is the same as a release and must be issued within 30 days of full payment
A withdrawal removes the public notice as if it had never been filed, but the taxpayer still owes the tax
explain: A withdrawal removes the public NFTL as though it was never filed, but the taxpayer remains liable. Grounds include a premature filing, entering an installment agreement (unless it provides otherwise), facilitating collection, or the best interest of the taxpayer and the government. A release, by contrast, must be issued within 30 days after the liability is paid or becomes unenforceable.
source: IRC 6323(j)(1), 6325(a); IRS, Understanding a Federal Tax Lien

q: Before levying on a taxpayer's bank account in a case that is not a jeopardy case, the IRS must have done all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Assessed the tax and sent notice and demand for payment
Waited at least 10 days after notice and demand without payment
Sent a final notice of intent to levy, with notice of hearing rights, at least 30 days before the levy
Obtained an order from a federal district court
explain: Administrative levy requires assessment, notice and demand, nonpayment for 10 days, and a written notice of intent to levy with collection due process (CDP) rights at least 30 days before the levy. No court order is needed for an ordinary levy. Court approval is required only in special cases such as levy on a principal residence.

q: All of the following are exempt from IRS levy EXCEPT:
choices: Unemployment compensation benefits
Workers' compensation benefits
Undelivered mail addressed to the taxpayer
Funds in the taxpayer's personal savings account
explain: Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6334(a) exempts items such as unemployment benefits, workers' compensation, undelivered mail, school books, certain service-connected disability payments and a minimum amount of wages. Bank account balances are not on the list and are a common levy source.

q: Which statement about an IRS levy on an employee's wages is correct?
choices: The levy is continuous until released, and the exempt amount depends on the employee's filing status, standard deduction and dependents
The levy must be served again each payday
The levy can take no more than 15% of each paycheck
Wages are fully exempt from levy if the employee has dependents
explain: A wage levy is continuous from the date it is first made until released, so it is served once. The weekly exempt amount is based on the standard deduction and dependents claimed on the employee's statement, from the tables in Pub 1494. The 15% limit applies to the continuous levy on certain federal payments, not to wages.

q: The IRS seized Ken's rental building and sold it at public auction on May 1, 2025. Ken now wants it back. Which is correct?
choices: Ken lost all rights once the sale was held
Ken may redeem the property within 1 year by paying the tax due
Ken may redeem the property within 180 days after the sale by paying the purchaser the price paid plus interest at 20% a year
Ken may redeem only if the sale was held more than 40 days after public notice
explain: After a sale of real property, the owner or other interested person may redeem within 180 days by paying the purchaser the amount paid plus interest at 20% per year. Before a sale, the owner can recover seized property by paying the amount due. The sale itself must be held 10 to 40 days after public notice.

q: The IRS places Gloria's account in currently not collectible status because paying would leave her unable to meet basic living expenses. All of the following are true EXCEPT:
choices: Future federal tax refunds may be applied to the balance
The IRS may file a Notice of Federal Tax Lien
The IRS may review her financial situation later
Penalties and interest stop accruing on the balance
explain: Currently not collectible (CNC) status delays collection but does not reduce the debt. Penalties and interest continue to accrue, refunds are applied to the balance, a notice of federal tax lien (NFTL) may be filed, and the IRS may review her finances and resume collection if her ability to pay improves.
source: IRS, Temporarily delay the collection process; IRS Pub 594; IRM 5.16.1.2.9

q: A revenue officer collecting Leo's assessed tax liability issues a summons to Leo's bank for his account records. Which statement is correct?
choices: The IRS must notify Leo within 3 days so he can petition to quash
Only the Tax Court can enforce the summons if the bank refuses
The bank must produce the records within 3 days of service
The IRS does not have to give Leo third-party summons notice because the summons is issued in aid of collecting an assessed liability
explain: The third-party notice and quash rules of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7609 do not apply to a summons issued in aid of collecting an assessment against the person whose liability is at issue. The appearance date must be at least 10 days after the summons date, and enforcement is in the federal district court where the summoned person resides or is found.

q: Dana, the controller of a struggling corporation, signs all checks and decides which bills to pay. Knowing that the payroll taxes withheld from employees were not deposited, she pays suppliers and rent to keep the business open, hoping to catch up on the taxes later. Which statement about the trust fund recovery penalty is correct?
choices: Dana is likely a responsible person who acted willfully, since paying other creditors while knowing the taxes were unpaid shows willfulness
Dana is not willful because she did not intend to cheat the government
Only the corporation's president can be liable
The penalty applies only to the employer's share of social security and Medicare tax
explain: A responsible person has the duty and power to direct the collecting, accounting and paying of trust fund taxes, which can include officers and employees with check-signing authority.
