Willfulness means knowing of the unpaid taxes and intentionally disregarding the law or being plainly indifferent; no evil motive is needed, and paying other creditors instead is a sign of it. The penalty covers withheld income tax and the employee share of Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA).
source: IRC 6672(a); IRM 8.25.1.3.1, 8.25.1.3.2; IRS, Employment taxes and the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty

q: A revenue officer concludes that Felix, who lives in the United States, is liable for the trust fund recovery penalty and sends him Letter 1153. Which is correct?
choices: Felix has 30 days to petition the Tax Court
The penalty is assessed immediately, and Felix can contest it only through collection due process (CDP)
Felix has 60 days from the date of the letter to file a protest and have Appeals review the proposed penalty before assessment
Felix must pay the penalty in full before he may appeal
explain: Letter 1153 proposes the trust fund recovery penalty (TFRP) and gives the person 60 days (75 days if addressed outside the United States) to protest to Appeals before assessment. If he does not respond, the IRS assesses the penalty and issues notice and demand.
source: IRC 6672(b); IRM 5.7.6.2, 5.7.6.4; IRS, Employment taxes and the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty

q: Carlos paid a $1,200 failure-to-file penalty on his 2023 return. He later learns that he qualifies for relief because a serious illness kept him from filing on time. He also forgot a $900 education credit on that return. Which forms should he use?
choices: Form 1040-X for both
Form 843 for both
Form 843 for the penalty refund and Form 1040-X for the education credit
Form 1040-X for the penalty and Form 843 for the credit
explain: Form 843 is used to claim a refund or abatement of penalties, interest and certain other taxes, including relief for reasonable cause. It cannot be used to claim a refund of income tax; changes to the income tax reported on Form 1040, such as a missed credit, go on Form 1040-X.

q: Ana timely filed her 2022 return on April 18, 2023, with no extension. Her $6,000 of withholding is treated as paid in April 2023. After an audit she paid an additional $2,000 on June 1, 2025. She files a refund claim on September 1, 2026. What is the most she can recover?
explain: The claim was filed more than 3 years after the return (April 18, 2026), but within 2 years of the June 1, 2025 payment, so it is timely under the 2-year rule. The refund is then limited to tax paid in the 2 years before the claim (September 1, 2024 to September 1, 2026), which is only the $2,000. The withholding paid in 2023 is outside that lookback period.

q: Which statement about a protective claim for refund is correct?
choices: It may be filed after the refund statute has expired if the contingency is resolved later
The IRS must act on it within 6 months
It must be filed on Form 843 for every type of tax
It preserves the right to a refund that depends on a future event, such as pending litigation, and need not state a specific dollar amount
explain: A protective claim is filed before the refund statute expires to preserve a refund whose amount depends on a contingency, such as the outcome of litigation. It must be written and signed and identify the contingency, but it does not need a specific dollar amount.

q: Which of the following individuals' tax debt may be certified to the State Department as seriously delinquent in 2025?
choices: Ana, who owes $70,000 assessed and is timely paying an installment agreement
Ben, who owes $60,000 assessed, after an IRS levy
Cal, who owes $70,000 assessed, after an IRS levy, with no collection alternative pending
Dee, who owes $90,000 assessed and whose account is currently not collectible due to hardship
explain: For 2025 a seriously delinquent tax debt is an assessed, legally enforceable federal tax debt over $64,000 (including penalties and interest) for which a notice of federal tax lien (NFTL) was filed and collection due process (CDP) rights were exhausted or lapsed, or a levy was made. Ben is under the threshold, and debts being timely paid under an installment agreement or in hardship currently not collectible (CNC) status are not certified.
source: IRC 7345(b); Rev. Proc. 2024-40, sec. 2.60; IRS, Revocation or denial of passport in cases of certain unpaid taxes

q: Chris filed his 2025 Form 1040 two months late and was charged failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties. He timely filed his 2022, 2023 and 2024 returns, and his only penalty in those years was an estimated tax penalty for 2023. Which is correct?
choices: He may qualify for first-time abatement of both the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties
He does not qualify for first-time abatement because of the 2023 estimated tax penalty
First-time abatement covers only the failure-to-file penalty
He must first be denied reasonable cause relief before first-time abatement is considered
explain: First-time abatement covers failure-to-file, failure-to-pay and failure-to-deposit penalties when the same type of return was timely filed for the prior 3 years with no penalties, other than an estimated tax penalty. The IRS considers this administrative waiver before reasonable cause.
source: IRM 20.1.1.3.3.2.1; IRS, Penalty relief due to First Time Abate or other administrative waiver

q: For a failure-to-pay penalty, each of the following may support reasonable cause relief EXCEPT:
choices: A fire that destroyed the taxpayer's records
Serious illness of the taxpayer
Death of a member of the taxpayer's immediate family
The taxpayer did not have enough money, with no other facts
explain: Reasonable cause exists when the taxpayer used ordinary business care and prudence but still could not comply, as with fires, disasters, serious illness, death or inability to get records. Lack of funds by itself is not reasonable cause. Reasonable cause also does not apply to the estimated tax penalty.
source: IRM 20.1.1.3.2; IRS, Penalty relief for reasonable cause

q: The IRS notified Irene in writing in February 2025 that her 2023 return was under examination. She supplied every document requested by April 2025. In May 2025 the revenue agent was permanently reassigned, and her file sat with no one assigned until January 2026. Which is correct about the interest for that delay?
choices: It cannot be abated because only ministerial acts qualify
It cannot be abated because the delay occurred before a deficiency was assessed
It may be abated because the reassignment decision is a managerial act that caused unreasonable delay after the IRS contacted her in writing
It is abated automatically, with no request needed
explain: Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6404(e) allows abatement of interest caused by unreasonable IRS error or delay in a ministerial or managerial act, after the IRS has contacted the taxpayer in writing, if no significant part of the delay is the taxpayer's fault. The regulations treat reassigning an agent and not reassigning the case as managerial acts. A decision about how to apply the tax law is not a ministerial or managerial act.
source: IRC 6404(e)(1); Treas. Reg. 301.6404-2(b) and Example 4; Form 843 instructions

q: Rosa runs a landscaping business as a sole proprietor and keeps all of her original books and records at her business office. The IRS opens a field examination of her Schedule C. Where will the examination generally take place?
choices: At the IRS office closest to her home
At her principal place of business, where her books and records are kept
At any IRS office the examiner chooses
Entirely by mail
explain: A field examination generally takes place where the original books, records and source documents are kept, which for a sole proprietor is usually the principal place of business. An office examination of an individual is generally held at the closest IRS office to the taxpayer's residence.

q: Jorge's 2022 return was examined for his charitable contribution deduction, and the IRS proposed no change. Now his 2024 return has been selected for examination of the same item. What should he do?
choices: Nothing, because Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7605(b) bars any later examination of the same issue
Contact the IRS and ask whether the examination should be discontinued under the repetitive examination policy
File Form 12153 to stop the examination
Ask the Tax Court to block the examination
explain: The IRS tries to avoid repeat examinations of the same items. If a return was examined for the same items in either of the 2 previous years and no change in tax was proposed, the taxpayer should contact the IRS to see if the exam should be discontinued. IRC 7605(b) is a different rule that limits the IRS to one inspection of books for each taxable year.

q: Dev, a self-employed consultant, has no receipts or logs. He testifies credibly that he spent about $6,000 on business travel away from home and about $1,200 on office supplies. Under the substantiation rules, which is correct?
choices: Both amounts may be estimated under the Cohan rule
Neither amount may be allowed under any circumstances
The travel may not be estimated because Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 274(d) requires adequate records or corroborating evidence, but a court may estimate the supplies
The supplies may not be estimated, but the travel may be
explain: Travel away from home, gifts and listed property must meet the strict substantiation rules of IRC 274(d), and the regulations state that this supersedes the Cohan rule. For other ordinary business expenses, a court may allow a reasonable estimate under Cohan when there is a basis for it, usually weighing it against the taxpayer.
source: IRC 274(d); Treas. Reg. 1.274-5T(a); Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)

q: Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 7491(a), the burden of proof on a factual issue shifts to the IRS in a court proceeding if an individual taxpayer introduces credible evidence and meets all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Substantiated the item as required by the Code
Maintained all required records
Cooperated with reasonable IRS requests for witnesses, information, documents, meetings and interviews
Agreed to extend the statute of limitations on assessment
explain: The burden shifts only if the taxpayer offers credible evidence, has substantiated the item, kept the required records and cooperated with reasonable requests. Agreeing to extend the statute is not a condition.

q: After a field examination, Ivan receives a 30-day letter with Form 4549 showing a proposed deficiency for 2023. He disagrees and does nothing by the deadline. What happens next?
choices: The IRS immediately assesses the tax and begins levying
The IRS issues a statutory notice of deficiency, giving him the right to petition the Tax Court
He loses all appeal rights, including the right to go to the Tax Court
The examination is closed with no change
explain: The 30-day letter lets the taxpayer agree, or request an Appeals conference in writing. If he does not respond, the IRS issues a notice of deficiency (90-day letter), and he can still petition the Tax Court before the tax is assessed.

q: Grace receives a CP2000 notice proposing additional tax because a brokerage reported a sale she left off her return. She agrees with the notice and has nothing else to report. What should she do?
choices: File Form 1040-X reporting the sale
Follow the notice instructions to agree; she does not need to amend her return
Wait for a 90-day letter, since a CP2000 is a bill
Request an office audit
explain: A CP2000 is not a bill or an audit; it proposes changes based on third-party information that does not match the return. If the taxpayer agrees and has no other items, she follows the notice instructions and does not need to file an amended return. If she does not respond, the IRS may issue a statutory notice of deficiency.
source: IRS, Understanding your CP2000 notice; IRS, Understanding your CP3219A notice

q: A 30-day letter proposes increases in tax and penalties of $18,000 for 2022 and $14,500 for 2023. The taxpayer wants Appeals to consider both years. Which is correct?
choices: A formal written protest is required because the total of $32,500 exceeds $25,000
A small case request may be used because the amount for each tax period is $25,000 or less
Appeals is not available because the total exceeds $25,000
The taxpayer must file separate formal protests for each year
explain: The $25,000 small case threshold is tested per tax period, not on the total. Since $18,000 and $14,500 are each $25,000 or less, a brief written request listing the disputed changes and reasons is enough. A formal protest, with facts, law and a penalties of perjury declaration, is needed when any period exceeds $25,000.
source: IRS Pub 5 (Rev. 4-2021); IRS Pub 556; IRS Pub 3498

q: Which statement about the IRS Independent Office of Appeals' settlement authority is correct?
choices: Appeals may settle a case based on the hazards of litigation, but not for nuisance value
Appeals may settle only if the taxpayer concedes every issue
Appeals must follow the examiner's findings of fact
Appeals may settle for nuisance value to avoid the cost of litigation
explain: Appeals weighs the hazards of litigation and the likely outcome if the case went to court. IRS policy (Policy Statement 8-47) bars any settlement based on nuisance value to either party.

q: While a case is pending in Appeals, the Appeals officer wants to discuss with the revenue agent the strengths and weaknesses of the agent's position. Under the ex parte rules, this is:
choices: Allowed at any time, because both are IRS employees
Prohibited unless the taxpayer or representative is given an opportunity to participate
Allowed only if the Appeals officer's manager approves
Prohibited in all cases, even for administrative matters
explain: Appeals may communicate with the originating function about ministerial, administrative or procedural matters without the taxpayer. Discussions of the substance of the issues, such as the strengths and weaknesses of the case, are prohibited unless the taxpayer or representative has an opportunity to take part.

q: Mia receives a statutory notice of deficiency for 2023 at her U.S. address. She does not petition the Tax Court and does not sign a waiver. Which is correct?
choices: The IRS may assess the tax as soon as the notice is mailed
The IRS may not assess the deficiency until the period to petition expires; after assessment she could still pay, claim a refund, and sue in a district court or the Court of Federal Claims
Once the petition period passes, she has no further way to contest the tax
She may still petition the Tax Court at any time before the tax is collected
explain: No deficiency may be assessed or collected by levy until the notice is mailed and the 90-day petition period ends (longer if a petition is filed). If she lets the period pass, the IRS assesses, but she can still pay, file a refund claim and, if it is denied, sue for a refund in a district court or the Court of Federal Claims.

q: A preparer's tax software runs its diagnostics on a client's return and reports no errors. Which statement best describes the preparer's responsibility?
choices: A clean diagnostic report satisfies the preparer's due diligence duty
The preparer needs to review the output only if the return claims a refund
Any understatement on the return becomes the software vendor's responsibility, not the preparer's
The preparer must still exercise due diligence, including reviewing the output for accuracy and for consistency with the client's information
explain: Circular 230 requires due diligence in preparing and filing returns, and the IRS states that software helps but cannot replace the preparer's professional judgment or responsibility. A clean diagnostic run is not a defense, because software cannot tell whether the data entered matches the client's real situation.
source: Treasury Circular 230, 10.22(a); IRS EITC Central, Due diligence requirements for tax preparers

q: Maria gives her preparer two 2025 Forms W-2: $52,000 from Employer A and $31,000 from Employer B. When reviewing the completed return before asking Maria to sign, the preparer sees wages of $135,000 on line 1a. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Employer B Form W-2 was entered twice
The Employer A Form W-2 was entered twice
Both Forms W-2 were entered twice
The software added Social Security wages to Medicare wages
explain: The correct wage total is $52,000 + $31,000 = $83,000. The return overstates wages by $135,000 - $83,000 = $52,000, which matches the Employer A W-2, so that form was entered twice. A duplicate Employer B entry would give $114,000, and comparing return totals to source documents is how a preparer catches this kind of duplicate entry.

q: Luis filed his 2023 Form 1040 on April 15, 2024, the due date. After an IRS notice, he paid additional tax of $1,800 on October 1, 2025. He then filed a claim for refund of that amount. Under IRS record-keeping guidance, he should keep the records supporting the claim until at least:
choices: April 15, 2027
October 1, 2027
April 15, 2030
April 15, 2031
explain: When a taxpayer files a claim for credit or refund, records are kept for 3 years from the date the original return was filed or 2 years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later. That is the later of April 15, 2027 (3 years from filing) or October 1, 2027 (2 years from payment), so October 1, 2027. The 6-year and 7-year periods apply only to a large omission of income or to worthless securities and bad debts.
source: IRS: How long should I keep records; IRC 6511(a)

q: Publication 1345 requires an electronic return originator (ERO) to keep which item only until the end of the calendar year, at the business address where the return was originated or a location it can readily access?
choices: The signed Form 8879
The earned income tax credit (EITC) due diligence records for a return claiming the credit
Copies of the taxpayer's Forms W-2, W-2G, and 1099-R
The record of employed preparers required under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 6060
explain: Pub 1345 lists copies of Forms W-2, W-2G and 1099-R, Form 8453 with supporting documents not sent electronically, signed consents to disclose, a complete copy of the electronic return, and the acknowledgment file as items kept until the end of the calendar year. The other three choices carry 3-year retention periods: Form 8879 from the later of the due date or IRS received date, due diligence records under the Form 8867 rules, and the IRC 6060 record of employed preparers.
source: IRS Pub 1345; IRC 6107(b); Treas. Reg. 1.6695-2(b)(4); IRC 6060

q: Rosa operates as an electronic return originator (ERO) only. On Friday afternoon she confirms that an intruder accessed her office system holding client tax data. Under Publication 1345, she must report the security incident to the IRS:
choices: As soon as possible, but no later than the next business day after confirmation, by contacting her local IRS stakeholder liaison
Within 72 hours, by filing a report through her tax software
Within 30 days, and only to the Federal Trade Commission
At her next IRS monitoring visit
explain: Pub 1345 requires all Authorized IRS e-file Providers to report security incidents as soon as possible but no later than the next business day after confirmation. Providers that are EROs only report through their local stakeholder liaison, who notifies IRS Criminal Investigation so fraudulent returns can be blocked. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notice under the Safeguards Rule is a separate duty and does not replace the IRS report.
source: IRS Pub 1345; IRS Pub 4557; IRS: Data theft information for tax professionals

q: On March 3, 2026, a tax firm discovers that an unauthorized person acquired unencrypted customer information on 650 clients. Under the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Safeguards Rule, the firm must notify the FTC no later than:
choices: It need not notify the FTC because fewer than 1,000 consumers were affected
March 4, 2026
April 2, 2026
explain: A notification event involving at least 500 consumers must be reported to the FTC as soon as possible and no later than 30 days after discovery: March 3 + 30 days = April 2, 2026. The threshold is 500 consumers, not 1,000, and the next-business-day deadline in Pub 1345 is for the separate report to the IRS.

q: Under the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Safeguards Rule, a tax preparation firm must use multi-factor authentication for:
choices: Any individual accessing any information system, unless the Qualified Individual approves equivalent or stronger controls in writing
Only access to IRS e-Services
Only employees who work remotely
Only firms that hold information on 5,000 or more consumers
explain: The rule requires multi-factor authentication for any individual accessing any information system, with the only exception being written approval by the Qualified Individual of equivalent or more secure controls. The small-firm exception for fewer than 5,000 consumers does not cover the multifactor authentication (MFA) requirement.

q: A sole practitioner keeps customer information on 1,200 consumers. Under the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Safeguards Rule, she is exempt from all of the following requirements EXCEPT:
choices: Writing an incident response plan
Having the Qualified Individual report in writing to the board or a senior officer at least annually
Annual penetration testing and vulnerability assessments every six months
Implementing multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing her information systems
explain: Institutions with information on fewer than 5,000 consumers are exempt from the written risk assessment criteria, the penetration testing and vulnerability assessment schedule, the written incident response plan, and the annual written report. All other elements, including multifactor authentication (MFA), encryption, a Qualified Individual and a written information security program, still apply.

q: The suitability check the IRS performs on a firm applying to be an Authorized IRS e-file Provider, and on its Principals and Responsible Officials, may include all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A tax compliance check
A check for prior noncompliance with IRS e-file requirements
A criminal background check
A credit history review
explain: Pub 3112 lists a tax compliance check, a check for prior e-file noncompliance, and a criminal background check as parts of the suitability check. A credit history review is not part of it. Applicants first create a Secure Access account, and Principals and Responsible Officials need e-Services accounts to complete the application.

q: A firm's IRS e-file application lists four Principals: an enrolled agent, a CPA with a current license, a licensed public accountant (LPA), and an officer of a publicly held corporation. Which of them must be fingerprinted?
choices: The licensed public accountant
The enrolled agent
The CPA
None of them
explain: Principals and Responsible Officials must be fingerprinted unless they provide professional credentials as an attorney, CPA or enrolled agent, or are an officer of a publicly held corporation or a bonded banking official. Pub 3112 specifically states that licensed public accountants must provide fingerprints.

q: A partnership applying for IRS e-file has four partners with these interests: 50%, 30%, 16%, and 4%. How many of the partners are Principals for the e-file application?
explain: For a partnership, each partner with a 5% or greater interest is a Principal. The partners holding 50%, 30% and 16% qualify, so there are 3. The 4% partner is not a Principal, though the firm could still list that person as a Responsible Official if he or she oversees the e-file operation at a location.

q: A firm that receives tax return data from electronic return originators (EROs) and from individual taxpayers, processes it, and forwards it to a transmitter is participating in IRS e-file as a(n):
choices: Software Developer
Online Provider
Reporting Agent
Intermediate Service Provider
explain: An Intermediate Service Provider processes return data, typically from an ERO or an individual taxpayer, and forwards it to a transmitter. A Software Developer writes origination or transmission software, a Reporting Agent originates certain returns for payroll clients, and an Online Provider lets taxpayers self-prepare returns and is only a secondary role paired with another option.

q: Ana, an Authorized IRS e-file Provider, sells her tax practice to Ben's newly formed corporation. Which statement is correct?
choices: The corporation must apply and get its own electronic filing identification number (EFIN), which only the IRS can issue
The corporation may use Ana's electronic filing identification number (EFIN) until the end of the processing year
Ana may transfer her electronic filing identification number (EFIN) to the corporation as part of the sale
The corporation may rent Ana's electronic filing identification number (EFIN) if she remains listed as a Principal
explain: EFINs cannot be sold, transferred, loaned, leased or rented. When a business is sold or transferred, the new entity must get its own EFIN from the IRS, and using another Provider's EFIN can lead to sanctions.

q: A small firm has three preparers who reasonably expect to file 3, 4, and 5 individual income tax returns, respectively, during calendar year 2026. None of them has a hardship waiver. Which preparers are specified tax return preparers who must e-file those returns?
choices: None of them, because no preparer expects to file 11 or more returns
Only the preparer expecting to file 5 returns
All three, because the firm's members in the aggregate expect to file 12 returns
Only the firm's owner
explain: For preparers who are members of a firm, the count is the total number of covered returns the firm's members expect to file in the aggregate: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, which is 11 or more. Every member is then a specified tax return preparer, even one who individually files fewer than the threshold.
source: Form 8948 instructions; Treas. Reg. 301.6011-7; IRS FAQs on e-file requirements for specified tax return preparers

q: Kim, a specified tax return preparer, prepares a client's 2025 Form 1040. The client insists on filing on paper and will mail the return herself. How should Kim handle this?
choices: Attach the client's signed choice statement to the paper return
Mail the paper return for the client with Form 8948 attached
File Form 8944 to request a hardship waiver for this return
Keep the client's signed choice statement in her own records, and attach Form 8948 to the paper return with the box checked showing the taxpayer chose to file on paper
explain: A taxpayer choice statement is kept with the preparer's records and is never attached to the return or sent to the IRS. Form 8948, with the box for taxpayer choice checked, goes with the paper return the client signs and mails. If Kim or her staff mailed it, Kim would be the one filing, so the taxpayer choice exception would not apply.
source: Form 8948 instructions; IRS FAQs on e-file requirements for specified tax return preparers

q: When the IRS rejects an e-filed return and the electronic return originator (ERO) cannot fix the problem, Publication 1345 requires the ERO to take reasonable steps to inform the taxpayer of the rejection within:
choices: 24 hours
3 business days
5 calendar days
10 calendar days
explain: The ERO must take reasonable steps to tell the taxpayer within 24 hours and give the business rules with an explanation. The 5 and 10 calendar day periods are the time allowed to fix and resubmit the return, or file on paper, and still be treated as timely.

q: An Authorized IRS e-file Provider may do all of the following in its advertising EXCEPT:
choices: Describe itself as an Authorized IRS e-file Provider
Operate under the business name "IRS Refund Center"
Use the IRS e-file logo to show it offers e-file, without combining it with the IRS eagle or the word "Federal"
State that e-filed refunds arrive faster, in terms consistent with official IRS publications
explain: A Provider may not use "IRS" or "Internal Revenue Service" in its doing business as name, and it may not carry Treasury or IRS seals. Once accepted, it may call itself an Authorized IRS e-file Provider, may use the e-file logo within the stated limits, and may make refund timing claims that match official IRS publications. Acceptance does not imply IRS endorsement.
source: IRS Pub 3112 (Rev. 11-2025); Rev. Proc. 2007-40; Treasury Circular 230, 10.30

q: An Authorized IRS e-file Provider ran a radio advertisement for its e-file services, and the ad last aired on March 10, 2026. Under Publication 3112, the Provider must keep a copy of the ad until:
choices: December 31, 2026
December 31, 2027
March 10, 2029
No copy is required for radio ads
explain: For radio, television and internet ads, the Provider keeps a copy of the text or recording until the end of the calendar year following the last transmission or use. The ad last aired in 2026, so the copy is kept until December 31, 2027, and it must be given to the IRS on request.

q: For which client may an electronic return originator (ERO) skip the in-person identity verification steps (inspecting a valid government photo ID, comparing the photo, and recording the name, Social Security number, address, and date of birth)?
choices: A returning client whose prior-year return this ERO originated
A new client who brings a copy of last year's return prepared by another firm
A new client referred by an existing client
A new client who shows only a Social Security card
explain: The ERO must confirm identity for in-person transactions unless there is a multi-year business relationship, meaning the ERO originated returns for the taxpayer for a prior tax year. A referral or a prior return from another firm does not create that relationship, and a Social Security card is not a government photo ID.

q: Under Publication 1345, which taxpayer is NOT eligible to sign an e-filed 2025 return using the Self-Select personal identification number (PIN) method?
choices: A taxpayer, age 15, filing as the primary taxpayer, who has never filed a return
A taxpayer who authenticates with last year's Self-Select PIN instead of prior-year adjusted gross income (AGI)
A retiree, age 72, who filed a return last year
A married couple whose electronic return originator (ERO) enters the five-digit PINs they chose
explain: Primary taxpayers under age 16 who have never filed are ineligible for the Self-Select PIN method, as are secondary taxpayers under 16 who did not file the prior year. The method authenticates with prior-year AGI or prior-year PIN, and an ERO may enter PINs the taxpayers choose. The Practitioner PIN method does not need prior-year AGI or PIN, but the taxpayer must sign Form 8879.

q: A client signed Form 8879 showing adjusted gross income (AGI) of $72,400 and a refund of $1,210. Before transmission, the preparer makes a correction. Which change requires the client to sign a new Form 8879?
choices: AGI increases by $45 and the refund decreases by $12
AGI increases by $50 and the refund decreases by $14
AGI is unchanged, but federal income tax withheld and the refund each increase by $15
Total income decreases by $30 and total tax decreases by $9
explain: A new signature is needed when changed amounts differ by more than $50 for total income or AGI, or by more than $14 for total tax, federal income tax withheld, refund or amount owed. A $15 change to withholding and refund exceeds $14. A change of exactly $50 or exactly $14 is not more than the tolerance, and the other choices fall below both limits.

q: Pat's e-filed return claims a dependent child under Form 8332 signed by the custodial parent. The electronic return originator (ERO) does not send Form 8332 electronically with the return. What should the ERO do with Form 8332?
choices: Attach it to Form 8879 and keep it in the ERO's files
Mail it with Form 8453 before transmitting the return
Attach it to Form 8453 and mail it to the IRS within 3 business days after receiving acknowledgment that the IRS accepted the return
Paper file the whole return, since Form 8332 cannot be filed with an e-filed return
explain: Supporting documents such as Form 8332 that are not sent electronically are attached to Form 8453 and mailed within 3 business days after the ERO receives acknowledgment that the IRS accepted the electronic return. Form 8453 is a transmittal and is not signed, and Form 8879 stays with the ERO.

q: An accepted electronic return originator (ERO) receives a client's signed Form 8879 and all other information needed to originate the return on Friday, February 27, 2026. To avoid stockpiling, the ERO must submit the return no later than:
choices: Saturday, February 28, 2026
Monday, March 2, 2026
Wednesday, March 4, 2026
April 15, 2026, the return's due date
explain: After acceptance into IRS e-file, stockpiling means waiting more than three calendar days to submit a return once the ERO has all necessary information. February 27 plus 3 calendar days is Monday, March 2, 2026. Counting 3 business days (March 4) is the most common error, and collecting returns before acceptance into e-file is also stockpiling.

q: All of the following statements about refund-related financial products are consistent with Publication 1345 EXCEPT:
choices: When the taxpayer gets a refund-related product, the IRS sends the refund to the financial institution, not directly to the taxpayer
A Provider may charge a separate fee for Direct Deposit of a refund
The IRS is not involved in or responsible for refund anticipation loans or checks
The Provider should inform taxpayers that refund anticipation loans are interest-bearing loans
explain: Providers must never charge a separate fee for Direct Deposit. The other three statements reflect Pub 1345: the product is a business contract between the Provider and the taxpayer, the refund goes to the financial institution, and refund anticipation loans (RALs) are interest-bearing loans.

q: The IRS told a Provider about a Level One infraction, and the Provider kept committing the same violation. The continued violation is a Level Two infraction, which may result in:
choices: A written reprimand only, with no suspension
Suspension from IRS e-file for one or two years, depending on severity
Permanent expulsion with no chance of reconsideration
A suspension of five years
explain: Level Two infractions include continued Level One violations after IRS notice and may lead to suspension for one or two years. A Level One infraction alone may draw a written reprimand. Level Three may bring a two-year suspension or expulsion; individuals of an expelled firm may be reconsidered after a five-year waiting period.

q: A Provider receives a letter dated May 4, 2026, proposing a Level Two suspension (not an immediate sanction). Which statement about administrative review is correct?
choices: The Provider must petition the Tax Court within 90 days
Sanctions for Level Two infractions cannot be reviewed
The Provider has 60 days to request review, and the suspension starts on the letter date

The Provider may request review in writing within 30 calendar days of the letter date, and the sanction generally takes effect the later of 30 days after the letter date or the date a reviewing office or IRS Appeals affirms it
explain: A written request for administrative review is due within 30 calendar days of the denial or sanction letter. In most cases a sanction is effective 30 days after the letter date or the date the reviewing office or IRS Independent Office of Appeals affirms it, whichever is later. An immediate sanction, such as one for a Level Three infraction, stays in effect during review.

q: An Authorized IRS e-file Provider did not e-file any returns in either the current or the prior processing year, and the IRS notifies it of removal from IRS e-file. How can the Provider keep its participation without submitting a new application?
choices: It may reply within 60 days and request reactivation
It does not need to do anything, because accepted Providers never have to reapply
It must file Form 8944 within 30 days
It must pass a new fingerprint check
explain: Accepted Providers need not reapply each year if they keep e-filing and remain suitable. If a Provider does not e-file for both the current and prior processing years, the IRS may notify it of removal, and it may be reactivated if it replies within sixty days asking for reactivation. Otherwise it must reapply.

q: A client's 2025 Form 1040, transmitted on April 15, 2026, the due date, is rejected the same day because the required Identity Protection Personal Identification Number was missing. The electronic return originator (ERO) tells the client right away. To keep the return treated as timely filed, the corrected electronic return must be resubmitted no later than:
choices: April 15, 2026
April 20, 2026
April 22, 2026
April 25, 2026
explain: A rejected return transmitted on or before the due date is timely if the electronic portion is corrected and resubmitted by the fifth calendar day after the due date: April 15 + 5 = April 20, 2026. April 22 is 5 business days, and April 25 is 10 days, the paper-filing window. A missing or incorrect Identity Protection Personal Identification Number (IP PIN) causes the reject, and the client can find the current IP PIN in the IRS Online Account.
source: IRS Pub 1345; IRS: Get an Identity Protection PIN

q: A client's timely transmitted 2025 Form 1040 was rejected, and the IRS sent the reject notification on April 14, 2026. The return cannot be corrected electronically, so the client will file on paper. To be treated as timely, the paper return must be filed by:
choices: April 15, 2026
April 20, 2026
April 24, 2026
April 28, 2026
explain: A paper return after a reject is timely if filed by the later of the due date or 10 calendar days after the IRS reject notification. April 14 + 10 calendar days = April 24, 2026, which is later than April 15. Counting 10 business days gives April 28, a common error, and the paper return should include an explanation of why it is filed after the due date.

q: Lena's e-filed 2025 Form 1040 is rejected because her son's Social Security number (SSN) was already claimed as a dependent on another return. She has confirmed the SSN with the Social Security Administration and that no one else may claim him. Lena, the primary taxpayer, has a valid Identity Protection Personal Identification Number (IP PIN). What can she do?
choices: Resubmit electronically with the son's birth certificate attached as a PDF
She must file a paper return, because duplicate-dependent returns can never be e-filed
Resubmit electronically including her valid IP PIN, since the IRS accepts duplicate-dependent returns when the primary taxpayer includes a valid IP PIN
Wait until the other return is corrected before filing
explain: Beginning with the 2025 filing season, the IRS accepts e-filed Forms 1040 that claim an already-claimed dependent if the primary taxpayer includes a valid IP PIN. Without an IP PIN, or for 2022 and 2023 returns, a paper return is needed.
source: IRS News Release IR-2024-294; IRS e-file FAQ: Age, name or SSN rejects, errors and correction procedures

q: Under the common law of agency, authority that a principal grants to an agent directly, in a written agency agreement or in clear oral instructions, is called:
choices: Apparent authority
Implied authority
Express authority
Authority by ratification
explain: Express authority is actual authority the principal grants in so many words, either in an agency agreement or by clear oral instructions. Implied authority is also actual authority, but it is inferred from the express grant or from the principal's conduct rather than stated outright, and apparent authority rests on what a third party reasonably believes, not on any grant to the agent.
source: Cornell LII Wex, express authority; Cornell LII Wex, actual authority

q: Rhoda owns a bakery. She tells her manager, Eli, "Get the delivery van's brakes fixed this week at whatever shop can do it." Eli takes the van to a repair shop and signs the shop's standard work order authorizing the brake repair in the bakery's name. Rhoda said nothing about signing work orders. Which statement is correct?
choices: Eli had implied actual authority to sign the work order, because it was reasonably necessary to carry out Rhoda's express instruction.
Eli had only apparent authority, because Rhoda never told him he could sign documents.
Eli had no authority to sign, and the bakery is bound only if Rhoda later ratifies the work order.
Eli had express authority to sign the work order, because any act an agent performs for the principal is expressly authorized.
explain: When a principal expressly authorizes a task, the agent also has implied actual authority to take the steps reasonably necessary to complete it, and signing the shop's work order is such a step. Apparent authority is the wrong label because it depends on a third party's reasonable belief created by the principal's conduct, while here Eli's authority came from Rhoda's own instruction to him.
source: Cornell LII Wex, implied authority; Cornell LII Wex, actual authority

q: Over the past year, Nadia, the office manager of a small firm, has several times ordered printer supplies on the firm's account without being told to. Each time the owner saw the invoice and paid it without objection, and he has never told her to stop. Nadia now places another, similar order. As between Nadia and the owner, Nadia most likely had:
choices: No authority, because actual authority must be granted to an agent expressly in words.
Express authority, because paying the earlier invoices was a written grant of authority.
Authority only if the owner ratifies this new order after it is placed.
Implied actual authority, because a principal's failure to object to an agent's prior acts can authorize the agent to repeat them.
explain: A principal's failure to object to an agent's prior actions can give the agent implied actual authority to repeat those actions. Actual authority does not have to be granted in words, so the choice saying no authority exists misstates the rule, and ratification is needed only when an agent acted without authority.
source: Cornell LII Wex, implied authority; Cornell LII Wex, agency

q: Apparent authority arises when:
choices: The agent reasonably understands, from the principal's instructions, that the principal wants the act done.
A third party reasonably believes, because of the principal's conduct, that the agent is authorized to act for the principal.
The agent tells a third party that the agent is authorized to act for the principal.
The principal approves an agent's unauthorized act after the act is done.
explain: Apparent authority exists only when a third party reasonably infers from the principal's own conduct that the principal gave the agent the power to act. An agent's reasonable understanding of the principal's instructions describes implied actual authority, and an agent's own claims of authority cannot create apparent authority because the belief must trace to the principal. Approval after the fact is ratification.
source: Cornell LII Wex, apparent authority; Cornell LII Wex, actual authority

q: Coastline Retail appoints Lee as manager of one of its stores. Store managers in the industry commonly sign supply contracts of $8,000 or more. Coastline privately instructs Lee in writing not to sign any supply contract over $5,000. Lee signs an $8,000 supply contract in Coastline's name with a vendor who does not know of the limit. Which statement is correct?
choices: Coastline is not bound, because Lee had no actual authority to sign a contract over $5,000.
Coastline is bound, because Lee had implied actual authority as store manager.
Coastline is bound, because Lee had apparent authority and the vendor did not know of the private limit.
Coastline is bound only if it ratifies the contract.
explain: Appointing someone to a position such as store manager gives that person apparent authority to do what people in that position are normally expected to do, and a principal's private limit on the agent does not cut off apparent authority when the third party does not know of it. Implied actual authority is wrong because an agent has no implied authority to do something the principal expressly prohibited. By ignoring the limit, Lee breached the duty of obedience to Coastline.
source: Cornell LII Wex, apparent authority; Cornell LII Wex, agency

q: Which statement about how an agency relationship is created is correct?
choices: It must be created by a written agreement signed by both the principal and the agent.
It exists only if the parties call their relationship an agency and intend its legal consequences.
It can arise from the parties' conduct showing consent that one will act on the other's behalf and subject to the other's control.
It arises only from the principal's statements to third parties about the agent.
explain: Whether an agency exists depends on conduct showing mutual consent that one person will act on behalf of the other and subject to the other's control, and an agency can exist even if the parties did not call it one or intend its legal consequences. No signed writing is needed in general, because authority can be granted by oral instructions. The principal's statements to third parties are what create apparent authority, not the agency itself.
source: Cornell LII Wex, fiduciary relationship (quoting A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, Inc., 309 N.W.2d 285 (Minn. 1981)); Cornell LII Wex, express authority

q: For five years Omar was the purchasing agent for Delta Builders, and he regularly ordered lumber on Delta's account from Pine Supply. Delta fired Omar on June 1 but did not tell Pine Supply. On June 10 Omar ordered lumber from Pine Supply in Delta's name and kept it. Pine Supply had no knowledge that Omar had been fired. Is Delta liable to Pine Supply for the lumber?
choices: Yes, because Omar's apparent authority continued until Pine Supply had notice that the agency had ended.
No, because firing Omar ended all of his authority on June 1.
No, because only Omar received the lumber, so only Omar is liable.
Yes, because Omar still had actual authority until Delta gave him written notice of termination.
explain: Ending the agency terminates the agent's actual authority, but apparent authority can continue until third parties who dealt with the agent have notice that the agency has ended. Pine Supply had dealt with Omar for years and was not told, so Delta is bound. The choice saying all authority ended on June 1 is wrong because it ignores this lingering apparent authority, and Omar's actual authority did end when he was fired.
source: Cornell LII Wex, fiduciary relationship; Cornell LII Wex, apparent authority

q: Paula signed a durable power of attorney naming her nephew, Sam, as her agent to manage her bank accounts. Paula died on March 3. On March 9, knowing that Paula had died, Sam withdrew funds from her account to pay a bill. Which statement is correct?
choices: Sam's authority continued, because a durable power of attorney survives the principal's death.
Sam's authority ended when Paula died, because even a durable power of attorney ends at the principal's death.
Sam's authority continued until a court appointed an executor for Paula's estate.
Sam's authority ended only when Paula's heirs revoked the power of attorney in writing.
explain: A power of attorney is effective only while the principal is alive. A durable power of attorney differs from an ordinary one only in that it stays in effect if the principal becomes incapacitated, so it still ends at the principal's death. The choice saying a durable power survives death confuses incapacity with death.
source: Cornell LII Wex, durable power of attorney; Cornell LII Wex, power of attorney

q: Without any authority, an agent signs a contract in her principal's name to buy a used delivery truck. Which statement about ratification of the contract is correct?
choices: The principal can ratify only by signing a written ratification.
Ratification makes the principal liable only for future deliveries, not for the purchase already agreed to.
The principal can ratify by conduct, such as accepting the benefits of the contract.
Ratification is not possible, because an unauthorized contract is void.
explain: Ratification is a principal's approval of an act that did not bind the principal when it was done, and it can be shown by conduct, including accepting the benefits of the contract, not only by a signed writing. Once ratified, the act binds the principal as if it had been authorized when done, so the choice limiting ratification to future performance is wrong.

q: A lease gives the tenant, Fenwick Co., an option to renew that must be exercised by notice to the landlord no later than March 1. On February 20, Fenwick's office assistant, who had no authority to do so, sent the landlord a notice exercising the option in Fenwick's name. Fenwick learned of the notice on March 10 and ratified it that day. Was the option validly exercised?
choices: Yes, because ratification relates back to February 20, when the notice was sent.
Yes, because the landlord received the notice before March 1.
No, because a lease option can never be exercised through an agent.
No, because a ratification is not effective against the landlord if it comes after the deadline for the act has passed.
explain: When an act must be done by a set time to create a right against another party, a ratification made after that time is not effective against the other party, because the person ratifying must be able to do the act both when it was done and when it is ratified. Fenwick could not have exercised the option itself on March 10, so ratification does not relate back to save it. The relation-back choice states the general effect of ratification but ignores this timing limit.
source: FEC v. NRA Political Victory Fund, 513 U.S. 88 (1994) (quoting Restatement (Second) of Agency section 90), via Cornell LII

q: Gina hires Raj as her agent to find and buy a parcel of land suitable for a warehouse. Raj finds a suitable parcel, secretly buys it in his own name, and then sells it to Gina at a profit without telling her that he owned it. The price Gina paid was fair market value. Which duty did Raj breach?
choices: The duty of loyalty
The duty of obedience
The duty of care
No duty, because Gina paid fair market value
explain: An agent is a fiduciary who must act in the principal's best interests and not for personal gain, and secretly dealing with the principal for the agent's own profit is self-dealing that breaches the duty of loyalty. A fair price does not cure the breach. The duty of obedience concerns following the principal's instructions, and Raj did deliver a suitable parcel as instructed.

q: Acting within his actual authority, Ben contracts in his own name to buy a building from Seller. He does not reveal that he is buying for Harbor Corp., and Seller believes Ben is buying for himself. Harbor Corp. later refuses to close, and Seller then learns that Ben was acting for Harbor. Whom may Seller hold liable on the contract?
choices: Only Ben, because Seller never agreed to deal with Harbor Corp.
Only Harbor Corp., because Ben acted within his actual authority.
Either Ben or Harbor Corp.
Neither, because the contract did not name the true buyer.
explain: Harbor Corp. is an undisclosed principal: its agent acted for it without revealing its existence. An undisclosed principal is bound by its agent's acts within actual authority, and the agent, who contracted as if for himself, is also liable, so the third party may pursue either the agent or, once it learns of it, the principal. The choice naming only Harbor Corp. is wrong because Ben, who signed in his own name, remains liable to Seller as well.

q: While making a delivery for her employer, a driver negligently runs a red light and injures a pedestrian. Under the doctrine of respondeat superior, which statement is correct?
choices: Only the employer is liable, because the driver was acting for the employer.
Both the employer and the driver may be held liable to the pedestrian.
Only the driver is liable unless the employer was negligent in hiring or supervising her.
The employer is liable only if it knew about the driver's careless driving before the accident.
explain: Respondeat superior makes an employer liable for the wrongful acts of an employee committed within the scope of employment, without regard to the employer's own fault or knowledge. The employee remains liable for her own tort, so the injured party typically sues both. The choice requiring negligent hiring or supervision describes the employer's direct liability, which is a separate theory that is not needed here.
source: Cornell LII Wex, respondeat superior; Cornell LII Wex, servant

q: A furniture company employs Dan as a delivery driver. In which situation is the company most likely liable under respondeat superior for Dan's negligent driving?
choices: During his delivery route, Dan drives a few blocks off the route to pick up lunch and collides with another car on the way back to his next stop.
On a Sunday when he is off duty, Dan takes the company van without permission to help a friend move to another city.
Driving his own car from home to the warehouse before his shift, Dan hits a cyclist.
Dan abandons his route for the afternoon to attend a friend's party in another town and has an accident at the party.
explain: A detour, a minor departure from the employee's duties, is still within the scope of employment, so the employer is liable for it, while a frolic, a major departure undertaken for the employee's own purposes, is outside the scope of employment. A short lunch stop during a route is a detour. Commuting to and from work is generally treated as outside the employment relationship, and the Sunday trip and the afternoon party are frolics.
source: Cornell LII Wex, frolic and detour; Cornell LII Wex, agency

q: A business that hires an independent contractor is generally not vicariously liable for the contractor's torts. Which of the following is an exception that can make the hiring business liable?
choices: The contractor is paid by the job rather than by the hour.
The contractor supplies its own tools and equipment.
The contractor performs similar work for many other customers.
The work the contractor was hired to do is an inherently dangerous activity.
explain: Respondeat superior applies to employees, not independent contractors, but some duties cannot be delegated, and a business that hires a contractor to perform an inherently dangerous activity remains liable for harm the work causes. The other choices are facts that point toward independent contractor status, so they support the general rule of no vicarious liability rather than an exception.
source: Cornell LII Wex, independent contractor; Cornell LII Wex, respondeat superior

q: On March 1, Rex Supply, a merchant that sells office furniture, sends Dana a signed letter offering to sell her 20 desks at $300 each. The letter states that the offer will remain open for 60 days. Dana gives nothing in return for this promise. On March 20, Rex notifies Dana that it revokes the offer. On March 30, Dana accepts. What is the result under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)?
choices: No contract was formed, because Dana gave no consideration to keep the offer open.
A contract was formed, because Rex's signed written assurance made the offer irrevocable for the 60 days stated.
No contract was formed, because the offeree, Dana, is not a merchant.
A contract was formed only for the desks Dana had already arranged to resell before March 20.
explain: Under the UCC firm offer rule, a merchant's offer to buy or sell goods in a signed writing that gives assurance it will be held open is irrevocable without consideration for the time stated, up to three months. Rex's March 20 revocation was ineffective, so Dana's March 30 acceptance formed a contract. The need for consideration to keep an offer open is the common-law option contract rule, which the firm offer rule displaces; only the offeror must be a merchant.
source: UCC 2-205; Cornell LII Wex, firm offer

q: Owen offers in writing to sell Paula a parcel of land for $200,000. Paula replies, 'I will pay $180,000.' Owen refuses. The next day Paula writes, 'All right, I accept your offer at $200,000.' Owen has not renewed his offer. Which statement is correct?
choices: A contract was formed at $200,000, because Paula accepted before Owen revoked his offer.
A contract was formed at $180,000, because Owen did not respond to Paula's reply in writing.
No contract was formed, because Paula's counteroffer rejected Owen's offer, and her later 'acceptance' is only a new offer.
No contract was formed, because an offer to sell land can be accepted only by a signed deed.
explain: A counteroffer is both a rejection of the original offer and a new offer, so it ends the offeree's power to accept the original offer. Paula's later attempt to accept at $200,000 is a new offer that Owen is free to accept or reject. The first choice is tempting, but once Paula rejected the offer by countering, there was nothing left to accept.
source: Cornell LII Wex, counteroffer; Cornell LII Wex, offer

q: Pat, who is not a merchant, gives Lee a signed note offering to sell Lee her used piano for $2,000 and promising to keep the offer open for 30 days. Lee gives nothing for the promise and does nothing in reliance on it. On day 10, Pat tells Lee she revokes the offer. On day 12, Lee tries to accept. Which statement is correct?
choices: Pat's revocation was effective, because the firm offer rule applies only to offers by merchants and Lee gave no consideration for an option.
Pat's revocation was ineffective, because the offer was a firm offer in a signed writing.
Pat's revocation was ineffective, because any written offer that states a time for acceptance is irrevocable for that time.
A contract was formed on day 12, because Lee accepted within the 30 days stated.
explain: The Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) firm offer rule applies only to an offer by a merchant, so Pat's signed promise does not make her offer irrevocable. Without consideration (an option contract) or detrimental reliance, an offeror may revoke an offer at any time before acceptance. The firm offer choice is the common trap: a signed writing alone is not enough when the offeror is not a merchant.
source: UCC 2-205; Cornell LII Wex, option contract; Cornell LII Wex, offer

q: On May 1, Ana mails Ben an offer to provide bookkeeping services for one year at $1,500 per month. The offer says nothing about how or when acceptance is effective. Ben mails a letter of acceptance on May 5, and Ana receives it on May 8. On May 6, Ana changes her mind and sends Ben a revocation, which Ben receives on May 7. Under the common-law rule most states follow, which statement is correct?
choices: No contract was formed, because Ben received the revocation before Ana received the acceptance.
No contract was formed, because the revocation was effective when Ana sent it on May 6.
A contract was formed on May 8, when Ana received the acceptance.
A contract was formed on May 5, when Ben mailed the acceptance.
explain: Under the mailbox rule, an acceptance sent by an invited medium is effective when it leaves the offeree's possession, not when the offeror receives it. A revocation, by contrast, works only when the offeree is notified of it before accepting. Ben accepted on May 5, so Ana's revocation, received May 7, came too late; the trap is to treat the acceptance as effective only on receipt.
source: Cornell LII Wex, mailbox rule (quoting Restatement (Second) of Contracts 63); Cornell LII Wex, offer

q: Hart Co., a merchant, sends Ivy Corp., a merchant, a purchase order for 500 valves at $40 each. The order states that acceptance is limited to its terms. Ivy returns a signed acknowledgment stating 'We accept your order' and adding a term that all disputes go to arbitration. The acknowledgment does not say acceptance is conditional on Hart's assent to the new term. Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), which statement is correct?
choices: No contract was formed, because the acknowledgment did not mirror the purchase order.
A contract was formed on the terms of the purchase order, and the arbitration term is not part of it.
A contract was formed that includes the arbitration term, because both parties are merchants.
A contract was formed that includes the arbitration term unless Hart objects in writing within 10 days.
explain: Under UCC 2-207(1), a definite expression of acceptance operates as an acceptance even though it adds terms, unless it is expressly conditional on assent to them. Between merchants an additional term becomes part of the contract unless, among other things, the offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms, as Hart's order did. The 'no contract' choice applies the common-law mirror image rule, which does not govern a sale of goods, and the 10-day objection period belongs to the merchant confirmation rule of the statute of frauds.
source: UCC 2-207(1), (2)(a); Cornell LII Wex, mirror image rule

q: Cara hires Dev, a contractor, to remodel her kitchen for $40,000. Halfway through, with no unforeseen difficulties, Dev says he will stop work unless Cara agrees to pay $45,000 for the same work. Cara signs a writing agreeing to pay $45,000. When Dev finishes, Cara pays only $40,000. Under the common-law rule most states follow, can Dev recover the extra $5,000?
choices: Yes, because a modification of a contract needs no consideration to be binding.
Yes, because Cara agreed to the modification in a signed writing.
No, because Dev gave no new consideration; he was already bound to do the work for $40,000.
No, because a contract for services can never be modified once performance begins.
explain: A remodeling contract is for services, so the common law governs. Under the pre-existing duty rule, a promise to pay more for work the other party is already bound to do is not supported by consideration and is not enforceable. The first choice states the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 2 rule for sales of goods, which does not apply to services, and a signed writing does not supply the missing consideration.
source: Cornell LII Wex, consideration; Cornell LII Wex, accord and satisfaction (pre-existing duty rule)

q: Under a written contract, Mill Co., a merchant, agreed to sell Baker Inc., a merchant, 1,000 bags of flour at $20 per bag. Before delivery, Mill's costs rose and it asked for $22 per bag. Baker agreed in a signed writing but received nothing new in return. Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), the modification is:
choices: Binding, because an agreement modifying a contract for the sale of goods needs no consideration.
Not binding, because Baker received no consideration for agreeing to pay more.
Binding only if a court finds Mill's cost increase made performance impracticable.
Voidable by Baker at any time before delivery.
explain: UCC 2-209(1) states that an agreement modifying a contract within Article 2 needs no consideration to be binding. Because the modified contract is still for goods of $500 or more, it must satisfy the statute of frauds, and Baker's signed writing does that. The 'not binding' choice applies the common-law pre-existing duty rule, which governs services and real estate, not sales of goods.

q: Under the doctrine of promissory estoppel, a court may enforce a promise that is not supported by consideration when:
choices: The promise is made in a writing signed by the promisor.
The promisor is a merchant who deals in goods of the kind.
The promisee pays a nominal sum, such as $1, for the promise.
The promisee reasonably relied on the promise to its detriment, the promisor could reasonably foresee that reliance, and enforcement is needed to avoid injustice.
explain: Promissory estoppel lets a promisee recover when it reasonably and detrimentally relied on a promise that the promisor could reasonably foresee would induce reliance, and enforcement is needed to avoid injustice. It applies even though there is no consideration. A signed writing by a merchant is the test for a firm offer under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), not for promissory estoppel.
source: Cornell LII Wex, promissory estoppel; Cornell LII Wex, contract

q: Jo, who is 16 and a minor under state law, buys a used laptop for $900 from Max, an adult. Which statement about the contract is correct under the majority rule?
choices: The contract is void, so neither Jo nor Max is bound by it.
The contract is voidable at Jo's option; Jo may disaffirm it, but Max is bound unless Jo disaffirms.
The contract is voidable at the option of either party, because one party lacked capacity.
The contract is fully enforceable against Jo, because the price was fair.
explain: Capacity is an element of a valid contract, and a contract made by a minor is generally voidable. Only the minor holds the option to disaffirm or affirm it; the adult party is bound unless the minor disaffirms. It is not void, which would mean it had no legal effect from the start for either party.
source: Cornell LII Wex, voidable; Cornell LII Wex, capacity; Cornell LII Wex, void

q: Gus agrees to pay Hal $5,000 if Hal steals a competitor's customer list. Hal takes the money but never performs. Gus sues Hal for breach of contract. What is the likely result?
choices: Gus recovers the $5,000 as compensatory damages.
Gus may enforce the agreement, because Hal accepted payment.
Gus loses, because an agreement to commit a crime lacks the legality element and is void.
Gus loses only if Hal raises the statute of frauds, because the agreement was not in writing.
explain: Legality, a lawful purpose, is one of the elements of a valid contract. An agreement whose object is a crime is void, meaning it has no legal effect from the start, so a court will neither compel performance nor award damages for nonperformance. The statute of frauds choice is wrong because the problem is the illegal purpose, not the lack of a writing.
source: Cornell LII Wex, contract; Cornell LII Wex, void

q: Lena posts a notice offering $500 to anyone who finds and returns her lost dog. Sam reads it and phones Lena to say, 'I promise I will find your dog.' The next day, before Sam has begun searching, Lena tells Sam she withdraws the reward. Which statement is correct?
choices: Lena is not bound, because her offer could be accepted only by performance and she revoked it before Sam began to perform.
Lena is bound, because Sam accepted by promising to find the dog, forming a bilateral contract.
Lena is bound, because a reward offer cannot be revoked once a person has read it.
Lena is bound to pay Sam half the reward for his promise.
explain: A reward offer seeks an act, not a promise, so it creates a unilateral contract that is formed only when the requested performance is completed. Sam's promise was not an acceptance, and the offeror may revoke a unilateral offer any time before the offeree begins performance. The bilateral contract choice is wrong because a bilateral contract is an exchange of promises, which Lena did not ask for.
source: Cornell LII Wex, unilateral contract; Cornell LII Wex, bilateral contract

q: Each of the following correctly describes a type of contract EXCEPT:
choices: A customer who sits in a barber's chair and gets a haircut without discussing price has formed a contract implied in fact.
A contract a party signed because of an unlawful threat is voidable by that party.
An express contract must be in writing to be a valid contract.
A contract that has every element of a contract but lacks a writing that the statute of frauds requires is unenforceable.
explain: An express contract is one whose terms the parties state in words, orally or in writing, so it need not be written. A contract implied in fact is shown by the parties' conduct, a contract induced by duress is voidable, and a contract that fails the statute of frauds is valid but unenforceable in court. The duress choice may look wrong to someone who thinks duress makes a contract void, but the victim may choose to affirm or avoid it.
source: Cornell LII Wex, express contract; Cornell LII Wex, implied contract; Cornell LII Wex, duress; Cornell LII Wex, unenforceable; Cornell LII Wex, statute of frauds

q: Under the statute of frauds, which of the following oral agreements is unenforceable?
choices: An agreement to paint a house for $12,000, to be finished within three months.
An agreement to employ a manager for a fixed term of two years beginning next month.
An agreement to sell a used bicycle for $300.
An agreement to provide consulting services for six months for $40,000.
explain: The statute of frauds requires a signed writing for, among others, contracts for the sale of an interest in land and contracts that cannot be completed within one year. A two-year employment term cannot be performed within one year, so the oral agreement is unenforceable. The large-dollar service contracts are tempting, but the common-law statute of frauds has no dollar threshold for services, and the $500 threshold for goods does not reach a $300 sale.
source: Cornell LII Wex, statute of frauds; UCC 2-201(1)

q: On June 1, Ace Co. and Bolt Inc., both merchants, orally agree that Bolt will buy 2,000 hinges from Ace for $9,000. On June 3, Ace sends Bolt a written confirmation of the terms, signed by Ace. Bolt receives it on June 5 and reads it but never responds. On July 1, Bolt refuses delivery and asserts the statute of frauds. Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), the contract is:
choices: Unenforceable against Bolt, because Bolt never signed a writing.
Enforceable only against Ace, because Ace signed the confirmation.
Unenforceable against both parties, because the contract was oral and the price was over $500.
Enforceable against Bolt, because Bolt did not give written notice of objection within 10 days after receiving the confirmation.
explain: Between merchants, a written confirmation received within a reasonable time that is sufficient against the sender satisfies the statute of frauds against the recipient who has reason to know its contents, unless the recipient gives written notice of objection within 10 days after receipt. Bolt received and read Ace's signed confirmation and did not object, so it cannot rely on the statute of frauds. The 'never signed' choice states the general rule, which this merchant exception overrides.

q: Bea's Bakery orally orders 300 canvas tote bags printed with the bakery's name and logo from Tote Works for $4,000. The bags are not suitable for sale to others. Before receiving any notice of repudiation, Tote Works has made a substantial beginning on making them. Bea's then cancels and argues that the oral contract is unenforceable. Which statement is correct under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC)?
choices: The contract is enforceable, because the goods are specially manufactured for the buyer and the seller made a substantial beginning on them before notice of repudiation.
The contract is unenforceable, because it is for goods priced at $500 or more and there is no signed writing.
The contract is enforceable only to the extent of the bags Bea's has paid for and accepted.
The contract is enforceable only if both parties are merchants.
explain: UCC 2-201(3)(a) makes an oral contract enforceable when the goods are to be specially manufactured for the buyer, are not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course of the seller's business, and the seller substantially began manufacture before notice of repudiation. The general $500 writing requirement in 2-201(1) gives way to this exception. The 'paid for and accepted' exception exists too, but here the specially manufactured goods exception covers the whole order.

q: Kent hires Jacobs Builders to build a house for $300,000. The contract specifies one brand of plumbing pipe. Without intending to deviate, Jacobs installs a different brand of the same quality, a defect that barely affects the home's value. Kent refuses to pay anything until the walls are torn out and the pipe replaced. Which statement is correct?
choices: Kent may refuse to pay, because Jacobs did not tender perfect performance.
Jacobs recovers nothing on the contract and may sue only for the reasonable value of the materials.
Kent may cancel the contract and recover all payments already made.
Jacobs substantially performed and may recover the contract price less damages for the deviation.
explain: A construction contract is governed by the common law, where the substantial performance doctrine treats an immaterial deviation that still fulfills the contract's purpose as performance. The builder recovers the contract price, and the owner may deduct damages for the difference caused by the deviation. The perfect tender choice borrows the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 2 rule for goods, which does not apply to building a house.

q: Under a single-delivery contract (not an installment contract), Fab Co. delivers 100 chairs to Dine Inc. Each chair is a separate commercial unit. Three chairs are scratched; the other 97 conform. The contract does not limit Dine's remedies. Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), what may Dine do?
choices: Dine must accept all 100 chairs, because Fab substantially performed.
Dine may reject the whole delivery, accept the whole delivery, or accept the 97 conforming chairs and reject the rest.
Dine may reject only if the defects substantially impair the value of the whole delivery.
Dine must accept all 100 chairs and may only deduct the cost of repairing the three scratched chairs.
explain: Under the perfect tender rule in UCC 2-601, if goods or the tender of delivery fail in any respect to conform, the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest. Substantial performance is a common-law doctrine for services and construction. The 'substantially impair' test applies to installment contracts under UCC 2-612, which this contract is not.
source: UCC 2-601; UCC 2-612(2); Cornell LII Wex, perfect tender rule

q: A contract requires Tech Co. to deliver 50 laptops of Model X to Lawson Partners by October 31. Tech delivers 50 laptops of Model Y on October 20, and Lawson rightfully rejects them on October 21. On October 22, Tech notifies Lawson that it will deliver 50 Model X laptops by October 30. Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), which statement is correct?
choices: Lawson may cancel the contract immediately, because the first tender was not perfect.
Tech may cure only if it had reasonable grounds to believe that Model Y would be acceptable.
Tech has a right to cure by making a conforming delivery by October 31, after seasonably notifying Lawson.
Tech may cure only with Lawson's written consent.
explain: Under UCC 2-508(1), when a nonconforming tender is rejected and the time for performance has not yet expired, the seller may seasonably notify the buyer of its intent to cure and then make a conforming delivery within the contract time. Tech still has until October 31. The 'reasonable grounds' test comes from 2-508(2), which gives a further reasonable time only after the contract time has run.

q: Tess hires Uma to manage Tess's rental properties for two years. After six months, Uma wants out. Tess, Uma and Vic all agree that Vic will take over Uma's duties for the rest of the term and that Uma is released from the contract. Which statement is correct?
choices: Uma is discharged, because the three parties made a novation substituting Vic for Uma.
Uma remains liable if Vic fails to perform, because a party can never escape a contract by transferring duties.
Uma is discharged only after Vic completes the remaining term.
The agreement is ineffective, because a novation requires new consideration from Tess.
explain: A novation is an agreement that substitutes a new party for an original party and excuses the party who is replaced; both original parties must agree to it. Because Tess agreed to release Uma and accept Vic, Uma is discharged now. The 'remains liable' choice ignores that Tess expressly agreed to release Uma, which is what makes this a novation rather than a simple transfer of duties.

q: Wes rents a hotel room for one night at triple the normal rate. Both Wes and the hotel know that he is renting it only to watch a once-a-year parade from its balcony. Before the date, the parade is canceled for the first time in its history. The room is still available and Wes could still stay in it. Which doctrine best fits Wes's argument that he is excused from paying?
choices: Impossibility of performance.
Mutual rescission.
Frustration of purpose.
Novation.
explain: Frustration of purpose excuses performance when an unforeseeable event destroys the principal purpose of the contract, even though performance is still possible. Impossibility is the tempting choice, but it applies only when performance itself cannot be done, and here the hotel can still provide the room and Wes can still pay. Mutual rescission would require both parties to agree to cancel.
source: Cornell LII Wex, frustration of purpose; Cornell LII Wex, impossibility; Cornell LII Wex, rescission

q: When Gear Co. contracted to sell Plant Inc. a replacement drive shaft for delivery by May 1, Plant told Gear that its production line would shut down without the part and that no other source could supply one in time. Gear delivered on May 15, and Plant lost $30,000 of profits while its line was down. Plant could not have obtained the part elsewhere. Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), can Plant recover the lost profits?
choices: No, because a buyer's damages for late delivery are limited to the difference between the market price and the contract price.
No, unless the contract expressly listed lost profits as recoverable damages.
Yes, but only as punitive damages for Gear's delay.
Yes, as consequential damages, because Gear had reason to know of Plant's needs when contracting and the loss could not have been prevented by cover.
explain: UCC 2-715(2)(a) lets a buyer recover consequential damages for losses from requirements and needs that the seller had reason to know of at the time of contracting and that could not reasonably be prevented by cover or otherwise. Plant told Gear about the shutdown risk and could not buy elsewhere, so the lost profits are recoverable. Punitive damages are generally not available for breach of contract.
source: UCC 2-715(2)(a); Cornell LII Wex, consequential damages; Cornell LII Wex, contract

q: Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), a liquidated damages clause in a contract for the sale of goods is enforceable if:
choices: The parties agreed to it in a signed writing, whatever the amount.
The amount is reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual harm from the breach, the difficulty of proving loss, and the difficulty of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy.
The amount is large enough to deter either party from breaching.
The actual damages can be calculated precisely at the time of contracting.
