explain: UCC 2-718(1) allows damages to be liquidated in the agreement only at an amount that is reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual harm, the difficulty of proof of loss, and the inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy. A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty, so an amount set to deter breach fails. Liquidated damages are used because actual damages are hard to prove, not because they are easy to calculate.

q: A county hires Luten Co. to build a bridge for $500,000. After Luten has spent $100,000, the county repudiates the contract and tells Luten to stop work. Luten ignores the notice, finishes the bridge, and sues for its full costs. Which statement is correct?
choices: Luten may not recover the costs it incurred after the county told it to stop, because it had a duty to mitigate damages.
Luten may recover all its costs, because the county breached first.
Luten may recover nothing, because it failed to stop work when told.
Luten may recover all its costs plus punitive damages, because the county's repudiation was intentional.
explain: Under the mitigation of damages doctrine, an injured party cannot recover damages it could have avoided with reasonable effort. Once Luten was told to stop, continuing to build only increased the losses, so the costs incurred after notice are not recoverable. Luten does not lose everything, because it can still recover damages caused by the breach up to the notice, and punitive damages are not available for breach of contract.
source: Cornell LII Wex, mitigation of damages; Cornell LII Wex, contract

q: Nora signs a contract to buy a lakefront lot from Seth for $250,000. Before closing, Seth refuses to convey the lot because he has received a higher offer. Nora still wants the lot. Which remedy is Nora most likely to obtain?
choices: Punitive damages, because Seth breached to get a higher price.
Nominal damages only, because she has not yet paid the price.
Specific performance, ordering Seth to convey the lot, because each parcel of land is treated as unique and money damages are inadequate.
Rescission of the contract, which is the only remedy for breach of a contract to sell land.
explain: Specific performance is an equitable remedy ordering a party to perform as promised when money damages are inadequate, most commonly for real property and rare or unique goods. Land is treated as unique, so Nora can obtain an order requiring Seth to convey the lot. Punitive damages are generally not available for breach of contract, even when the breach is deliberate.
source: Cornell LII Wex, specific performance; Cornell LII Wex, contract; UCC 2-716(1)

q: Under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), when a buyer wrongfully rejects goods, the seller may do all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Withhold delivery of the goods.
Resell the goods in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner and recover the difference between the contract price and the resale price, plus incidental damages.
Cancel the contract.
Cover by buying substitute goods and recover the difference between the cost of cover and the contract price.
explain: UCC 2-703 lists the aggrieved seller's remedies, including withholding delivery, reselling and recovering damages under 2-706, recovering damages for nonacceptance, and canceling. Cover, buying substitute goods and recovering the difference between the cost of cover and the contract price, is a buyer's remedy when the seller fails to deliver or the buyer rightfully rejects or revokes acceptance. Mixing up the buyer's cover remedy with the seller's resale remedy is a common error.

q: Pat bought equipment from Seller and signed a promissory note payable to Seller. Kim signed the note as an accommodation party (a surety) for Pat. Seller now sues Kim on the note. Kim may raise all of the following defenses EXCEPT:
choices: Seller fraudulently induced Pat to sign the note by lying about the equipment.
Pat was a minor when Pat signed the note.
Seller fraudulently induced Kim to sign as surety.
Seller never delivered the equipment Pat paid for with the note.
explain: A surety may raise its own defenses and most of the principal debtor's defenses, such as the creditor's fraud or failure to deliver what was promised. The principal's personal defenses of infancy, lack of legal capacity and discharge in insolvency proceedings are not available to the surety, because protecting the creditor against exactly those risks is why a surety is taken. Fraud on the principal is the tempting wrong choice, but it goes to the underlying obligation, so the surety can use it.

q: Sam signed a promissory note to Bank as an accommodation party (a surety) for Ron, the borrower. Ron later received a discharge in bankruptcy that included the note. Bank now demands payment from Sam. What is the result?
choices: Sam is released, because a surety may assert every defense the principal debtor has.
Sam is released, because the principal debtor's discharge extinguishes the debt for all obligors.
Sam remains liable, because the principal debtor's discharge in bankruptcy is not a defense the surety may raise.
Sam remains liable only if Bank first filed a claim in Ron's bankruptcy case.
explain: Discharge of the principal debtor in an insolvency proceeding is one of the principal's personal defenses that a surety cannot raise. Sam stays liable to Bank on the note. The idea that a surety may assert every defense of the principal is wrong because infancy, lack of capacity and discharge in insolvency are carved out.

q: Lee signed Tom's promissory note to Lender as an accommodation party, next to the words "collection guaranteed." Tom missed a payment. Before Lender may collect from Lee, Lender generally must:
choices: make no demand on anyone, because a guarantor is liable as soon as the principal debtor misses a payment.
first try to collect from Tom, for example by obtaining a judgment that is returned unsatisfied, unless Tom is insolvent, cannot be served or payment from Tom is otherwise plainly unobtainable.
obtain Lee's written consent to proceed.
repossess and sell any collateral Tom pledged and sue Lee only for a deficiency.
explain: A guarantor of collection is liable only after the creditor shows that payment cannot be obtained from the principal debtor, such as when an execution of judgment is returned unsatisfied, the debtor is insolvent or cannot be served. A guarantor of payment, by contrast, may be pursued as soon as the debtor defaults, with no prior resort to the debtor. The first choice describes a guaranty of payment, not of collection.

q: Kim signed Pat's promissory note to Bank as an accommodation party (a surety). When Pat defaulted, Kim paid Bank the full balance. Which statement correctly describes Kim's rights?
choices: Kim may recover from Pat only if Pat signed a separate written promise to reimburse Kim.
Kim and Pat must share the loss equally, because both signed the note.
Kim has no claim against Pat, because Kim's payment discharged the note.
Kim is entitled to reimbursement from Pat and may enforce the note against Pat in Bank's place.
explain: A surety who pays the principal debtor's obligation is entitled to reimbursement from the principal debtor and may enforce the instrument against the principal, stepping into the creditor's position (subrogation). No separate reimbursement promise is needed. Sharing the loss describes contribution among co-sureties, not the relationship between a surety and the principal debtor, who bears the whole debt.

q: Ann and Bo each signed Cy's promissory note to Bank as co-makers for Cy's accommodation (co-sureties). When Cy defaulted, Bank collected the entire balance from Ann. Which right lets Ann recover part of what she paid from Bo?
choices: Contribution
Exoneration
Reimbursement
Setoff
explain: Co-sureties with the same liability are jointly and severally liable to the creditor, and one who pays more than its share may recover from the other through contribution. Reimbursement is the surety's right against the principal debtor, Cy, for the full amount paid, not a right against a fellow surety.

q: Dee signed Ed's promissory note to Bank as an accommodation party (a surety), and Bank knew Dee signed as surety. The note was secured by a perfected security interest in Ed's delivery truck. Without Dee's consent, Bank released its security interest in the truck and took no substitute collateral. The note contains no waiver of suretyship defenses. Ed then defaulted. What is the effect of the release on Dee?
choices: None, because Dee promised to pay if Ed did not, regardless of collateral.
Dee is fully discharged, because any act by the creditor without the surety's consent releases the surety.
Dee is discharged to the extent the release impaired the value of the collateral.
Dee is discharged only if Bank also released Ed from the debt.
explain: When the creditor impairs collateral securing the principal debtor's obligation, for example by releasing it without substitute collateral, a surety the creditor knows of is discharged to the extent of the impairment. The surety is not released in full, only by the value lost. The first choice ignores that the surety had a right to look to that collateral after paying.

q: Under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code, a security interest attaches to collateral when all of the following have occurred EXCEPT:
choices: the secured party has given value.
the debtor has rights in the collateral.
the debtor has signed a security agreement describing the collateral, or the secured party has possession or control of the collateral under the agreement.
a financing statement covering the collateral has been filed.
explain: Attachment requires value, the debtor's rights in the collateral, and either a signed security agreement describing the collateral or the secured party's possession or control under the agreement. Filing a financing statement is a method of perfection, not a requirement for attachment.

q: Lender lent $20,000 to Gail and, in a phone call, Gail agreed that Lender would have a security interest in Gail's piano. Nothing was put in writing or signed, and the piano stayed in Gail's home. Lender then filed a financing statement naming Gail and describing the piano. Is Lender's security interest enforceable against Gail?
choices: Yes, because Lender gave value and Gail owns the piano.
Yes, because the financing statement satisfies the writing requirement.
No, because there is no signed security agreement and Lender does not have possession of the piano.
No, because a security interest in household goods can be created only by a purchase-money seller.
explain: A security interest is enforceable only if, in addition to value and rights in the collateral, the debtor signs a security agreement describing the collateral or the secured party takes possession or control under the agreement. An oral agreement with the collateral left with the debtor fails that test. Filing a financing statement does not substitute for the security agreement; a financing statement may be filed before attachment, but it does not cause attachment.

q: Appliance Store sold a refrigerator on credit to Dana for use in her home. Dana signed a security agreement giving the store a security interest in the refrigerator to secure the unpaid price. The store did not file a financing statement. The store's security interest is:
choices: unperfected, because a financing statement must be filed to perfect a security interest in goods.
perfected automatically when it attached, because it is a purchase-money security interest in consumer goods.
perfected only if the store files within 20 days after Dana receives the refrigerator.
perfected only while the store keeps possession of the refrigerator.
explain: A purchase-money security interest in consumer goods is perfected when it attaches, without filing. The refrigerator is a consumer good because Dana bought it primarily for household use, and the store's interest secures its price. The 20-day period is the grace period that lets a purchase-money filing defeat intervening lien creditors and buyers, or gain priority in non-inventory collateral, not a condition for perfecting this interest.

q: Appliance Store holds a purchase-money security interest (PMSI) in a refrigerator it sold on credit to Dana for her home, perfected automatically without filing. Dana later sold the refrigerator for cash to her neighbor Eli, who bought it for his own home and did not know of the store's interest. The store never filed a financing statement. Can the store reclaim the refrigerator from Eli?
choices: Yes, because the PMSI was perfected.
Yes, because a security interest follows the collateral into the hands of any buyer.
No, because Eli is a buyer in ordinary course of business.
No, because Eli bought for value, without knowledge, for household use, and before any financing statement was filed.
explain: A buyer of consumer goods from a consumer takes free of a security interest, even a perfected one, if the buyer gives value without knowledge of it, buys primarily for personal, family or household use, and buys before a financing statement covering the goods is filed. Had the store filed, Eli would have taken subject to its interest. Eli is not a buyer in ordinary course because Dana is not in the business of selling refrigerators.

q: Bank holds a security interest in all of Motor Dealer's inventory, perfected by filing. Rita bought a car from Dealer's showroom lot in the usual way, paid in full and drove it home. Rita knew Bank financed Dealer's inventory. Dealer then defaulted on the Bank loan. Which statement is correct?
choices: Rita takes the car free of Bank's security interest.
Bank may repossess the car, because its security interest was perfected before Rita bought.
Bank may repossess the car, because Rita knew of Bank's security interest.
Rita takes free of Bank's interest only if she bought the car primarily for business use.
explain: A buyer in ordinary course of business takes free of a security interest created by its seller, even if the interest is perfected and the buyer knows it exists. Rita bought in good faith, in the usual way, from a dealer in the business of selling cars. Knowing of the security interest does not defeat her; only knowing that the sale violates the secured party's rights would.

q: Under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code, a financing statement is sufficient if it provides all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: the name of the debtor.
the name of the secured party or its representative.
an indication of the collateral covered.
the amount of the debt the collateral secures.
explain: A financing statement is sufficient if it gives the debtor's name, the name of the secured party or a representative, and an indication of the collateral. It is a notice filing that tells searchers to inquire further; it need not state the amount of the secured debt.

q: Lender took a security interest from Oak Corp. Both the signed security agreement and the filed financing statement described the collateral only as "all of the debtor's assets." Which statement is correct?
choices: Both descriptions are sufficient.
The financing statement's description is sufficient, but the security agreement's description does not reasonably identify the collateral.
The security agreement's description is sufficient, but the financing statement must list each item of collateral.
Neither description is sufficient.
explain: A financing statement may indicate the collateral as all assets or all personal property, because it only gives notice. A security agreement must reasonably identify the collateral, and a supergeneric description such as "all the debtor's assets" does not, so the security interest does not attach on that description.

q: First Bank lent money to Nova Inc. and took a security interest in Nova's checking account at Second Bank. How may First Bank perfect its security interest in the deposit account?
choices: By filing a financing statement in the state where Nova is organized
By taking possession of Nova's checkbook and bank statements
By obtaining control, such as through a signed agreement among Nova, First Bank and Second Bank that Second Bank will follow First Bank's instructions about the funds without Nova's further consent
No action is needed, because a security interest in a deposit account is perfected when it attaches
explain: A security interest in a deposit account, as original collateral, may be perfected only by control. A secured party that is not the depositary bank gets control through an agreement among the debtor, the secured party and the bank that the bank will follow the secured party's instructions without the debtor's further consent, or by becoming the bank's customer on the account. Filing, the usual method for most collateral, does not perfect a security interest in a deposit account.

q: Gary borrowed money from Lender and, under a signed security agreement, delivered his valuable painting to Lender to hold as collateral. Lender filed no financing statement. Two months later, at Gary's request, Lender returned the painting to Gary. Which statement is correct?
choices: Lender's security interest was perfected while Lender held the painting and became unperfected when Lender returned it.
Lender's security interest was never perfected, because no financing statement was filed.
Lender's security interest stays perfected after the return, because it was perfected when the loan was made.
Lender's security interest stays perfected for 20 days after the return in every case.
explain: A secured party may perfect a security interest in goods by taking possession, without filing, and perfection by possession lasts only while the secured party keeps possession. Once Lender returned the painting with no financing statement on file, its interest became unperfected. The 20-day temporary perfection rules cover narrow cases such as goods held by a bailee or instruments released for sale or collection, not an ordinary return of goods to the debtor.

q: On March 1, Alpha Bank filed a financing statement covering Kane Co.'s equipment while it negotiated a loan. On April 1, Beta Bank lent money to Kane, took a signed security agreement covering the same equipment and filed its own financing statement. On May 1, Alpha made its loan and Kane signed Alpha's security agreement. Neither interest is a purchase-money security interest. Which bank has priority in the equipment?
choices: Beta, because its security interest attached and was perfected before Alpha's.
Beta, because Alpha's filing was ineffective when made before a security agreement existed.
Alpha, because priority among perfected security interests dates from the earlier of filing or perfection.
They share pro rata, because both interests are perfected.
explain: Conflicting perfected security interests rank by the earlier of the time a filing covering the collateral is first made or the time the interest is first perfected. A financing statement may be filed before a security agreement is made, so Alpha's priority dates from its March 1 filing, ahead of Beta's April 1 filing. Beta's argument that it attached and perfected first is the common mistake; the rule is first to file or perfect, not first to perfect.

q: Bank holds a security interest in all of Rook Corp.'s present and after-acquired equipment, perfected by a financing statement filed in 2024. On June 1, Seller sold Rook a new machine for use in its plant on credit, took a signed security agreement in the machine to secure the price, and delivered the machine that day. Seller filed a financing statement on June 15. Which party has priority in the machine?
choices: Bank, because it filed first.
Bank, because Seller did not notify Bank before delivering the machine.
Seller, because a purchase-money seller always has priority, whenever it files.
Seller, because its purchase-money security interest in non-inventory goods was perfected within 20 days after Rook received the machine.
explain: A perfected purchase-money security interest in goods other than inventory or livestock has priority over a conflicting security interest in the same goods if it is perfected when the debtor receives possession or within 20 days after. Seller filed 14 days after delivery, so it beats Bank's earlier-filed after-acquired property interest. Advance notice to earlier secured parties is required only for a purchase-money interest in inventory or livestock.

q: Finance Co. has a security interest in Vale Corp.'s equipment under a signed security agreement, but it never filed a financing statement or took possession. A judgment creditor of Vale then had the sheriff levy on the equipment, obtaining a judicial lien. Neither party has a purchase-money interest. Who has priority in the equipment?
choices: The judgment creditor, because an unperfected security interest is subordinate to a person who becomes a lien creditor before the security interest is perfected.
Finance Co., because its security interest attached before the levy.
Finance Co., because a judgment creditor is an unsecured creditor.
They share pro rata.
explain: A security interest is subordinate to the rights of a person who becomes a lien creditor before the security interest is perfected, or before a financing statement is filed with a security agreement in place. Attachment alone makes the interest enforceable against the debtor, but it must be perfected to beat a lien creditor. A judgment creditor that levies is a lien creditor, not merely an unsecured creditor.

q: In a Chapter 7 liquidation, after secured creditors have been satisfied from their collateral, the trustee distributes the remaining property of the estate in which order?
choices: General unsecured claims, then priority claims under 11 U.S.C. 507, then the debtor
Priority claims under 11 U.S.C. 507 in their listed order, then timely filed general unsecured claims, then the debtor
All unsecured claims pro rata, with no distinction between priority and general claims, then the debtor
Claims of the debtor's insiders, then priority claims, then general unsecured claims
explain: Secured creditors are paid first from the value of their collateral. The estate's remaining property then goes to priority claims in the order 11 U.S.C. 507 lists them, then to timely filed general unsecured claims, then to later-ranked items such as late claims, penalties and postpetition interest, and anything left goes to the debtor. Within a class, claims share pro rata, but priority claims as a group are paid before general unsecured claims.

q: Under 11 U.S.C. 507(a), which allowed unsecured claim is given first priority?
choices: Administrative expenses of the bankruptcy estate
Unpaid wages owed to the debtor's employees
Domestic support obligations, such as child support owed to a former spouse
Income taxes owed to the federal government
explain: Section 507(a)(1) gives first priority to allowed unsecured claims for domestic support obligations owed to a spouse, former spouse or child of the debtor, or assigned to a governmental unit, subject to a carve-out for certain trustee administrative expenses. Administrative expenses are the tempting choice, but they rank second. Wages rank fourth and most taxes eighth.

q: Rex Corp. filed a Chapter 7 petition on October 1 while still operating. Which employee claim qualifies for priority under 11 U.S.C. 507(a)(4), up to the statutory dollar cap?
choices: Wages Tina earned in January of the same year, about nine months before the petition
A loan Uma made to Rex the month before the petition
Wages Val will earn from the trustee after the petition
Vacation pay Sid earned in August, two months before the petition
explain: Section 507(a)(4) gives fourth priority, up to a per-person cap, to wages, salaries, commissions, and vacation, severance and sick pay earned within 180 days before the petition or the end of the business, whichever is first. Sid's vacation pay was earned within that window. Tina's wages were earned more than 180 days before the petition, so her claim is a general unsecured claim, and any wage claim above the cap is also general unsecured.

q: In a Chapter 7 case, Bank's allowed claim is secured by a perfected security interest in equipment worth less than the amount Bank is owed. How is Bank's claim treated?
choices: As a secured claim up to the value of the equipment and a general unsecured claim for the rest
As a secured claim for the full amount owed, payable first from all estate property
As a general unsecured claim for the full amount, because the collateral does not cover the debt
As a priority claim under 11 U.S.C. 507 for the amount the collateral does not cover
explain: An allowed claim secured by a lien is a secured claim to the extent of the value of the creditor's interest in the collateral and an unsecured claim for the rest. The shortfall shares with other general unsecured creditors; it gets no priority under section 507 and no claim on other estate property ahead of other creditors.

q: In a bankruptcy case, a creditor's allowed claim is secured by collateral worth more than the claim. Under 11 U.S.C. 506(b), the creditor may also recover from the collateral:
choices: nothing beyond the amount of the claim on the petition date.
interest on its claim and reasonable fees, costs or charges provided for in the agreement under which the claim arose.
priority under 11 U.S.C. 507 for any deficiency.
the full value of the collateral, including the excess over its claim.
explain: An oversecured creditor is allowed interest on its claim, plus reasonable fees, costs or charges provided for under the agreement or state statute, to the extent the collateral's value exceeds the claim. It is not entitled to the excess value itself; any equity above the claim belongs to the estate. Creditors whose collateral is worth less than the claim do not earn this postpetition interest.

q: Finance Co. had a signed security agreement covering Lark Inc.'s equipment but never filed a financing statement or otherwise perfected. Lark then filed a Chapter 7 petition. What is the trustee's position with respect to Finance Co.'s security interest?
choices: The trustee must honor the security interest, because it attached before the petition.
The trustee may avoid it only if Finance Co. is an insider of Lark.
The trustee may avoid it, because the trustee has the rights of a hypothetical lien creditor as of the petition date, so Finance Co. is left with a general unsecured claim.
The trustee may avoid it only if Lark granted the security interest within 90 days before the petition.
explain: Under the strong-arm clause the trustee has, as of the start of the case, the rights of a creditor holding a judicial lien on the debtor's property, whether or not such a creditor exists. An unperfected security interest is subordinate to a lien creditor, and the Uniform Commercial Code treats a trustee in bankruptcy as a lien creditor from the petition date. Finance Co. loses its collateral and shares as a general unsecured creditor; the 90-day and insider periods belong to the separate preference rules.

q: In a Chapter 7 case, the estate's unencumbered property is not enough to pay every claim. Which of the following allowed unsecured claims is paid first?
choices: An income tax claim of the federal government entitled to priority
A supplier's claim for goods sold on open account
A claim for wages earned within 180 days before the petition
The trustee's fees and other administrative expenses of the estate
explain: Among these claims, administrative expenses rank second under 11 U.S.C. 507(a)(2), ahead of wages within 180 days (fourth) and priority tax claims (eighth). The supplier's open-account claim has no priority and is paid only after all priority claims. Wages are the tempting choice, but administrative expenses come first so that the case can be run.

q: Delta Corp., an insolvent manufacturing corporation, wants to keep operating while it restructures its debts under a court-confirmed plan. Under which chapter of the Bankruptcy Code may Delta file a voluntary petition to do this?
choices: Chapter 7, which lets a business keep operating under a repayment plan
Chapter 11
Chapter 13
None, because a corporation can be put into bankruptcy only by an involuntary petition of its creditors
explain: Chapter 11 (reorganization) is open to corporations and other persons that may be Chapter 7 debtors, and lets the business keep operating under a confirmed plan. Chapter 13 is limited to an individual with regular income (or an individual and spouse) within the Chapter 13 debt limits, so a corporation cannot use it. Chapter 7 is liquidation, and any entity that may be a debtor under a chapter can file a voluntary petition under it.

q: All of the following statements about involuntary bankruptcy petitions are correct EXCEPT:
choices: An involuntary case may be commenced only under Chapter 7 or Chapter 11.
Creditors may file an involuntary Chapter 13 petition against an individual who has regular income.
An involuntary petition may not be filed against a farmer.

If the debtor has 12 or more qualifying creditors (holders of claims that are not contingent or in bona fide dispute, not counting employees, insiders and transferees of avoidable transfers), at least three of them must join in the petition.
explain: An involuntary case can be commenced only under Chapter 7 or Chapter 11; Chapter 13 is available only by the debtor's own voluntary petition. Farmers, family farmers and nonbusiness (charitable) corporations cannot be put into bankruptcy involuntarily. Three petitioning creditors are needed when there are 12 or more qualifying creditors, and one is enough when there are fewer than 12, as long as the petitioners' undisputed unsecured claims meet the statutory minimum.

q: Kim, an individual, files a voluntary Chapter 7 petition. Which of the following may continue without relief from the automatic stay?
choices: A credit card issuer's calls and letters demanding payment of a balance Kim owed before the petition
A lender's repossession of Kim's car for payments she missed before the petition
A pending state criminal prosecution of Kim for writing bad checks
A creditor's enforcement of a money judgment it won against Kim before the petition
explain: Filing a petition automatically stays acts to collect prepetition claims, to enforce prepetition judgments, and to take possession of or enforce liens against the debtor's property. Criminal proceedings against the debtor are an express exception, as are certain domestic support actions, governmental police and regulatory actions, and tax audits. A creditor that wants to repossess collateral must first get relief from the stay from the court.

q: Which statement about the trustee's power to avoid preferential transfers is correct?
choices: A payment to any creditor made within one year before the petition can be avoided, whether or not the creditor is an insider.
The trustee must prove that the creditor knew the debtor was insolvent when it received the payment.

A payment to an insider creditor can be avoided if made within one year before the petition, while a payment to a creditor that is not an insider generally must be made within 90 days before the petition.

A cash purchase of inventory that the debtor and seller intended to be, and that in fact was, a substantially contemporaneous exchange for new value can be avoided if made within 90 days before the petition.
explain: A preference is a transfer to or for a creditor on an antecedent debt, made while the debtor was insolvent, that lets the creditor receive more than it would in a Chapter 7 liquidation; the look-back period is 90 days, extended to one year for insiders. Using the one-year period for a creditor that is not an insider is the common mistake. The creditor's knowledge is not an element, the debtor is presumed insolvent during the 90 days before the petition, and a substantially contemporaneous exchange for new value is an exception, along with ordinary course payments and bona fide domestic support payments.

q: On June 1, 2024, Rita, who was insolvent, sold land worth $400,000 to Ben, an unrelated buyer, for $150,000. Rita had no intent to hinder, delay or defraud her creditors. She filed a Chapter 7 petition on September 1, 2025. Can the trustee avoid the sale under the Bankruptcy Code as a fraudulent transfer?
choices: No, because the sale was made more than one year before the petition
No, because the trustee must prove Rita actually intended to defraud her creditors
Yes, but only if Ben was an insider
Yes, because Rita received less than reasonably equivalent value while insolvent, within two years before the petition
explain: The trustee may avoid a transfer made within 2 years before the petition either with actual intent to hinder, delay or defraud creditors, or (constructive fraud) for less than reasonably equivalent value while the debtor was insolvent. No intent is needed for constructive fraud, and the one-year period belongs to insider preferences, not fraudulent transfers. If Ben bought in good faith, he keeps a lien on the land to the extent of the $150,000 he paid.

q: Which of the following would cause the court to deny an individual debtor a Chapter 7 discharge of all debts, rather than only leaving a particular debt undischarged?
choices: The debtor owes past-due child support to a former spouse.
Eight months before the petition, the debtor gave her boat to a friend with intent to hinder her creditors.
The debtor owes a judgment for injuries she caused while driving intoxicated.
The debtor owes a debt for money she embezzled from a former employer.
explain: Transferring or concealing property with intent to hinder, delay or defraud creditors within one year before the petition is a ground to deny the discharge entirely, as are destroying financial records, making a false oath in the case, and receiving a Chapter 7 discharge in a case filed within 8 years before. Domestic support obligations, debts for embezzlement, and debts for injury caused by intoxicated driving are only excepted from the discharge: those debts survive, but the debtor's other debts are still discharged. An embezzlement debt survives only if the creditor timely asks the court to except it; support and drunk-driving debts survive automatically.

q: Granite Inc., a privately held corporation organized in Texas, has no securities registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and files no SEC reports. To win a government contract, its president wires money from a Texas bank account to a foreign defense ministry official. Which statement is correct under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)?
choices: No violation occurred, because the anti-bribery provisions apply only to issuers with securities registered with the SEC.
No violation occurred, because the official received the payment outside the United States.
Granite violated the books and records provisions, which apply to every business organized in the United States.
Granite violated the anti-bribery provisions, which apply to domestic concerns as well as to issuers.
explain: The FCPA anti-bribery provisions cover issuers, domestic concerns (United States citizens and residents, and businesses organized in the United States or with their principal place of business here), and other persons acting within the United States. A corrupt payment to a foreign official to obtain business, made using a means of interstate commerce such as a wire from a United States bank, is prohibited even though the official is abroad. The books and records and internal control provisions apply only to issuers, so they do not reach a private company like Granite.

q: A corporation whose stock is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) pays a foreign customs clerk a small fee to speed up the routine processing of import papers for goods the company is entitled to bring into the country. Which statement is correct under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)?
choices: The payment violates the FCPA, because any payment of value to a foreign official is prohibited.
The payment is permitted only because its amount is small.
The payment falls within the exception for facilitating or expediting payments made to secure routine governmental action.
The same exception would cover a payment to the official who decides whether to award the company a new government contract.
explain: The anti-bribery provisions do not apply to a facilitating or expediting payment whose purpose is to secure routine governmental action, such as processing papers, issuing permits, or scheduling inspections. The exception turns on the nature of the action, not the size of the payment. A decision whether, or on what terms, to award new business or continue business with a party is never routine governmental action.

q: Under the anti-bribery provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), which of the following is an affirmative defense?
choices: Payments of this kind are customary in the foreign country, even though no written law permits them.
The payment was lawful under the written laws and regulations of the foreign official's country.
The company paid the official through a local agent instead of paying the official directly.
The foreign official, rather than the company, first asked for the payment.
explain: The FCPA has two affirmative defenses: the payment was lawful under the written laws and regulations of the official's country, and the payment was a reasonable and bona fide expenditure, such as travel and lodging, directly related to promoting or demonstrating products or services or performing a contract with a foreign government. Local custom without a written law is not a defense. Paying through an agent while knowing the money will go to the official is itself prohibited, and a request from the official does not excuse the payment.

q: Lee is an unpaid, volunteer member of the board of directors of a tax-exempt charity. He serves solely in an honorary capacity, takes no part in the day-to-day or financial operations, and did not know that payroll taxes withheld from employees were not paid over. The charity's paid executive director, who signs the checks, is liable for the trust fund recovery penalty. Which statement about Lee is correct?
choices: Lee is liable for the penalty, because every director has authority over the organization's finances.
Lee is liable for the penalty, because it applies to every board member whether or not he knew of the failure.
Lee is not liable, but only because a tax-exempt organization owes no Social Security or Medicare tax.

Lee is not liable, because the penalty does not apply to an unpaid, volunteer, honorary board member of a tax-exempt organization who does not take part in its day-to-day or financial operations and did not know of the failure.
explain: The trust fund recovery penalty falls on a person required to collect, account for and pay over the tax who willfully fails to do so, and the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) exempts unpaid, volunteer board members of tax-exempt organizations who serve only in an honorary capacity, stay out of day-to-day and financial operations, and lack actual knowledge of the failure. The exception does not apply if it would leave no one liable, but here the executive director is liable. Tax-exempt status does not remove an employer's duty to withhold and pay Social Security and Medicare taxes.

q: Coastal Corp. paid wages to an employee but failed to withhold the employee's share of Social Security and Medicare taxes. Which statement about liability for the employee's share is correct?
choices: Coastal is liable for the employee share it failed to withhold, as well as for its own matching employer share.
Only the employee is liable for the employee share, because that tax is imposed on the employee's wages.
Coastal is liable only for its employer share, and the employee pays the rest as self-employment tax.
No one is liable for the employee share, because it was not withheld when the wages were paid.
explain: The employee share of Social Security and Medicare tax is imposed on the employee, but the employer must collect it by deducting it from wages and is liable for paying it, whether or not it actually withheld it. The employer separately owes an equal employer share. Federal unemployment tax is imposed only on the employer and is not withheld from wages.

q: Pat repairs equipment for Delta Co. The written contract calls Pat an independent contractor. Delta supplies the tools, pays Pat by the hour, and has the right to tell Pat when, where and how to do the work, though it rarely gives instructions because Pat is experienced. Pat has no investment in the business and works only for Delta. Under the common-law rules, Pat is most likely:
choices: An independent contractor, because the written contract says so
An independent contractor, because Delta rarely exercises control over the work
An employee, because Delta has the right to control how the work is done, even though it seldom uses that right
An employee only if Pat works at least 30 hours a week
explain: Under the common-law rules, a worker is an employee if the business has the right to control what will be done and how it will be done, even if it gives the worker freedom of action; the right to control, not its use, is what matters. The label in the contract does not decide status, and whether the worker is full time or part time makes no difference. Hourly pay, tools supplied by the business and no investment by the worker also point to employee status.
source: IRS Pub 15-A, Common-Law Rules; Rev. Rul. 87-41

q: Throughout 2024, Bolt Inc. employed an average of 80 full-time employees (at least 30 hours of service a week) and is not part of a controlled group. In 2025 it offers no health coverage to any employee. One full-time employee enrolls in a qualified health plan through the Health Insurance Marketplace and is allowed a premium tax credit for 2025. Which statement is correct?
choices: Bolt owes no payment, because the employer mandate applies only when at least 95% of its full-time employees receive a premium tax credit.
Bolt is an applicable large employer for 2025 and owes an employer shared responsibility payment, because it offered no coverage and at least one full-time employee received a premium tax credit.
Bolt owes no payment, because the law requires an employer only to pay part of the premiums for employees who ask for coverage.
Bolt owes a payment only for the one employee who received the premium tax credit.
explain: An employer is an applicable large employer for a year if it averaged at least 50 full-time employees (counting full-time equivalents) in the preceding calendar year. An applicable large employer that fails to offer coverage to its full-time employees owes a payment for any month in which at least one full-time employee is allowed a premium tax credit, and that payment is figured on all of its full-time employees minus the first 30, not just the employee who got the credit. The payment for one employee only applies when an employer does offer coverage but it is unaffordable or lacks minimum value.

q: Each of the following single individuals enrolled in a qualified health plan through the Health Insurance Marketplace for all of 2025, has household income of at least 100% of the federal poverty line, is not claimed as anyone's dependent, and is not eligible for Medicare, Medicaid or other government coverage. Which one cannot be allowed a premium tax credit for 2025?
choices: Alan, who has no offer of employer coverage and household income of 450% of the federal poverty line
Beth, who has no offer of employer coverage and household income of 200% of the federal poverty line
Carl, who declined his employer's offer of coverage because his required contribution exceeded the affordability percentage
Dana, who declined her employer's offer of self-only coverage that is affordable and provides minimum value
explain: An employee who is eligible for employer coverage that is affordable and provides minimum value is not allowed a premium tax credit, even if she declines it and buys Marketplace coverage instead. Employer coverage that is unaffordable to the employee does not bar the credit. For 2021 through 2025 the 400% of the federal poverty line ceiling on household income does not apply, so Alan is not barred by his income.

q: Under the individual shared responsibility provision of the Affordable Care Act, what payment does an individual owe for going without minimum essential coverage for all of 2025, if no exemption applies?
choices: A flat amount of $695 per adult
2.5% of household income above the filing threshold
The greater of a flat dollar amount or a percentage of income, capped at the national average bronze plan premium
explain: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reduced the individual shared responsibility payment to zero for 2019 and later years by setting both the flat dollar amount and the percentage of income at zero. The requirement to have minimum essential coverage is still in the law, but no federal payment is owed for failing it. The flat amount and percentage formulas in the other choices applied only to earlier years.
source: IRC 5000A(c)(2)(B), (c)(3)(A); IRS, Questions and answers on the individual shared responsibility provision

q: Ana and Ben run a food truck together. They split the profits equally and both decide the menu and the schedule. They never signed a written agreement and never filed anything with the state, and both say they never meant to become partners. A supplier claims the business is a general partnership. Which statement is correct?
choices: No partnership exists, because a general partnership requires a written partnership agreement
No partnership exists, because a general partnership is created only by filing with the secretary of state
A general partnership exists, because two persons are carrying on as co-owners a business for profit, whatever they intended
No partnership exists, because neither of them intended to form one
explain: A general partnership is formed when two or more persons associate to carry on as co-owners a business for profit; no written agreement or state filing is needed. Courts look at what the parties did, not their subjective intent, so it does not matter that Ana and Ben never meant to be partners. A state filing is needed to create a limited partnership, not a general partnership.
source: Cornell LII Wex, partnership; Cornell LII Wex, copartner (Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 202, profit-sharing presumption); Cornell LII Wex, limited partnership

q: Cara is a partner in a general partnership that sells office furniture. The partnership agreement bars any partner from buying inventory without the other partners' consent. Without asking them, Cara orders desks for resale from Delta Supply. Before taking the order, Delta's sales manager had been told about the restriction. Is the partnership bound by the order?
choices: Yes, because buying inventory is in the ordinary course of the partnership's business
No, because Cara had no authority to place the order and Delta knew it
Yes, because every general partner has unlimited authority to bind the partnership
No, because a partner can never bind a partnership without the written consent of all partners
explain: Each partner is an agent of the partnership and generally binds it when acting in the ordinary course of the partnership's business. The exception is when the partner had no authority for the act and the third party knew she had none. Delta knew of the restriction, so the ordinary-course rule does not protect it. This matches the Revised Uniform Partnership Act, sections 301(1) and 306.
source: Cornell LII Wex, general partner; Cornell LII Wex, partner

q: Partners in a general partnership that is not a limited liability partnership are liable for the partnership's obligations:
choices: only up to the amount of each partner's capital contribution
only for obligations that the partner personally incurred or approved
only for a share of each obligation equal to the partner's share of profits
jointly and severally, so each partner can be personally liable for the full obligation
explain: General partners have unlimited joint and several personal liability, so one partner can be held liable for the whole obligation and then seek contribution from the other partners. The partnership, and so each general partner, is liable for a loss caused by another partner's wrongful act in the ordinary course of the business. Liability capped at the capital contribution describes a limited partner, not a general partner. Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act, a creditor generally must first try to collect from the partnership before reaching a partner's personal assets.
source: Cornell LII Wex, general partner; Cornell LII Wex, joint and several liability; Cornell LII Wex, limited partnership

q: After a general partnership is dissolved, its business is wound up. Winding up includes all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Selling the partnership's assets
Paying the partnership's debts
Distributing any remaining proceeds to the partners
Taking on new long-term business to grow the partnership
explain: Dissolution ends the partners' relationship as a going business, and the partnership's assets are then liquidated in winding up. Winding up means collecting and selling the assets, settling the debts and distributing what is left. Starting new long-term business is the opposite of winding up.
source: Cornell LII Wex, winding up; Cornell LII Wex, liquidating partner

q: Which of the following is required to create a limited partnership but is NOT required to create a general partnership?
choices: A partnership agreement signed by all partners
Registering the partnership with the appropriate state agency
At least two general partners
Equal capital contributions from all partners
explain: A general partnership can arise from conduct alone, but a limited partnership must be registered with the appropriate state agency to be created. A limited partnership needs only one general partner, and neither form requires equal contributions. A signed partnership agreement is common for both but is not what creates a limited partnership.
source: Cornell LII Wex, limited partnership; Cornell LII Wex, partnership

q: Gail is the only general partner of Hill Limited Partnership. Ivan is a limited partner who contributed $50,000 and has taken no part in managing the business. The partnership fails, owing creditors $200,000 more than the value of its assets. Which statement is correct?
choices: Gail is personally liable for the unpaid debts, and Ivan's loss is limited to his $50,000 contribution
Gail and Ivan are each personally liable for half of the unpaid debts
Neither Gail nor Ivan is personally liable, because a limited partnership shields all of its partners
Ivan is personally liable for the unpaid debts, but only after Gail's personal assets are used up
explain: A limited partnership must have at least one general partner with unlimited personal liability, while a limited partner's liability generally does not exceed the partner's contribution. Gail, as general partner, is personally liable for the shortfall. Ivan is a limited partner, so his loss is limited to his $50,000 contribution.
source: Cornell LII Wex, limited partnership; Cornell LII Wex, silent partner

q: Kim and Lou are partners in an accounting firm organized as a limited liability partnership. A client wins a malpractice judgment against the firm because of Lou's negligent work on an engagement. Kim had no part in that engagement. The firm's assets do not cover the judgment. Can the client collect the rest from Kim's personal assets?
choices: No, because a partner in a limited liability partnership is not personally liable for the malpractice of another partner
Yes, because a limited liability partnership is a general partnership and every partner is jointly and severally liable
Yes, but only up to Kim's share of the partnership's profits
No, but only because Kim took no part in managing the firm
explain: The point of a limited liability partnership is that a partner is not personally liable for the tort damages, such as malpractice, caused by other partners. Unlike a limited partner, a partner in a limited liability partnership keeps that protection even while managing the business, so Kim's role in management does not matter. In an ordinary general partnership Kim would be jointly and severally liable.
source: Cornell LII Wex, limited liability partnership (LLP); Cornell LII Wex, general partner

q: Which feature distinguishes a limited liability partnership from a limited partnership?
choices: A limited liability partnership must have at least one partner with unlimited personal liability
A limited liability partnership can be formed with only one partner
Every partner in a limited liability partnership can take part in management and still keep limited liability
Partners in a limited liability partnership are personally liable for the torts of the other partners
explain: In a limited liability partnership every partner has limited liability for the other partners' torts, even partners who stay involved in management. A limited partnership, by contrast, must have at least one general partner with unlimited liability, and its limited partners typically keep their distance from management. Like a general partnership, a limited liability partnership must have two or more partners.
source: Cornell LII Wex, limited liability partnership (LLP); Cornell LII Wex, limited partnership

q: To form a limited liability company (LLC), its organizers must:
choices: file the LLC's operating agreement with the secretary of state
adopt bylaws and elect a board of directors
file a certificate of limited partnership naming at least one general partner
file articles of organization with the state
explain: An LLC comes into existence when articles of organization, called a certificate of formation in some states, are filed with and approved by the state, usually the secretary of state. The operating agreement is a private contract among the members and is not what creates the LLC. Bylaws and a board of directors belong to a corporation.
source: Cornell LII Wex, articles of organization; Cornell LII Wex, certificate of formation; Cornell LII Wex, operating agreement

q: Mia is one of three members of a member-managed limited liability company (LLC) and takes an active part in running its business every day. The LLC defaults on a bank loan that Mia did not personally guarantee. There is no fraud or misuse of the company. Is Mia personally liable on the loan?
choices: Yes, because a member who manages the business is treated as a general partner
No, because members of an LLC have limited liability even when they take part in management
Yes, because all members of a member-managed LLC are jointly and severally liable for its debts
No, but only if Mia contributed at least as much capital as each of the other members
explain: LLC members can control the business much as general partners do, yet they have limited liability like limited partners. Taking part in management does not cost a member that shield, and the stem rules out the misconduct that could lead a court to pierce it. Mia risks only her investment, because she did not guarantee the loan.
source: Cornell LII Wex, member; Cornell LII Wex, limited liability company (LLC)

q: Which statement about the operating agreement of a limited liability company (LLC) is correct?
choices: It must be filed with the secretary of state before the LLC can exist
It binds only members who later approve it at an annual shareholders' meeting
It is the members' governing contract and can set whether members or managers run the LLC
It cannot change how the LLC is managed, because management is fixed by statute
explain: The operating agreement is the contract among the members that governs the LLC's affairs, including whether it is run by its members or by managers, and it overrides the state statute's default rules. Without one, the LLC runs under those default rules. The document filed with the state to create the LLC is the articles of organization, not the operating agreement.
source: Cornell LII Wex, operating agreement; Cornell LII Wex, limited liability company (LLC); Cornell LII Wex, articles of organization

q: Before Pine Corp. was incorporated, its promoter, Raj, signed a one-year office lease for the corporation. After Pine was incorporated, its board adopted the lease, and the landlord, Raj and Pine all agreed that Pine would replace Raj as tenant and that Raj would be released. Pine later defaults on the lease. Is Raj liable to the landlord?
choices: No, because the novation substituted Pine for Raj and released him
Yes, because a promoter can never be released from a contract signed before incorporation
Yes, because a corporation cannot take over a contract made before it existed
Yes, because the landlord, as the other original party, cannot agree to release Raj
explain: A promoter organizes the corporation, and the corporation can adopt the promoter's acts once its board is in place. A novation, which needs the agreement of both original parties and the new party, substitutes a new party and releases the original one. Because the landlord, Raj and Pine all agreed, Raj is released and only Pine is liable.
source: Cornell LII Wex, promoter; Cornell LII Wex, novation; Cornell LII Wex, assignee

q: Which document must be filed with the state to create a corporation and generally states the number and classes of shares the corporation may issue?
choices: The bylaws
The articles of incorporation
The operating agreement
The minutes of the board's first meeting
explain: The articles of incorporation, also called the corporate charter, are filed with the state at incorporation and set out matters such as the number and classes of shares. Bylaws are the internal rules for meetings, elections and officers' duties and are not filed to create the corporation. An operating agreement governs a limited liability company.
source: Cornell LII Wex, articles of incorporation; Cornell LII Wex, corporate charter; Cornell LII Wex, bylaws

q: Shareholders who own 70% of the voting stock of Quill Corp. are unhappy with the corporation's president and want her removed. The articles of incorporation and bylaws say nothing special about removing officers. Who has the power to remove the president?
choices: The majority shareholders, by giving written notice to the president
The other officers, by majority vote
Only a court, in a derivative suit brought by the shareholders
The board of directors
explain: Shareholders elect the directors, the board appoints and removes the officers, and the officers run the day-to-day business as the corporation's agents. Owning a majority of the stock does not let shareholders fire an officer directly. Their route is to elect directors who will.
source: Cornell LII Wex, officer; Cornell LII Wex, corporate officers; Cornell LII Wex, board of directors

q: The directors of Reed Corp., none of whom has a personal interest in the decision, study market reports and an outside consultant's analysis for two months and then vote in good faith to open a new plant. The plant loses money and closes a year later. A shareholder sues the directors for breach of the duty of care. What is the most likely result?
choices: The directors are protected by the business judgment rule
The directors are liable, because their decision caused the corporation a loss
The directors are liable, because they relied on an outside consultant instead of their own judgment
The directors must prove that the decision was entirely fair to the corporation
explain: Under the business judgment rule, courts uphold a director's decision made in good faith, with the care of a reasonably prudent person and in the reasonable belief that it serves the corporation, even if it turns out badly. The rule is a presumption for the board, and only proof of gross negligence, bad faith or a conflict of interest overcomes it. The burden to prove fairness shifts to the directors only when the rule does not apply.
source: Cornell LII Wex, business judgment rule; Cornell LII Wex, duty of care

q: Sam is a director of Tide Corp., a boat dealer. Through his position he learns that a nearby boat dealership is for sale at a bargain price. Tide has the money to buy it and has been looking to expand. Without telling Tide's board, Sam buys the dealership for himself. Which statement is correct?
choices: Sam breached only his duty of care
Sam did nothing wrong, because a director may buy any business in his own name
Sam breached his duty of loyalty by taking a corporate opportunity
Sam is protected by the business judgment rule because he acted in good faith
explain: The duty of loyalty requires a director to put the corporation's interests ahead of his own and bars diverting a corporate opportunity: one in the corporation's line of business that it can afford and is interested in. Sam had to present the opportunity to the board first. The business judgment rule does not protect a director with a personal conflict of interest.
source: Cornell LII Wex, duty of loyalty; Cornell LII Wex, corporate opportunity; Cornell LII Wex, business judgment rule

q: A shareholder who brings a derivative suit against a corporation's directors generally must meet all of the following requirements EXCEPT:
choices: Have been a shareholder when the challenged act or omission occurred
Make a written demand that the corporation act, and generally wait 90 days unless the demand is rejected or waiting would cause irreparable harm
Fairly and adequately represent the corporation's interests
Agree that any recovery will be paid to the shareholder personally
explain: In a derivative suit the shareholder enforces a claim that belongs to the corporation, so any recovery goes to the corporation, not to the shareholder, who may recover only reasonable litigation costs. The shareholder must have owned shares when the wrong occurred, make a written demand and fairly represent the corporation. A shareholder who was harmed personally brings a direct suit instead.
source: Cornell LII Wex, shareholder derivative suit; Cornell LII Wex, shareholder's derivative action

q: All of the following can support a court's decision to pierce the corporate veil and hold a shareholder personally liable for a corporation's debts EXCEPT:
choices: The shareholder pays personal bills from the corporation's bank account and mixes personal and corporate funds
The corporation simply cannot pay a creditor in full, and there is no other misconduct
The corporation was formed with too little capital for its foreseeable obligations
The corporation ignores corporate formalities and keeps no separate records
explain: Courts presume against piercing the corporate veil and do it only for serious misconduct, such as commingling personal and corporate assets, undercapitalization and disregard of corporate formalities. A creditor's inability to collect is the very risk that limited liability puts on creditors, so the injustice must be something more than an unpaid debt. Otherwise shareholders risk only their investment.
source: Cornell LII Wex, piercing the corporate veil; Cornell LII Wex, disregarding the corporate entity; Cornell LII Wex, limited liability

q: The articles of incorporation of Vale Corp. say nothing about preemptive rights. The board approves issuing 10,000 new shares to an outside investor. Wanda, who owns 20% of the outstanding shares, demands the right to buy 20% of the new shares before they are offered to anyone else. Under most state corporation laws, which statement is correct?
choices: Wanda has a preemptive right, because every shareholder has one by law
Wanda can block the issue by bringing a derivative suit, because any new issue dilutes her stake
Wanda has a preemptive right only if she has held her shares for more than one year
Wanda has no preemptive right, because preemptive rights exist only if the articles of incorporation grant them
explain: A preemptive right lets existing shareholders buy newly issued shares before outsiders, to protect against dilution. Courts once treated the right as automatic, but most state laws now deny it unless the corporate charter grants it. Vale's articles are silent, so Wanda has no preemptive right.

q: The board and shareholders of Wren Corp. approve its dissolution, and Wren makes the required state filings. After dissolution, which of the following may Wren do?
choices: Sign a five-year contract to open a new line of business
Distribute all of its assets to its shareholders before paying its creditors
Collect its assets, pay its debts and distribute any remaining assets to its shareholders
Nothing at all, because it ceases to exist at dissolution and can no longer sue or be sued
explain: A dissolved corporation generally may carry on only the business of winding up its affairs: collecting and selling assets, settling its liabilities and distributing what remains to shareholders. Creditors are paid before shareholders receive anything. A dissolved corporation can still sue and be sued during winding up, so it does not simply vanish.
source: Cornell LII Wex, dissolution of corporation; Cornell LII Wex, winding up a corporation; Cornell LII Wex, winding up

q: Gina, Hal and Ivy are partners in a general partnership at will. Their partnership agreement says nothing about dissociation, dissolution or buyouts. Gina dies, and Hal and Ivy want to keep running the business. Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act, which statement is correct?
choices: The partnership is dissolved by Gina's death and must be wound up, although Hal and Ivy may then form a new partnership
Gina is dissociated as a partner, the partnership continues, and the partnership must cause her interest to be purchased for a buyout price
Gina's estate becomes a partner in her place, with her full management rights
Gina is not dissociated until her estate gives the partnership written notice that she is withdrawing
explain: A partner's death dissociates that partner, but in a partnership at will only a partner's express will to withdraw dissolves the partnership, so the business continues without Gina. When a dissociation does not cause dissolution, the partnership must cause the dissociated partner's interest to be bought out, and her estate is not a partner. Dissolution on any partner's departure was the rule of the original 1914 Uniform Partnership Act, which the revised act changed.
source: Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-601(7)(A); Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 603 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-603(a)); Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 701 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-701(a)); Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 801 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-801 and comment)

q: Unless the partnership agreement provides otherwise, which of the following events dissolves a general partnership at will that has five partners?
choices: One partner dies
One partner becomes a debtor in bankruptcy
The other four partners expel one partner under an expulsion clause in the partnership agreement
The partnership learns that one partner has expressed the will to withdraw as a partner
explain: In a partnership at will, the partnership is dissolved when it knows or has notice of a partner's express will to withdraw. Death, bankruptcy and expulsion each dissociate the partner involved, but under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act they do not dissolve the partnership; the official comments note that even expelling a partner from a partnership at will does not dissolve it. Instead the remaining partners continue the business and buy out the dissociated partner's interest.
source: Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 801(1) (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-801(1) and comment); Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-601(3), (6)(A), (7)(A); Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 701 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-701(a))

q: Jo, Kai and Lee formed a general partnership for a definite term of five years. After two years, with no other partner having left, Jo gives the partnership written notice that she is withdrawing immediately. The partnership agreement says nothing about withdrawal or buyouts, and Kai and Lee continue the business. Which statement is correct?
choices: Jo's withdrawal has no effect, because a partner in a partnership for a definite term cannot withdraw before the term ends
Jo's withdrawal automatically dissolves the partnership, and its business must be wound up
Jo is dissociated, and because the dissociation is wrongful, she is liable for the damages it causes, which may be offset against her buyout price
Jo is dissociated and is entitled to immediate payment of her full buyout price, with no deduction for damages
explain: A partner always has the power to dissociate by express will, but withdrawing from a partnership for a definite term before the term ends is wrongful, and the partner is liable to the partnership and the other partners for the damages caused. Those damages are offset against the buyout price, and a wrongfully dissociating partner generally gets no payment until the term expires unless a court finds that earlier payment will not cause undue hardship to the business. A wrongful dissociation does not dissolve a term partnership unless at least half of the remaining partners agree to wind up within 90 days, and Kai and Lee chose to continue.
source: Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-602(a), (b)(2)(A), (c); Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 701 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-701(c), (h)); Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 801 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-801(2)(A))

q: Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act, a person to whom a partner has transferred the partner's entire transferable interest, and whom the partners have not admitted as a partner, is entitled while the partnership continues to:
choices: receive the distributions the transferor would otherwise have received, but not to take part in management or to see the partnership's records
vote on partnership matters in the transferor's place, because the transferee holds the transferor's entire interest
inspect the partnership's books and records, but not to receive any distributions until the partnership dissolves
an ownership share in specific partnership property equal to the transferor's share of the profits
explain: A transferee of a transferable interest has the right to receive, in accordance with the transfer, the distributions to which the transferor would otherwise be entitled. The transferee has no right to take part in management or to access partnership records or information, except an account of the partnership's transactions from the date of dissolution if the partnership dissolves. A partner has no transferable interest in specific partnership property, so the transferee cannot acquire one.
source: Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 503 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-503(a)(3), (b), (c)); Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-501

q: Olga, a partner in a four-partner general partnership, gives all of her transferable interest in the partnership to her daughter. The partnership agreement says nothing about transfers or expulsion. Which statement is correct?
choices: Olga is automatically dissociated as a partner when the transfer takes effect
The partnership is dissolved, and its business must be wound up
Olga remains a partner with all of a partner's duties, although the other three partners may expel her by unanimous vote
Olga remains a partner but is released from her duties to the partnership, because she no longer has an economic interest in it
explain: A transfer of a transferable interest does not by itself dissociate the transferor or dissolve the partnership, and the transferor keeps the rights of a partner other than the interest transferred and all the duties and obligations of a partner. Because Olga transferred all of her transferable interest, the other partners may expel her by the affirmative vote or consent of all of them. Until they do, she is still a partner.
source: Revised Uniform Partnership Act section 503 (Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-503(a)(2), (f)); Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-601(4)(B)

q: Pat, a partner in a general partnership, owes Quinn a personal debt unrelated to the partnership's business. Quinn obtains a court judgment against Pat that remains unpaid. Which remedy may Quinn use to collect the judgment from Pat's interest in the partnership?
choices: Levy on and sell specific partnership equipment in proportion to Pat's share of the partnership
Obtain a charging order, which requires the partnership to pay Quinn any distributions that would otherwise be paid to Pat
Take Pat's place as a partner and vote on partnership decisions until the judgment is paid
Obtain a court order requiring the partnership to make distributions large enough to pay the judgment
explain: A judgment creditor of a partner may obtain a charging order against the partner's transferable interest; it is a lien that requires the partnership to pay the creditor any distribution that would otherwise be paid to the partner, and it is the creditor's exclusive remedy against that interest. The creditor has no say in the timing or amount of distributions and cannot interfere in the management of the partnership. Specific partnership property belongs to the partnership, not to Pat, so it cannot be seized for Pat's personal debt.
source: Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-504(a), (g) and comment; Uniform Business Organizations Code 3-501

q: On March 1, 2025, Kim, an individual, transfers investment land she has held for six years, with an adjusted basis of $50,000 and a fair market value (FMV) of $200,000, to an existing business for a 25% ownership interest. Lou and Max, who own the other 75%, transfer nothing at that time. The business is not an investment company. What gain does Kim recognize, and what is her basis in her ownership interest, if the business is (1) a C corporation or (2) a limited liability company (LLC) taxed as a partnership?
choices: C corporation: $0 gain and $50,000 basis; LLC: $0 gain and $50,000 basis
C corporation: $150,000 gain and $200,000 basis; LLC: $0 gain and $50,000 basis
C corporation: $150,000 gain and $200,000 basis; LLC: $150,000 gain and $200,000 basis
C corporation: $0 gain and $50,000 basis; LLC: $150,000 gain and $200,000 basis
explain: Section 351 applies only if the transferors of property own at least 80% of the corporation right after the exchange; Kim is the only transferor and owns 25%, so she recognizes $200,000 - $50,000 = $150,000 of gain and takes a $200,000 cost basis in the stock. Section 721 has no control requirement, so a contribution to an LLC taxed as a partnership is tax free and her basis in the interest is her $50,000 basis in the land. Assuming section 351 protects her because the business is still owned by the same people overlooks that Lou and Max transferred nothing.

q: Four individuals are organizing a new business in 2025. They want every owner protected from personal liability for the business's debts, every owner free to take part in management without losing that protection, income taxed only once at the owner level, the ability to give one owner 60% of profits while she holds 40% of capital, and to admit an owner who is a nonresident alien. Without any special tax election, which entity best meets all of these goals?
choices: A corporation that elects S corporation status
A limited partnership
A limited liability company (LLC) with two or more members
A C corporation
explain: A domestic LLC with two or more members gives every member limited liability even when the member manages, and by default it is taxed as a partnership, so income is taxed once to the members and the operating agreement can allocate profits differently from capital. An S corporation cannot have a nonresident alien shareholder or more than one class of stock, so it cannot admit that owner or skew profit shares. A limited partnership must have at least one general partner who is personally liable, and a C corporation's income is taxed at the corporate level and again when distributed.
source: Treas. Reg. 301.7701-3(b)(1); IRC 1361(b)(1)(C), (D); IRC 701, 704(a), (b); IRC 11(b); Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act

q: P Corp. has owned 85% of the stock of Sub Corp. (by both vote and value) for six years, with a stock basis of $100,000. Dee, an individual, owns the other 15%, with a stock basis of $10,000. In 2025 Sub Corp. adopts a plan of complete liquidation and distributes land A (fair market value (FMV) $850,000, adjusted basis $300,000) to P Corp. and land B (FMV $150,000, adjusted basis $60,000) to Dee. What gain does Sub Corp. recognize, what gain does P Corp. recognize, and what is P Corp.'s basis in land A?
choices: Sub Corp. $90,000; P Corp. $0; basis $300,000
Sub Corp. $640,000; P Corp. $0; basis $850,000
Sub Corp. $0; P Corp. $750,000; basis $850,000
Sub Corp. $0; P Corp. $0; basis $100,000
explain: P Corp. owns at least 80% of Sub Corp.'s vote and value, so P Corp. recognizes no gain under section 332, Sub Corp. recognizes no gain on land A distributed to P Corp. under section 337, and P Corp. takes Sub Corp.'s $300,000 carryover basis. The distribution to the minority shareholder is taxed under section 336, so Sub Corp. recognizes $150,000 - $60,000 = $90,000 of gain, and Dee recognizes $150,000 - $10,000 = $140,000 under section 331 with a $150,000 basis in land B. Recognizing gain on both parcels, or taxing P Corp. on $850,000 - $100,000, applies the ordinary liquidation rules to an 80% corporate parent.

q: Two unrelated individuals each own 50% of an entity. Each owner's basis in the ownership interest is $100,000. The entity's only assets are two identical parcels of investment land it bought with cash, each with an adjusted basis of $100,000 and a fair market value (FMV) of $250,000. It has no liabilities. In 2025 the entity liquidates and distributes one parcel to each owner. Ignore any income tax the entity owes. Which statement correctly compares the results if the entity is a C corporation or a partnership?
choices: C corporation: no gain to the corporation, $150,000 of gain to each owner, and a $250,000 basis in each parcel. Partnership: no gain to anyone, and a $250,000 basis in each parcel.
C corporation: $300,000 of gain to the corporation, no gain to the owners, and a $100,000 basis in each parcel. Partnership: no gain to anyone, and a $100,000 basis in each parcel.

C corporation: $300,000 of gain to the corporation, $150,000 of gain to each owner, and a $250,000 basis in each parcel. Partnership: $300,000 of gain to the partnership, and a $250,000 basis in each parcel.
C corporation: $300,000 of gain to the corporation, $150,000 of gain to each owner, and a $250,000 basis in each parcel. Partnership: no gain to anyone, and a $100,000 basis in each parcel.
