explain: A liquidating C corporation recognizes gain as if it sold each parcel at FMV, 2 x ($250,000 - $100,000) = $300,000, and each shareholder treats the parcel as payment for the stock, recognizing $250,000 - $100,000 = $150,000 and taking a $250,000 FMV basis. A partnership recognizes no gain on a distribution, a partner recognizes gain only if money received exceeds outside basis (no money here), and each partner's basis in the parcel equals the $100,000 basis in the partnership interest. Giving the partners an FMV basis applies the corporate rule to a partnership and would let the $150,000 of appreciation escape tax.

q: On June 1, 2025, Ron contributes equipment with an adjusted basis of $80,000 and a fair market value (FMV) of $50,000, and Sue contributes $50,000 cash, to a new entity in which each receives a 50% interest. If the entity is a corporation, the transfer qualifies under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 351 and no election is made to reduce Ron's stock basis instead. What is the entity's basis in the equipment immediately after the contribution if it is (1) a corporation or (2) a partnership?
choices: Corporation $80,000; partnership $80,000
Corporation $50,000; partnership $80,000
Corporation $50,000; partnership $50,000
Corporation $80,000; partnership $50,000
explain: When a section 351 transferor's property has a net built-in loss, the corporation's basis is limited to FMV, $50,000, unless the transferor and corporation jointly elect to cut the transferor's stock basis to FMV instead; Ron's stock basis stays $80,000. A partnership takes the contributing partner's $80,000 basis, but section 704(c)(1)(C) lets only Ron take the $30,000 built-in loss into account and treats the basis as $50,000 for the other partners. Giving the corporation a full $80,000 carryover basis would let the same $30,000 loss be deducted twice, once on the stock and once on the equipment.

q: A calendar-year C corporation had a $450,000 net operating loss (NOL) for 2022 that it has not used. For 2025 its taxable income before any NOL deduction is $500,000, and it has no deduction under section 199A or section 250 and no other carryovers. Using the 21% corporate rate, by how much does the NOL deduction reduce the corporation's 2025 federal income tax, and how much of the NOL carries forward to 2026?
choices: $94,500 reduction; $0 carries forward
$75,600 reduction; $90,000 carries forward
$84,000 reduction; $50,000 carries forward
$105,000 reduction; $0 carries forward
explain: A loss arising in a tax year beginning after 2017 can offset only 80% of taxable income figured before the NOL deduction, so the 2025 deduction is the lesser of $450,000 or 80% x $500,000 = $400,000. That saves $400,000 x 21% = $84,000, and the unused $50,000 carries forward with no expiration. Deducting the full $450,000 for $94,500 of savings ignores the 80% limit, and applying 80% to the loss itself ($360,000) is a misreading of the rule.

q: A calendar-year C corporation has a $30,000 net capital loss from its 2020 tax year. It had no capital gains in 2017 through 2024, so none of the loss has been used. It has no other capital transactions in 2025 and expects positive ordinary taxable income in 2025 and 2026. It owns investment land, a capital asset held for five years, that it can sell at a $30,000 gain with a closing date of either December 15, 2025, or January 5, 2026, at the same price. Using the 21% corporate rate, how much federal income tax does closing in 2025 save compared with closing in 2026?
choices: $0, because a corporation's capital loss carries forward indefinitely
explain: A corporation carries a net capital loss back 3 years and forward 5 years, so a 2020 loss can be used through 2025 and then expires. Closing in 2025 lets the $30,000 carryover, treated as a short-term capital loss, offset the $30,000 gain, while a 2026 closing leaves the gain fully taxed: $30,000 x 21% = $6,300. Indefinite carryforward and the $3,000 offset against ordinary income ($630 of tax) are rules for individuals, not corporations.

q: A calendar-year C corporation had taxable income of $1,300,000 in 2021, $600,000 in 2022, $400,000 in 2023 and $250,000 in 2024. Its 2024 return, for a full 12-month year, showed tax of $52,500. It expects 2025 tax of $160,000 and will not use the annualized income or adjusted seasonal installment method. The corporation is not a member of a controlled group. What is the smallest amount it can pay for each 2025 installment and still avoid the underpayment penalty?
choices: $13,125 for each of the four installments
$13,125 for the first installment, $66,875 for the second, and $40,000 for each of the last two
$40,000 for each of the four installments
$14,437.50 for each of the four installments
explain: A large corporation is one with taxable income of $1,000,000 or more in any of the 3 preceding tax years; for 2025 that testing period is 2022 through 2024, so the 2021 income does not count and the corporation may base every installment on 100% of last year's tax: $52,500 / 4 = $13,125. The second choice is the large-corporation rule, which allows the prior-year amount only for the first installment and adds the $26,875 shortfall ($40,000 - $13,125) to the second. The 110% figure is a rule for higher-income individuals, not corporations.

q: An accrual-method, calendar-year C corporation does business only in State X; all of its sales, property and payroll are there, so 100% of its income is apportioned to State X. State X has enacted an increase in its corporate income tax rate from 6% for 2025 to 9% for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. The federal rate is 21% in both years. The corporation can finish and bill a $200,000 project either in December 2025 or in January 2026, and can incur a $50,000 deductible repair expense either in December 2025 or in January 2026. State X follows federal rules for when income and deductions are taken into account. Ignoring federal tax effects and the time value of money, which plan minimizes State X income tax, and how much does it save compared with putting both items in 2026?
choices: Put both items in 2025; it saves $7,500
Put the income in 2025 and keep the repair expense in 2026; it saves $6,000
Put the repair expense in 2025 and keep the income in 2026; it saves $1,500
Timing makes no difference, because the corporate tax rate is a flat 21% in both years
explain: When rates are rising, income should be accelerated into the lower-rate year and deductions deferred into the higher-rate year. Moving the $200,000 of income into 2025 saves $200,000 x (9% - 6%) = $6,000, and keeping the $50,000 deduction in 2026 preserves its 9% value. Moving both items into 2025 actually saves only $6,000 - $1,500 = $4,500, because the deduction is worth $1,500 less at 6%; adding the $1,500 instead of subtracting it gives the $7,500 distractor.

q: Gina owns 100% of a calendar-year C corporation with ample earnings and profits. The corporation holds investment land, held for four years, with an adjusted basis of $150,000 and a fair market value (FMV) of $90,000. In 2025 it also has $100,000 of capital gains from other sales. It is considering two plans for 2025: (A) distribute the land to Gina, or (B) sell the land to an unrelated buyer for $90,000 and distribute the $90,000 cash to Gina. Using the 21% corporate rate, which statement is correct?
choices: Under plan A the corporation recognizes a $60,000 capital loss, and Gina takes a $150,000 basis in the land.
Under plan A Gina has a $150,000 dividend, equal to the corporation's adjusted basis in the land.
Under plan B the corporation recognizes a $60,000 capital loss that offsets its capital gains and saves $12,600 of tax; under plan A it recognizes no loss.
Selling the land to Gina for $90,000 cash would give the corporation the same $60,000 deductible loss as plan B.
explain: A corporation recognizes gain, but never loss, when it distributes property to a shareholder, so plan A wastes the $60,000 built-in loss; Gina would have a $90,000 dividend and a $90,000 FMV basis in the land. Selling to an unrelated buyer produces a $150,000 - $90,000 = $60,000 capital loss that offsets the corporation's capital gains, saving $60,000 x 21% = $12,600, and Gina still has a $90,000 dividend. A sale to Gina is not an alternative, because she owns more than 50% of the stock and the loss on a sale between related persons is disallowed.

q: A calendar-year C corporation elected S status effective January 1, 2022. On that date it owned land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $120,000, and its net unrealized built-in gain was $80,000. The corporation proposes to sell the land for $120,000 in 2025. Apart from the sale, its 2025 operations will produce a $30,000 loss, so its 2025 taxable income figured as if it were a C corporation, without a net operating loss deduction or special deductions, would be $50,000. It has no carryforwards or credits. If it sells in 2025, what is its 2025 built-in gains tax, and what happens to the rest of the built-in gain?
choices: $16,800; all $80,000 of built-in gain is taxed in 2025
$10,500; the remaining $30,000 is treated as recognized built-in gain in 2026
$0, because the corporation has been an S corporation for more than three years
$10,500; the remaining $30,000 permanently escapes the built-in gains tax
explain: The 2025 sale falls inside the 5-year recognition period (2022 through 2026). Net recognized built-in gain is the lesser of the $80,000 recognized built-in gain or the $50,000 taxable income limit, so the tax is $50,000 x 21% = $10,500. The $30,000 cut off by the taxable income limit carries to 2026 as recognized built-in gain; it is not taxed in full in 2025 ($16,800) and does not disappear.

q: Lena owns all the stock of a calendar-year corporation whose S election was revoked effective January 1, 2025. On that date its accumulated adjustments account (AAA) was $60,000, and it had no earnings and profits from earlier C corporation years. As a C corporation, it has $90,000 of current earnings and profits for 2025. On June 1, 2025, it distributes $50,000 cash to Lena, whose stock basis just before the distribution is $70,000. The corporation makes no election to have distributions come from earnings and profits first. How is the distribution treated?
choices: $50,000 dividend; Lena's stock basis falls to $20,000
$0 dividend; Lena's stock basis stays $70,000
$0 dividend; Lena's stock basis falls to $20,000
$50,000 dividend; Lena's stock basis stays $70,000
explain: The post-termination transition period runs from January 1, 2025 to the later of December 31, 2025 or the extended due date of the 2024 S return, so the June 1 cash distribution falls inside it. A cash distribution in that period reduces stock basis tax free to the extent of the AAA, so the full $50,000 is applied against basis: $70,000 - $50,000 = $20,000. Treating it as a dividend from the 2025 current earnings and profits ignores this transition rule.

q: A calendar-year corporation has been an S corporation since 2018. It had accumulated earnings and profits from its C corporation years at the close of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and passive investment income was more than 25% of its gross receipts in each of those years. All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
choices: If it had distributed all of its accumulated earnings and profits by December 31, 2025, the election would not have terminated
Its S election terminates effective January 1, 2026
Its S election terminates retroactively to January 1, 2025, the first day of the third year
It owes the corporate-level tax on excess net passive income for any of those years in which it had excess net passive income
explain: Termination requires accumulated earnings and profits at the close of each of 3 consecutive S years and passive investment income above 25% of gross receipts in each, and it takes effect on the first day of the next tax year, January 1, 2026, not retroactively. Because the test looks at earnings and profits at the close of each year, distributing all accumulated earnings and profits before December 31, 2025 (for example, by electing to distribute them first) would have prevented termination. The passive income tax applies separately in each year the conditions are met.

q: In 2022 Kai lent $50,000 to his S corporation, evidenced by a written note. By the end of 2024, flow-through losses had reduced his stock basis to zero and his basis in the note to $20,000. In 2025 the corporation repays $25,000 of principal. For 2025 the corporation has no income, loss or other items, so there is no net increase to restore basis. What does Kai report for 2025 on the repayment?
choices: No gain, because a repayment of a shareholder's own loan is a return of capital
$15,000 long-term capital gain
$5,000 long-term capital gain
$15,000 ordinary income
explain: Each repayment of reduced-basis debt is partly a recovery of basis and partly income, in the ratio of basis to face: $25,000 x ($20,000 / $50,000) = $10,000 of basis, so $15,000 is gain. Debt evidenced by a formal note is a capital asset, and Kai held it more than one year, so the gain is long-term capital gain; an open account advance would produce ordinary income. Subtracting the whole $20,000 basis from the $25,000 payment ($5,000) ignores that the rest of the note is still outstanding.
source: IRC 1367(b)(2), 1271(a)(1); Treas. Reg. 1.1367-2(c)-(d); Instructions for Form 7203 (12/2022), line 34

q: A calendar-year S corporation has $15,000 of accumulated earnings and profits from its C corporation years. At the end of 2025, before distributions, its accumulated adjustments account (AAA) is $40,000. Tom, its sole shareholder, has a stock basis of $60,000 before distributions. To purge the earnings and profits, the corporation distributes $20,000 cash to Tom in December 2025 and, with his consent, elects to distribute earnings and profits first. What is the result?
choices: $15,000 dividend; Tom's stock basis is $40,000
$20,000 dividend; Tom's stock basis is $60,000
$15,000 dividend; Tom's stock basis is $55,000
$0 dividend; Tom's stock basis is $40,000
explain: With the election, the distribution comes first from accumulated earnings and profits ($15,000 dividend) and then from the AAA ($5,000 tax free). Only the $5,000 that is not taxed reduces stock basis, so basis is $60,000 - $5,000 = $55,000. Without the election, the whole $20,000 would come from the AAA tax free; the election exists so the corporation can clear out earnings and profits.

q: In 2023 Ann, an investor, contributed land she held as a capital asset, with an adjusted basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $30,000, to a partnership for a 50% interest. Bob contributed $30,000 cash for the other 50%. The partnership is a real estate dealer and holds the land as inventory. In 2025 it sells the land to a customer for $26,000. What is Ann's share of the loss, and its character?
choices: $12,000 ordinary loss
$20,000 capital loss and $2,000 ordinary loss
$22,000 capital loss
$22,000 ordinary loss
explain: The partnership's tax loss is $24,000 ($50,000 - $26,000). The $20,000 built-in loss at contribution is allocated only to Ann, and because the land was a capital asset to her and is sold within 5 years, that $20,000 is a capital loss; the $4,000 decline after contribution is an ordinary inventory loss shared equally, $2,000 each. Splitting the whole $24,000 equally ($12,000) ignores section 704(c), and treating all of Ann's loss as ordinary ignores section 724(c).

q: Kim and Lee are equal partners. For 2025 the partnership agreement pays Kim a $50,000 guaranteed payment for services, determined without regard to partnership income. Before the guaranteed payment, the partnership's ordinary business income is $30,000, and it has no other items. Kim has enough basis to absorb any loss. What does Kim report for 2025?
choices: $15,000 of ordinary income; the $50,000 is a distribution that reduces her basis
$50,000 of guaranteed payment income and a $10,000 ordinary loss
$50,000 of guaranteed payment income and $15,000 of ordinary income
$30,000 of income, because guaranteed payments cannot exceed partnership income
explain: The partnership deducts the guaranteed payment, turning $30,000 of income into a $20,000 ordinary loss, and Kim's 50% share is a $10,000 loss. She also reports the full $50,000 guaranteed payment as ordinary income, for a net of $40,000. Giving her a $15,000 share of income double counts the $50,000, because it ignores the partnership's deduction.
source: IRC 707(c), 702(a); Treas. Reg. 1.707-1(c), Example 3; IRS Pub 541

q: Lia's basis in her partnership interest is $26,000. In a nonliquidating distribution in 2025, she receives $6,000 cash, parcel A (partnership basis $24,000, fair market value $30,000) and parcel B (partnership basis $10,000, fair market value $6,000). The partnership has no unrealized receivables or inventory items, neither parcel was contributed by a partner, and her share of liabilities does not change. What are Lia's bases in the parcels?
choices: Parcel A $24,000; parcel B $10,000, with $14,000 of gain recognized
Parcel A $14,000; parcel B $6,000
Parcel A $20,000; parcel B $0
Parcel A $16,000; parcel B $4,000
explain: The cash is less than her basis, so no gain; the parcels share the $20,000 of basis left ($26,000 - $6,000), a $14,000 decrease from their $34,000 partnership basis. The decrease goes first to parcel B up to its $4,000 of unrealized depreciation (B to $6,000), and the remaining $10,000 is split by adjusted bases of $24,000 and $6,000: A is reduced $8,000 to $16,000 and B $2,000 to $4,000. Writing B down to $0 is wrong because the first step stops at each property's unrealized depreciation.

q: On September 1, 2025, Nora sells her partnership interest, held for five years, for $70,000 cash, and the buyer takes over her $10,000 share of partnership liabilities. Her basis in the interest, including that share of liabilities, is $50,000. Her share of the partnership's assets includes cash-method accounts receivable with a basis of $0 and a fair market value of $15,000, and inventory with a basis of $10,000 and a fair market value of $12,000. How is her gain characterized?
choices: $30,000 long-term capital gain
$17,000 ordinary income and $3,000 long-term capital gain
$15,000 ordinary income and $15,000 long-term capital gain
$17,000 ordinary income and $13,000 long-term capital gain
explain: Her amount realized is $80,000 ($70,000 cash plus $10,000 of liability relief), so total gain is $30,000. On a sale of an interest, all unrealized receivables and inventory items are hot assets, whether or not the inventory is substantially appreciated, so $15,000 + $2,000 = $17,000 is ordinary income and the other $13,000 is capital gain. The substantial appreciation test applies only to distributions, and leaving out the liability relief understates the gain.

q: In 2022 Ann contributed land with an adjusted basis of $10,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 to a partnership. On March 1, 2025, the partnership distributes the land, now worth $50,000, to Ben, another partner, in a nonliquidating distribution. The partnership uses the traditional method for section 704(c), and Ann receives nothing in 2025. As a result of the distribution, Ann recognizes gain of:
explain: Contributed property distributed to another partner within 7 years of its contribution makes the contributing partner recognize the gain that would have been allocated to her under section 704(c) had the property been sold for its value at distribution, which is the $30,000 precontribution gain ($40,000 - $10,000). The $10,000 of appreciation after contribution would have been shared, not allocated only to Ann, so $35,000 and $40,000 overstate it. Ann's basis in her interest and the partnership's basis in the land both increase by the $30,000.

q: On April 8, 2025, Marcus exchanges a warehouse held for use in his business (adjusted basis $200,000, fair market value $500,000, subject to a $120,000 mortgage that the other party assumes) for another warehouse to be held for business use (fair market value $420,000, no mortgage). Marcus also pays the other party $40,000 cash. What are Marcus's realized gain and recognized gain?
choices: $300,000 realized gain and $80,000 recognized gain
$300,000 realized gain and $120,000 recognized gain
$300,000 realized gain and no recognized gain
$340,000 realized gain and $120,000 recognized gain
explain: Marcus realizes $300,000: the $420,000 warehouse plus $120,000 of debt relief, minus his $200,000 basis and the $40,000 cash he paid. Debt relief counts as boot, but the regulations let cash he pays offset the liabilities he is relieved of, so net boot is $120,000 minus $40,000, or $80,000, and that is his recognized gain. The $120,000 choice ignores this offset. The opposite rule is different: liabilities a taxpayer takes on never offset cash he receives.

q: On June 2, 2025, Grace exchanges land held for investment (adjusted basis $300,000, fair market value $600,000, subject to a $200,000 mortgage that the other party assumes) for an office building to be held for investment (fair market value $450,000, subject to a $50,000 mortgage that Grace assumes). No cash changes hands. What are Grace's recognized gain and her basis in the office building?
choices: $150,000 recognized gain and $300,000 basis
$200,000 recognized gain and $350,000 basis
$150,000 recognized gain and $250,000 basis
No recognized gain and $150,000 basis
explain: Grace realizes $300,000 ($450,000 building plus $200,000 debt relief, minus $300,000 basis and $50,000 debt assumed). The $50,000 she assumes offsets the $200,000 she is relieved of, so net boot and recognized gain are $150,000, and $150,000 is deferred. Her basis is $300,000 old basis plus $50,000 debt assumed plus $150,000 gain recognized minus $200,000 debt relieved, or $300,000, which equals the $450,000 value minus the $150,000 deferred gain; the $250,000 choice forgets to add the debt she assumed.

q: On August 14, 2025, Nina exchanges land held for investment (adjusted basis $500,000, fair market value $400,000) for a rental duplex (fair market value $350,000) plus $50,000 cash. There are no liabilities. What is the result to Nina?
choices: No loss is recognized, and her basis in the duplex is $450,000
A $50,000 loss is recognized, and her basis in the duplex is $400,000
A $100,000 loss is recognized, and her basis in the duplex is $350,000
No loss is recognized, and her basis in the duplex is $500,000
explain: Nina realizes a $100,000 loss ($400,000 received minus $500,000 basis), but no loss is recognized in a like-kind exchange even when cash boot is received. Her basis is the $500,000 basis given up minus the $50,000 cash received, or $450,000, which preserves the $100,000 deferred loss ($350,000 value plus $100,000). The $500,000 choice forgets to subtract the cash.

q: On March 10, 2025, a fire destroyed a warehouse that Victor used in his business. His adjusted basis was $180,000, and in May 2025 he received $400,000 of insurance proceeds. In June 2026 he bought a replacement warehouse for his business for $350,000 and elected to postpone gain under Section 1033. What are Victor's recognized gain and his basis in the new warehouse?
choices: $50,000 recognized gain and $180,000 basis
$50,000 recognized gain and $350,000 basis
$220,000 recognized gain and $350,000 basis
No recognized gain and $180,000 basis
explain: Victor realizes $220,000 ($400,000 minus $180,000). He bought replacement property within the replacement period, so he recognizes gain only to the extent the proceeds exceed the cost of the replacement, $400,000 minus $350,000, or $50,000, and $170,000 is postponed. His basis is the $350,000 cost minus the $170,000 postponed gain, or $180,000; the $350,000 choice forgets to reduce the cost by the postponed gain.

q: In 2025 each of the following taxpayers realized a gain on an involuntary conversion and bought replacement property within the replacement period. The gain can be postponed under Section 1033 in each case EXCEPT:
choices: A factory that Ruth used in her own manufacturing business was destroyed by fire, and she used the insurance proceeds to buy an apartment building to rent to tenants
An office building that Sam held for rental was condemned by the state, and he used the award to buy vacant land to hold for investment

A machine that Tara used in her business was destroyed by fire, and she used the insurance proceeds to buy 80% of the voting stock and 80% of all other stock of a corporation that owns a similar machine
A delivery truck used in Uma's business was stolen, and she used the insurance proceeds to buy a delivery truck to use the same way
explain: For an owner-user, replacement property must be similar or related in service or use, meaning it must function the same way, and a rental apartment building does not function like a factory Ruth operated. The looser like-kind standard that lets Sam replace a rental building with investment land applies only to condemned real property held for business or investment, not to a fire. Buying a controlling interest (at least 80%) in a corporation that owns similar property is an allowed form of replacement.
source: IRC 1033(a)(1), (a)(2)(A), (a)(2)(E), (g)(1); IRS Pub 544 (2025), ch. 1, Similar or related in service or use

q: On March 3, 2025, Jordan transferred a rental building with a fair market value of $800,000 to a qualified intermediary to start a deferred like-kind exchange. The values of all properties below do not change during the exchange period. Jordan's identification of replacement property meets the Treasury Regulations if, within the 45-day identification period, he:
choices: Identifies five properties with an aggregate fair market value of $1,500,000 in a written document he signs and delivers to the qualified intermediary

Identifies four properties with an aggregate fair market value of $1,700,000 in a signed writing, and he receives, after the 45-day identification period ends but within the exchange period, one of them worth $900,000
Identifies two properties with an aggregate fair market value of $900,000 in a phone call to the qualified intermediary

Identifies six properties with an aggregate fair market value of $2,000,000 in a signed writing, and he receives, after the 45-day identification period ends but within the exchange period, three of them worth $1,800,000
explain: Any number of properties may be identified if their aggregate value does not exceed 200% of the relinquished property's value ($1,600,000), so five properties worth $1,500,000 are valid. The $1,700,000 and $2,000,000 identifications exceed both the three-property and 200% limits, and they are saved only if Jordan receives at least 95% of the identified value; $900,000 is 53% and $1,800,000 is 90%. Identification must be in a written document signed by the taxpayer, so a phone call does not count.

q: In 2025 Helen, an individual, had the following results from property used in her business and held more than one year: a $30,000 gain on the sale of land used as a parking lot, a $12,000 loss on the sale of equipment, an $8,000 gain when a storm destroyed a building depreciated straight-line (insurance exceeded adjusted basis, and she did not replace it), and a $20,000 loss when equipment was stolen. She has no nonrecaptured net Section 1231 losses from earlier years. How much of these results is treated as long-term capital gain?
explain: Casualty and theft gains and losses on business property are netted first; because the $20,000 theft loss exceeds the $8,000 storm gain, neither enters Section 1231 netting, and both are ordinary. The remaining Section 1231 items net to a $18,000 gain ($30,000 minus $12,000), which is long-term capital gain. The $6,000 choice wrongly puts the casualty items into the main Section 1231 netting.

q: Olivia, an individual, had a net Section 1231 loss of $25,000 in 2021, which she deducted as an ordinary loss. In 2023 she had a net Section 1231 gain of $10,000, all of which was properly treated as ordinary income under the lookback rule. She had no other Section 1231 gains or losses from 2020 through 2024. In 2025 she has a net Section 1231 gain of $40,000. How is her 2025 net Section 1231 gain treated?
choices: $15,000 ordinary income and $25,000 long-term capital gain
$25,000 ordinary income and $15,000 long-term capital gain
$40,000 long-term capital gain
$40,000 ordinary income
explain: A net Section 1231 gain is ordinary income to the extent of nonrecaptured net Section 1231 losses from the 5 preceding years (2020 through 2024). The 2021 loss of $25,000 was already recaptured by $10,000 in 2023, leaving $15,000 nonrecaptured, so $15,000 is ordinary income and the remaining $25,000 is long-term capital gain. The $25,000 ordinary choice forgets the 2023 recapture.
source: IRC 1231(c); IRS Pub 544 (2025), ch. 3, Nonrecaptured section 1231 losses; Form 4797 instructions

q: In 2016 Elena, an individual, bought a residential rental property for $325,000, of which $275,000 was allocable to the building and $50,000 to the land. She claimed $90,000 of straight-line depreciation on the building. On June 20, 2025, she sold the property for $400,000, of which $300,000 was allocable to the building and $100,000 to the land. She had no other Section 1231 transactions and no nonrecaptured net Section 1231 losses. How is her $165,000 gain characterized?
choices: No ordinary income, $90,000 of unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, and $75,000 of other long-term capital gain
$90,000 of ordinary income and $75,000 of long-term capital gain
No ordinary income, $115,000 of unrecaptured Section 1250 gain, and $50,000 of other long-term capital gain
$18,000 of ordinary income and $147,000 of long-term capital gain
explain: The building gain is $115,000 ($300,000 minus the $185,000 adjusted basis) and the land gain is $50,000. Section 1250 makes only depreciation in excess of straight-line ordinary income, so there is none; unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is the building gain up to the depreciation taken, $90,000, and the other $75,000 is long-term capital gain. The $90,000 ordinary choice applies Section 1245 rules to real property, and the $18,000 choice applies the 20% Section 291 rule that reaches only corporations.

q: In 2025 Derek, an individual, sold three assets used in his business, each held more than one year. Machine A cost $60,000, had $40,000 of depreciation, and sold for $45,000. Machine B cost $50,000, had $20,000 of depreciation, and sold for $20,000. Land cost $28,000 and sold for $40,000. He has no nonrecaptured net Section 1231 losses from earlier years. How are these sales treated?
choices: $25,000 ordinary income and $2,000 long-term capital gain
$27,000 long-term capital gain
$15,000 ordinary income and $12,000 long-term capital gain
$25,000 ordinary income, $12,000 long-term capital gain, and a $10,000 ordinary loss
explain: Machine A has a $25,000 gain ($45,000 minus $20,000 adjusted basis), all ordinary under Section 1245 because recapture is the lesser of the gain or the $40,000 depreciation. Machine B has a $10,000 loss ($20,000 minus $30,000) and the land a $12,000 gain; both are Section 1231 items that net to a $2,000 gain, which is long-term capital gain. Recapture income is not netted with Section 1231 losses, so the $15,000 ordinary choice is wrong.

q: Jen bought stock directly from a domestic corporation at its original issuance in 2020 for $150,000 cash. The stock qualified as Section 1244 small business stock. In 2025 she sold all of it to an unrelated buyer for $20,000. Jen and her husband, Mike, file a joint return for 2025. Mike owns no stock, and they have no other capital gains or losses for 2025. How is the $130,000 loss treated on their 2025 return?
choices: $100,000 ordinary loss and a $30,000 capital loss, of which $3,000 is deductible in 2025 and $27,000 carries forward
$50,000 ordinary loss, because only Jen owned the stock, and an $80,000 capital loss, of which $3,000 is deductible in 2025
$130,000 ordinary loss, all deductible in 2025
$100,000 ordinary loss and a $30,000 capital loss, all deductible in 2025
explain: On a joint return the Section 1244 ordinary loss limit is $100,000 a year, whether the loss is sustained by one spouse or both, so $100,000 is ordinary and the other $30,000 ($130,000 - $100,000) is a capital loss. With no capital gains, only $3,000 of that capital loss offsets other income in 2025 and $27,000 carries forward. The $50,000 limit applies only to a taxpayer who does not file a joint return.

q: In each case below, the stock was Section 1244 stock when the corporation issued it, and the holder sold it at a loss in 2025. All of the following individuals may treat the loss as an ordinary loss under Section 1244 EXCEPT:
choices: Lena, who bought her shares for cash directly from the corporation when it issued them
Omar, who was a partner in a partnership when the partnership bought shares from the corporation at issuance, and whose distributive share includes the partnership's loss on those shares
Paul, who bought his shares for cash from Lena, the original holder
Rosa, who received her shares from the corporation at issuance in exchange for equipment whose basis equaled its fair market value
explain: Only the individual to whom the corporation issued the stock, or an individual who was a partner when a partnership acquired the stock at issuance, can claim a Section 1244 ordinary loss. Anyone who acquires the stock from a shareholder, by purchase, gift or otherwise, has a capital loss, so Paul does not qualify. Stock issued for property other than stock or securities, such as Rosa's equipment, can qualify.

q: In September 2025 Nina, a sole proprietor, sold business equipment that cost $200,000 and on which she had claimed $120,000 of depreciation. The selling price was $300,000: the buyer assumed a $50,000 loan secured by the equipment, paid $50,000 cash at closing, and gave a note for $200,000 with adequate stated interest, with principal payments starting in 2026. Nina paid $10,000 of selling expenses and reports on the installment method. How much gain must she recognize for 2025?
explain: The $120,000 of Section 1245 recapture is recognized in full in the year of sale and is added to basis, so installment sale basis is $80,000 + $10,000 selling expenses + $120,000 = $210,000 and gross profit is $90,000. The assumed loan does not exceed that basis, so the contract price is $300,000 - $50,000 = $250,000 and the gross profit percentage is 36%; the $50,000 payment gives $18,000, for a 2025 total of $120,000 + $18,000 = $138,000. Dividing gross profit by the selling price instead of the contract price gives 30% and the wrong $135,000.

q: On March 1, 2025, Frank sold land he held for investment to his son for $300,000. Frank's basis was $120,000, and there were no selling expenses. The son paid $30,000 at closing and gave a note for $270,000 with adequate stated interest, payable in installments beginning March 1, 2026. On November 15, 2025, the son resold the land to an unrelated buyer for $320,000 cash. Frank reports on the installment method. How much gain must Frank recognize for 2025?
explain: Frank's gross profit percentage is 60% ($180,000 / $300,000). Because his son is a related person and resold the land within two years, Frank is treated as receiving the lesser of the son's $320,000 amount realized or the $300,000 contract price, minus the $30,000 already received, or $270,000; total 2025 payments are $300,000, and 60% of that is $180,000. The $200,000 answer wrongly uses the son's resale price, and $18,000 ignores the related-party resale rule.

q: All of the following pairs are related persons under Section 267(b), so that a loss on a 2025 sale between them is disallowed, EXCEPT:
choices: An individual and a corporation in which she owns 40% of the stock by value and her husband owns 15%
The grantor of a trust and the trust's fiduciary
An individual and his wife's brother
An S corporation and a C corporation when the same persons own more than 50% in value of the outstanding stock of each
explain: A brother-in-law is not family under Section 267(c)(4), which covers only siblings, a spouse, ancestors and lineal descendants, so an individual and his wife's brother are not related. The wife in the first choice owns 55% (her 40% plus her husband's 15% by family attribution), which is more than 50%, so she and the corporation are related; the grantor and fiduciary, and the commonly controlled S and C corporations, are also listed relationships.

q: Zeta Corp., a C corporation, has 1,000 shares of one class of stock outstanding, owned as follows: Mark 300, Mark's sister 200, Mark's grandson 100, Mark's father 100, Yolo Corp. 200, and an unrelated individual 100. Mark owns 40% of the only class of Yolo Corp. stock, and unrelated individuals own the rest. What percentage of Zeta stock is Mark treated as owning, directly and constructively, under Section 267(c) and under Section 318(a)?
choices: 78% under Section 267(c) and 50% under Section 318(a)
78% under both Section 267(c) and Section 318(a)
70% under Section 267(c) and 50% under Section 318(a)
78% under Section 267(c) and 70% under Section 318(a)
explain: Under Section 267(c) Mark owns his 300 shares plus his sister's, grandson's and father's 400 shares as family, plus 40% of Yolo's 200 shares (80) because stock held by a corporation is attributed proportionately to any shareholder: 780 shares, or 78%. Under Section 318(a) family means only a spouse, children, grandchildren and parents, so the sister's shares are excluded, and corporate stock is attributed only to a shareholder owning 50% or more in value, so Yolo's shares are excluded: 300 + 100 + 100 = 500 shares, or 50%. Treating a sibling as family under Section 318 is the most common error.

q: In February 2025 Joan sold land she held for investment to her daughter, Kate, for $60,000, its fair market value. Joan's adjusted basis was $90,000. In October 2025 Kate sold the land to an unrelated buyer for $75,000. What are the 2025 results for Joan and Kate?
choices: Joan deducts no loss, and Kate recognizes no gain
Joan deducts no loss, and Kate recognizes a $15,000 gain
Joan deducts a $15,000 loss when Kate resells, and Kate recognizes no gain
Joan deducts no loss, and Kate recognizes a $15,000 loss because she takes Joan's $90,000 basis
explain: Joan's $30,000 loss ($60,000 - $90,000) is disallowed because a daughter is a related person. Kate's basis is her $60,000 cost, so she realizes a $15,000 gain, which is recognized only to the extent it exceeds Joan's $30,000 disallowed loss, so none is recognized; the other $15,000 of disallowed loss is lost for good and never returns to Joan. Kate does not take Joan's basis, so she has no loss.

q: Sam owns 80% of the value of the outstanding stock of Delta Corp., a C corporation; unrelated persons own the rest. In June 2025 Sam sold Delta a warehouse building (not the land) that he had used in his sole proprietorship since 2015. The building cost $400,000, and he had claimed $100,000 of straight-line depreciation. Delta paid $450,000, its fair market value, and will depreciate the building. How is Sam's $150,000 gain characterized?
choices: $100,000 of unrecaptured Section 1250 gain and $50,000 of other Section 1231 gain
$100,000 of ordinary income and $50,000 of Section 1231 gain
$150,000 of ordinary income
$150,000 of Section 1231 gain
explain: Section 1239 treats all gain on a sale of property between a person and a corporation of which he owns more than 50% in value as ordinary income if the property is depreciable in the buyer's hands, so the full $150,000 ($450,000 - $300,000 adjusted basis) is ordinary. Without Section 1239 there would be no Section 1250 ordinary recapture on straight-line depreciation; the gain would be Section 1231 gain, of which $100,000 would be unrecaptured Section 1250 gain. Section 1239 does not stop at the depreciation taken.

q: On January 1, 2025, Ruth made an interest-free demand loan of $90,000 to her son. It was the only loan between them and was outstanding all of 2025, and tax avoidance was not a principal purpose. The son's 2025 net investment income was $3,000. Assume the blended annual rate (the applicable federal rate for a demand loan outstanding for the full year) is 4%. How much interest income must Ruth report for 2025 under Section 7872?
explain: Forgone interest at the applicable federal rate is $90,000 x 4% = $3,600, but for a gift loan between individuals of $100,000 or less, the interest treated as paid back to the lender cannot exceed the borrower's net investment income, so Ruth reports $3,000. The $0 answer would apply only if the son's net investment income were $1,000 or less, or the loans totaled $10,000 or less.

q: On July 1, 2025, Ruth sold land she held for investment to her son for $400,000, payable in one lump sum on July 1, 2028, with no stated interest. Ruth made no other sales to her son in 2025, and neither of them is a nonresident alien. Assume the applicable federal rate for the note is 7%, compounded semiannually. Which statement about imputed interest on the sale is correct?
choices: Unstated interest is imputed at 6%, compounded semiannually; it is interest income to Ruth and reduces the selling price
Unstated interest is imputed at 7%, the applicable federal rate, because Section 1274 applies to sales over $250,000
No interest is imputed because the sale is between family members
Unstated interest is imputed at 6%, compounded semiannually, and is added to Ruth's capital gain on the land
explain: For a sale of land by an individual to a family member, the discount rate under Section 483 is capped at 6%, compounded semiannually, on up to $500,000 of sales between the same individuals in a calendar year, and Section 1274 does not apply to the extent this rule does. The unstated interest is taxed as interest, so less of the $400,000 is selling price for figuring Ruth's gain. Using the 7% applicable federal rate ignores the related-party land rule.

q: On March 3, 2023, Ellen's employer granted her nonqualified stock options to buy 2,000 shares of its stock at $15 a share. The options had no readily ascertainable fair market value when granted. On May 12, 2025, she exercised all of the options when the stock was worth $40 a share, and on December 1, 2025, she sold all 2,000 shares for $46 a share. How does Ellen report these events for 2025?
choices: $50,000 of ordinary compensation income and a $12,000 short-term capital gain
$50,000 of ordinary compensation income and a $12,000 long-term capital gain
No income at exercise and a $62,000 long-term capital gain on the sale
$62,000 of ordinary compensation income and no capital gain
explain: An option with no readily ascertainable value is not taxed at grant; at exercise Ellen has compensation equal to the spread, ($40 minus $15) times 2,000, or $50,000, and her basis becomes $40 a share. The sale at $46 gives a $12,000 gain that is short-term, because the holding period of the shares began at exercise in May 2025, not at the 2023 grant. Deferring all tax to the sale and getting capital gain treatment is the rule for qualifying incentive stock options, not nonqualified options.

q: On January 10, 2024, Raj was granted incentive stock options to buy 1,000 shares of his employer's stock at $20 a share, the stock's value on that date. On February 3, 2025, he exercised the options when the stock was worth $50 a share. On November 14, 2025, he sold all 1,000 shares on the open market for $45 a share. What are the 2025 results for regular tax and for the alternative minimum tax (AMT)?
choices: $25,000 of ordinary compensation income for regular tax, and a $30,000 positive AMT adjustment
$25,000 long-term capital gain for regular tax, and a $30,000 positive AMT adjustment
$30,000 of ordinary compensation income and a $5,000 short-term capital loss for regular tax, and no AMT adjustment
$25,000 of ordinary compensation income for regular tax, and no AMT adjustment for the options
explain: Selling within 1 year of exercise (and 2 years of grant) is a disqualifying disposition, and because the sale is at a price below the value at exercise, ordinary income is limited to the gain actually realized: ($45 minus $20) times 1,000, or $25,000, with no capital gain or loss. For AMT, the same limit applies when the exercise and the sale fall in the same tax year, so AMT income from the options is also $25,000 and there is no adjustment. The $30,000 adjustment applies only when the shares are still held at the end of the year of exercise.

q: On February 3, 2025, Nina's employer transferred 5,000 shares of restricted stock to her for no payment. The shares vest only if she is still employed on February 3, 2028. The shares were worth $4 each ($20,000) on the transfer date, and Nina filed a Section 83(b) election on February 20, 2025. All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
choices: Nina includes $20,000 of ordinary compensation income in 2025.
Nina recognizes no income when the shares vest in 2028, and her basis in the shares is $20,000.
Nina's holding period begins just after February 3, 2025, so a sale in March 2028 produces long-term capital gain or loss.
If Nina quits in 2026 and forfeits the shares, she may deduct a $20,000 capital loss.
explain: Under the election Nina is taxed on the $20,000 value at transfer, gets a $20,000 basis, owes nothing at vesting, and starts her holding period at the transfer. If the shares are forfeited, her loss is limited to what she paid for them minus anything received, which is zero here, so the $20,000 she included is never recovered. That forfeiture risk is the main cost of making the election.

q: Omar is a cash-method sole proprietor. His marginal income tax rate is 35% for 2025 and will be 24% for 2026 because he is cutting back his work. In mid-December 2025 he can either bill a client for $20,000 of work completed in December, so that payment arrives by December 31, 2025, or wait and bill in January 2026, so that payment arrives in January. He also owes a $10,000 deductible advertising bill for services received in 2025, which he can pay on December 29, 2025, or in January 2026. Ignoring self-employment tax, the qualified business income deduction and the time value of money, which plan minimizes his combined 2025 and 2026 income tax, and how much does it save compared with billing in December 2025 and paying the advertising bill in January 2026?
choices: Bill in January 2026 and pay the advertising bill in January 2026; $2,200
Bill in January 2026 and pay the advertising bill in December 2025; $3,300
Bill in December 2025 and pay the advertising bill in December 2025; $1,100
Bill in January 2026 and pay the advertising bill in December 2025; $10,500
explain: A cash-method taxpayer reports income when received and deducts expenses when paid, so Omar should push the income into the lower-rate year and pull the deduction into the higher-rate year. Deferring the $20,000 saves $20,000 times (35% minus 24%), or $2,200, and paying the $10,000 bill in 2025 saves $10,000 times 11%, or $1,100, for $3,300 in total. The $10,500 choice looks only at 2025 tax (35% of $30,000) and ignores the tax that still comes due in 2026.
source: IRC 451(a); IRC 461(a); Treas. Reg. 1.451-1(a); Treas. Reg. 1.451-2(a); Treas. Reg. 1.461-1(a)(1)

q: Lena is single. Her 2024 return, for a full 12-month year, showed adjusted gross income (AGI) of $210,000 and total tax of $40,000. She projects, accurately, that her 2025 total tax will be $60,000, and her employer will withhold $20,000 of federal income tax evenly during 2025. She will not use the annualized income installment method. What is the smallest equal estimated tax payment she can make on each of the four 2025 due dates and still avoid an underpayment penalty?
explain: The required annual payment is the lesser of 90% of the 2025 tax ($54,000) or, because her 2024 AGI exceeded $150,000, 110% of the 2024 tax ($44,000). Subtracting the $20,000 of withholding leaves $24,000 of estimated payments, or $6,000 per installment. The $5,000 choice uses 100% of the prior-year tax, which is not available above $150,000 of AGI, and $8,500 uses the 90% current-year test even though the prior-year test is lower.

q: Ted owns an interest in a retail store, which is not a personal service activity. Under the passive activity regulations, Ted materially participates in the store for 2025 if any of the following is true EXCEPT:
choices: He participates in the store for 520 hours during 2025.
He participates for 110 hours during 2025, and no other individual, including employees who are not owners, participates more than he does.
He materially participated in the store in 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2023.
He materially participated in the store in 2022, 2023 and 2024, and in no earlier year.
explain: Material participation in any 3 prior years qualifies only for a personal service activity, such as a consulting or law practice; a retail store needs material participation in any 5 of the 10 preceding years, which the 2016 to 2023 history meets even though the years are not consecutive. More than 500 hours, and more than 100 hours with no other individual participating more, are separate tests that each qualify on their own.

q: Priya is single. She owns a rental house and actively participates in managing it, and in 2025 the house produced a $30,000 loss. She also has $4,000 of net income from a limited partnership interest in which she does not materially participate. Her modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) for the special allowance is $130,000. She has no other passive activities and no suspended losses from earlier years. How much of the rental loss can she use in 2025, and how much is suspended?
choices: $14,000 used ($4,000 against the partnership income and $10,000 against nonpassive income); $16,000 suspended
$10,000 used; $20,000 suspended
$29,000 used ($4,000 against the partnership income and $25,000 against nonpassive income); $1,000 suspended
$4,000 used, all against the partnership income; $26,000 suspended
explain: Passive income and losses are netted first, so $4,000 of the rental loss offsets the partnership income, leaving a $26,000 net passive loss from rental real estate. The $25,000 allowance is reduced by 50% of MAGI over $100,000, or $15,000, leaving $10,000 that can offset nonpassive income, for $14,000 used and $16,000 suspended. The $10,000 choice skips the netting step, and the $4,000 choice reduces the allowance by the full $30,000 excess instead of half of it.

q: Marco owns a limited partnership interest in which he does not materially participate, with $40,000 of suspended passive losses from earlier years. On September 30, 2025, he sold his entire interest to an unrelated buyer for cash in a fully taxable sale. For 2025 the partnership allocated him a $5,000 operating loss, and he had a $15,000 gain on the sale. He also owns a second limited partnership interest, also passive, that produced $6,000 of net income in 2025. He has enough basis and amount at risk to cover all losses. How much loss is treated as not from a passive activity in 2025?
explain: On a fully taxable disposition of an entire interest to an unrelated person, the activity's loss for the year, counting suspended losses and the gain on the sale, is $5,000 plus $40,000 minus $15,000, or $30,000. That loss first offsets the $6,000 of net income from his other passive activity, and the remaining $24,000 is treated as nonpassive and can offset his other income. The $30,000 choice forgets to net against the other passive income, and $45,000 ignores both the gain and the other income.

q: Jade is a limited partner in a partnership that runs a restaurant, and she does not materially participate. At the start of 2025 her basis in the partnership interest is $30,000, which includes a $10,000 share of partnership nonrecourse liabilities that are not qualified nonrecourse financing. Her amount at risk is $20,000. Her share of the partnership's 2025 ordinary loss is $45,000, and she has no passive income. How is the loss treated in 2025?
choices: $25,000 suspended under the at-risk rules and $20,000 suspended under the passive activity rules
$15,000 suspended under the basis limit, $10,000 suspended under the at-risk rules and $20,000 suspended under the passive activity rules
$15,000 suspended under the basis limit and $30,000 suspended under the passive activity rules
$45,000 suspended under the passive activity rules
explain: The limits apply in order: basis first, then at-risk, then passive. Basis allows $30,000 and suspends $15,000; of the $30,000, only her $20,000 at risk passes the at-risk limit, suspending $10,000 because the nonrecourse debt is not at risk; the remaining $20,000 is a passive loss with no passive income to absorb it, so none is deducted. Applying the at-risk test to the full $45,000 skips the basis step.
source: IRC 704(d); IRC 465(a), (b); IRC 469(a); Temp. Treas. Reg. 1.469-2T(d)(6); IRS Pub 925 (2025)

q: Hal owned an interest in a passive activity with $50,000 of suspended passive losses. He died on June 10, 2025, and the interest passed to his daughter. Hal's adjusted basis in the interest just before his death was $60,000, and the daughter's basis, its fair market value at Hal's death, is $80,000. How are the suspended losses treated?
choices: $50,000 is deducted on Hal's final 2025 return.
$30,000 is deducted on Hal's final 2025 return, and $20,000 is added to the daughter's basis.
None is deducted on Hal's final return, and the $50,000 carries over to the daughter.
$30,000 is deducted on Hal's final 2025 return, and $20,000 is never deductible.
explain: When a passive interest passes at death, suspended losses are allowed on the decedent's final return only to the extent they exceed the basis step-up, here $80,000 minus $60,000, or $20,000; so $30,000 is deductible and the other $20,000 is lost for good. Adding the disallowed loss to the recipient's basis is the rule for a gift of a passive interest, not a transfer at death.
source: IRC 469(g)(2); IRC 469(j)(6); IRC 1014(a); IRS Pub 925 (2025), Dispositions by death

q: Helen made each of the following transfers in 2025. Which one is a completed gift in 2025 for federal gift tax purposes?
choices: She deposited $50,000 in a joint bank account with her son, from which she can withdraw the entire balance without his consent. Her son withdrew nothing in 2025.
She transferred $200,000 of securities to a revocable living trust that names her children as beneficiaries.
She bought a $10,000 U.S. savings bond registered as payable to "Helen or her nephew." The nephew did not cash it in 2025.
She transferred $80,000 of stock to an irrevocable trust for her niece and kept no power to revoke the trust or change its beneficiaries.
explain: A gift is complete when the donor parts with dominion and control and keeps no power to change its disposition, which is true of the irrevocable trust with no retained powers. A transfer to a revocable trust is incomplete because Helen can take the property back. For a joint bank account or a bond payable to either owner, the gift occurs only when the other owner withdraws the funds or cashes the bond for his own benefit, which did not happen in 2025.

q: In 2025 Ray gave his daughter land with a fair market value (FMV) of $419,000. His adjusted basis in the land was $119,000. Ray had used all of his unified credit on earlier gifts. Assume the 2025 annual exclusion is $19,000. He made no other 2025 gifts and paid $160,000 of gift tax on this gift. What is the daughter's basis in the land?
explain: The donee's basis is the donor's basis increased by the gift tax attributable to the net appreciation: net appreciation is $419,000 - $119,000 = $300,000, and the amount of the gift after the annual exclusion is $419,000 - $19,000 = $400,000, so the increase is $160,000 x $300,000 / $400,000 = $120,000 and the basis is $119,000 + $120,000 = $239,000. Adding the full $160,000 of tax ($279,000) ignores the net appreciation fraction, and dividing by the $419,000 fair market value (FMV) instead of the $400,000 gift after the exclusion gives $233,558.
source: IRC 1015(a) and (d)(6); Treas. Reg. 1.1015-5(c); IRS Pub 551 (Property Received as a Gift)

q: Mark, age 70, plans to keep all his property until death, expects his estate to owe estate tax, and is in the same income tax bracket as his daughter. In 2025 he wants to give her one asset worth $60,000. Asset A: stock with a $100,000 basis that is not expected to grow. Asset B: stock with a $55,000 basis that is expected to grow sharply. Asset C: land with a $10,000 basis that is not expected to grow. Which gift best reduces the family's combined future estate and income taxes?
choices: Asset A, because his daughter takes his $100,000 basis and can deduct the $40,000 loss when she sells it
Asset B, because its future growth is kept out of his estate while little built-in gain loses the step-up in basis at death
Asset C, because removing the asset with the largest built-in gain from his estate saves the most estate tax
Asset A sold to his daughter for $60,000 instead of given, so that he can deduct the $40,000 loss
explain: Gifted property counts in the estate tax base only at its value on the date of the gift, so giving the asset expected to grow keeps its future growth out of Mark's estate, and with only $5,000 of built-in gain little is lost by giving up the step-up in basis at death. For a loss gift, the daughter's basis for loss is the $60,000 fair market value, so the $40,000 loss disappears, and a sale to his daughter is a related-party sale whose loss is disallowed. Giving away Asset C saves no more estate tax than any other $60,000 asset, since estate tax uses value, not basis, and it gives up a $50,000 step-up.
source: IRC 1014(a); IRC 1015(a); IRC 2001(b); IRC 267(a)(1), (b)(1) and (c)(4); IRS Pub 551; IRS Pub 544

q: In 2025 Ana paid $50,000 of tuition directly to her grandson's university and paid $8,000 to her grandson to reimburse him for hospital bills he had already paid. She also gave him $15,000 in cash. Assume the 2025 annual exclusion is $19,000. She made no other gifts and does not elect gift-splitting. What is the amount of her 2025 taxable gifts?
explain: Tuition paid directly to the school is excluded without limit, but the exclusion for medical care requires payment directly to the provider, so the $8,000 reimbursement is an ordinary gift. The gifts that count are $8,000 + $15,000 = $23,000, less the $19,000 annual exclusion, or $4,000. Treating the reimbursement as an excluded medical payment gives $0, which is wrong because Ana did not pay the hospital directly.
source: IRC 2503(b) and (e); Treas. Reg. 25.2503-6(b) and (c), Examples 1 and 4

q: In 2025 Tom gave his wife, a U.S. citizen, $500,000 in cash and gave his son $100,000 in cash. Assume the 2025 annual exclusion is $19,000. Tom made no other gifts and does not elect gift-splitting. What are his 2025 taxable gifts, and must he file Form 709?
choices: $81,000 of taxable gifts, and Form 709 is required
$562,000 of taxable gifts, and Form 709 is required
$62,000 of taxable gifts, and Form 709 is required
$0 of taxable gifts, because the unified credit covers the gift to his son, and Form 709 is not required
explain: Outright gifts to a citizen spouse qualify for an unlimited marital deduction for the amount left after the annual exclusion, so the $500,000 gift produces no taxable gift. The gift to his son is $100,000 - $19,000 = $81,000 taxable, and because it exceeds the annual exclusion Tom must file Form 709 even though the unified credit means no tax is due. Ignoring the marital deduction gives $562,000.
source: IRC 2523(a); IRC 2524; IRC 2503(b); IRC 6019; Form 709 instructions (2025), Who Must File and Schedule A Part 4

q: Ann was born in March 1951. In 2025 she still works full time for a company in which she owns 2% of the stock, and its 401(k) plan lets employees who are still working delay required minimum distributions (RMDs) until they retire. She holds a traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA), pretax and designated Roth accounts in the 401(k), and a Roth IRA. Which of these accounts require an RMD for 2025?
choices: Only the traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA)
The traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA) and the pretax 401(k) account
The traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA), the pretax 401(k) account and the designated Roth account
None of them, because she is still working
explain: Ann turned 72 after 2022, so her applicable age is 73, which she reached in 2024, and IRA distributions must start then whether or not she works. The still-working delay applies only to an employer plan of a non-5% owner, so her pretax 401(k) account is deferred, and designated Roth accounts (for years after 2023) and Roth IRAs have no RMDs during the owner's life. Assuming the still-working rule also covers her IRA is the common error.

q: In 2025 Ken, age 50, has 2025 modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) of $300,000. He converts $50,000 from his only traditional individual retirement arrangement (IRA), which holds no nondeductible contributions, to a Roth IRA and pays the tax from savings. Which statement is correct?
choices: The conversion is not allowed because his modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) exceeds the Roth IRA contribution limit
The $50,000 is included in his 2025 gross income and is also subject to a $5,000 additional tax because he is under age 59 1/2
The $50,000 is included in his 2025 gross income, no 10% additional tax applies to the conversion, and he cannot later recharacterize it
The $50,000 is included in his 2025 gross income, but he can undo the conversion by recharacterizing it by the extended due date if the account loses value
explain: A conversion is treated as a distribution, so the $50,000 of pretax money is included in gross income, but the statute turns off the 10% additional tax on early distributions for the converted amount. There is no income limit on conversions, and conversions made after 2017 cannot be recharacterized, so he cannot undo it if the investments fall.
source: IRC 408A(d)(3)(A) and (C); IRC 408A(d)(6)(B)(iii); IRC 408A(c)(3); IRS Pub 590-A (2025)

q: Maya is the beneficiary of a 529 plan her parents opened in 2008. The account is worth $40,000, of which $6,000 is contributions made in the last 5 years and the earnings on them. In 2025 Maya earns $250,000 of wages, which puts her modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) above the Roth individual retirement arrangement (IRA) phaseout range, and she contributes $3,000 to a traditional IRA. Assume the 2025 IRA contribution limit is $7,000. She has never rolled 529 money to a Roth IRA. What is the most she can move tax free by direct transfer from the 529 plan to a Roth IRA for her in 2025?
explain: A 529-to-Roth rollover is capped each year at the IRA contribution limit less the beneficiary's other IRA contributions for the year, so $7,000 - $3,000 = $4,000, and the lifetime cap is $35,000. The account has been open more than 15 years and $34,000 is old enough to qualify, so those limits do not bind. The Roth income limit is raised by the rollover amount, so her high modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) does not block it.

q: In March 2023 Ann sold a $500,000 policy on her own life to Bob, her friend, for $40,000. Bob is not her business partner and has no business or family relationship with her, and he named himself the beneficiary. Bob paid $12,000 of premiums after buying the policy. Ann died in August 2025, and Bob collected $500,000. How much must Bob include in his 2025 gross income?
explain: Under the transfer-for-value rule, a buyer of a life insurance policy excludes only what he paid for it plus the premiums he paid afterward, so Bob includes $500,000 - $40,000 - $12,000 = $448,000. The full exclusion would apply only if he fit an exception, such as being the insured, her partner, or a corporation in which she was a shareholder or officer. Subtracting only the $40,000 price gives $460,000.

q: Pam was disabled for 6 months of 2025 and received $12,000 of benefits from a group long-term disability policy whose premiums her employer paid without including them in her wages. She also received $12,000 from an individual disability policy she bought and paid for with after-tax dollars. How much of the $24,000 is included in her 2025 gross income?
explain: Disability benefits from a policy the individual paid for with after-tax dollars are excluded, so the $12,000 from her own policy is tax free. Benefits from a plan paid for by the employer with premiums not included in her income are taxable, so $12,000 is included. This is why buying disability coverage with after-tax dollars protects the full benefit if a disability occurs.
source: IRC 104(a)(3); IRC 105(a); IRS Pub 525 (2025), Sickness and Injury Benefits

q: A calendar-year C corporation reports the following for 2024: gross income from operations of $300,000, deductible operating expenses of $420,000, $100,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 30% of the stock (by vote and value), and $10,000 of cash charitable contributions. It has no other items and no carryovers into 2024. For 2025 its taxable income before any net operating loss (NOL) deduction is $90,000, and it has no deduction under section 199A or section 250. What is the corporation's 2024 NOL, and how much of it carries forward to 2026?
choices: $85,000 NOL; $13,000 carries forward to 2026
$85,000 NOL; $0 carries forward to 2026
$95,000 NOL; $23,000 carries forward to 2026
$20,000 NOL; $0 carries forward to 2026
explain: Before special deductions the corporation has a $20,000 loss ($300,000 - $420,000 + $100,000). The 65% dividends received deduction of $65,000 is allowed in full because the taxable income limit of section 246(b) does not apply in a year with an NOL, but no charitable deduction is allowed because taxable income for the 10% limit is below zero, so the NOL is $85,000. In 2025 the deduction is capped at 80% x $90,000 = $72,000, leaving $13,000 to carry forward; deducting the whole $85,000 ignores the 80% limit, and $95,000 wrongly deducts the charitable contributions.

q: P Corp., a domestic C corporation, has for six years owned 85% of the only class of stock of S1 Corp. and 75% of the only class of stock of S2 Corp., both domestic C corporations. P Corp. and S1 Corp. file a consolidated return for 2025, and S2 Corp. files its own return. For 2025, P Corp.'s separate taxable income, not counting any dividends received, is $500,000; S1 Corp.'s is $200,000; and S2 Corp.'s is $100,000. During 2025 S1 Corp. paid P Corp. a $50,000 dividend and S2 Corp. paid P Corp. a $40,000 dividend, both out of earnings and profits. There are no other intercompany transactions. What is the consolidated taxable income for 2025?
explain: S1 Corp. is an includible member because P Corp. owns at least 80% of its vote and value, so its $50,000 dividend to P Corp. is an intercompany distribution excluded from P Corp.'s income. S2 Corp. fails the 80% test, so it cannot join the group, and its $40,000 dividend is taxable to P Corp. with a 65% dividends received deduction: $40,000 x 35% = $14,000. Consolidated taxable income is $500,000 + $200,000 + $14,000 = $714,000; $800,000 wrongly treats S2 Corp. as a member and $740,000 forgets the dividends received deduction.

q: In 2025 Delta Inc., a domestic C corporation, earns the following gross income: $10,000 of interest on a loan to a German corporation that has no trade or business in the United States; $20,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation; $30,000 of royalties from a domestic company for the right to use Delta's patent only in France; $40,000 of rent from a Canadian company for a warehouse Delta owns in Texas; and $50,000 of fees from a domestic customer for engineering services that Delta's employees performed entirely in Canada. How much of this gross income is foreign-source income?
explain: Interest is sourced by the payer's residence, so the German corporation's $10,000 is foreign source; royalties are sourced where the property is used, so the $30,000 for use in France is foreign source; and service income is sourced where the work is performed, so the $50,000 for work in Canada is foreign source, for $90,000 in total. The dividends from a domestic corporation and the rent on Texas property are United States source. Answering $50,000 applies a payer-residence rule to every item, but only interest and dividends follow the payer.

q: On June 1, 2025, a calendar-year C corporation distributes investment land to Ivy, an individual shareholder, in a nonliquidating distribution. The land has an adjusted basis of $70,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 and is not subject to any liability. The corporation has $200,000 of accumulated earnings and profits and $100,000 of current earnings and profits for 2025, before considering the distribution. Which statement is correct?
choices: The corporation recognizes no loss; Ivy has a $40,000 dividend and a $40,000 basis in the land; the corporation's earnings and profits decrease by $70,000.
The corporation recognizes a $30,000 loss; Ivy has a $40,000 dividend and a $40,000 basis in the land; the corporation's earnings and profits decrease by $40,000.
The corporation recognizes no loss; Ivy has a $40,000 dividend and a $70,000 basis in the land; the corporation's earnings and profits decrease by $70,000.
The corporation recognizes no loss; Ivy has a $70,000 dividend and a $70,000 basis in the land; the corporation's earnings and profits decrease by $70,000.
explain: A corporation recognizes gain, but never loss, on a nonliquidating distribution of property, so the $30,000 decline in value is not deductible. Ivy's distribution is measured at the land's $40,000 fair market value, which is a dividend because earnings and profits are ample, and her basis is that same $40,000. Earnings and profits fall by the land's adjusted basis of $70,000; only appreciated property is reduced at fair market value after earnings and profits are first increased by the gain.

q: Max owns 90% of a calendar-year C corporation with ample earnings and profits and works full time as its chief executive. In 2025 the corporation pays him a $600,000 salary. On audit, the IRS establishes that reasonable compensation for his services is $400,000 and that the excess was paid in proportion to his stockholding. All of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:
choices: The corporation may deduct $400,000 as compensation for 2025.
The $200,000 excess is treated as a dividend to Max.
Max includes the full $600,000 in his 2025 gross income.
Max may exclude the $200,000 excess from gross income because the corporation cannot deduct it.
explain: A corporation deducts only a reasonable allowance for salaries, and an excess paid to a shareholder in proportion to stockholding is a distribution of earnings, so the corporation deducts $400,000 and the $200,000 is a nondeductible dividend. Max still reports all $600,000: $400,000 as wages and $200,000 as dividend income. Losing the deduction at the corporate level creates double taxation of the $200,000; it does not give Max an exclusion.

q: Ana owns all the stock of a calendar-year S corporation, and her stock basis is $25,000. On March 1, 2025, she transfers land to the corporation in exchange for additional shares in a transaction that qualifies under section 351. The land has an adjusted basis of $70,000 and a fair market value of $120,000 and is subject to a $30,000 mortgage that Ana took out in 2019 to buy it; the corporation assumes the mortgage. Immediately after the transfer, what is Ana's basis in all her stock, and what is the corporation's basis in the land?
choices: Stock basis $65,000; land basis $70,000
Stock basis $95,000; land basis $70,000
Stock basis $65,000 plus $30,000 of debt basis; land basis $70,000
Stock basis $115,000; land basis $120,000
explain: The assumed mortgage is less than the land's basis, so Ana recognizes no gain, but it is treated as money received and reduces the basis of her new shares to $70,000 - $30,000 = $40,000, for total stock basis of $25,000 + $40,000 = $65,000. The corporation takes Ana's $70,000 carryover basis in the land. Unlike a partner, an S corporation shareholder gets no basis for corporate liabilities, even one she transferred, so the $30,000 does not create debt basis.

q: Bo is the sole shareholder of a calendar-year corporation that has been an S corporation since it was formed in 2015 and has no accumulated earnings and profits. His stock basis on January 1, 2025, is $50,000, and he has no debt basis. On July 1, 2025, the corporation distributes to Bo investment land it has held for six years, with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $60,000. The corporation has no other items for 2025. Which statement is correct?
choices: A $40,000 long-term capital gain passes through to Bo; his stock basis at year end is $30,000, and his basis in the land is $60,000.
No gain is recognized; Bo's stock basis at year end is $30,000, and his basis in the land is $20,000.
A $40,000 long-term capital gain passes through to Bo, and he also recognizes a $10,000 gain on the distribution; his stock basis is $0, and his basis in the land is $60,000.
A $40,000 long-term capital gain passes through to Bo; his stock basis at year end is $70,000, and his basis in the land is $60,000.
explain: An S corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property as if it sold the land, and the $40,000 ($60,000 - $20,000) passes through to Bo, raising his stock basis to $90,000. The income adjustment is made before the distribution, so the $60,000 distribution reduces basis to $30,000 with no gain, and Bo's basis in the land is its $60,000 fair market value. Applying the distribution before the gain would wrongly create a $10,000 gain, and the no-gain answer applies partnership distribution rules.

q: In 2023 Lee lent $40,000 to his calendar-year S corporation in exchange for a written note. By December 31, 2024, flow-through losses had reduced his stock basis to $0 and his basis in the note to $15,000, and he has no suspended losses. For 2025 his share of the corporation's items is $20,000 of ordinary business income and $2,000 of noncapital, nondeductible expenses. The corporation makes no distributions and no loan repayments in 2025. What are Lee's stock basis and debt basis on December 31, 2025?
choices: Stock basis $0; debt basis $33,000
Stock basis $18,000; debt basis $15,000
Stock basis $0; debt basis $35,000
Stock basis $20,000; debt basis $13,000
explain: When debt basis was reduced in an earlier year, a later year's net increase restores debt basis before any of it goes to stock basis. The net increase is the $20,000 of income minus the $2,000 of nondeductible expenses, or $18,000, so debt basis rises from $15,000 to $33,000, which is still below the $40,000 note, and stock basis stays at $0. Adding the income to stock basis first is the most common error, and restoring $20,000 ignores that the nondeductible expenses reduce the net increase.
source: IRC 1367(a), 1367(b)(2)(B); Treas. Reg. 1.1367-2(c)(1); Instructions for Form 7203 (Rev. December 2022)

q: On January 1, 2025, Kai's stock basis in his calendar-year S corporation is $30,000, and his basis in a $10,000 note for money he lent the corporation in 2024 is $10,000. For 2025 his share of the corporation's ordinary business loss is $45,000, and on March 1, 2025, he receives a $12,000 cash distribution. The corporation has no accumulated earnings and profits and no other items. Considering only the basis limitation, which statement is correct?
choices: Kai deducts $28,000 of the loss, $17,000 carries forward, and he recognizes no gain on the distribution.
Kai deducts $40,000 of the loss, $5,000 carries forward, and he recognizes a $12,000 capital gain on the distribution.
Kai deducts $18,000 of the loss, $27,000 carries forward, and he recognizes no gain on the distribution.
Kai deducts $40,000 of the loss, $5,000 carries forward, and he recognizes no gain on the distribution.
explain: Stock basis is reduced by distributions before losses, so the $12,000 distribution is tax free and leaves stock basis of $18,000. The loss then uses the $18,000 of stock basis and the $10,000 of debt basis, so Kai deducts $28,000 and carries $17,000 forward indefinitely. Taking the loss first would allow $40,000 but leave no stock basis for the distribution, creating a $12,000 gain, and debt basis is never reduced by distributions, never by distributions.

q: On May 1, 2025, Cara buys Dan's one-third interest in a partnership for $150,000 cash. The partnership has a section 754 election in effect and no liabilities, and none of its property was contributed by a partner. Its assets are cash (adjusted basis and fair market value $60,000), land held for investment (adjusted basis $120,000, fair market value $270,000) and corporate stock held for investment (adjusted basis $90,000, fair market value $120,000). Cara's share of the partnership's adjusted basis in its property is one-third. What is the section 743(b) basis adjustment, and how is it allocated?
choices: A $60,000 increase, allocated $50,000 to the land and $10,000 to the stock, with respect to Cara only
A $180,000 increase to the partnership's common basis, allocated $150,000 to the land and $30,000 to the stock, shared by all partners
No adjustment; Cara takes over Dan's $90,000 share of the inside basis, and her basis in her interest is $90,000
A $60,000 increase with respect to Cara only, allocated $41,538 to the land and $18,462 to the stock in proportion to their fair market values
explain: Cara's outside basis is her $150,000 cost, and her share of the inside basis is $90,000 (one-third of $270,000), so the section 743(b) increase is $60,000. It is allocated to the land and stock by the gain Cara would be allocated on a hypothetical sale: one-third of $150,000 for the land ($50,000) and one-third of $30,000 for the stock ($10,000). The adjustment belongs to Cara alone and does not change common basis, so stepping up all of the partnership's appreciation ($180,000) is wrong.

q: On August 1, 2025, Eli buys a 25% interest in a partnership from Fay for $300,000 cash. The partnership has never made a section 754 election and has no liabilities. Immediately after the sale, the partnership's property has a total adjusted basis of $1,600,000 and a total fair market value of $1,200,000, and Eli's share of the adjusted basis is 25%. Which statement is correct?
choices: No adjustment is made, because the partnership has no section 754 election in effect
No adjustment is made, because Eli would be allocated a loss of only $100,000 if the partnership sold all its property at fair market value
The partnership must reduce the basis of its property by $100,000 with respect to Eli only
The partnership must reduce the common basis of its property by $400,000 for all partners
