explain: After the documentation completion date, the auditor may add or modify documentation, for example to clarify existing documentation in response to monitoring comments, but must document the specific reasons for the change and when and by whom it was made and reviewed. The auditor may not delete or discard documentation before the end of the retention period, so replacing or backdating the original workpaper is not allowed. Clarifying a conclusion already reached does not call for new procedures or a new report date.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, the auditor identified a significant deficiency in controls over changes to the vendor master file, which management fixed in February 2026 while the audit was in progress. The auditor also found a deficiency in petty cash reconciliations that is not a significant deficiency but merits management's attention. The entity's board of directors is separate from management, and the auditor's report was released on March 13, 2026. Which approach meets the auditor's communication requirements?
choices: Communicate the significant deficiency orally to the board and leave it out of any written communication, because it was fixed before the report date
Communicate both deficiencies in writing to the board before the date of the auditor's report, because communication after the report release date is not permitted
Communicate the significant deficiency in writing only to management, which is responsible for internal control, and state in writing that no other significant deficiencies were identified
Communicate the significant deficiency in writing to the board and to management, and the petty cash deficiency to management in writing or orally, no later than 60 days after March 13, 2026
explain: Significant deficiencies and material weaknesses, including those remediated during the audit, must be communicated in writing to those charged with governance and to management, while other deficiencies that merit management's attention may go to management in writing or orally. These communications must be made no later than 60 days after the report release date; making them by the release date is best practice but not required. The auditor should not issue a written statement that no significant deficiencies were identified.

q: While planning an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ending December 31, 2025, the auditor meets with the entity's audit committee. One member asks for the dates of the surprise cash counts and the list of customer accounts that will be selected for confirmation. Which response is most appropriate?
choices: Provide the dates and the list, because the auditor must share the detailed audit plan with those charged with governance
Give an overview of the planned scope and timing, including the significant risks identified, without disclosing detailed procedures in a way that would make them predictable
Decline to discuss the planned scope and timing at all, because the overall audit strategy and audit plan are solely the auditor's responsibility
Provide the list and let the audit committee approve any changes to the nature and extent of the planned procedures
explain: The auditor must communicate an overview of the planned scope and timing of the audit, including the significant risks identified, but care is needed so as not to compromise the audit, because communicating the nature and timing of detailed procedures may make them too predictable. Refusing any discussion is wrong because the overview is required; the auditor's sole responsibility for the strategy and plan means the committee does not approve procedures, not that scope and timing go unmentioned.

q: A registered public accounting firm audits the financial statements of an issuer, and the issuer's audit committee pre-approved each of the services below. Under the independence rule of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in section 210.2-01 of Title 17 of the Code of Federal Regulations, providing all of the following services to the issuer during the audit and professional engagement period would impair the firm's independence EXCEPT:
choices: Performing reference checks on the two finalists for the issuer's open chief financial officer position
At the issuer's request, interviewing candidates for controller and advising the issuer on each candidate's competence for the role
Performing the issuer's outsourced internal audit work on its internal accounting controls over revenue
Designing and implementing the software system that aggregates the source data underlying the issuer's general ledger
explain: The SEC rule bars human resources services such as reference checks for an executive position, but it permits the firm, at the client's request, to interview candidates and advise on their competence for financial accounting, administrative or control positions, which includes a controller. Outsourced internal audit work on internal accounting controls and designing a system that aggregates source data for the financial statements are prohibited, because their results will be subject to audit procedures. Audit committee pre-approval does not make a prohibited service permissible; it is an added requirement for services that are allowed.

q: Tanya Ruiz, an audit manager at a registered public accounting firm, spent more than 40 hours from April through June 2025 on the firm's audit engagement team for an issuer with a calendar fiscal year, reviewing its interim financial information for the quarter ended March 31, 2025. She left the firm on June 30, 2025, and has no capital balance or financial arrangement with it. The issuer filed its 2025 annual report with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on March 2, 2026, and hired Tanya as its controller on September 1, 2026. Under the SEC independence rule for an audit of an issuer, which statement about the firm's audit of the issuer's 2026 financial statements is correct?
choices: The firm is independent, because more than one year passed between Tanya leaving the firm and starting work as the issuer's controller
The firm is not independent, because Tanya was on the audit engagement team during the year before audit procedures for 2026 began on March 3, 2026
The firm is independent, provided Tanya does not take part in or influence any audit of a period during which she was employed by the firm
The firm is independent if the audit committee knows of her prior role, because a controller holds an accounting role, not a financial reporting oversight role
explain: Audit procedures for 2026 are deemed to begin the day after the 2025 annual report is filed, March 3, 2026, so the look-back year runs from March 3, 2025 to March 2, 2026. Tanya worked on the engagement team inside that year, and the SEC rule names a controller as a financial reporting oversight role, so the firm is not independent for the 2026 audit. The 14 months between her leaving the firm and her hire date are not the test, because the year is measured back from the date audit procedures began for the fiscal period that includes her hire date.

q: Pat Okafor served as the lead partner on a registered public accounting firm's audits of an issuer's financial statements for fiscal years 2021 through 2025. The firm has more than 10 partners and more than five audit clients that are issuers. Under the partner rotation rule of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for an audit of an issuer, Pat
choices: may not serve as lead partner or as engagement quality reviewer on that issuer's audits for fiscal years 2026 through 2030
may serve as engagement quality reviewer on that issuer's 2026 audit, because the five-year limit applies to each role separately
may return as lead partner on that issuer's audit for fiscal year 2028, after the required two-year time-out period
may continue as lead partner for fiscal years 2026 and 2027 if the issuer's audit committee approves the extension
explain: Under the SEC rule, the lead partner and the engagement quality reviewer may serve no more than five consecutive years and then may not perform either role, or a combination of them, for the next five consecutive years, so Pat may not return in either role before fiscal year 2031. The two-year time-out applies to other audit partners, who may serve up to seven consecutive years. The audit committee cannot extend the limit; the only exemption is for a firm with fewer than five issuer audit clients and fewer than ten partners whose engagements the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board reviews at least once every three years.

q: A CPA firm is engaged to audit an employee benefit plan's financial statements for the plan's annual report on Form 5500 filed with the Department of Labor (DOL). Under the DOL interpretive bulletin on the independence of an accountant retained by an employee benefit plan, which relationship would cause the DOL not to recognize the firm as independent?
choices: The firm's tax department also prepares the plan sponsor's corporate income tax return each year under a separate engagement
An actuary associated with the firm renders actuarial services to the plan sponsor during the period of the plan audit
A partner of the firm keeps the plan's accounting records, posting contributions, benefit payments and investment income each month
The firm hires a former employee of the plan sponsor who has completely disassociated from it and does not audit any plan period when she worked there
explain: The bulletin states that the DOL will not consider an accountant independent if the accountant or a member of the firm, which includes every partner, maintains financial records for the plan, because the firm would be auditing records it keeps. Being engaged by the plan sponsor for other professional work, such as its tax return, or having an associated actuary serve the plan or sponsor does not by itself impair independence, although the DOL considers all relationships. A former sponsor employee may join the firm if she has completely disassociated from the sponsor and does not audit plan periods covering her employment.

q: Under Statement on Quality Management Standards (SQMS) No. 1, A Firm's System of Quality Management, a firm's system of quality management addresses eight components. All of the following are among those components EXCEPT:
choices: Governance and leadership
Information and communication
Control activities
The monitoring and remediation process
explain: SQMS No. 1 lists eight components: the firm's risk assessment process, governance and leadership, relevant ethical requirements, acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements, engagement performance, resources, information and communication, and the monitoring and remediation process. Control activities is a component of an entity's internal control under the Internal Control Integrated Framework, not of a firm's system of quality management, where the policies and procedures that address quality risks are called responses.

q: A CPA firm designed and implemented its system of quality management under Statement on Quality Management Standards (SQMS) No. 1 by December 15, 2025, and assigned its managing partner ultimate responsibility and accountability for the system. In the first annual evaluation, as of September 30, 2026, the firm finds an identified deficiency in one small regional office: widespread noncompliance with firm policies, caused by local leaders' focus on financial targets. The firm judges the deficiency severe but not pervasive, and remediation is not yet complete. Which statement is correct?
choices: The managing partner should conclude that the system provides reasonable assurance except for matters related to the deficiency, and the firm should act promptly
The managing partner should conclude that the system does not provide reasonable assurance, because any severe deficiency not yet remediated requires that conclusion
The partner with operational responsibility for monitoring and remediation should make the conclusion, which may be unmodified once a remediation plan is approved
The firm should postpone the evaluation until the regional office's remediation is complete, provided it is finished before December 15, 2027
explain: At least annually, the individual assigned ultimate responsibility and accountability evaluates the system as of a point in time and reaches one of three conclusions; a deficiency that is severe but not pervasive, such as one confined to a small office, leads to the "except for" conclusion, and the firm must then take prompt action and communicate to engagement teams and, under its policies, to external parties. The conclusion that the system does not provide reasonable assurance is for deficiencies that are severe and pervasive. The evaluation cannot be handed to the operational monitoring role or deferred, and the first one was due within one year after December 15, 2025.

q: A CPA firm has three partners. For its audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ending December 31, 2026, the firm's policies require an engagement quality review (EQR) because the firm assessed a quality risk from substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern. Partner A is the 2026 engagement partner, and Partner B is on the 2026 engagement team. Partner C was the engagement partner on the 2025 audit and has no role in 2026. Under Statements on Quality Management Standards (SQMS) No. 1 and No. 2, which statement is correct?
choices: No EQR is needed, because SQMS No. 1 requires one only for audits of issuers and for engagements on which law or regulation requires one
Partner B may serve as the EQR, provided that Partner B does not sign the auditor's report or supervise the other staff assigned to the audit
Partner C may not serve as the EQR until two years have passed, which is the cooling-off period SQMS No. 2 sets for a former engagement partner
The firm may appoint Partner C if its policies on the threat to objectivity from C's 2025 role are met, or may appoint an eligible outside individual
explain: SQMS No. 1 requires an EQR both where law or regulation requires one and where the firm decides an EQR is an appropriate response to a quality risk, so this audit needs one, and the reviewer may be a partner, another individual in the firm, or an external individual, but not a member of the engagement team, which rules out Partner B. SQMS No. 2 does not set a fixed cooling-off period; it requires the firm's policies to address the threat to objectivity, mainly self-review, when a former engagement partner becomes the reviewer, and a firm may choose a cooling-off period that fits the facts.

q: A CPA firm requires an engagement quality review for its audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ending December 31, 2026. Under Statement on Quality Management Standards (SQMS) No. 2, Engagement Quality Reviews, the engagement quality reviewer should do all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Discuss with the engagement partner the significant matters and significant judgments made in planning, performing and reporting on the audit
Evaluate the basis for the engagement partner's determination that relevant ethical requirements relating to independence have been fulfilled
Obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence of the reviewer's own to support the opinion to be expressed on the financial statements
Evaluate the basis for the engagement partner's determination that the partner's involvement was sufficient and appropriate throughout the audit
explain: An engagement quality review is an objective evaluation of the significant judgments the engagement team made and the conclusions reached, so the reviewer discusses those judgments with the engagement partner and evaluates the basis for the partner's conclusions on independence and on the sufficiency of the partner's own involvement. The reviewer is not a member of the engagement team and is not required to obtain evidence to support the opinion, although the team may obtain more evidence in response to matters the reviewer raises.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ending December 31, 2026, the firm requires an engagement quality review. On March 10, 2027, the engagement partner believes sufficient appropriate audit evidence has been obtained, but the engagement quality reviewer still disagrees with the team's conclusion on the valuation of a significant investment and has not notified the partner that the review is complete. The client wants the report that day. Under generally accepted auditing standards, the engagement partner should
choices: date and release the auditor's report, because the engagement partner, not the reviewer, has overall responsibility for the audit and the reviewer's concerns are only advisory
follow the firm's policies to resolve the difference of opinion, and neither date the report until it is resolved nor release it until the review is complete
date and release the auditor's report on March 10 and document the reviewer's disagreement in the audit file
release the report on March 10 if the firm's managing partner approves, because the managing partner holds ultimate responsibility for quality
explain: Under AU-C section 220, a difference of opinion between the engagement team and the engagement quality reviewer is resolved under the firm's policies, the engagement partner may not date the auditor's report until it is resolved, and the partner may not release the report until the engagement quality review is complete. The partner does keep overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the audit, but that does not allow the partner to override an incomplete review, and releasing the report while documenting the disagreement breaks the rule on release. The bar on dating the report before the difference is resolved was added by Statement on Auditing Standards No. 146 (AU-C 220.38(c)).

q: An issuer is neither a large accelerated filer nor an accelerated filer, as the Securities and Exchange Commission defines those terms in Rule 12b-2, and is not an emerging growth company. Under sections 302 and 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which statement about the issuer's annual report for 2026 is correct?
choices: Because section 404(c) exempts smaller issuers from section 404, the annual report need not include management's internal control report
The annual report must include management's assessment of its internal control over financial reporting, but the auditor need not attest to it
The auditor must attest to and report on management's internal control assessment in an engagement separate from the financial statement audit
The principal executive and financial officers need not certify the annual report, because the certification applies only to accelerated filers
explain: Section 404(a) requires every annual report to include management's internal control report with an assessment as of fiscal year end, and section 404(c) exempts an issuer that is neither a large accelerated filer nor an accelerated filer only from section 404(b), the auditor's attestation. Section 302 certification by the principal executive and financial officers applies to every annual and quarterly report, whatever the filer status. When an attestation is required, section 404(b) says it may not be the subject of a separate engagement.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, the auditor was engaged in February 2026 and could not observe the December 31, 2025 physical inventory count. Inventory is $600,000 of total assets of $9,000,000, and materiality for the financial statements as a whole is $150,000. Alternative procedures did not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the quantities. The auditor concludes that the possible effects of undetected misstatements are material but confined to inventory and cost of sales and are not a substantial proportion of the financial statements. All other areas are satisfactory. Which opinion and wording should the auditor use?
choices: An adverse opinion, because the auditor cannot conclude that inventory is fairly stated
A qualified opinion stating that, except for the possible effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the financial statements present fairly
A qualified opinion stating that, except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the financial statements present fairly
A disclaimer of opinion, because the auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about a material account
explain: An inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence whose possible effects are material but not pervasive calls for a qualified opinion, and because the problem is missing evidence rather than a known misstatement, the opinion says "except for the possible effects" and the Basis for Qualified Opinion section gives the reasons. "Except for the effects" is the wording for a material misstatement the auditor has found. A disclaimer is for possible effects that are both material and pervasive, and an adverse opinion is for actual misstatements that are material and pervasive.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, management recognizes revenue on all of its long-term construction contracts when each contract is signed, which is not in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. Management refuses to correct the resulting misstatements, which affect revenue, receivables, contract liabilities, income taxes and equity, and the auditor concludes they are material and pervasive. Management asks that the report also include an unmodified opinion on cash and on property and equipment, where the auditor found no misstatements. Which report is appropriate?
choices: A qualified opinion, with the effects of the revenue misstatements quantified in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
A disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole, with an unmodified opinion on cash and on property and equipment
An adverse opinion on the financial statements as a whole, with an unmodified opinion on cash and on property and equipment
An adverse opinion on the financial statements as a whole, with no separate opinion on cash or on property and equipment
explain: Misstatements that are both material and pervasive require an adverse opinion, with the matter described and its effects quantified unless that is impracticable in the Basis for Adverse Opinion section. When the opinion on the financial statements as a whole is adverse or a disclaimer, the report may not also give an unmodified opinion on specific accounts or items (a piecemeal opinion), because that would contradict the overall opinion. A disclaimer is for an inability to obtain evidence, not for misstatements the auditor has found, and a qualified opinion understates a pervasive misstatement.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, which are presented comparatively with the 2024 financial statements, the auditor considers four matters for additional paragraphs in the report. Which matter belongs in an other-matter paragraph rather than an emphasis-of-matter paragraph?
choices: The 2024 financial statements were audited by a predecessor auditor, whose report on them is not reissued
A fire in November 2025 destroyed the entity's main plant, and the loss is fully disclosed in the notes
The outcome of unusually important litigation against the entity, disclosed in the notes, is uncertain
Significant transactions with related parties during 2025 are appropriately disclosed in the notes
explain: An other-matter paragraph covers a matter not presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report, and when a predecessor's report is not reissued the auditor must use one to say that a predecessor audited the prior period, the type of opinion it expressed and the date of its report. The other three matters are appropriately disclosed in the financial statements, so if the auditor judges one fundamental to users' understanding, it goes in an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that refers to the note and states that the opinion is not modified.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, management refuses to give the auditor access to the accounting records of its largest operating division and will not remove the limitation. The auditor informs those charged with governance, finds no alternative procedures, and concludes that the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive. Withdrawal is not practicable, so the auditor disclaims an opinion. The auditor's report should include all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A statement that the auditor was engaged to audit the financial statements, in place of a statement that they were audited
A Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section that describes the reasons for the inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
A statement that the auditor believes the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for the auditor's opinion
A statement that the auditor is required to be independent of the entity and to meet the auditor's other ethical responsibilities
explain: In a disclaimer, the report states that the auditor was engaged to audit the statements, explains the reasons for the inability in the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section, and keeps the statement about independence and ethical responsibilities in the shortened description of the auditor's responsibilities. It leaves out the statement that the evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate, because a disclaimer means it is not. The report also omits any Key Audit Matters or Other Information section.

q: In an integrated audit of a nonissuer, the auditor audits the financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of that date. The auditor identifies a material weakness in the review of the allowance for credit losses, which management describes in its report. Management records the auditor's proposed adjustment, and the auditor concludes that the financial statements are presented fairly in all material respects. The scope of the audit was not limited, and the auditor issues separate reports. Which is appropriate?
choices: A qualified opinion on ICFR, stating that except for the material weakness ICFR is effective, and an unmodified opinion on the financial statements
An adverse opinion on ICFR that states whether the opinion on the financial statements was affected, an unmodified opinion on the financial statements, and both reports dated the same day
An adverse opinion on ICFR and a qualified opinion on the financial statements, because a material weakness always requires a modified opinion on the financial statements
An adverse opinion on ICFR dated when management's report is finalized, and an unmodified opinion on the financial statements dated earlier, when the audit evidence was complete
explain: When one or more material weaknesses exist as of the date of management's assessment and the scope is not limited, the auditor must express an adverse opinion on ICFR, not a qualified one. The auditor determines the effect on the financial statement opinion, which stays unmodified here because the misstatement was corrected, and the ICFR report states in a separate paragraph whether that opinion was affected. Because the two audits are integrated, separate reports must carry the same date.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's comparative financial statements for 2025 and 2024, each of the following has a material effect on comparability and is properly accounted for and disclosed. Each requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph in the auditor's report EXCEPT:
choices: A voluntary change in 2025 from the first-in, first-out method to the weighted-average method of inventory, which the entity has justified as preferable
A restatement of the 2024 financial statements to correct a material misstatement in the previously issued 2024 financial statements
Presentation of consolidated financial statements in 2025 in place of the separate parent-only financial statements presented before
A change in the reporting entity that results from the entity's purchase of a new subsidiary during 2025
explain: A material change in accounting principle that meets the standard's criteria, an adjustment to correct a material misstatement in previously issued financial statements, and a change in reporting entity that does not result from a transaction or event, such as presenting consolidated statements in place of individual ones, each require an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that refers to the entity's disclosure. A change in reporting entity that results from a transaction or event, such as buying a subsidiary, does not require recognition in the auditor's report.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, management has acknowledged in writing that its annual report consists of the financial statements, the auditor's report, a president's letter and a page of operating highlights, and the auditor obtains the final version of all of it before the report date of March 10, 2026. The operating highlights say revenue grew 12% in 2025, while the audited financial statements, which are fairly presented, show growth of 4%. The auditor concludes this is a material misstatement of the other information, and management and those charged with governance refuse to correct it. If the auditor issues the report, it should include:
choices: A qualified opinion on the financial statements, with the misstated growth figure described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
An emphasis-of-matter paragraph drawing users' attention to the difference between the operating highlights and the financial statements
An Other Information section stating that an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information exists and describing it
No reference to the matter, because the auditor's opinion does not cover the other information and gives no assurance on it
explain: When the auditor concludes that an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information exists, the Other Information section must say so and describe it; the alternatives are to withhold the report or withdraw. The financial statements themselves are not misstated, so there is no basis for a qualified opinion, and an emphasis-of-matter paragraph may refer only to matters presented or disclosed in the financial statements. The opinion does not cover the other information, but that does not remove the duty to report the uncorrected misstatement.

q: An auditor who performed the audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, is engaged to review the nonissuer's interim financial information for the quarter ended March 31, 2026. At the end of the review, management refuses to provide a written representation that all transactions have been recorded and are reflected in the interim financial information. What should the auditor do?
choices: Withdraw from the engagement to review the interim financial information
Issue the review report with a modified conclusion that describes management's refusal
Issue a review report stating that the auditor does not express a conclusion on the interim financial information
Issue the standard review report, because the auditor is not required to corroborate management's responses
explain: The representation that all transactions have been recorded is one of those whose absence requires the auditor to withdraw from the review of interim financial information, so no review report is issued. The auditor need not corroborate management's responses to inquiries, but that does not excuse a missing written representation. Modifying the review report is the response to a departure from the applicable financial reporting framework, not to a refusal to provide representations.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, the auditor is also engaged to report on whether consolidating schedules, presented as supplementary information with the financial statements, are fairly stated in relation to the financial statements as a whole. Because of a management-imposed scope limitation whose possible effects are material and pervasive, the auditor disclaims an opinion on the financial statements. The schedules were reconciled to the underlying records without exception. If the auditor does not withdraw from the engagement to report on the schedules, the report on them should:
choices: State that the schedules are fairly stated, in all material respects, in relation to the financial statements as a whole, because they agree with the records
State that, because of the significance of the matter disclosed in the auditor's report, it is inappropriate to, and the auditor does not, express an opinion on the schedules
State an opinion on the schedules based on a materiality level set for the schedules themselves rather than for the financial statements as a whole
State that, except for the effects of the matter described in the auditor's report, the schedules are fairly stated in relation to the financial statements as a whole
explain: An opinion on supplementary information in relation to the financial statements as a whole requires an audit report on those statements that contains neither an adverse opinion nor a disclaimer. With a disclaimer, the auditor is precluded from opining on the schedules and, if not withdrawing, states that it is inappropriate to, and the auditor does not, express an opinion on them. The "except for" wording applies only when the financial statement opinion is qualified, and procedures on supplementary information use the same materiality as the financial statement audit.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer, a partnership, the financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, are prepared on the basis of accounting the partnership uses for income tax purposes, and under its partnership agreement management has no choice of financial reporting framework. The auditor concludes that the financial statements are presented fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with that basis, which differs from accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (GAAP). Which does the auditor's report require?
choices: An other-matter paragraph restricting use of the report to the partners and the taxing authorities, which is required for every special purpose framework
A qualified opinion, because the financial statements depart from GAAP
An emphasis-of-matter paragraph stating that the financial statements are prepared on the income tax basis, a basis of accounting other than GAAP, with a reference to the note that describes it
An opinion on fair presentation in accordance with GAAP, plus a separate opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared in accordance with the income tax basis
explain: Except for regulatory basis statements intended for general use, a report on special purpose financial statements must include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that states the framework used, refers to the note describing it and says it is a basis other than GAAP, and the opinion is on fair presentation in accordance with the tax basis. An other-matter paragraph restricting use is required for contractual and regulatory bases (other than a regulatory basis intended for general use) and for an other basis when AU-C 905 requires it, but for the tax basis it is optional. The dual opinion on GAAP and on the framework is only for regulatory basis statements intended for general use.

q: Harbor Fund, a nonissuer investment partnership, engages a practitioner to perform an assertion-based examination engagement on a schedule of investment performance statistics for the year ended December 31, 2026. Delta Advisors, the fund's outside investment manager, prepares the schedule and is the responsible party; Harbor Fund is the engaging party. Delta Advisors states orally that the schedule is presented in accordance with the criteria and answers the practitioner's inquiries, but it refuses to provide a written assertion. If the practitioner can otherwise obtain sufficient appropriate evidence, what should the practitioner do?
choices: Withdraw from the engagement, because an examination cannot be completed without a written assertion from the responsible party
Report directly on the schedule, disclose Delta Advisors' refusal to provide a written assertion in the report, and restrict the use of the report to Harbor Fund
Express an opinion on Delta Advisors' oral assertion and add an alert restricting the use of the report to Harbor Fund and Delta Advisors
Disclaim an opinion, because the missing written assertion is a scope limitation whose possible effects are pervasive
explain: When the engaging party is not the responsible party, the practitioner need not withdraw if the responsible party refuses a written assertion: the practitioner may report on the subject matter but must disclose the refusal and restrict use of the report to the engaging party. Withdrawal is the required response only when the engaging party is itself the responsible party and refuses. A report on an assertion needs a written assertion, so the practitioner reports on the schedule itself, not on the oral statement.

q: A practitioner performs a review engagement under the attestation standards on a nonissuer's written assertion that its schedule of greenhouse gas emissions for the year ended December 31, 2026, is presented in accordance with stated criteria. The practitioner finds that the schedule omits emissions from two of the entity's three plants, and management will not revise it. Management's written assertion acknowledges the omission. The practitioner concludes that the misstatement is both material and pervasive. How should the practitioner report?
choices: Express a qualified conclusion on management's assertion, because the assertion itself discloses the omission
Express an unmodified conclusion on management's assertion, because the assertion acknowledges the omission, and add a paragraph emphasizing it
Express an adverse conclusion directly on the schedule, not on the assertion, with a separate paragraph describing the omission
Disclaim a conclusion, because limited assurance cannot support a finding that the schedule is materially misstated
explain: In a review engagement, a material and pervasive misstatement calls for an adverse conclusion, and the practitioner must express it directly on the subject matter, not on the assertion, even when the assertion acknowledges the misstatement. The report adds a separate paragraph describing the matter and, if practicable, its effects. Reporting on an assertion that admits the omission would let a fairly stated assertion hide a misstated schedule, which the standard does not allow.

q: A practitioner is performing a review engagement under the attestation standards on a nonissuer's schedule of royalties payable to a licensor for the year ended December 31, 2026. Management will not allow the practitioner to make inquiries of the sales staff or to apply analytical procedures to the underlying sales data, and the practitioner cannot obtain sufficient appropriate review evidence any other way. Law and regulation do not prevent withdrawal. What should the practitioner do?
choices: Disclaim a conclusion and state that the scope of the work was not sufficient to express a conclusion
Express a qualified conclusion and describe the procedures that could not be performed
Issue the review report with an alert restricting its use to management
Withdraw from the engagement
explain: In a review engagement under the attestation standards, an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate review evidence is a scope limitation, and the practitioner should withdraw when law and regulation allow it. A disclaimer is the response to a pervasive scope limitation in an examination engagement, not in a review, so the most tempting choice applies the examination rule to the wrong engagement.

q: A bank engages a practitioner to perform an agreed-upon procedures engagement on a borrower's schedule of trade accounts receivable as of September 30, 2026. The borrower is a nonissuer and is the responsible party. In the written agreement, the bank tells the practitioner not to report differences of $500 or less. Which of the following should the practitioner's agreed-upon procedures report include?
choices: A statement that nothing came to the practitioner's attention indicating that the schedule is not fairly stated, in all material respects
A description of the $500 threshold for reporting exceptions, along with the findings from each procedure, including details of the exceptions above it
A statement that the practitioner applied a $500 materiality threshold that the practitioner set based on the total of the schedule
An opinion on the existence of the receivables, limited to the customer accounts the practitioner selected
explain: The practitioner reports all findings, and when the engaging party has set a threshold for reporting exceptions, the report must describe it. A threshold applies only if the engaging party establishes it, so the practitioner does not set one. A report of procedures and findings gives no opinion or conclusion, and the standard names "nothing came to our attention" wording as language that should not be used to report findings.

q: An accountant is engaged to prepare a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, in a preparation engagement. The entity's bank requires the statements to be submitted on the bank's own template, so the accountant cannot include a statement on each page that no assurance is provided. Each of the following is an acceptable response EXCEPT:
choices: Issue a disclaimer that makes clear that no assurance is provided on the financial statements
Perform a compilation engagement on the financial statements instead
Withdraw from the engagement and tell management the reasons for withdrawing
Release the financial statements without any statement or disclaimer, because a preparation engagement does not require a report
explain: In a preparation engagement the accountant must put a statement on each page that, at a minimum, says no assurance is provided. If that is not possible, the accountant must issue a disclaimer making clear that no assurance is provided, perform a compilation engagement instead, or withdraw and tell management why. It is true that a preparation engagement needs no report, but the statements still cannot go out with nothing indicating that no assurance is provided.

q: An accountant performs a compilation engagement on a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (GAAP). Management has chosen not to recognize several leases that GAAP requires it to recognize, and will not revise the statements. The departure is material. Management has not determined its effects, and they are not readily known to the accountant from the compilation procedures. The accountant concludes that modifying the report is adequate to disclose the departure. What should the compilation report do?
choices: State in a separate paragraph that, because of the departure, the financial statements are not in accordance with GAAP
Disclose the departure in a separate paragraph and state that management has not determined its effects on the financial statements
Disclose the departure and quantify its effects, which the accountant must determine with additional procedures
Include a qualified conclusion, with a basis paragraph that describes the departure
explain: When modifying the compilation report is adequate, the accountant discloses the known departure in a separate paragraph and discloses its effects only if management has determined them or they are readily known; otherwise the accountant need not determine them but must state that management has not determined them. The report must not state that the financial statements are not in conformity with the framework. A compilation gives no assurance, so it never contains a qualified conclusion; that wording belongs to a review report.

q: Midway through a review engagement on a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, an accountant learns that a member of the engagement team holds a direct financial interest in the entity, which impairs the firm's independence. The entity still needs a report from the firm on those financial statements. Which response complies with the Statements on Standards for Accounting and Review Services?
choices: Complete the review and add a final paragraph to the review report stating that the firm is not independent
Complete the review and describe every reason for the impairment in the review report, which allows a review conclusion to be issued
Withdraw from the review engagement; the firm may instead perform a compilation engagement and state its lack of independence in the final paragraph of the compilation report
Withdraw from the review engagement and decline any other engagement on those financial statements, because a compilation engagement also requires independence
explain: An accountant must be independent to perform a review, so the accountant who finds independence impaired during the review should withdraw from it, and nothing prohibits a compilation of the same statements instead. A compilation report may be issued without independence if it states the lack of independence in a final paragraph; if the accountant chooses to describe the reasons, all of them must be included. Disclosing the impairment is the compilation rule, and it does not rescue a review report.

q: In a review engagement on a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (GAAP), the accountant finds that inventory is overstated by $180,000 because obsolete items were not written down. Management will not adjust. The accountant judges the misstatement material but not pervasive, and the amount is known. How should the accountant's review report address the matter?
choices: An unmodified conclusion, followed by a separate paragraph disclosing the overstatement as a known departure from GAAP
An adverse conclusion stating that the financial statements are not in accordance with GAAP, because any uncorrected departure requires one in a review
A qualified opinion stating that, except for the overstatement, the financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with GAAP

A Qualified Conclusion section stating that, except for the effects of the matter described, the accountant is not aware of any material modifications needed, preceded by a Basis for Qualified Conclusion paragraph that describes the overstatement and quantifies it at $180,000
explain: A material but not pervasive misstatement in a review calls for a qualified conclusion under a Qualified Conclusion heading, with a basis paragraph immediately before it that describes the misstatement and quantifies its effects when they are known. An adverse conclusion is reserved for misstatements that are both material and pervasive. A review gives limited assurance, so the report never expresses an opinion that the statements present fairly; that is audit language.

q: An auditor audits the financial statements of Pell Co., a nonissuer, for the year ended December 31, 2025, in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards (GAAS). The audit is not also performed under Government Auditing Standards. The auditor expresses an adverse opinion because Pell Co. did not consolidate a material subsidiary. Pell Co.'s loan agreement asks the auditor for a report on compliance with the agreement's financial covenants, insofar as they relate to accounting matters. The auditor identified no instances of noncompliance. What should the auditor do?
choices: Issue a report on compliance stating that nothing came to the auditor's attention indicating noncompliance, together with a statement describing the adverse opinion
Express an opinion on compliance with the covenants, because the covenants relate to accounting matters subjected to the audit procedures
Not issue a report on compliance, because after an adverse opinion such a report is issued only when instances of noncompliance are identified
Issue a report on compliance with an alert restricting its use, since the alert removes the need to consider the opinion on the financial statements
explain: Negative assurance on compliance in connection with an audit is permitted only when the auditor found no noncompliance and expressed an unmodified or qualified opinion on the related financial statements. After an adverse opinion or a disclaimer, the auditor issues a report on compliance only to describe identified noncompliance, so with none identified no report is issued. Describing the adverse opinion does not help, because the negative assurance itself is not permitted after an adverse opinion, and an audit never yields an opinion on covenant compliance.

q: Rivera Health, a nonissuer that receives a state grant, asks a practitioner for an attestation engagement on its compliance with the grant's requirements for the year ending December 31, 2026. Management accepts responsibility for compliance and for internal control over compliance, and it evaluates its compliance. The practitioner may accept each of the following engagements EXCEPT:
choices: An examination of Rivera Health's compliance with the specified grant requirements
An agreed-upon procedures engagement related to Rivera Health's compliance with the specified grant requirements
An agreed-upon procedures engagement related to Rivera Health's internal control over compliance with the grant requirements
A review engagement that gives limited assurance on Rivera Health's compliance with the specified grant requirements
explain: The compliance attestation standard covers examinations of compliance and agreed-upon procedures engagements on compliance or on internal control over compliance. The review standard says a practitioner should not perform a review of compliance with specified laws, regulations, rules, contracts or grants, so limited assurance is not available for this subject matter. An agreed-upon procedures engagement on internal control over compliance is allowed and gives findings rather than assurance.

q: A CPA firm audits the financial statements of Calder Tool Co., a nonissuer and an attest client. The lead engagement partner on the audit primarily practices in the firm's Denver office. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, each of the following individuals is a covered member with respect to Calder EXCEPT
choices: a tax manager in the firm's Chicago office who provided 14 hours of tax planning services to Calder during Calder's current fiscal year
an audit partner in the Denver office who has never worked on any engagement for Calder
a staff accountant in the Denver office who has never worked on any engagement for Calder
the firm's managing partner in Chicago, who directly supervises the partner who oversees the lead engagement partner
explain: Covered members include partners and partner equivalents in the office where the lead engagement partner primarily practices, but not staff in that office who have no role on the engagement. The tax manager is covered because a partner, partner equivalent or manager who provides 10 or more hours of nonattest services to the attest client in a fiscal year is a covered member. The managing partner is covered as an individual in a position to influence the attest engagement, which includes every successively senior level above the engagement partner through the firm's chief executive.

q: A CPA firm has audited the annual financial statements of Brightwater Supply, a nonissuer and an attest client, for six years, and neither the firm nor Brightwater has given notice of ending the relationship. Ana Kim is the lead engagement partner each year. The firm issued its report on the 2025 financial statements on March 12, 2026. Kim's spouse bought 100 shares of Brightwater stock on April 6, 2026, and sold them on June 22, 2026. The engagement letter for the 2026 audit was signed on August 3, 2026. The shares were immaterial to Kim and her spouse. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, what is the effect on the firm's independence for the 2026 audit?
choices: Independence is impaired, because the period of the professional engagement continued after the 2025 report was issued
Independence is not impaired, because the period of the professional engagement ended on March 12, 2026, and began again when the 2026 engagement letter was signed
Independence is not impaired, because the shares were immaterial and were sold before the 2026 engagement letter was signed
Independence is not impaired, because shares owned by a spouse are an indirect financial interest of the covered member and were immaterial
explain: The period of the professional engagement lasts for the entire professional relationship and ends only on notice of termination or issuance of a report, whichever is later, so it does not stop when one year's report is issued and restart with the next year's engagement letter. A covered member's immediate family must comply with the Independence Rule, and any direct financial interest, even an immaterial one, held during that period impairs independence. Shares the spouse owns outright are a direct financial interest, so materiality and the early sale do not help.

q: Maya Chen, a senior on the engagement team for the audit of Ostrow Instruments, a nonissuer and an attest client, owns shares of a nondiversified mutual fund worth $500,000. The fund has net assets of $25 million, so Chen owns 2 percent of its outstanding shares, and 8 percent of the fund's assets are invested in Ostrow common stock. Chen does not control the fund or take part in its investment decisions. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, how should Chen evaluate her interest in Ostrow?
choices: Because she owns 5 percent or less of the fund's outstanding shares, the fund's underlying investments are immaterial indirect financial interests and no further evaluation is needed
Her $40,000 indirect financial interest in Ostrow is compared with her net worth combined with that of her immediate family, and independence is impaired only if it is material
Because the fund holds Ostrow stock, her $500,000 investment in the fund is a direct financial interest in Ostrow that impairs independence whatever its amount
Her $40,000 indirect financial interest in Ostrow is compared with the fund's $25 million of net assets, and independence is impaired only if it is material to the fund
explain: Chen's interest in Ostrow is $500,000 x 8% = $40,000, and because she does not control the fund or direct its investments it is an indirect financial interest, which impairs independence only if material, judged against her net worth combined with her immediate family's. The 5 percent safe harbor applies only to a diversified fund, so for a nondiversified fund she must look through to the underlying holdings. Her fund shares are a direct financial interest in the fund, not in Ostrow.

q: A CPA firm audits the financial statements of Harmon Community Bank, a nonissuer and an attest client that makes loans as part of its normal business. Assume no regulator imposes requirements stricter than the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs. Each loan below is held by a different member of the engagement team, and each was made under the bank's normal lending procedures, terms and requirements. Which loan impairs independence?
choices: A home mortgage obtained in 2019, before Harmon became an attest client in 2023, with payments current and the home's estimated fair value exceeding the balance
An automobile loan obtained in March 2026, while the borrower was on the engagement team, secured by the automobile and with payments current
Two credit cards issued by Harmon with an aggregate outstanding balance of $7,200 on a current basis
A home equity loan obtained in 2020, before Harmon became an attest client, whose maturity date Harmon extended by five years in 2026 at the borrower's request
explain: A grandfathered home mortgage or other secured loan stays permitted only if, after the borrower becomes a covered member, the loan is kept current and its terms do not change in any way the original agreement did not provide for, and a new or extended maturity date is a changed term. Automobile loans secured by the automobile may be obtained at any time under normal lending terms, and consumer loans such as credit cards are permitted when the aggregate balance from the same lending institution is $10,000 or less on a current basis. The 2019 mortgage was obtained before Harmon became an attest client and meets the collateral test.

q: A CPA firm audits the financial statements of Ridgeview Manufacturing, a nonissuer and an attest client. None of the relatives below holds a key position at Ridgeview, and none of the holdings gives the relative significant influence over Ridgeview. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, which situation impairs independence?
choices: A staff auditor on the engagement team knows that her sister owns Ridgeview shares that are material to the sister's net worth

A partner in the office where the lead engagement partner primarily practices, who does not work on the engagement, knows that his brother owns Ridgeview shares that are material to the brother's net worth
A senior on the engagement team has a father who works at Ridgeview as a warehouse supervisor and owns no Ridgeview shares
A manager on the engagement team has an adult, nondependent son who owns Ridgeview shares that are immaterial to the son
explain: A sister is a close relative, and for an individual on the attest engagement team, a close relative's financial interest impairs independence if the individual knows or has reason to believe it is material to the relative or if it gives the relative significant influence. For a partner in the lead engagement partner's office who is not on the team, both conditions must be met, so the brother's material but noninfluential holding does not impair independence. A close relative employed by the attest client outside a key position, or holding an immaterial, noninfluential interest, does not impair independence.

q: A CPA firm audits the financial statements of Linden Dental Group, a nonissuer and an attest client, for the year ending December 31, 2026, and will also prepare Linden's financial statements from its trial balance. Linden's owner accepts responsibility for the financial statements and designates the office manager, who has bookkeeping experience and understands the service well enough to oversee it and evaluate the results but could not prepare the statements herself, to oversee the work. Before the work began, the engagement partner and the owner agreed orally on the objectives, the services, each party's responsibilities and the limitations of the engagement, but the firm never put that understanding in writing. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, which statement is correct?
choices: Independence is impaired, because the individual who oversees a nonattest service must be able to perform or reperform it
Independence is impaired, because the understanding with the attest client was not documented in writing before the service was performed
Independence is not impaired, but the failure to document the understanding in writing violates the Compliance With Standards Rule
Independence is impaired, because preparing an attest client's financial statements is a management responsibility
explain: When the firm established the understanding with the attest client but failed to document it in writing, independence is not impaired, but the missing documentation violates the Compliance With Standards Rule. The individual who oversees the service must have suitable skill, knowledge or experience and understand the service well enough to oversee it, but need not have the expertise to perform or reperform it. Preparing financial statements is a nonattest service the firm may perform under the general requirements; the management responsibility is accepting responsibility for their preparation and presentation, which the owner kept.

q: A CPA firm audits the financial statements of Harbor Components, Inc., a nonissuer and an attest client. Harbor is wholly owned by Lakeline Holdings, which also wholly owns Westfield Logistics. Harbor and Westfield are each material to Lakeline, so Lakeline and Westfield are affiliates of Harbor. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, which of the following impairs independence with respect to Harbor?
choices: The spouse of a covered member is the controller of Westfield, a position with no responsibility for or influence over Harbor's financial statements
A covered member owns a small ownership interest in Lakeline that is immaterial to the covered member's net worth
A covered member has a personal loan from a director of Westfield who has no ability to affect decision-making at Harbor

The firm designs Westfield's financial information system, a service that would impair independence if performed for Harbor, and the system's results will not be subject to audit procedures in the Harbor audit
explain: A member applies the Independence Rule and its interpretations to a financial statement attest client's affiliates, except in situations the Client Affiliates interpretation lists, and a financial interest in an affiliate is not among those exceptions, so even an immaterial direct financial interest in the parent impairs independence. The listed exceptions permit an immediate family member to hold a key position at a sister entity that is not a key position with respect to the attest client, and a loan from a director of an affiliate who cannot affect the attest client's decision-making. A service that would be prohibited for the attest client may be provided to a sister entity when its results will not be subject to audit procedures, with safeguards applied to any remaining threats such as management participation.

q: Dana Ortiz was the accounts payable supervisor of Alder Foods, a nonissuer, until May 31, 2026, and joined a CPA firm as an audit senior on June 15, 2026. The firm audits Alder's calendar-year financial statements. Before joining the firm, Ortiz sold her Alder stock, transferred her vested balance out of Alder's retirement plan and left Alder's health plan, and she has no loans to or from Alder. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, may Ortiz serve on the engagement team for the audit of Alder's financial statements for the year ending December 31, 2026?
choices: Yes, because she disassociated from Alder before becoming a covered member
Yes, provided she is not assigned to audit accounts payable or other areas she worked on
Yes, because an accounts payable supervisor does not hold a key position at Alder
No, because the audit covers a period that includes her employment at Alder
explain: If a covered member participates on the attest engagement, or is in a position to influence it, for any period that includes the member's former employment with the attest client, independence is impaired and safeguards cannot fix it. The 2026 financial statements cover January 1 to May 31, 2026, when Ortiz worked at Alder, so her disassociation from Alder's plans, stock and loans does not cure the problem, and the rule does not depend on whether her former position was a key position. Keeping her away from accounts payable is not a safeguard the interpretation allows.

q: A CPA firm is about to issue its report, dated March 20, 2026, on the financial statements of Garnet Logistics, a nonissuer and an attest client, for the year ended December 31, 2025. Garnet, which is not in bankruptcy, still owes the firm $48,000 for consulting services the firm completed in January 2025, and the amount is significant to the firm. The firm concludes that threats to its independence are not at an acceptable level. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, each of the following could serve as a safeguard EXCEPT
choices: communicating the unpaid fees and the firm's evaluation of them to Garnet's board of directors, with no other action
obtaining partial payment before the report is issued, so that the remaining balance is insignificant to the firm
obtaining Garnet's agreement to a payment schedule before the report is issued
having a reviewer who has not provided attest or nonattest services to Garnet review the attest work before the report is issued
explain: When unpaid fees are significant to the covered member and relate to services provided more than one year before the current-year attest report, threats are not at an acceptable level, and the firm must apply safeguards such as partial payment that leaves an insignificant balance, an agreed payment schedule or an independent review of the attest work, all before the report is issued. Communicating with those charged with governance is not a sufficient safeguard when applied alone, although it may count when combined with another safeguard. Before the revision effective December 31, 2022, any unpaid fees for services more than one year old impaired independence regardless of safeguards; the current interpretation allows safeguards.

q: During planning for the audit of Pellham Outdoor, a nonissuer and an attest client, the engagement partner learns that the audit senior and Pellham's controller have been close friends for years and take vacations together. No independence interpretation addresses this relationship. Under the conceptual framework in the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of CPAs, how should the firm proceed?
choices: Conclude that no independence issue exists, because the Code does not address friendships with client personnel
Identify the familiarity threat, evaluate whether it is at an acceptable level, and if it is not, apply and document safeguards such as reassigning the senior
Treat the friendship as a self-interest threat that no safeguard can reduce, and resign from the engagement
Rely on the controller's written promise not to discuss audit matters with the senior, which reduces the threat to an acceptable level by itself
explain: When no interpretation addresses a relationship, the member applies the conceptual framework: identify threats, evaluate whether a reasonable and informed third party would conclude each is at an acceptable level, and if not, apply safeguards and document the threats and safeguards. A team member's close friendship with someone in a key position at the attest client is the Code's example of a familiarity threat, which safeguards such as removing the senior from the team can address. A safeguard implemented by the attest client cannot be relied on alone to reduce a significant threat.

q: Ana is a CPA in public practice whose firm audits nonissuers and also provides tax and consulting services. Ben is a CPA in business who prepares his employer's financial statements. Under the Objectivity and Independence principle in the Principles of Professional Conduct in the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which statement is correct?
choices: Ana should be independent in fact and appearance when providing auditing and other attestation services, and should maintain objectivity and avoid conflicts of interest when providing all other services
Ana should be independent in fact and appearance in every professional service she provides, including tax and consulting services
Ben should be independent in fact and appearance of his employer when he prepares its financial statements
Only Ana has an obligation to maintain objectivity, because the principle applies only to members in public practice who perform attestation services
explain: The principle requires independence in fact and appearance only for auditing and other attestation services; for all other services a member in public practice should maintain objectivity and avoid conflicts of interest. A member in business such as Ben cannot maintain the appearance of independence from his employer, but he carries the same responsibility for objectivity as a member in public practice, so objectivity is not limited to attest work.

q: Reyes and Lin, CPAs, provides tax and consulting services to the clients described below and performs no audit, review, compilation or other attest services for any of them. Under the Integrity and Objectivity Rule of the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which situation is a violation that no safeguard can cure?
choices: The firm advises two clients that are competing to acquire the same company, after disclosing the conflict to both, obtaining each client's specific consent, and staffing separate engagement teams with restricted access to files
A partner attends a dinner hosted by a client after a business meeting, along with representatives of other clients; the cost is reasonable and breaks no law or policy of the client or the firm

A partner accepts $900 concert tickets from a client's chief financial officer, knowing that the client's written policy bars gifts over $100 to service providers, and reports the gift to the firm's ethics partner, who then reviews the partner's work for that client

A partner advises a client to invest in a business in which the partner's spouse holds an interest, after concluding the threat is at an acceptable level, disclosing the spouse's interest and obtaining the client's specific consent
explain: Accepting a gift that the member knows violates the client's policy puts the threat beyond an acceptable level and the member is presumed to lack integrity; review by an ethics partner is a safeguard, and the Code says no safeguard can fix this. The competing bidders and the spouse's interest are conflicts of interest, which the member may handle by reducing threats to an acceptable level and disclosing the conflict and obtaining consent (required even when threats are already acceptable), and reasonable entertainment tied to business is at an acceptable level.

q: Dana Okoro, CPA, prepares the corporate income tax return of Brightline Inc., a nonissuer for which her firm performs no attest services. Brightline's chief executive officer tells Dana that the company will not award her firm a planned consulting engagement unless she stops disagreeing with management about how a deduction should be reported on the return. Under the Conceptual Framework for Members in Public Practice in the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which statement is correct?
choices: The statement creates a self-interest threat that Dana can reduce to an acceptable level by relying solely on a safeguard implemented by the client, such as review of the return by Brightline's board of directors

The statement creates an undue influence threat; if Dana concludes it is not at an acceptable level and no safeguard can reduce it, she should determine whether to decline or discontinue the service or resign from the engagement
Because a threat now exists, Dana is already in violation of the Integrity and Objectivity Rule, whatever safeguards she applies
The statement creates an advocacy threat, and Dana may use the conceptual framework to justify reporting the deduction the way management wants if she documents the safeguards she applied
explain: The Code lists a client's statement that it will not award additional engagements if the firm keeps disagreeing on an accounting or tax matter as an example of an undue influence threat, and when no safeguard can reduce a threat to an acceptable level the member should decide whether to decline, discontinue or resign. The existence of a threat is not itself a violation, safeguards implemented by the client cannot be relied on alone, and the framework can never be used to overcome the prohibition on subordinating judgment.

q: In an audit of a nonissuer's financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025, prepared under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), management departs from a requirement of the Financial Accounting Standards Board Accounting Standards Codification. Under the Accounting Principles Rule of the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which circumstance could justify the departure as one in which literal application of the principle would make the financial statements misleading?
choices: The departure has an unusually large effect on the financial statements, so applying the principle would dominate the reported results
Other entities in the same industry commonly follow a practice that conflicts with the promulgated principle
The entity's lender has asked management to use a method the lender considers more useful for its credit analysis
New legislation or a new form of business transaction that the promulgated principle did not anticipate
explain: The Code gives new legislation and the evolution of a new form of business transaction as circumstances that may justify a departure from GAAP, and the member then complies with the rule by describing the departure, its approximate effects if practicable, and why compliance would be misleading. It names an unusual degree of materiality and conflicting industry practices as circumstances that do not justify a departure, and a user's preference for another method is not an unusual circumstance.

q: Harbor CPAs prepares individual income tax returns, a nonattest service, for its clients. It plans to engage an outside vendor whose staff use the vendor's artificial intelligence (AI) platform to extract data from clients' tax documents and prepare draft returns, which Harbor's staff will then review. Under the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which approach meets Harbor's obligations before it discloses confidential client information to the vendor?
choices: Inform clients, preferably in writing, that it may use a third-party service provider, and either sign a contract requiring the vendor to keep the information confidential, with reasonable assurance that the vendor has procedures to prevent unauthorized release, or obtain each client's specific consent
Take no client-facing steps, because using a vendor's technology platform is an administrative support service, like software application hosting, that clients need not be told about
Obtain each client's specific written consent, because a confidentiality agreement with the vendor can never satisfy the Confidential Client Information Rule
Tell clients about the vendor after the returns are filed, and rely on the vendor to review its own output, because the vendor is responsible for the quality of the drafts it prepares
explain: Because the vendor assists in providing the professional service, Harbor should tell clients beforehand, preferably in writing, that it may use a third-party service provider, and before disclosing confidential information it should either have a confidentiality contract with reasonable assurance about the vendor's procedures or obtain the client's specific consent. The administrative support exception covers services such as record storage or software hosting, not a vendor whose staff prepare the returns. Harbor also remains subject to the General Standards Rule and the Compliance With Standards Rule, so it must check the vendor's qualifications and plan and supervise its work.

q: A member in public practice audits the financial statements of Elm Street Bakery, a nonissuer, and has not obtained Elm Street's consent to any disclosure. Under the Confidential Client Information Rule of the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), disclosing Elm Street's confidential information in each of the following situations would be permitted EXCEPT:
choices: Producing Elm Street's records in response to a validly issued and enforceable subpoena, without telling Elm Street about the subpoena
Giving the member's professional liability insurance carrier the information needed solely to defend a threatened claim against the member
Responding to an inquiry from the investigative body of the state board of accountancy about the member's work on the engagement
Submitting Elm Street's gross margin and payroll data, which are not publicly available, to an industry benchmarking organization that has promised not to name the bakery
explain: Confidential client information may not be disclosed for a benchmarking study, even when the client will not be named, unless the client gives specific consent, preferably in writing. The rule does not prohibit compliance with an enforceable subpoena, and the member need not notify the client, nor does it prohibit responding to a board of accountancy's investigative inquiry; disclosure to the member's liability carrier to defend a claim is also permitted.

q: A CPA firm has the four arrangements below for the year ending December 31, 2026. Each client is a nonissuer, and the firm discloses every commission and referral fee to the affected client in writing. Under the Contingent Fees Rule and the Commissions and Referral Fees Rule of the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which arrangement is prohibited?
choices: For a tax client for which the firm performs no attest services, a fee that depends on the outcome of the firm's representation of the client in a revenue agent's examination of its federal income tax return

For a client whose 2026 financial statements the firm compiles for use by the client's bank, with a compilation report that discloses the firm's lack of independence, a commission for referring the client to a payroll software vendor
For a client whose 2026 financial statements the firm is engaged to review in a review engagement, a commission from a software vendor for recommending its inventory system to the client
For a new client referred by another CPA firm, a referral fee the firm pays to that firm for the referral
