explain: A member may not receive a commission for recommending a product to a client for which the firm performs an audit or review of financial statements, during the engagement and the period the statements cover, and disclosure does not cure this. A compilation is covered only when a third party is expected to use the statements and the report does not disclose a lack of independence, so the payroll referral is permitted with written disclosure. The Code lists a contingent fee for representing a client in a revenue agent's examination as permitted, and a referral fee paid to obtain a client is allowed once disclosed to the client.

q: Kim Alvarez, CPA, a member in public practice, prepared the 2025 federal income tax return of Lakeside Pottery, a nonattest client. While preparing it she proposed adjusting journal entries that Lakeside had not recorded and that she was not engaged to prepare. The return is complete, but Kim has not released it because Lakeside has not paid her $4,000 fee for that return. On March 2, 2026, Lakeside ends the engagement and asks for the original bank statements and invoices it gave her, the adjusting entries, the completed return and her working papers. No agreement with Lakeside and no state board rule provides otherwise. Under the Records Requests interpretation of the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), what must Kim make available?
choices: The bank statements, invoices and adjusting entries, because member-prepared records may never be withheld for unpaid fees
Only the bank statements and invoices, which she may not withhold for the unpaid fee, no later than 45 days after the request absent extenuating circumstances
Nothing until Lakeside pays the $4,000 fee, because all of the requested records relate to the unpaid engagement
All four items, including the working papers, because a former client is entitled to every record that relates to its engagement
explain: Client-provided records must be made available even when fees are unpaid, as soon as practicable and, absent extenuating circumstances, within 45 days. Member-prepared records such as the adjusting entries are owed only for a completed and issued work product and may be withheld when fees for that work product are due, the return itself may be withheld for its unpaid fee, and working papers are the member's property that she need not provide.

q: Walsh and Ortiz, CPAs, audits the financial statements of several nonissuers and plans to admit non-CPA owners. Under the Form of Organization and Name Rule of the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and the Council resolution it refers to, which ownership plan is permitted?
choices: CPAs hold 60% of both the financial interests and the voting rights; the non-CPA owners, a data analytics director and an information technology consultant who work full time in the firm, use the title "principal" and do not hold themselves out as CPAs
CPAs hold 70% of both the financial interests and the voting rights, and a private equity fund whose personnel do not work in the firm holds the other 30%
CPAs hold 55% of the financial interests but only 45% of the voting rights, and all of the non-CPA owners work full time in the firm
CPAs hold 80% of both the financial interests and the voting rights, and a non-CPA owner who works full time in the firm takes ultimate responsibility for its compilation engagements
explain: A firm that performs audits must have CPAs owning a majority of both the financial interests and the voting rights, every non-CPA owner must be actively engaged in the firm, and non-CPA owners may use titles such as principal but may not hold themselves out as CPAs. Ownership by investors not actively engaged in the firm is prohibited, and a CPA must have ultimate responsibility for the firm's audit, review, compilation and similar engagements.
source: ET 1.800.001.01, 1.800.001.05; ET Appendix B, Council Resolution Concerning the Form of Organization and Name Rule, paragraphs A.1, A.2 and A.3

q: Priya Shah, CPA, is the controller of Carver Tools Inc., a nonissuer, and is not in public practice. Her annual bonus equals 2% of reported operating income, and she is setting the year-end reserve for obsolete inventory, which directly affects that income. Under the Conceptual Framework for Members in Business in the Code of Professional Conduct of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA), which statement is correct?
choices: The bonus creates a management participation threat, which no safeguard can reduce, because Priya makes management decisions for her employer
The bonus creates a self-review threat, and only safeguards applied by Carver's external auditor can reduce it to an acceptable level

The bonus creates a self-interest threat, and safeguards implemented by the employing organization, such as an audit committee charter with independent audit committee members, may help reduce it to an acceptable level
No threat exists, because a member in business cannot be independent of her employer and the Code therefore does not require her to be objective
explain: A performance bonus whose value is directly affected by the member's own decisions is the Code's example of a self-interest threat for members in business, and their safeguards come from the profession, legislation or regulation and from the employing organization, including an audit committee charter with independent members. The management participation threat appears only in the framework for members in public practice, and members in business must maintain objectivity even though they cannot appear independent.
